documents.title: High Blood Pressure in Adults

chunks.content: Introduction Essential hypertension is one of the most common cardiovascular risk factors, affecting 43% to 58% of adults worldwide. Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and ventricular remodelling caused by hypertension are the leading causes of cardiovascular death and disability. Unfortunately, the blood pressure control rates required for hypertension treatment is low and the pathogenesis of hypertension is not fully understood. , Periodontitis is another common disease that affects more than half of the global population. Approximately 10% of the population is affected by severe periodontitis. Recently, epidemiological surveys have found that patients with periodontitis have higher blood pressure levels than those with healthy periodontium. Periodontitis is also considered to be one of the factors contributing to a poor antihypertensive effect and a low rate of blood pressure control among patients with hypertension. A meta-analysis has shown that periodontitis can increase the risk of hypertension, especially in patients with severe periodontitis. Using blood pressure as the primary outcome variable, our randomized controlled trial on periodontitis treatment showed that intensive periodontal therapy alone (without antihypertensive medication) effectively reduced blood pressure , the finding that aligns with a 2020 meta-analysis. It has been suggested that periodontitis may be a new factor contributing to the development of hypertension, with the condition labelled ‘dental hypertension’. However, the mechanism by which periodontitis causes elevated blood pressure is unknown. , MMPs are a family of Zn 2+ /Ca 2+ -dependent peptide chain endonucleases that breakdown almost all proteins in the extracellular matrix (ECM) and play a critical role in tissue remodelling. MMPs together with tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs) maintain ECM stability. MMP-9 is a member of the MMP family, which was previously found to be associated with cardiovascular remodelling in cardiovascular diseases. Recently, MMP-9 has been found to be associated with hypertension. For example, serum MMP-9 levels are significantly higher in prehypertensive and hypertensive patients than in individuals with normal blood pressure. Our previous experiments showed that injecting exogenous MMP-9 into rats could significantly increase their blood pressure. In periodontitis patients, previous studies have revealed elevated levels of MMP-9 in the gingival tissue and gingival crevicular fluid (GCF) and the local application of nonspecific MMP inhibitors was observed to alleviate periodontitis. , , In terms of the systemic effects, it has been found that serum MMP-9 levels in periodontitis patients are significantly higher than those with healthy periodontum. Likewise, serum MMP-9 levels and the MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio in hypertensive patients with periodontitis were found to be significantly higher than those in patients with simple hypertension. However, whether lowering the serum MMP-9 level can reduce blood pressure in patients with periodontitis is not yet clear. JNJ0966 is a specific MMP-9 inhibitor that reduces both the precursor and the active form of MMP-9. Its high specificity allows it to have almost no effect on the activity of other MMPs. JNJ0966 has been used in in vivo and in vitro studies and has shown good specific inhibition of MMP-9. , The primary aim of this study is to elucidate whether elevated serum MMP-9 constitutes a causal factor underlying the increase in arterial blood pressure in periodontitis and to explore the potential mechanism linking periodontitis, serum MMP-9 elevation and hypertension. Materials and methods Experimental periodontitis animal model construction and MMP-9 inhibitor intervention experiment Thirty-six 12-week-old male SHRs, weighing 249 to 280 g, were purchased from Beijing Viton Lihua Experimental Animal Technology Co., Ltd., license number SCXK 2016-0006 and kept in individually ventilated cages (temperature 22 ± 3 °C, humidity 60%, 12 hours light/dark cycles) at the First Affiliated Hospital of Guangdong Pharmaceutical University Experimental Animal Centre. Six animals were housed per cage and supplied with sufficient food and water. After 1 week of acclimatisation feeding (ie, 13th week of age), 36 animals were randomly by means of a raffle method, divided into the experimental periodontitis group (SHR-L, n = 18) and nonperiodontitis group (SHR-C, n = 18). The experimental periodontitis rat model was induced using a previously reported method, where animals were fasted for 12 hours before the modelling procedure and 3% pentobarbital sodium (40 mg/kg, intraperitoneal injection) was used for anaesthesia. The SHR-L group was subjected to ligation of the maxillary first and second molars bilaterally with a 4-0 silk thread in an “8” shape. The silk thread was pressed into the gingival sulcus at the cervical region of the teeth. If the silk thread was dislodged, it was religated until the end of the experiment. The SHR-C group was anaesthetised in the same way but without molar ligation. At 4 weeks postmodelling, the rats in both groups were randomly divided into 3 subgroups and were administered JNJ0966 (Selleck) by gavage once per day for 7 days. JNJ0966 was dissolved in 20% hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin (Sigma) and was not administered to the SHR-C-0 and SHR-L-0 groups. The JNJ0966 solution was administered at a dose

an “8” shape. The silk thread was pressed into the gingival sulcus at the cervical region of the teeth. If the silk thread was dislodged, it was religated until the end of the experiment. The SHR-C group was anaesthetised in the same way but without molar ligation. At 4 weeks postmodelling, the rats in both groups were randomly divided into 3 subgroups and were administered JNJ0966 (Selleck) by gavage once per day for 7 days. JNJ0966 was dissolved in 20% hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin (Sigma) and was not administered to the SHR-C-0 and SHR-L-0 groups. The JNJ0966 solution was administered at a dose of 10 mg/kg for the SHR-C-10 and SHR-L-10 groups and 30 mg/kg for the SHR-C-30 and SHR-L-30 groups ( n = 6 for each group). Noninvasive tail artery manometry (Anhui Zhenghua Biological Instrument Equipment Co., Ltd) was used to measure SHR systolic blood pressure (SBP). Manometry was performed in the morning at a constant temperature (36-38 °C) in a quiet light-protected cage, systolic blood pressure was measured 3 times and the mean value was calculated. Blood pressure and body weight were measured before modelling and weekly after surgery. After 1 week of JNJ0966 intervention, the rats were anaesthetised again as previously described. Whatman #3 filter paper was cut into 10 × 1 mm strips and 6 strips were randomly selected and placed into marked EP tubes and weighed. Physical isolation with cotton rolls, combined with continuous suction and air-drying, ensures that the fluid collected on the paper strip originates from the gingival crevice and is not diluted or contaminated by saliva. The preweighed filter paper strips were placed into the gingival sulcus of the buccolingual sides of the left first molar for 30 seconds. After removal, all 6 filter papers were placed into the original EP tube. The difference between the 2 weights was the weight of the tooth’s GCF. A blunt-tipped periodontal probe was used to probe the bottom of the gingival sulcus along the surface of the left first molar by a single experienced periodontists (Qianbing Zhou) and the depths of 6 points were measured (mesio-buccal, mid-buccal, disto-buccal, mesio-lingual, mid-lingual and disto-lingual). The values of each point were averaged to measure the probe depth (PD). Similarly, a blunt-tipped periodontal probe was used to lightly probe the gingival sulcus or the bottom of the periodontal pocket and the degree of bleeding was observed 30 seconds after removing the probe. The bleeding was scored on a scale from 0 to 5 to obtain the bleeding index (BI). After the PD and BI measurements, approximately 5 mL of blood was collected from the abdominal aorta with a vacuum blood collection tube with a red top. The blood was then left for 2 hours and centrifuged at 3000 r/min for 15 minutes at 4 °C and the upper layer of serum was collected and stored at −80 °C. The gingival tissue around the left first molar of each SHR was taken, treated with liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C. The left first molar and surrounding alveolar bone were collected, fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 48 hours, decalcified in 4% hydrochloric acid for 7 days (decalcification endpoint confirmed by needle probing), rinsed under flowing water for 8 hours, embedded in paraffin and longitudinally sectioned along the mesiodistal axis for histopathological examination. MMP-9 and TIMP-1 level measurements and histopathology of SHR alveolar bone All −80 °C frozen specimens were thawed at room temperature (20-25 °C). The GCF was added to 200 μL of Tris-HCl solution (pH 7.5, Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd) per tube, shaken for 1 hour and centrifuged at 10,000 r/min for 10 minutes at 4 °C and the supernatant was collected as GCF solution. The GCF solution and serum MMP-9, TIMP-1 and Ang II concentrations were measured using an ELISA kit (R&D Systems) and the MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio was calculated. The SHR gingival tissue was cut into smaller pieces with ophthalmic scissors and RIPA protein lysis solution (Beyotime Institute of Biotechnology) was added to extract the total protein. The total protein concentration of the tissue samples was quantified using a BCA protein concentration quantification kit (Beyotime Institute of Biotechnology) on the preformulated SDS‒PAGE electrophoresis gel lane. After electrophoresis, the separated proteins were transferred to PVDF membranes (Millipore Corporation) and blocked with protein sealing solution (Beyotime Institute of Biotechnology) to prevent nonspecific binding of proteins. Next, the PVDF membranes were incubated with primary antibody (MMP-9 protein, Abcam and β-actin, Abcam), overnight at 4 °C on a shaker, then incubated with secondary antibody (Guangzhou AKEA Biotechnology company) for 1 hour on a shaker at room temperature. Finally, the proteins were incubated with chemiluminescence enhancement reagents (Beyotime Institute of Biotechnology). After sectioning the alveolar bone tissue, haematoxylin-eosin staining was performed. Image-Pro Plus 6.0 image analysis software (Media Cybernetics, Inc. Version 6.0.0.260) was used to

Next, the PVDF membranes were incubated with primary antibody (MMP-9 protein, Abcam and β-actin, Abcam), overnight at 4 °C on a shaker, then incubated with secondary antibody (Guangzhou AKEA Biotechnology company) for 1 hour on a shaker at room temperature. Finally, the proteins were incubated with chemiluminescence enhancement reagents (Beyotime Institute of Biotechnology). After sectioning the alveolar bone tissue, haematoxylin-eosin staining was performed. Image-Pro Plus 6.0 image analysis software (Media Cybernetics, Inc. Version 6.0.0.260) was used to calculate the percentage of alveolar bone area (BAr) to total interradicular area (TAr) and the BAr/Tar ratio was calculated. The BAr/Tar ratio can reflect the degree of bone resorption and destruction of the alveolar bone ( ). Statistical analysis All experimental data were statistically analysed using SPSS 25.0 software. The normality of the data was first tested with Shapiro-Wilk normality test. Data conforming to a normal distribution were presented as the mean ± standard deviation ( ¯X ± SD). Data not conforming to a normal distribution were summarised as the median. The numerical variables of the 2 groups were compared using the independent samples t test or Mann-Whitney U test. For the identification of differences between 2 or more groups of quantitative data, 1-way ANOVA was used if there was homogeneity of variance. The LSD method was used for 2-way comparisons and the nonparametric rank sum test was used if there was no homogeneity of variance. Pearson correlation analysis was used to evaluate correlations. Statistical differences were denoted as P <0.05. Results The weight of the SHRs gradually decreased and blood pressure gradually increased in the periodontitis group during the modelling process. There were no differences in the baseline body weight and blood pressure between the 2 groups at 13 weeks of age. After modelling, the weight of the SHR-C group gradually increased over time, whereas the weight of the SHR-L group decreased at 14 weeks of age and increased again at 15 weeks but remained lower than that of the SHR-C group ( P < 0.0001). The blood pressure of the SHR-L group increased at 14 weeks of age and was significantly higher than that of the SHR-C group at 15 weeks ( P = 0.0198, ). Blood pressure was significantly higher in SHRs with periodontitis than in SHRs without periodontitis and JNJ0966 reduced blood pressure and body weight, especially in the periodontitis group. After 1 week of JNJ0966 intervention, there was no significant difference in body weight between the SHR-L-0 and SHR-C-0 groups, but both the SHR-C-30 and SHR-L-30 groups had lower body weights than the SHR-C-0 and SHR-L-0 groups, respectively ( P = 0.0494, A). Blood pressure was significantly higher in the SHR-L-0 group than in the SHR-C-0 group and significantly lower in the SHR-C-30 group than in the SHR-C-0 group ( P = 0.0230, B). Blood pressure values in the SHR-L-10 and SHR-L-30 groups were significantly lower than those in the SHR-L-0 group ( P = 0.0096 and P = 0.0075, B). The PD, BI and GCF weight were significantly increased in the periodontitis group compared with the nonperiodontitis group. The JNJ0966 intervention did not significantly alleviate these periodontitis-induced increases. The PD, BI and GCF weights were significantly higher in the SHR-L-0 group than in the SHR-C-0 group ( P = 0.0115, P = 0.0210 and P = 0.0093), but they were not significantly different between the subgroups within the SHR-C and SHR-L groups after 1 week of intervention with different concentrations of JNJ0966 ( P > 0.05, C-E). Alveolar bone destruction was obvious in the periodontitis group and the JNJ0966 intervention did not significantly reverse this damage. Histopathological examination of the alveolar bone showed that bone destruction and resorption in the SHR-L group were significant compared with those in the SHR-C group and the BAr/TAr (%) ratio was significantly decreased ( P < 0.0001). In contrast, no significant changes were observed in the BAr/TAr (%) ratio of the alveolar bone after 1 week of intervention with different concentrations of JNJ0966 ( P > 0.05, ). Serum MMP-9 levels and the MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio were significantly higher in the periodontitis group than in the nonperiodontitis group and were significantly decreased after JNJ0966 intervention. The serum MMP-9 concentration and MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio were significantly higher in the SHR-L-0 group than in the SHR-C-0 group ( P = 0.0471 and P = 0.0136). After 1 week of intervention with different concentrations of JNJ0966, serum MMP-9 levels were significantly lower in the SHR-C-30 group than in the SHR-C-0 group ( P = 0.0280), while the MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio exhibited a decreasing trend. Serum MMP-9 levels and the MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio in the SHR-L-10 and SHR-L-30 groups were significantly decreased compared with those in

in the periodontitis group than in the nonperiodontitis group and were significantly decreased after JNJ0966 intervention. The serum MMP-9 concentration and MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio were significantly higher in the SHR-L-0 group than in the SHR-C-0 group ( P = 0.0471 and P = 0.0136). After 1 week of intervention with different concentrations of JNJ0966, serum MMP-9 levels were significantly lower in the SHR-C-30 group than in the SHR-C-0 group ( P = 0.0280), while the MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio exhibited a decreasing trend. Serum MMP-9 levels and the MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio in the SHR-L-10 and SHR-L-30 groups were significantly decreased compared with those in the SHR-L-0 group ( P = 0.0074 and P = 0.0032). And the MMP9/TIMP 1 ratio in the SHR-L-10 and SHR-L-30 groups also were significantly decreased compared with SHR-L-0 group ( P < 0.0001 and P < 0.0001). A decreasing trend was observed in the SHR-L-30 group compared to the SHR-L-10 group, but this decrease was not statistically significant ( A and B). Further, the serum MMP-9 level was moderately correlated with blood pressure ( r = 0.389, P = 0.019), while the serum MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio was moderately associated with blood pressure ( r = 0.390, P = 0.019) ( C and D). The Serum Ang II levels were significantly higher in the periodontitis group than in the nonperiodontitis group and significantly decreased after the JNJ0966 intervention. Serum Ang II levels were significantly initially higher in the SHR-L-0 group than in the SHR-C-0 group ( P = 0.0248). After 1 week of intervention with JNJ0966, the serum Ang II level in the SHR-C-30 group was significantly lower than that in the SHR-C-0 group ( P = 0.0203), while there was a nonsignificant decrease in the SHR-C-10 group. Both the SHR-L-10 and SHR-L-30 groups with periodontitis had significantly decreased serum Ang II levels compared with those in the SHR-L-0 group ( P = 0.0127 and P = 0.0028), while the SHR-L-30 group had a decreasing trend compared to the SHR-L-10 group ( E). The GCF MMP-9 level and MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio were significantly increased in the periodontitis group and they were both decreased after the JNJ0966 intervention. The MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio decreased more significantly. Compared with those in the SHR-C-0 group, the GCF MMP-9 concentration and MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio were significantly higher in the SHR-L-0 group ( P = 0.0086 and P = 0.0025). After 1 week of intervention with different concentrations of JNJ0966, the differences in the GCF MMP-9 level and MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio between the SHR-C subgroups were not statistically significant. However, the GCF MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratios in the SHR-L-10 and SHR-L-30 groups were both significantly decreased ( P = 0.0302 and P = 0.0188) compared with those in the SHR-L-0 group, while the MMP-9 level tended to decline ( F and G). MMP-9 levels were significantly higher in the gingival tissue of the periodontitis group and significantly decreased after JNJ0966 intervention.. Western blot assays showed that the gingival tissue MMP-9 protein level was significantly higher in the SHR-L-0 group than in the SHR-C-0 group ( P = 0.0034). After intervention with different concentrations of JNJ0966, the changes in the MMP-9 protein concentrations in the gingival tissues of the SHR-C subgroups were not statistically significant. After JNJ0966 intervention, the MMP-9 concentrations in the gingival tissues of the SHR-L-10 and SHR-L-30 groups were significantly decreased compared with those of the SHR-L-0 group ( P = 0.0077 and P = 0.0055; A and B). Discussion Although epidemiological and clinical studies have found an association between periodontitis and hypertension, the mechanism underlying this relationship is not yet fully elucidated. Previous studies have primarily indicated that systemic immune abnormalities, triggered by local inflammatory lesions associated with periodontitis, may lead to immune-mediated damage to both the kidneys and arterial system. This process also involves the production and release of vasoconstrictive active substances, such as the activation of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system. Furthermore, inflammatory mediators may contribute to endothelial damage and potentially induce the production of specific microRNAs, resulting in cardiovascular remodelling. However, the specific substances involved in these processes remain incompletely understood. , , In this study, an SHR model was successfully established and SHRs with periodontitis were found to have significantly higher arterial blood pressure than control SHRs. This finding is in support of the hypothesis that periodontitis can elevate blood pressure in rats. Given that periodontitis can increase blood pressure, elevated MMP-9 levels in periodontal tissue and serum are often observed in patients with periodontitis and MMP-9 expression may increase blood pressure, we hypothesised that elevated blood pressure in periodontitis patients may, in part, be related to elevated serum MMP-9 levels. However, there is a lack of direct evidence to support this assertion. In this study, by comparing serum MMP-9 levels in SHR with and without periodontitis, we found that serum MMP-9 levels were significantly higher in rats

finding is in support of the hypothesis that periodontitis can elevate blood pressure in rats. Given that periodontitis can increase blood pressure, elevated MMP-9 levels in periodontal tissue and serum are often observed in patients with periodontitis and MMP-9 expression may increase blood pressure, we hypothesised that elevated blood pressure in periodontitis patients may, in part, be related to elevated serum MMP-9 levels. However, there is a lack of direct evidence to support this assertion. In this study, by comparing serum MMP-9 levels in SHR with and without periodontitis, we found that serum MMP-9 levels were significantly higher in rats with periodontitis. Importantly, the MMP-9-specific inhibitor (JNJ0966) significantly reduced serum MMP-9 levels and simultaneously lowered arterial blood pressure. This finding provides the first direct experimental evidence that elevated serum MMP-9 is a mechanistic link between periodontitis and hypertension. This study used a silk thread ligation method reported in the literature to induce experimental periodontitis in SHRs and found that compared with the nonperiodontitis control group (SHR-C-0 group), the periodontitis model control group (SHR-L-0 group) had a significantly higher PD and BI and significantly increased GCF weight. The pathological sections showed more alveolar bone and resorption destruction, which is consistent with previous reports. , These observations are also similar to those of human periodontitis, suggesting successful periodontitis modelling. The MMP-9 level and MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio in the GCF of the SHR-L-0 group were significantly higher than those of the SHR-C-0 group. The MMP-9 protein level in the gingival tissues of the SHR-L-0 group was also significantly higher than that of the SHR-C-0 group by Western blot. The MMP-9 level and MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio in the serum of the SHR-L-0 group were significantly higher than those of the SHR-C-0 group. These results are similar to the previous clinical studies of periodontitis patients, , , and thus, this model is considered a suitable model for further exploring the role of MMP-9 in periodontitis-induced hypertension. TIMP-1 inhibits the activity of MMP-9 and the effect of MMP-9 is enhanced when the MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio is increased . The current study found that the MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio was significantly increased in both GCF and serum, so the net effect of MMP-9 was enhanced in SHRs with periodontitis. To further confirm that increased serum MMP-9 levels are a factor in the elevated blood pressure observed in periodontitis model rats, a specific systemic MMP-9 inhibitor intervention was used in SHRs with and without periodontitis. The results revealed that the periodontitis group showed a significant decrease in GCF and serum MMP-9 levels and MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratios and a significant reduction in MMP-9 in gingival tissue after MMP-9 inhibitor intervention. Importantly, a significant decrease in overall blood pressure followed. Correlation analysis showed that the serum MMP-9 level and MMP-9/TIMP-1 ratio were moderately correlated with blood pressure, respectively. This finding confirms that elevated serum MMP-9 is 1 factor that contributes to elevated blood pressure in SHR with periodontitis. The benefits of the systemic application of MMP inhibitors in the adjuvant treatment of periodontal disease have been confirmed. For example, low-dose oral doxycycline at a nonantibacterial concentration can significantly reduce the MMP concentration in the periodontal tissue and GCF, which is significantly positively correlated with improvement in the periodontal tissue and alveolar bone destruction. Therefore, orally administered, low-dose doxycycline is recognised as one of the nonsurgical treatments for periodontal disease. However, the efficacy of the systemic application of MMP inhibitors in the treatment of periodontitis combined with hypertension has rarely been reported. The results of this study provide direct evidence for the systemic use of MMP-9-specific inhibitors in the treatment of elevated blood pressure in periodontitis. There are few reports on the effect of increased MMP-9 on blood pressure. , The serum Ang II level in the SHR-L-0 group was significantly higher than that in the SHR-C-0 group. Following the JNJ0966 intervention, with a decrease in serum MMP-9 levels, the serum Ang II levels in the SHR-L-10, SHR-L-30 and SHR-C-30 groups were all significantly lower than those in the corresponding nonintervention groups. This finding suggests that MMP-9 may elevate blood pressure by increasing Ang II levels in serum, as previously reported. However, the mechanism is unknown and it is speculated that it may operate similarly to angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), such as elevating ACE levels so that more Ang I can be converted to Ang II. In addition, MMP-9 interacts with reactive oxygen radicals to increase the secretion of vasoconstrictive substances, such as endothelin-1 and phenylephrine and decrease endothelial nitric oxide production, reducing endothelial diastole function mediated by diastolic substances. This process results in increased vasoconstriction and blood pressure. MMP-9 can breakdown the ECM and cause migration of vascular smooth muscle cells, leading to vascular remodelling, especially thickening of the arterial wall, which causes an increase in vascular resistance. However, to determine whether MMP-9 has a direct vasoconstrictive

enzyme (ACE), such as elevating ACE levels so that more Ang I can be converted to Ang II. In addition, MMP-9 interacts with reactive oxygen radicals to increase the secretion of vasoconstrictive substances, such as endothelin-1 and phenylephrine and decrease endothelial nitric oxide production, reducing endothelial diastole function mediated by diastolic substances. This process results in increased vasoconstriction and blood pressure. MMP-9 can breakdown the ECM and cause migration of vascular smooth muscle cells, leading to vascular remodelling, especially thickening of the arterial wall, which causes an increase in vascular resistance. However, to determine whether MMP-9 has a direct vasoconstrictive effect, further studies are needed. Significant decreases in the serum MMP-9 level and blood pressure were also observed in the nonperiodontitis group with high-dose JNJ0966, which may be because SHR itself increased MMP-9 levels. In the present study, the decreases in serum MMP-9 and blood pressure in the periodontitis group after intervention with an MMP-9 inhibitor did not show significant dose dependence. This phenomenon may be due to a higher dose of JNJ0966 in the ‘low-dose’ group and an insufficient dose in the ‘high-dose’ group. Combined with the fact that the high-dose MMP-9 inhibitor subgroup of the nonperiodontitis group exhibited more significant decreases in serum MMP-9 levels and blood pressure compared to those in the low-dose MMP-9 inhibitor group, it can be speculated that there is a dose-dependent relationship between the MMP-9 inhibitor and the reductions in serum MMP-9 levels and blood pressure. In this study, the MMP-9 levels in GCF were significantly decreased in the periodontitis group after intervention with JNJ0966, but periodontitis indices such as the PD value, BI score, GCF weight and BAr/TAr (%) ratio did not significantly improve. There are several possible reasons for these results. First, the periodontal ligature silk thread was not removed and local irritation persisted, which could lead to the continued progression of periodontitis. Second, other MMPs were not inhibited and it has been shown that there are multiple MMPs are highly expressed in the GCF of periodontitis patients. Third, other inflammatory factors, such as IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α and NF-κB, were not blocked, aggravating alveolar bone destruction and resorption. , Finally, the intervention time was short and the repair of alveolar bone may take longer. Therefore, this result does not demonstrate that the systemic application of MMP inhibitors is ineffective in the treatment of periodontitis. It should be noted that since the silk ligature that induced periodontitis remained in place throughout the experiment, this study could not objectively evaluate the effect of systemic MMP-9 inhibitor application on periodontitis itself. Furthermore, this study only investigated the role of MMP-9 in odontogenic hypertension by treating an experimental periodontitis model in rats with MMP-9 specific inhibitors. As this was not naturally occurring periodontitis, whether differences exist compared to clinically occurring odontogenic hypertension remains unclear, which requires further observation and confirmation in individuals with naturally occurring periodontitis. The reason for the increase in serum MMP-9 levels in individuals with periodontitis is not fully understood. Although previous studies and this study have both found that MMP-9 in the GCF of periodontitis individuals is significantly increased, no significant correlations between the levels of MMP-9 in GCF and serum have been observed. , It can be seen that the increased MMP-9 in serum is not caused by the direct infiltration of high concentrations of MMP-9 into the blood but is more likely to be a systemic reaction to periodontitis. Previous studies have suggested that periodontitis causes a systemic chronic inflammatory response with upregulated expression of proinflammatory factors and this stimulates inflammation-related gene expression and increases the number of inflammatory cells. , , Moreover, Porphyromonas gingivalis can directly enter the blood circulation and invade the vascular wall, aggravating and activating inflammatory cells and monocytes. The antigen of P. gingivalis enhances the immune activity of the patient and activates the immune system and macrophages. Inflammatory cells, macrophages and immune cells can promote MMP-9 secretion, , increasing serum MMP-9 levels. It has been found that the blood neutrophils of patients with periodontitis are significantly increased, and neutrophils are inflammatory cells rich in MMP-9. Because serum MMP-9 is not primarily derived from the osmosis of periodontal fluid, the effect of simple local periodontal treatment on blood pressure is not satisfactory. , In this study, systemic application of MMP-9 inhibitors significantly decreased the serum MMP-9 level and resulted in a significant decrease in blood pressure. This offers a novel approach for lowering blood pressure in hypertensive patients with periodontitis. This finding may help to improve the rate of antihypertensive achievement in patients with refractory hypertension complicated by periodontitis. Of course, this study is based on animal models and must be further confirmed in human patients. Conclusion Serum MMP-9 levels were higher in SHRs with periodontitis than in those without periodontitis. Specific inhibition of MMP-9

treatment on blood pressure is not satisfactory. , In this study, systemic application of MMP-9 inhibitors significantly decreased the serum MMP-9 level and resulted in a significant decrease in blood pressure. This offers a novel approach for lowering blood pressure in hypertensive patients with periodontitis. This finding may help to improve the rate of antihypertensive achievement in patients with refractory hypertension complicated by periodontitis. Of course, this study is based on animal models and must be further confirmed in human patients. Conclusion Serum MMP-9 levels were higher in SHRs with periodontitis than in those without periodontitis. Specific inhibition of MMP-9 reduced blood pressure in SHRs with experimental periodontitis, suggesting that elevated serum MMP-9 levels may be one of the mechanisms underlying elevated blood pressure in individuals with periodontitis. chunks.content: T-cell engager (TCE) therapies are bispecific or multispecific antibodies that simultaneously bind a T-cell receptor complex (usually CD3) and a tumor-associated antigen on target cells, thereby redirecting cytotoxic T cells to recognize and kill tumor cells. TCEs have significantly improved the prognosis of patients with hematologic malignancies and are being explored in solid tumors, resulting in expanding clinical indications. TCEs are now approved for several B-cell and plasma-cell malignancies, including blinatumomab for B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia; teclistamab, talquetamab, and elranatamab for multiple myeloma; and glofitamab and epcoritamab for B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphomas. , Other agents, such as cevostamab, are under advanced clinical investigation. Compared with chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy, TCEs are “off-the-shelf” biologics that can be administered immediately without patient-specific cell manufacturing, offering broader accessibility and facilitating integration into clinical practice. However, like other immune-based therapies, TCEs have important treatment-related toxicities, including cytokine-release syndrome (CRS), immune effector cell–associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS), infusion-related reactions, systemic infections, cytopenias, and tumor flare reactions. Although cardiovascular complications following other immunotherapies, such as immune checkpoint inhibitors or CAR T-cell therapy, are well described (reported prevalence 0.4%-2.0% and 14.0%-18.0%, , respectively), data on cardiovascular complications associated with TCE therapy are scarce. Recently, Sayed et al described bispecific TCE therapy–related cardiovascular adverse events using the U.S. Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS). However, FAERS is limited by reporting bias and does not capture all drug-exposed individuals, precluding accurate incidence estimation or causal inference. In this retrospective study, we aimed to describe the frequency of cardiovascular complications and baseline factors associated with these events in a large cohort of patients with cancer treated with TCE therapy. Methods Study design This retrospective cohort study included consecutive patients with a cancer diagnosis who received TCE therapy between January 2016 and December 2024 at 2 large cancer centers: the Massachusetts General Brigham (MGB) Health System and the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. The study protocol was approved by the MGB Institutional Review Board, and the requirement for informed consent was waived given the retrospective nature of this study. Study population We queried the MGB Research Patient Data Registry to identify adult patients with cancer (≥18 years) who initiated their first course of Food and Drug Administration–approved bispecific TCE therapy (blinatumomab, teclistamab, talquetamab, elranatamab, glofitamab, epcoritamab) between January 2016 and December 2024, including both research and nonresearch use. Patients who received at least 1 full dose of TCE therapy were included. The electronic medical records of those identified were manually reviewed (O.I.B.Z., A.N.) to obtain demographic and clinical data (including TCE therapy–related complications and management), as well as laboratory and imaging data. Definition of individual cardiovascular events Left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction was defined as either: 1) a new reduction in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of ≥10 percentage points from baseline to an LVEF <50%; or 2) a new reduction in LVEF of <10 percentage points from baseline to an LVEF of 40% to 49% with either a new relative decline in LV global longitudinal strain (GLS) of >15% from baseline or a new rise in cardiac biomarkers. , Because LV GLS and troponin measurements at baseline and during active therapy were infrequently obtained in our cohort, LV dysfunction was effectively defined by criterion 1 (a new reduction in LVEF of ≥10 percentage points from baseline to an LVEF <50%). Symptomatic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) was defined as LV systolic dysfunction accompanied by symptoms of heart failure (dyspnea and/or orthopnea). Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) was defined as at least 1 heart failure symptom (dyspnea and/or orthopnea) plus 1 or more objective signs of volume overload (chest imaging with pulmonary infiltrates and/or pulmonary edema and/or N-terminal prohormone of brain natriuretic peptide above the normal range) that responded to loop diuretics. Atrial arrhythmia events were defined as new-onset atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter (AF) or known AF complicated by rapid ventricular response requiring intravenous rate control or pharmacologic or electrical cardioversion. Supraventricular tachycardia included atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia or atrial tachycardia and was considered a cardiovascular event when associated with rapid ventricular response requiring intravenous rate control or pharmacologic or electrical cardioversion. Ventricular arrhythmias were defined as ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation. High-degree atrioventricular conduction disease was defined as second-degree Mobitz II or third-degree atrioventricular block on a 12-lead electrocardiogram. Acute coronary syndrome was defined per the 2025 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (AHA) guideline for the management of patients with acute coronary syndrome. Cerebrovascular accident (CVA) and transient ischemic attack (TIA) were defined per the 2021 AHA/American Stroke Association guideline for the prevention of stroke. TCE therapy–related complications CRS and ICANS were graded according to the American Society for Transplantation and Cellular Therapy consensus criteria ( ). Clinical covariates Preexisting cardiovascular disease and cardiovascular risk factors were extracted by manual chart review,

conduction disease was defined as second-degree Mobitz II or third-degree atrioventricular block on a 12-lead electrocardiogram. Acute coronary syndrome was defined per the 2025 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (AHA) guideline for the management of patients with acute coronary syndrome. Cerebrovascular accident (CVA) and transient ischemic attack (TIA) were defined per the 2021 AHA/American Stroke Association guideline for the prevention of stroke. TCE therapy–related complications CRS and ICANS were graded according to the American Society for Transplantation and Cellular Therapy consensus criteria ( ). Clinical covariates Preexisting cardiovascular disease and cardiovascular risk factors were extracted by manual chart review, including hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, current or former smoking (self-report), AF, prior CVA/TIA, HFrEF, light-chain (AL) amyloid cardiomyopathy, and obstructive coronary artery disease (defined as diameter stenosis of 50% or more in the left main coronary artery or stenosis of 70% or more in a major epicardial vessel). AL amyloid cardiomyopathy was defined by Congo red–positive endomyocardial biopsy or cardiac magnetic resonance imaging findings compatible with amyloid infiltration in the presence of AL amyloid deposits confirmed by a positive Congo red stain and liquid chromatography mass spectrometry typing in a different organ. Established cardiovascular disease was defined as baseline AF, coronary artery disease, CVA/TIA, and/or HFrEF. Cardiac testing was performed at the discretion of the treating clinician and was not prespecified. Echocardiographic variables (LVEF, LV GLS, pericardial effusion [included if more than trivial]) were collected at baseline and during TCE therapy based on the formal interpretations documented in the echocardiography reports. Inflammatory biomarkers before and during TCE therapy were drawn per institutional protocols; peak values were identified. Biomarkers included C-reactive protein (normal reference range 0-3 mg/L), interleukin-6 (normal reference range <7.1 pg/mL), and ferritin (normal reference range 30-400 μg/L). Study outcomes Cardiovascular events and survival were assessed during TCE therapy, defined as the interval from the first TCE dose to 90 days after the last TCE dose. Cardiovascular events were defined as a composite of new LV systolic dysfunction with or without symptomatic heart failure (HFrEF), HFpEF, acute coronary syndrome, AF, clinically significant supraventricular tachycardias, ventricular arrhythmias, high-degree atrioventricular conduction disease, and TIA/CVA. Other outcomes of interest included individual cardiovascular events, all-cause mortality, and cardiovascular mortality. Mortality status and cause of death (cardiovascular vs other) were determined from the electronic medical record or death certificates, where available. Statistical analysis Continuous variables were reported as median (25th-75th percentiles [Q1-Q3]) and categorical variables as frequencies and proportions. Baseline characteristics were summarized descriptively without formal hypothesis testing between groups because of informative censoring in the time-to-event framework. Paired comparisons of LVEF and GLS between baseline and during active therapy were performed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Follow-up was assessed using restricted mean follow-up time because the reverse Kaplan-Meier curve did not reach 50% and median follow-up could not be estimated. For time-to-event analyses, restricted mean time to first cardiovascular event (restricted mean time to failure) was calculated as a measure of average event-free time during the active TCE treatment period with CIs estimated using nonparametric bootstrap resampling (1,000 iterations). Cumulative incidence function (CIF) curves were generated using the Aalen-Johansen estimator to account for competing risks. Because analyses were restricted to events occurring during TCE therapy, patients who completed therapy without an event were treated as a competing risk rather than censored because they were no longer at risk once treatment ended. CIFs were calculated for the composite cardiovascular events outcome and for all-cause mortality, treating each outcome as a competing event for the other. In a separate analysis, the CIF for cardiovascular mortality was estimated, treating noncardiovascular death as a competing event. Before model construction, collinearity among candidate variables was assessed using variance inflation factors. For analysis of the composite cardiovascular endpoint, known AF with rapid ventricular response events were excluded to reduce misclassification bias. Univariable Fine-Gray models were used to evaluate associations with the composite endpoint; variables with P < 0.05 were considered for multivariable analysis, with age and sex forced into the model. Multivariable Fine-Gray models were constructed using forward stepwise selection guided by the Akaike information criterion (AIC) to minimize overfitting. Fine-Gray model results are presented as the subdistribution HR with 95% CI. Covariates retained in the stepwise procedure were subsequently incorporated as baseline covariates in cause-specific Cox proportional hazards models evaluating cardiovascular events, with CRS and/or ICANS grades ≥2 included as a time-dependent covariate. For all-cause mortality, univariable Cox proportional hazards models were first fitted. Variables meeting the prespecified selection criteria ( P < 0.05, with age and sex forced into the model) were entered into a forward stepwise AIC-guided multivariable Cox model. The composite cardiovascular event endpoint, including known AF with rapid ventricular response, was incorporated as a time-dependent exposure to assess its association with subsequent mortality. Cox model results are presented as the HR with 95% CI.

Variables meeting the prespecified selection criteria ( P < 0.05, with age and sex forced into the model) were entered into a forward stepwise AIC-guided multivariable Cox model. The composite cardiovascular event endpoint, including known AF with rapid ventricular response, was incorporated as a time-dependent exposure to assess its association with subsequent mortality. Missing data were handled using complete-case analysis, resulting in the exclusion of 4 patients with missing baseline estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). A 2-sided P value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Statistical analysis was performed using RStudio, version 1.4.1106. Results Baseline characteristics The study cohort included 567 patients with cancer who received their first course of TCE therapy between January 2016 and December 2024. Baseline characteristics are shown in . Median age at the first TCE infusion was 67 years (Q1-Q3: 57-75), and 46.0% (n = 261) were female. Among these patients, 8.6% (n = 49) had a history of obstructive coronary artery disease, 15.3% (n = 87) had AF, 7.4% (n = 42) had known HFrEF or amyloid cardiomyopathy, and 3.7% (n = 21) had a history of CVA/TIA. The most common malignancies were multiple myeloma (n = 232, 40.9%), including 13 with concomitant AL amyloidosis, and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (n = 202, 35.6%). Overall, 217 (38.3%) patients were previously treated with anthracyclines, 130 (22.9%) with carfilzomib, and 125 (22.0%) with CAR T-cell therapy. Clinical characteristics during TCE therapy The restricted mean follow-up was 248 days (range: 0-973) and the most frequently used TCE agents were CD19-targeting blinatumomab (n = 212, 37.4%) and B-cell maturation antigen–targeting teclistamab (n = 167, 29.5%) ( ). CRS and ICANS occurred in 256 (45.1%) and 46 (8.1%) patients, respectively, and were most frequent during the first cycle of TCE therapy. Grade ≥2 CRS and/or ICANS occurred in 88 (15.5%) patients. Cardiovascular outcomes during active TCE therapy During TCE therapy, a total of 65 cardiovascular events were observed. summarizes the number of patients experiencing each distinct cardiovascular event category, with 4 patients experiencing more than 1 event type. The 943-day cumulative incidence of a first cardiovascular event was 10.4% (95% CI: 8.1-13.1) in the presence of competing risks ( ). Cardiovascular events occurred early after TCE initiation, with a restricted mean time to failure of 91.3 days (95% CI: 65.1-113.3). The most common cardiovascular events were new LV dysfunction (n = 13, cumulative incidence of 2.3%; 95% CI: 1.3-3.8; 11 of 13 were symptomatic HFrEF) and new-onset AF (n = 12, cumulative incidence 2.1%; 95% CI: 1.2-3.6). Nine patients experienced acute coronary syndrome (cumulative incidence 1.6%; 95% CI: 0.8-2.9); 6 of 9 had acute myocardial infarction. Baseline characteristics of patients with and without a cardiovascular event are shown in . Among patients with concomitant multiple myeloma and AL amyloidosis (n = 13), 4 cardiovascular events were documented: new AF (n = 1), clinically significant supraventricular tachycardia (n = 1), acute coronary syndrome (n = 1), and stroke (n = 1). No heart failure events were documented. Echocardiographic findings during therapy Baseline echocardiography was available in 491 patients (86.6%), with a median LVEF of 62% (Q1-Q3: 58-66). During TCE therapy, 291 patients (51.3%) underwent echocardiography at a median of 61 days (Q1-Q3: 0-101) after TCE initiation; median LVEF was 60% (Q1-Q3: 57-65) ( ). Among patients with paired baseline and on-treatment echocardiograms (n = 256), LVEF did not change significantly (paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test; P = 0.50) ( , ). Similar LVEF findings were observed in patients with established cardiovascular disease at baseline (n = 84 pairs; P = 0.87) and in those without established cardiovascular disease (n = 172 pairs; P = 0.35) ( ). LV GLS was available at baseline in 135 patients and during therapy in 99 patients, with 32 paired measurements; there was no significant change from baseline to on-treatment (paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test; P = 0.99). Hemodynamically insignificant pericardial effusions were observed in 4.6% of patients (n = 12) during TCE therapy; no patients presented with acute pericarditis. Clinical factors associated with cardiovascular events In univariable Fine-Gray analyses, older age, reduced renal function, baseline coronary artery disease, hypertension, dyslipidemia, prior pomalidomide/thalidomide exposure, and elranatamab therapy were associated with a higher incidence of composite cardiovascular events ( ). Forward stepwise Fine-Gray selection using AIC, with age and sex forced into the model, identified coronary artery disease and eGFR as covariates that improved multivariable model fit. In the final model, coronary artery disease remained the only variable independently associated with cardiovascular events (subdistribution HR: 4.06; 95% CI: 2.02-8.15), whereas

Forward stepwise Fine-Gray selection using AIC, with age and sex forced into the model, identified coronary artery disease and eGFR as covariates that improved multivariable model fit. In the final model, coronary artery disease remained the only variable independently associated with cardiovascular events (subdistribution HR: 4.06; 95% CI: 2.02-8.15), whereas age, sex, and eGFR were not statistically significant ( ). Among patients with preexisting coronary artery disease, treatment-associated cardiovascular events included acute coronary syndrome (n = 5), HFrEF (n = 4), atrial fibrillation (n = 6), supraventricular tachycardia (n = 2), HFpEF (n = 1), ventricular arrhythmia (n = 1), and cerebrovascular events (n = 1). The cumulative incidence of events stratified by baseline coronary artery disease is shown in (Gray’s test; P < 0.001). To evaluate the contribution of acute immunotoxicity to cardiovascular risk, grade ≥2 CRS and/or ICANS was included as a time-dependent covariate in a cause-specific Cox proportional hazards model using the same AIC-selected baseline covariates. In univariable analysis, this exposure was associated with more than a 2-fold increase in the instantaneous risk of cardiovascular events (HR: 2.37; 95% CI: 1.26-4.46). This association remained significant after adjustment for age, sex, coronary artery disease, and eGFR (HR: 2.27; 95% CI: 1.20-4.29; P = 0.012) ( , ). Coronary artery disease remained independently associated with cardiovascular risk (HR: 3.70; 95% CI: 1.94-7.06; P < 0.001), whereas age, sex, and eGFR were not significantly associated with this outcome. The cumulative incidence of cardiovascular events stratified by CRS and/or ICANS status is shown in . Cardiovascular and all-cause mortality Among the 106 patients who died during TCE therapy, 2 died from cardiovascular causes (severe valvular disease and deterioration of preexisting cardiomyopathy), corresponding to a cumulative incidence of 0.4% (95% CI: 0.1-1.2). depicts on-treatment cardiovascular, noncardiovascular, and all-cause mortality. In univariable Cox models, older age, sex, reduced renal function, a history of cardiomyopathy/HFrEF, lower baseline LVEF, prior pomalidomide/thalidomide exposure, anthracycline exposure, and cancer/TCE agent category were each associated with higher on-treatment all-cause mortality ( ). To identify baseline predictors of mortality at the time of TCE initiation, a multivariable Cox model was constructed using forward stepwise selection guided by the AIC, with age and sex forced into the model. In the final multivariable Cox model, teclistamab (HR: 4.10; 95% CI: 1.90-8.84), epcoritamab (HR: 3.95; 95% CI: 1.86-8.40), and prior anthracycline exposure (HR: 2.72; 95% CI: 1.42-5.23) remained independently associated with higher on-treatment mortality along with older age and sex ( ). To assess whether incident cardiovascular toxicity was associated with subsequent mortality risk, a multivariable Cox model was constructed in which the composite cardiovascular event endpoint was incorporated as a time-dependent covariate. The occurrence of a cardiovascular event was associated with subsequent mortality, with event onset conferring nearly a 7-fold increase in hazard (HR: 6.76; 95% CI: 4.19-10.92), independent of age, sex, TCE agent, and prior anthracycline exposure ( , ). Discussion To our knowledge, this is the first study to systematically characterize TCE-related cardiovascular complications and their association with all-cause mortality in a large, real-world cohort of patients with hematologic malignancies ( ). In this dual-center cohort of 567 patients treated with TCEs, the cumulative incidence of on-treatment cardiovascular events was 10.4% (95% CI: 8.1-13.1), with LV dysfunction, and AF, representing the most common presentations. Coronary artery disease was the only baseline variable independently associated with cardiovascular events, whereas development of high-grade CRS and/or ICANS was associated with a significant time-dependent increase in cardiovascular risk. Cardiovascular events were, in turn, associated with subsequent all-cause mortality. In addition, prior anthracycline exposure and treatment with teclistamab or epcoritamab were independently associated with higher mortality. Immunotherapy has transformed cancer treatment and improved survival outcomes. However, off-target immune activation has been associated with adverse cardiovascular events. Acute myocarditis, although rare (0.4%-2%), is a potentially fatal complication of immune checkpoint inhibitors, with reported mortality rates ranging from 5% to 46%. , In contrast, CAR T-cell therapy–related cardiovascular complications occur in 14% to 16% of patients , and primarily include atrial arrhythmias (8%) and HFrEF (8%), with substantially lower cardiovascular mortality rates (0.50%-0.65%). , In a pharmacovigilance analysis of 3,668 systemic adverse events linked to TCE therapy, cardiovascular events comprised a small subset and included heart failure (1.4%), tachyarrhythmias (1.2%), myocarditis (0.2%), pericarditis (0.1%), and sudden death (0.05%). Collectively, data suggest that TCE therapy is associated with a more favorable cardiovascular safety profile relative to other immunotherapeutic modalities. cardiovascular complications occur in 14% to 16% of patients , and primarily include atrial arrhythmias (8%) and HFrEF (8%), with substantially lower cardiovascular mortality rates (0.50%-0.65%). , In a pharmacovigilance analysis of 3,668 systemic adverse events linked to TCE therapy, cardiovascular events comprised a small subset and included heart failure (1.4%), tachyarrhythmias (1.2%), myocarditis (0.2%), pericarditis (0.1%), and sudden death (0.05%). Collectively, data suggest that TCE therapy is associated with a more favorable cardiovascular safety profile relative to other immunotherapeutic modalities. Consistent with this, our findings demonstrate a cumulative incidence of TCE therapy–related cardiovascular events (10.4%), most commonly HFrEF and AF, with cardiovascular mortality remaining rare (0.4%). No cases of TCE-related acute myocarditis were identified on detailed manual chart review. Although our ability to detect subclinical myocardial injury was limited by inconsistent biomarker assessments, clinical suspicion for myocarditis was low. This aligns with observations from large CAR T-cell therapy studies in which CRS and ICANS are common complications and myocarditis has not been reported. , Another notable finding in this cohort was the relatively low cumulative incidence of high-grade CRS or ICANS (16%), a pattern that may reflect contemporary practice characterized by heightened clinical vigilance and early use of targeted anticytokine therapies such as tocilizumab and anakinra. Nevertheless, among patients receiving TCE therapy, development of grade ≥2 CRS and/or ICANS was associated with more than a 2-fold increase in cardiovascular event risk, mirroring observations from CAR T-cell therapy in which more severe CRS is associated with greater cardiotoxicity. , Together, these findings reinforce the need for close hemodynamic and cardiac monitoring during episodes of significant immune activation. Further research is needed to establish evidence-based surveillance protocols for early detection and management of cardiovascular toxicity in this setting. Established cardiovascular disease was present at baseline in 26% (n = 147) of the cohort, reflecting the growing inclusion of patients with substantial comorbidities undergoing advanced cancer therapies. Although the cumulative incidence of cardiovascular events during TCE therapy was 10.4%, baseline coronary artery disease was independently associated with a higher risk of subsequent cardiovascular events, including acute coronary syndrome. These findings highlight the importance of thorough cardiovascular assessment and optimization in patients with preexisting coronary artery disease before and throughout TCE therapy. Study limitations First, the cohort was drawn from 2 cancer centers, which may limit generalizability. Second, analyses were restricted to on-treatment cardiovascular events; therefore, we cannot comment on longer-term cardiovascular effects associated with TCE therapy. Third, because TCE dosing schedules varied and the study was retrospective, inflammatory and cardiac biomarkers were measured inconsistently, limiting our ability to assess their temporal relationship with cardiovascular events or to detect subclinical myocardial injury or inflammation. Fourth, this study evaluated TCE-related cardiovascular complications over a 10-year period during which treatment protocols, dosing schedules, premedication, and supportive care strategies evolved. Newly approved TCEs and improvements in monitoring and management of immune-related toxicities also may have influenced cardiovascular outcomes over the study period. Conclusions In summary, this study provides the first detailed characterization of cardiovascular toxicity during TCE therapy in a large real-world cohort. Although overall event rates were modest, preexisting coronary artery disease and development of grade ≥2 CRS and/or ICANS identified patients at substantially higher cardiovascular risk. These events were, in turn, associated with higher mortality, underscoring the clinical relevance of early recognition and coordinated cardio-oncology care. As TCE use continues to expand, prospective studies are needed to refine risk stratification and define evidence-based surveillance and management strategies. Perspectives COMPETENCY IN MEDICAL KNOWLEDGE: In patients receiving TCE therapies, baseline coronary artery disease and development of grade ≥CRS and/or ICANS identify those at heightened cardiovascular risk; cardiovascular events are significantly associated with higher subsequent mortality. Clinicians should incorporate targeted cardiovascular assessment and closer monitoring in patients with preexisting coronary disease, prior anthracycline exposure, or grade ≥2 CRS and/or ICANS to facilitate timely detection and management of cardiotoxicity. TRANSLATIONAL OUTLOOK: Future prospective studies are needed to establish standardized surveillance protocols and determine whether tailored preventive or therapeutic strategies can improve outcomes in patients treated with TCE therapy.
