chunks.content: 1 Introduction Metabolic syndrome (MetS) comprises central obesity, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and hypertension, all of which contribute to systemic metabolic dysfunction. Emerging evidence suggests that MetS plays a critical role in reproductive health, affecting both male and female fertility. While individual components of MetS have been studied extensively, their combined and synergistic effects on infertility require comprehensive evaluation. 1.1 Metabolic syndrome Metabolic syndrome was first described by Reaven in 1988 as “Syndrome X,” emphasizing insulin resistance as the central mechanism linking glucose intolerance, dyslipidemia, and hypertension to increased cardiovascular disease risk [ , , ]. It is now recognized as a cluster of metabolic abnormalities—including abdominal obesity, hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia, and elevated blood pressure—that collectively increase the risk of diabetes and cardiovascular diseases [ ]. According to the National Cholesterol Education Program-Third, Adult Treatment Panel (NCEP ATP III) criteria, diagnosis requires the presence of at least three of these components [ ]. Globally, metabolic syndrome affects approximately 20–25% of adults, with prevalence rising due to obesity and sedentary lifestyles [ , , , ]. In Ethiopia, prevalence has been reported at 27–35%, depending on diagnostic criteria [ ]. Although its pathogenesis is not fully understood, visceral obesity is considered a key driver, contributing to insulin resistance, chronic inflammation, and oxidative stress, which play central roles in disease development [ , , ]. 1.2 Infertility Infertility is defined as the failure to achieve pregnancy after 12 months of regular, unprotected intercourse and may be primary or secondary, with about 20% of cases unexplained [ ]. Male infertility is mainly due to poor semen quality, while female infertility involves disorders of the ovaries, uterus, fallopian tubes, or endocrine system [ ]. Globally, infertility affects 10–15% of couples, with male factors contributing to nearly half of the cases. Lifestyle factors also play a significant role by influencing hormonal balance and reproductive function [ , , , ]. 2 Methodology This study was conducted as a narrative review of the literature examining the relationship between metabolic syndrome and infertility. The review aimed to discuss current evidence regarding pathophysiological mechanisms, clinical associations, and therapeutic consequences in both male and female populations. This narrative review provides a novel and integrative perspective by examining infertility as a dual-condition involving both male and female factors. In contrast to the majority of existing narrative and systematic reviews, which predominantly address infertility in a sex-specific manner, our approach discusses evidence across both partners to reflect the inherently coupled nature of reproductive outcomes. Methodologically, this review adopts a structured and comprehensive literature synthesis to critically evaluate shared and interacting pathophysiological mechanisms. Clinically, this dual framework offers greater relevance by aligning with real-world infertility management, where both partners are evaluated concurrently, thereby supporting more holistic diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. A comprehensive literature search was conducted using the electronic databases PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. The search covered studies published from January 1980 to 2025. The following keywords were used in various combinations: Metabolic Syndrome, Infertility, Male infertility, Female infertility, Insulin resistance, Obesity, Hypertension, Dyslipidemia, Reproductive hormones, Testosterone, Polycystic ovary syndrome, Erectile dysfunction. Boolean operators (AND, OR) were applied to refine the search strategy. 2.1 Ethical considerations As this study is a review of previously published literature, ethical approval was not required. 3 The impact of metabolic syndrome on infertility Metabolic syndrome (MetS) is strongly associated with infertility in both males and females [ ]. In men, MetS contributes to hypogonadism, impaired spermatogenesis, reduced sperm count and motility, and increased sperm DNA damage, largely driven by systemic inflammation and elevated cytokines such as TNF-α [ , ]. In women, MetS is closely linked to polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), characterized by chronic anovulation, menstrual irregularities, hyperandrogenism, and insulin resistance [ ]. Although numerous studies have examined the relationship between MetS and infertility, a comprehensive evaluation integrating both male and female reproductive outcomes remains limited. Such a holistic approach is essential to better understand the cumulative impact of MetS on reproductive health and to inform improved prevention, early diagnosis, and management strategies [ , ]. The effects of MetS on male and female reproductive function are illustrated in . 3.1 Obesity and infertility The transition of Homo sapiens from hunting and gathering to agriculture during the Neolithic period marked a significant dietary shift toward carbohydrate-rich foods [ ]. In modern times, reduced physical activity combined with increased consumption of calorie-dense foods is widely recognized as a primary driver of the rising prevalence of obesity [ ]. The spread of the Western-style diet (WSD), characterized by high levels of simple carbohydrates and saturated fats, has been a major contributor to this trend, nearly doubling global obesity rates [ ]. Obesity is defined as an excessive accumulation of body fat that negatively affects health. Clinically, it is commonly assessed using body mass index (BMI), where

agriculture during the Neolithic period marked a significant dietary shift toward carbohydrate-rich foods [ ]. In modern times, reduced physical activity combined with increased consumption of calorie-dense foods is widely recognized as a primary driver of the rising prevalence of obesity [ ]. The spread of the Western-style diet (WSD), characterized by high levels of simple carbohydrates and saturated fats, has been a major contributor to this trend, nearly doubling global obesity rates [ ]. Obesity is defined as an excessive accumulation of body fat that negatively affects health. Clinically, it is commonly assessed using body mass index (BMI), where obesity is classified as a BMI greater than 30 kg/m 2 and morbid obesity as a BMI greater than 35 kg/m 2 [ ]. However, BMI does not distinguish between lean mass and fat mass, limiting its accuracy. Therefore, body fat percentage is considered a more precise measure of adiposity [ ]. Current consensus indicates that the risk of obesity-related complications increases when body fat exceeds 25% in males and 30% in females [ ]. The global rise in obesity, driven largely by dietary transitions and reduced physical activity, has been strongly associated with impaired reproductive function. While the epidemiological association between obesity and infertility is well established, the underlying mechanisms and their clinical significance remain variably supported by evidence of differing quality [ , ]. The HPG axis is the most important regulating endocrine axis in the reproductive system, as displayed in [ ]. The pulsatile release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) from the hypothalamus triggers the release of gonadotropins, which coordinate the processes of steroidogenesis and spermatogenesis by acting on their receptors on testicular cells, Leydig cells, and Sertoli cells. Adiponectin and both of its receptors, AdipoR1 and AdipoR2, have been found in the human hypothalamus and pituitary, indicating their involvement in the HPG axis's regulation mechanism. Moreover, its deficiency affects reproductive functions by inhibiting FSH and LH secretion [ ]. Obesity and insulin resistance have been consistently associated with impaired oocyte quality, particularly in experimental animal models. In studies using female mice fed a high-fat diet (HFD), a well-established model for inducing both obesity and insulin resistance, significant alterations in reproductive outcomes have been observed. HFD-exposed mice demonstrated a reduced likelihood of ovulation; however, among those that did ovulate, an increased ovulation rate was paradoxically reported. Despite comparable fertilization rates between HFD and control groups, embryos derived from HFD mice exhibited delayed progression across multiple developmental milestones, suggesting compromised developmental competence [ ]. At the ovarian level, obesity was associated with a marked increase in apoptotic follicles, alongside a reduction in both the number and size of mature oocytes. These findings indicate that the adverse effects of obesity on oocyte quality may be mediated indirectly through disruption of the follicular microenvironment rather than direct effects on the oocyte itself. Complementary evidence from human studies supports these observations, demonstrating that oocytes retrieved from smaller follicles are associated with lower fertilization and cleavage rates, further underscoring the clinical relevance of follicular development dynamics in reproductive success [ ]. Overall, while animal models provide strong mechanistic insights into the impact of obesity and insulin resistance on oocyte competence, translating these insights to human fertility outcomes requires cautious interpretation given physiological differences and variability across clinical contexts. Evidence linking obesity to infertility derives from a combination of epidemiological studies, clinical observations, and experimental animal models, each with distinct strengths and limitations. Observational human studies consistently demonstrate associations between elevated body mass index (BMI) and reduced fertility outcomes in both males and females, providing moderate-to-strong evidence of a clinical relationship. However, these studies are often confounded by lifestyle, metabolic comorbidities, and socioeconomic factors [ ]. Altered mitochondrial function has been proposed as a key mechanistic pathway underlying compromised oocyte quality and adverse reproductive outcomes in obese females. Mitochondria are central to oocyte competence, as their quality, quantity, and spatial distribution within the ooplasm are critical for energy production, calcium homeostasis, and regulation of early embryonic development. Consequently, mitochondrial dysfunction can impair the capacity of embryos to successfully progress through pre-implantation stages [ ]. Evidence from animal models indicates that oocytes from obese mice exhibit significant mitochondrial abnormalities, including increased inner mitochondrial membrane potential, heterogeneous and uneven mitochondrial distribution, elevated production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and a shift toward a more oxidized intracellular redox state. These alterations suggest a state of mitochondrial hyperactivity coupled with oxidative imbalance. Furthermore, obesity has been associated with compensatory upregulation of mitochondrial biogenesis, reflected by increased mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) copy number. While this response may initially aim to meet heightened demands, it paradoxically exacerbates oxidative stress, leading to cumulative damage to mtDNA and impairment of mitochondrial integrity [ ]. Such damage is particularly detrimental in oocytes, where mitochondrial function is essential for fertilization and early embryogenesis. Taken together,

These alterations suggest a state of mitochondrial hyperactivity coupled with oxidative imbalance. Furthermore, obesity has been associated with compensatory upregulation of mitochondrial biogenesis, reflected by increased mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) copy number. While this response may initially aim to meet heightened demands, it paradoxically exacerbates oxidative stress, leading to cumulative damage to mtDNA and impairment of mitochondrial integrity [ ]. Such damage is particularly detrimental in oocytes, where mitochondrial function is essential for fertilization and early embryogenesis. Taken together, these findings support the hypothesis that mitochondrial dysregulation—characterized by oxidative stress, altered bioenergetics, and mtDNA damage—represents a critical link between obesity and reduced oocyte developmental competence. However, the extent to which these mechanisms translate to human reproductive physiology remains an area requiring further investigation [ ]. Mechanistic insights—such as the role of hyperinsulinemia, hyperleptinemia, oxidative stress, and chronic inflammation—are largely supported by experimental and animal studies [ ] . These models allow controlled investigation of causality but may not fully replicate human reproductive physiology. For instance, studies using high-fat diet (HFD)-induced obesity in mice demonstrate impaired oocyte quality, altered mitochondrial function, and increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, suggesting plausible biological pathways. Nevertheless, the translation of these findings to humans remains limited due to interspecies differences. Hormonal dysregulation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal (HPG) axis is one of the most consistently reported mechanisms, supported by both clinical and experimental data [ ]. Alterations in gonadotropin secretion, reduced anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), and disrupted steroidogenesis provide a coherent framework linking metabolic dysfunction to reproductive impairment. Human studies provide further evidence that obesity adversely affects female reproductive endocrinology and ovarian reserve. Obese women have been shown to exhibit reduced levels of luteinizing hormone (LH) and anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH)—a granulosa cell–derived marker of ovarian reserve—suggesting diminished follicular capacity compared to normal-weight women [ ]. In addition, decreased inhibin B in premenopausal obese women further indicates impaired granulosa cell function. Alterations in gonadotropin dynamics are also evident, as women with BMI >25 demonstrate reduced excretion of gonadotropins and luteal phase progesterone metabolites, implying compromised corpus luteum function. Collectively, these findings support the presence of underlying follicular dysfunction in obese women, even in cases where ovulation is preserved [ ]. In males, obesity negatively impacts fertility through multifactorial mechanisms, including disruption of the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal (HPG) axis, impaired steroidogenesis, and broader metabolic dysregulation involving insulin, inflammatory cytokines, and adipokines. These alterations are associated with reduced sperm concentration, motility, and viability, as well as abnormal morphology. At the molecular level, obesity has been linked to defective chromatin condensation, increased DNA fragmentation, enhanced apoptosis, and epigenetic modifications that may be transmitted to offspring [ ]. A key contributing factor is oxidative stress, with excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) damaging sperm membrane integrity and function [ ]. However, evidence from animal studies remains partially inconsistent. For example, one study in high-fat diet (HFD)–fed male mice reported no significant differences in sperm viability or fertilizing capacity (both in vivo and in vitro), despite reductions in epididymal weight and altered body composition, including increased gonadal fat mass [ ]. Similarly, comparable fertilization rates and embryo development to the blastocyst stage were observed between HFD and control groups, suggesting preserved functional competence under certain experimental conditions [ ]. These findings highlight a discrepancy between structural or metabolic alterations and measurable reproductive outcomes. Additionally, hormonal imbalances appear to play a critical role in both obesity and infertility. Reduced testosterone-to-estradiol ratios have been observed in both infertile and obese men compared to appropriate control groups, indicating a shift toward estrogenic dominance likely driven by increased aromatase activity in adipose tissue [ ]. Overall, while a substantial body of evidence supports the detrimental effects of obesity on both female and male reproductive function, variability across studies—particularly between animal models and human data—suggests that these effects may be context-dependent. Differences in study design, degree and duration of obesity, and compensatory physiological mechanisms likely contribute to these inconsistencies. From a clinical perspective, these findings underscore the importance of metabolic health in reproductive outcomes, while also highlighting the need for more standardized and longitudinal human studies to clarify causality and long-term effects. Despite general agreement on the negative impact of obesity on fertility, significant inconsistencies exist across studies, particularly in experimental models. For example, while some animal studies report reduced ovulation rates and impaired embryonic development, others demonstrate no significant differences in fertilization rates or sperm viability between obese and control groups. These discrepancies may arise from variations in study design, including differences in diet composition, duration of obesity exposure, genetic background of animal models, and endpoints measured. Similarly, in human studies, the degree to which obesity affects male fertility remains debated. While many reports indicate reduced sperm quality and hormonal

effects. Despite general agreement on the negative impact of obesity on fertility, significant inconsistencies exist across studies, particularly in experimental models. For example, while some animal studies report reduced ovulation rates and impaired embryonic development, others demonstrate no significant differences in fertilization rates or sperm viability between obese and control groups. These discrepancies may arise from variations in study design, including differences in diet composition, duration of obesity exposure, genetic background of animal models, and endpoints measured. Similarly, in human studies, the degree to which obesity affects male fertility remains debated. While many reports indicate reduced sperm quality and hormonal imbalances, others find minimal or no significant associations after controlling for confounders. This suggests that obesity alone may not be a sufficient determinant of infertility, but rather acts in combination with other metabolic or environmental factors. Another area of inconsistency involves mitochondrial dysfunction in oocytes. Although experimental evidence strongly supports mitochondrial alterations as a key mechanism, direct clinical evidence in humans is limited due to methodological challenges in assessing mitochondrial function in vivo. A critical distinction must be made between experimental findings and their clinical applicability. Animal studies provide valuable mechanistic insights, particularly regarding oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and hormonal dysregulation. However, these findings often represent controlled, extreme condition s (e.g., high-fat diets inducing rapid obesity), which may not accurately reflect the gradual and multifactorial development of obesity in humans. Clinically, the most relevant outcomes include reduced fecundity, menstrual irregularities, impaired assisted reproductive technology (ART) outcomes, and decreased semen quality. While experimental data suggest profound cellular and molecular damage, the clinical manifestations in humans are often more heterogeneous and less severe, indicating potential compensatory mechanisms. Furthermore, some experimental findings—such as unchanged fertilization rates in certain obese animal models—highlight the possibility that early reproductive processes may remain intact, while later stages (e.g., embryo development or implantation) are more vulnerable. This has important implications for clinical management, particularly in the context of ART. Overall, the relationship between obesity and infertility is supported by strong epidemiological evidence and moderate mechanistic evidence, but is complicated by inconsistencies across studies and limitations in translating experimental findings to clinical practice. The heterogeneity of results suggests that obesity should be viewed not as a singular causal factor, but as part of a complex, multifactorial network involving metabolic, hormonal, and environmental influences. 3.2 Dyslipidemia and infertility Dyslipidemia, a central component of metabolic syndrome, is characterized by elevated triglycerides, reduced high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, and increased levels of small dense low-density lipoprotein (LDL), all of which contribute to an atherogenic profile [ ]. Beyond its established role in cardiovascular disease, emerging evidence suggests that dyslipidemia may also adversely affect reproductive function in both males and females [ ]. In addition to reproductive implications, elevated serum triglyceride (STG) levels have been associated with an increased risk of malignancies, including prostate cancer in men and cervical cancer in women [ ]. Mechanistically, hypertriglyceridemia promotes oxidative stress and excessive generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which can induce DNA damage, enhance cellular proliferation, and inhibit apoptosis—processes that are relevant not only to carcinogenesis but also to impaired gamete integrity [ , ]. Experimental animal studies provide mechanistic insights into the reproductive consequences of dyslipidemia. In hypercholesterolemic rat models, significant reductions in fertility index, testicular weight, sperm count, motility, and viability have been observed, alongside increased sperm abnormalities. Importantly, therapeutic interventions with α-tocopherol (vitamin E) or simvastatin resulted in significant improvements in these parameters, with combined treatment demonstrating additive or synergistic effects [ , ]. These findings highlight the potential reversibility of lipid-induced reproductive dysfunction, although their direct applicability to human populations remains uncertain. Human data further support an association between dyslipidemia and impaired reproductive outcomes, particularly in females. A retrospective cohort study conducted in China reported that women with dyslipidemia exhibited significantly reduced bilateral antral follicle counts and lower basal follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) levels, indicating diminished ovarian reserve [ ]. Additionally, elevated levels of triglycerides (TG), total cholesterol (TC), and LDL were inversely correlated with the number of normally fertilized oocytes and negatively associated with the proportion of high-quality embryos [ ]. These findings suggest that lipid abnormalities may compromise both oocyte competence and early embryonic development. Overall, oxidative stress appears to be a unifying mechanism linking dyslipidemia to reproductive dysfunction. However, despite consistent associations, the strength of evidence varies across study designs. Animal studies provide strong mechanistic support but may overestimate effect sizes, whereas human studies—often observational—are limited by potential confounding factors such as obesity, insulin resistance, and lifestyle variables. Consequently, while dyslipidemia is increasingly recognized as a modifiable risk factor for infertility, further well-controlled, longitudinal studies are needed to establish causality and inform targeted clinical interventions [ ]. The effect is summarized in . 3.3 Diabetic mellitus and infertility Type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T1DM and T2DM) are increasingly prevalent global health conditions, with a particularly rapid rise in T2DM among adolescents and young adults [ ]. This epidemiological shift has heightened concern regarding the reproductive consequences of diabetes, especially in women of reproductive age. In T1DM, reproductive dysfunction is common, with up to 40% of affected women experiencing menstrual irregularities or other reproductive disorders during their lifetime [ ]. Mechanistically, chronic hyperglycemia exerts direct neuroendocrine toxicity, disrupting the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal (HPG) axis. Experimental evidence demonstrates that hyperglycemia impairs gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) secretion and increases apoptosis in GnRH-producing cells, alongside a diminished luteinizing hormone (LH) response to GnRH stimulation [ , ]. Additional animal studies show that uncontrolled hyperglycemia induces a catabolic state characterized by reduced adiposity and decreased leptin levels, which suppress kisspeptin expression—an essential upstream regulator of GnRH—thereby further impairing reproductive signaling [ , ]. Insulin itself plays a pivotal regulatory role in reproductive physiology. In T1DM, exogenous insulin administered subcutaneously bypasses hepatic first-pass metabolism, leading to supraphysiological peripheral insulin levels [ ]. Given the widespread expression of insulin receptors in reproductive tissues—including the ovaries, uterus, hypothalamus, and pituitary—this altered insulin distribution has significant functional implications [ ]. At the ovarian level, insulin enhances granulosa cell steroidogenesis, supports follicular development, and potentiates follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)-mediated steroid secretion. It also promotes early follicular recruitment through gonadotropic effects on folliculogenesis [ ]. Consequently, dysregulated insulin signaling can disrupt ovarian development and function through multiple, interrelated pathways [ , ]. In T2DM, the combination of hyperinsulinemia and insulin resistance contributes to distinct but overlapping reproductive abnormalities. Excess insulin stimulates granulosa cell activity, leading to increased recruitment of small follicles and the development of enlarged ovaries with multiple immature follicles, a phenotype consistent with polycystic ovarian morphology [ ]. Simultaneously, insulin resistance impairs the selection of a dominant follicle, contributing to anovulation and menstrual irregularities [ , ]. Clinically, diabetic women may also experience sexual dysfunction, including dyspareunia, reduced libido, and impaired arousal, further compounding reproductive challenges [ ]. Evidence from animal models reinforces the central role of insulin signaling in reproductive regulation. For example, neuronal-specific insulin receptor knockout models exhibit severe metabolic derangements, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and infertility, largely attributable to GnRH deficiency [ ]. In males, diabetes is also associated with reduced reproductive capacity. A large cohort study of individuals with childhood-onset T1DM demonstrated significantly lower fertility rates in both males and females compared to controls, with a more pronounced reduction observed in women [ ]. At the gamete level, diabetic men exhibit reduced semen volume and increased mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) deletions in sperm, indicating compromised mitochondrial integrity and function [ , ]. Hormonal alterations further contribute to male reproductive dysfunction. Population-based studies report that diabetic men have significantly lower testosterone and sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), despite similar levels of other sex steroids such as estradiol and androstenedione [ ]. Moreover, markers of insulin resistance, including C-peptide and HOMA-IR, are inversely correlated with total, free, and bioavailable testosterone levels. Notably, the association appears strongest for total testosterone, although adjustment for SHBG attenuates these differences, suggesting a complex interaction between insulin resistance and androgen bioavailability [ , ]. Overall, diabetes mellitus exerts multifaceted effects on reproductive function through disruptions in metabolic, hormonal, and neuroendocrine pathways. While mechanistic studies—particularly in animal models—provide strong evidence for causal links, human data are largely observational and subject to confounding factors such as obesity, disease duration, and glycemic control. Clinically, these findings underscore the importance of early metabolic management and endocrine monitoring in preserving reproductive health among diabetic individuals. Both male and female diabetic animals exhibit a marked hypogonadotropic state, characterized by reduced basal gonadotropins and sex steroids, diminished luteinizing hormone (LH) pulsatility, and impaired gonadotropic responses to gonadectomy—an indicator of disrupted hypothalamic–pituitary negative feedback regulation [ , , , ]. These findings highlight a central defect at the level of the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal (HPG) axis. Rodent models of type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) have provided robust mechanistic evidence linking uncontrolled diabetes to profound reproductive endocrine dysfunction. Both male and female diabetic animals exhibit a marked hypogonadotropic state, characterized by reduced basal gonadotropins and sex steroids, diminished luteinizing hormone (LH) pulsatility, and impaired gonadotropic responses to gonadectomy—an indicator of disrupted hypothalamic–pituitary negative feedback regulation [ , , , ]. These findings highlight a central defect at the level of the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal (HPG) axis. In female models, additional abnormalities include disruption of the estradiol-mediated positive feedback mechanism, delayed or absent preovulatory LH surges, and consequent anovulation. Importantly, these dysfunctions are at least partially reversible following insulin administration, supporting a causal role of insulin deficiency and metabolic imbalance in reproductive impairment [ , ]. This reversibility underscores the dynamic interaction between metabolic control and reproductive endocrine function. Beyond reproductive dysfunction, hyperinsulinemia—commonly associated with hyperglycemia and insulin resistance—has been implicated in carcinogenesis. Elevated insulin levels increase the circulating bioavailability of Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), a potent mitogenic and anti-apoptotic factor. Activation of insulin and IGF-1 receptor signaling pathways promotes cellular proliferation, inhibits apoptosis, and facilitates tumor invasion and metastasis, contributing to the development of malignancies such as endometrial and ovarian cancer [ ]. Furthermore, both cancer itself and its therapeutic interventions (e.g., chemotherapy, radiotherapy) can adversely affect gonadal function, thereby compounding infertility risk in affected women [ ]. Overall, these findings illustrate the dual impact of diabetes on reproductive health: direct disruption of neuroendocrine reproductive regulation and indirect effects mediated through increased oncogenic risk and its consequences. While animal studies provide strong causal insights, translation to human populations necessitates careful consideration of disease heterogeneity, treatment effects, and long-term metabolic control. 3.4 Hypertension and infertility Hypertension (HTN), a core component of metabolic syndrome and a major contributor to cardiovascular disease, is defined by the Adult Treatment Panel III (ATP III) criteria as systolic blood pressure ≥130 mmHg and/or diastolic blood pressure ≥85 mmHg [ ]. Increasing evidence suggests a bidirectional relationship between hypertension and reproductive dysfunction, wherein both the condition itself and its treatment may adversely affect reproductive health. In males, hypertension has been consistently associated with reduced androgen levels, particularly total testosterone, and with a higher prevalence of sexual dysfunction [ ]. This association is multifactorial, involving vascular impairment, endothelial dysfunction, and hormonal alterations. Notably, certain classes of antihypertensive medications—such as diuretics, central α-agonists, and non-selective β-blockers—have been shown to exert more pronounced negative effects on sexual function compared to calcium channel blockers and angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, which appear to have more neutral or less detrimental profiles [ , ]. Erectile dysfunction (ED) represents one of the most clinically significant yet under-recognized complications of hypertension. Epidemiological data indicate that the prevalence of ED in hypertensive men is approximately twice that observed in normotensive individuals [ ]. This association is sufficiently robust that the European Society of Hypertension/European Society of Cardiology 2013 guidelines formally incorporated erectile dysfunction into the clinical assessment of hypertensive patients [ ]. Supporting these findings, population-based data from North Norway demonstrate that hypertensive men exhibit significantly lower levels of total testosterone, free testosterone, and sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) compared to normotensive controls [ ]. In females, hypertension has also been linked to adverse reproductive outcomes, including an increased risk of endometrial cancer [ ]. Additionally, hypertensive disorders such as preeclampsia further highlight the intersection between vascular dysfunction and reproductive health, although causal pathways remain incompletely defined. The relationship between hypertension and androgen deficiency appears to be complex and potentially bidirectional. While hypertension may contribute to reduced androgen levels through vascular and metabolic mechanisms, emerging evidence suggests that androgen deficiency itself may predispose to hypertension by promoting increased arterial stiffness. This is supported by studies demonstrating that androgen deprivation therapy in men is associated with increased aortic and arterial stiffness, indicating a potential causal role of androgens in maintaining vascular elasticity [ , ]. Overall, the evidence supports a multifaceted interaction between hypertension, hormonal regulation, vascular function, and reproductive health. However, much of the available data is observational, limiting causal inference. Clinically, these findings emphasize the importance of considering sexual and reproductive health in the management of hypertensive patients, as well as the need for careful selection of antihypertensive therapies to minimize adverse reproductive effects. Careful consideration of these variables is essential when interpreting findings from both clinical and epidemiological studies. Age is one of the most significant confounders, as reproductive capacity naturally declines with advancing age in both males and females. In women, age-related reductions in ovarian reserve and oocyte quality may independently contribute to infertility, while in men, aging is associated with gradual declines in testosterone levels and sperm quality. Since the prevalence of metabolic syndrome also increases with age, failure to adjust for this variable may overestimate its effect on fertility outcomes [ ]. Lifestyle factors , including physical inactivity, poor dietary habits, smoking, and alcohol consumption, are strongly associated with both metabolic syndrome and impaired fertility. For instance, smoking has been linked to oxidative stress and DNA damage in gametes, while sedentary behavior contributes to obesity and insulin resistance. These overlapping pathways make it difficult to isolate the independent contribution of metabolic syndrome without proper adjustment [ ]. Obesity , although a core component of metabolic syndrome, may act as an independent confounder when not appropriately stratified. Adiposity influences reproductive function through hormonal dysregulation, inflammation, and altered leptin signaling. Distinguishing the independent effects of obesity from the broader metabolic syndrome phenotype remains a methodological challenge in many studies [ ]. Hormonal disorders , such as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) in women and hypogonadism in men, represent important confounders. PCOS, in particular, shares key features with metabolic syndrome, including insulin resistance and dyslipidemia, and is a well-established cause of infertility. Similarly, male hypogonadism may coexist with metabolic disturbances, complicating causal interpretation [ ]. Medication use is another critical confounding factor. Antihypertensive drugs, lipid-lowering agents, and antidiabetic medications may independently influence reproductive hormones, sexual function, or gametogenesis. For example, certain antihypertensive agents have been associated with erectile dysfunction, while some lipid-lowering drugs may affect steroid hormone synthesis [ ]. Chronic systemic inflammation and comorbidities —such as cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease—may also confound the association. These conditions share common inflammatory and metabolic pathways with metabolic syndrome and may independently impair reproductive health [ ]. Socioeconomic status and environmental exposures further confound. Limited access to healthcare, nutritional disparities, and exposure to endocrine-disrupting chemicals (e.g., pesticides, industrial pollutants) may influence both metabolic health and fertility outcomes [ ]. Psychological stress and mental health conditions should also be considered, as they are associated with both metabolic dysregulation (via neuroendocrine pathways) and reduced reproductive function [ ]. In summary, the interplay of these confounding factors highlights the need for well-designed studies that incorporate appropriate statistical adjustments and stratified analyses. Failure to account for these variables may lead to biased estimates and misinterpretation of the true relationship between metabolic syndrome and infertility. 4.2 Interaction between components of metabolic syndrome in relation to infertility Metabolic syndrome is not merely a collection of independent risk factors; rather, it represents a cluster of interrelated metabolic disturbances that interact synergistically to amplify adverse effects on reproductive function. The combined presence of central obesity, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and chronic low-grade inflammation creates a complex pathophysiological network that exerts a greater detrimental impact on fertility than any single component alone [ ]. Central obesity and insulin resistance underpin this interaction. Excess adipose tissue—particularly visceral fat—acts as an active endocrine organ, releasing adipokines and pro-inflammatory cytokines that promote systemic insulin resistance. In turn, hyperinsulinemia exacerbates adipose tissue dysfunction by enhancing lipogenesis and inhibiting lipolysis, creating a self-perpetuating cycle. This interaction disrupts the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal (HPG) axis, leading to altered gonadotropin secretion and impaired steroidogenesis in both sexes [ ]. The interaction between insulin resistance and dyslipidemia further intensifies reproductive dysfunction. Hyperinsulinemia promotes increased hepatic production of very-low-density lipoproteins (VLDL), contributing to elevated triglyceride levels and reduced high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol. These lipid abnormalities enhance oxidative stress through excessive generation of reactive oxygen species, which can damage sperm DNA, impair sperm motility, and negatively affect oocyte maturation and embryo development [ ]. Obesity and dyslipidemia also act synergistically to disrupt reproductive outcomes. Elevated free fatty acids and cholesterol accumulation in reproductive tissues can impair testicular function, reduce sperm quality, and alter ovarian follicular environments. Lipotoxicity within ovarian and testicular cells induces mitochondrial dysfunction and apoptosis, further compromising gametogenesis [ ]. The interplay between hypertension and endothelial dysfunction represents another critical mechanism. Chronic elevation of blood pressure is associated with vascular damage and reduced nitric oxide bioavailability, leading to impaired blood flow to reproductive organs. Elevated free fatty acids and cholesterol accumulation in reproductive tissues can impair testicular function, reduce sperm quality, and alter ovarian follicular environments. Lipotoxicity within ovarian and testicular cells induces mitochondrial dysfunction and apoptosis, further compromising gametogenesis [ ]. The interplay between hypertension and endothelial dysfunction represents another critical mechanism. Chronic elevation of blood pressure is associated with vascular damage and reduced nitric oxide bioavailability, leading to impaired blood flow to reproductive organs. When combined with other MetS components—particularly insulin resistance and inflammation—this vascular impairment may contribute to erectile dysfunction in men and reduced endometrial receptivity in women [ ]. Chronic low-grade inflammation acts as a unifying link among all components of metabolic syndrome. Adipose tissue–derived cytokines (e.g., TNF-α, IL-6) exacerbate insulin resistance, promote endothelial dysfunction, and disrupt hormonal signaling. This inflammatory milieu interferes with folliculogenesis, spermatogenesis, and implantation processes, thereby amplifying infertility risk [ ]. Importantly, these interactions are often bidirectional and mutually reinforcing. For example, insulin resistance promotes dyslipidemia and hypertension, while dyslipidemia and inflammation further worsen insulin sensitivity. This interconnected network creates a cumulative and synergistic effect on reproductive health, making it difficult to attribute infertility to a single metabolic abnormality [ ]. From a clinical perspective, these findings underscore the importance of a holistic approach to the management of metabolic syndrome in infertile individuals. Targeting multiple components simultaneously—rather than addressing isolated risk factors—may yield more effective improvements in reproductive outcomes [ ]. In conclusion, the interaction between components of metabolic syndrome plays a pivotal role in mediating infertility. The synergistic and self-reinforcing nature of these disturbances highlights the need for integrated therapeutic strategies and further research to disentangle their combined effects on reproductive physiology. This is summarized in and illustrated in . 4.3 Reverse causality in the relationship between metabolic syndrome and infertility While substantial evidence supports the role of metabolic syndrome (MetS) in impairing reproductive function, the possibility of reverse causality should be carefully considered. Infertility itself may contribute to the development or worsening of metabolic disturbances, creating a bidirectional relationship that complicates causal interpretation. One important pathway involves hormonal dysregulation secondary to infertility. In women, conditions such as anovulation and diminished ovarian reserve can alter estrogen and progesterone balance, which in turn affects insulin sensitivity, lipid metabolism, and fat distribution. Similarly, in men, infertility associated with hypogonadism is characterized by reduced testosterone levels, which are known to promote increased visceral adiposity, insulin resistance, and dyslipidemia. In this context, reproductive dysfunction may precede and contribute to the development of MetS components [ ]. Psychological stress and behavioral changes associated with infertility also play a significant role. Infertility is often accompanied by chronic stress, anxiety, and depression, which can activate the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis, increasing cortisol levels. Elevated cortisol promotes central fat accumulation, insulin resistance, and hypertension. Additionally, affected individuals may adopt unhealthy coping behaviors—such as reduced physical activity, poor diet, smoking, or alcohol use—which further increase the risk of metabolic syndrome [ ]. Medical interventions for infertility may also contribute to metabolic alterations. Hormonal treatments, including ovulation induction agents and assisted reproductive technologies (ART), can influence body weight, insulin sensitivity, and lipid profiles. For example, repeated exposure to exogenous hormones may exacerbate underlying metabolic imbalances, particularly in susceptible individuals. In women, infertility-related conditions such as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) highlight the challenge of reverse causality, as PCOS is both a leading cause of infertility and a metabolic disorder characterized by insulin resistance, obesity, and dyslipidemia. This overlap makes it difficult to determine whether metabolic abnormalities are the cause or consequence of reproductive dysfunction. Likewise, in men, testosterone deficiency may both result from and contribute to metabolic syndrome, reinforcing a bidirectional cycle [ ]. Furthermore, reduced reproductive activity and delayed childbearing, often associated with infertility, may indirectly influence metabolic health. Advancing age and prolonged exposure to adverse metabolic conditions can exacerbate weight gain, hypertension, and glucose intolerance, further strengthening the apparent association. Overall, reverse causality underscores the bidirectional and self-reinforcing nature of the relationship between metabolic syndrome and infertility. Failure to account for this dynamic may lead to overestimation of causal effects in observational studies. Longitudinal designs, temporality assessment, and mechanistic investigations are therefore essential to disentangle cause-and-effect relationships [ ]. In summary, recognizing reverse causality is critical for accurate interpretation of the association between metabolic syndrome and infertility. Future research should aim to clarify temporal sequences and identify early markers that distinguish primary metabolic dysfunction from infertility-driven metabolic changes, thereby improving both prevention and treatment strategies. 5 Conclusion Metabolic syndrome represents a growing global health challenge with far-reaching consequences beyond cardiovascular and metabolic disorders, extending significantly into reproductive health. This review demonstrates substantial evidence supporting an inverse relationship between metabolic syndrome and fertility, mediated through multiple interconnected pathophysiological pathways. Future research should aim to clarify temporal sequences and identify early markers that distinguish primary metabolic dysfunction from infertility-driven metabolic changes, thereby improving both prevention and treatment strategies. 5 Conclusion Metabolic syndrome represents a growing global health challenge with far-reaching consequences beyond cardiovascular and metabolic disorders, extending significantly into reproductive health. This review demonstrates substantial evidence supporting an inverse relationship between metabolic syndrome and fertility, mediated through multiple interconnected pathophysiological pathways. Obesity, a central component of metabolic syndrome, exerts detrimental effects on male reproductive function by impairing semen parameters—including sperm concentration, motility, viability, and morphology—while also promoting chromatin abnormalities and DNA fragmentation. In females, obesity is associated with reduced oocyte quality and compromised reproductive potential. Dyslipidemia, particularly elevated serum triglycerides and hypercholesterolemia, further exacerbates reproductive dysfunction by inducing oxidative stress, increasing reactive oxygen species production, and causing DNA damage. These alterations not only impair gametogenesis but are also linked to an increased risk of hormone-related cancers, including prostate and cervical cancers. Additionally, hyperinsulinemia and associated insulin resistance disrupt endocrine homeostasis, leading to reduced levels of bioavailable and total testosterone, as well as sex hormone-binding globulin. These hormonal imbalances, coupled with elevated insulin-like growth factor-1 activity, contribute to both impaired fertility and enhanced carcinogenic potential. Hypertension and its pharmacological management also play a significant role in reproductive impairment, being associated with decreased testosterone levels, erectile dysfunction, and an increased risk of endometrial cancer. Collectively, these findings underscore the multifactorial and systemic nature of metabolic syndrome in disrupting reproductive health. Given these insights, prevention and management of metabolic syndrome through lifestyle modification—including dietary regulation, physical activity, and weight control—alongside appropriate medical interventions, are essential strategies to mitigate its adverse effects on fertility. Future research should focus on elucidating the precise molecular and cellular mechanisms linking individual components of metabolic syndrome—such as insulin resistance, central obesity, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and chronic inflammation—to reproductive dysfunction. A more detailed mechanistic understanding will enable the development of targeted therapeutic approaches aimed at restoring hormonal balance, improving gonadal function, and ultimately enhancing fertility outcomes in affected individuals. 6 Future Perspectives Despite growing evidence linking metabolic syndrome (MetS) with impaired reproductive function, significant gaps remain in our understanding of the precise mechanisms and optimal management strategies. Future research should focus on molecular and translational research to identify biomarkers that predict reproductive dysfunction in individuals with MetS. These may include inflammatory markers, adipokines, oxidative stress indicators, and genetic or epigenetic modifications. Understanding these pathways could enable the development of targeted therapies to re-establish reproductive potential. Interventional studies are also crucial. While lifestyle modification - such as weight reduction, dietary optimization, and physical activity - has shown promise in improving metabolic parameters, further randomized controlled trials are needed to determine whether these interventions directly enhance fertility outcomes. Furthermore, the reproductive effects of pharmacological treatments for metabolic syndrome, including insulin-sensitizing agents, antihypertensive drugs, and lipid-lowering therapies, warrant further investigation to optimize treatment protocols without compromising reproductive health. Another important area for future investigation is the impact of early metabolic disturbances during adolescence and young adulthood on long-term reproductive capacity. Preventive strategies targeting metabolic health at earlier stages of life may reduce the burden of infertility later on. Finally, a multidisciplinary approach integrating endocrinology, reproductive medicine, cardiology, nutrition, and public health is indispensable. Personalized medicine strategies that tailor metabolic and fertility treatments based on individual risk profiles may ultimately improve reproductive outcomes in patients with metabolic syndrome. Progressing research in these areas will not only deepen our understanding of the interplay between metabolic health and fertility but also contribute to more effective prevention and management strategies for infertility in the context of the global rise in metabolic disorders. chunks.content: Key Findings ▪ Landmark randomized clinical trials have established the efficacy of implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) therapy in patients with a history of arrhythmic sudden death. The survival benefit of ICD therapy in the secondary prevention of sudden death was primarily observed in patients with significantly reduced left ventricular function (left ventricular ejection fraction ≤35%). ▪ Patients historically excluded from randomized trials of ICD efficacy in secondary prevention, including those thought to have a reversible etiology of arrhythmia (eg, acute ischemia, electrolyte aberration), remain at increased risk of arrhythmic and all-cause mortality. ▪ A systematic diagnostic protocol in secondary prevention patients including coronary evaluation, imaging (transthoracic echocardiography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging), and, when appropriate, exercise testing, provocative drug challenge, genetic and invasive electrophysiology testing, is vital to the delineation of arrhythmic arrest etiology and guidance of subsequent therapy. ▪ The subcutaneous ICD may be reasonable to consider in select secondary prevention ICD recipients. The use of a long detection interval for fast ventricular arrhythmias (cycle length ≤320 ms) is associated with reduced ICD therapies in secondary prevention patients. ▪ In patients meeting criteria for secondary prevention ICD, early catheter ablation may reduce the risk of ICD therapies and recurrent ventricular arrhythmia as compared to antiarrhythmic drug therapy. For patients treated with antiarrhythmic drug therapy with recurrent ventricular arrhythmia, catheter ablation lowers the risk of recurrent ventricular arrhythmia as compared to escalated antiarrhythmic drug therapy. Introduction Sudden cardiac death is estimated to account for 15%–20% of global mortality and remains a pressing public health challenge. Sudden death is frequently attributed to lethal ventricular arrhythmia and coronary heart disease (CHD) is the most common underlying substrate in the Western world. For survivors of cardiac arrest attributed to ventricular tachycardia (VT) or ventricular fibrillation (VF), or those with sustained VT not due to a reversible cause, contemporary consensus guidelines recommend implantation of an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) in patients with greater than 1 year life expectancy. While the use of ICD therapy in this context is seemingly straightforward, there remain substantial knowledge gaps regarding the secondary prevention of sudden death. This review summarizes the landmark clinical trials evaluating the efficacy of ICD therapy for secondary prevention, reviews clinical outcomes in survivors of sudden cardiac death, highlights the role for systematic diagnostic evaluation, discusses the invasive electrophysiological management in this population, and frames future challenges and needs to advance the care for secondary prevention patients. Landmark Trials in Secondary Prevention Anti-arrhythmic Versus Implantable Defibrillator Trial The Anti-arrhythmic Versus Implantable Defibrillator (AVID) trial (enrollment 1993–1997) evaluated the efficacy of ICD therapy in 1016 patients with resuscitated VF arrest, sustained VT with syncope, or sustained VT with a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) ≤40% and symptoms suggestive of hemodynamic compromise ( ). The majority of participants had underlying CHD (81%) and left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction (mean LVEF 32% ± 13%). Approximately one-half of trial participants qualified on the basis of a resuscitated VF arrest, the remainder with sustained VT. Participants were randomized to ICD therapy vs antiarrhythmic drugs (AAD), which was predominantly amiodarone (96% of the AAD arm at hospital discharge). Over a mean follow-up of 18 months, after which the trial was prematurely terminated on the basis of ICD efficacy, crude mortality was 15.8% in the ICD arm vs 24% in the AAD arm. At 3 years, the average unadjusted survival attributed to ICD therapy was 2.7 months and the estimated number needed to treat to save 1 life with an ICD was 12. There were notable differences in background medical therapy and morbidities between the randomized groups, including a greater prevalence of β-blocker therapy in the ICD vs AAD arm (eg, 42% vs 16% at hospital discharge) and lower prevalence of heart failure (55% vs 60%). While the survival benefit of ICD therapy persisted following adjustment for these differences, the possibility of residual confounding could not be entirely excluded. In subgroup analysis, there was no statistical difference in survival benefit of ICD therapy when stratified by qualifying indication (VF arrest vs sustained VT), prevalent CHD, or LVEF, although numerically, the survival benefit of ICD therapy was observed to accrue only in patients with an LVEF ≤35%. Cardiac Arrest Study Hamburg The Cardiac Arrest Study Hamburg (CASH) evaluated the efficacy of ICD vs medical therapy (amiodarone or β-blocker) in 288 patients with resuscitated cardiac arrest and sustained ventricular arrhythmia (VT or VF), enrolling between 1986 and 1997. The original design of the study included propafenone as a randomized arm, but this was discontinued in light of interim analysis demonstrating a significant 61% increased mortality when compared to participants randomized to ICD therapy. An important limitation of CASH was the notably long recruitment period (11 years), over which time there were notable changes in therapies—both procedural and pharmacotherapy—for patients with coronary disease and cardiomyopathy. (CASH) evaluated the efficacy of ICD vs medical therapy (amiodarone or β-blocker) in 288 patients with resuscitated cardiac arrest and sustained ventricular arrhythmia (VT or VF), enrolling between 1986 and 1997. The original design of the study included propafenone as a randomized arm, but this was discontinued in light of interim analysis demonstrating a significant 61% increased mortality when compared to participants randomized to ICD therapy. An important limitation of CASH was the notably long recruitment period (11 years), over which time there were notable changes in therapies—both procedural and pharmacotherapy—for patients with coronary disease and cardiomyopathy. Notable exclusion criteria for the study included arrests occurring within 72 hours of acute myocardial infarction (MI), cardiac surgery, electrolyte abnormalities, or proarrhythmic medications. VF was the most common qualifying subtype of cardiac arrest (84% of trial participants). The majority of participants had symptomatic heart failure (80%) and CHD was the most common underlying substrate (73%). There were differences in background medical therapy among the groups, most notably the 0% prevalence of β-blocker use in the ICD and amiodarone arms of the study. Over a mean follow-up of 57 months, crude mortality was lower in the ICD arm compared to the AAD arm (36.4% vs 44.4%), although this difference was not statistically significant (1-sided P = .08). In cause-specific mortality analysis, ICD therapy was associated with a significant reduction in sudden death as compared to AAD therapy (13% vs 33%, P = .005). Subgroup analysis did not identify any difference in ICD efficacy within strata of LV function, NYHA class, or prevalent CHD, although—as observed in AVID—there was a numerically greater reduction in mortality associated with ICD therapy in patients with LVEF ≤35%. Likewise, the absolute risk reduction in mortality associated with ICD vs AAD therapy (∼8%) was similar in the 2 studies. Canadian Implantable Defibrillator Study The Canadian Implantable Defibrillator Study (CIDS) evaluated the efficacy of ICD therapy vs amiodarone in 659 participants with resuscitated VT/VF arrest, sustained VT and syncope, sustained VT and symptoms of hemodynamic compromise in the setting of LV dysfunction (LVEF ≤35%), or syncope and the presence of nonsustained VT or inducible VT by programmed stimulation. The trial enrolled between 1990 and 1997. Similar to AVID, approximately one-half of participants qualified on the basis of resuscitated VT/VF arrest (50.1%), the majority had LV dysfunction (mean LVEF 33.3%) and CHD (75%), and the prevalence of β-blocker use was numerically higher in those randomized to ICD therapy (33.5% vs 21.4% at hospital discharge). Over a mean follow-up of 3 years, there was no statistical difference in all-cause and arrhythmic mortality in patients randomized to ICD therapy compared to amiodarone. There were numeric absolute risk reductions in all-cause mortality (ICD vs amiodarone: 23.3% vs 27.0%) and arrhythmic mortality (ICD vs amiodarone: 9.8% vs 11.9%) at 3 years, although these did not reach statistical significance. Similar to AVID and CIDS, the potential efficacy of ICD therapy was not different within strata of qualifying arrhythmia, LV function, prevalent CHD, or heart failure although there was numerically greater benefit in those with LVEF ≤35%. Meta-analysis In response to the premature termination of AVID (which may have therefore overestimated treatment efficacy) and the relatively smaller sample sizes of CIDS and CASH (which may have therefore been underpowered to detect a treatment effect), a meta-analysis of these 3 trials was performed to further evaluate the relative efficacy of ICD therapy compared to amiodarone for the secondary prevention of sudden death. As highlighted above, the inclusion criteria for CIDS and AVID were similar, , whereas participants in CASH were more likely to have had antecedent VF arrest (84% of CASH vs ∼50% of CIDS/AVID), higher LV function (mean LVEF CASH 45% vs 32%–34% in CIDS/AVID), and lower rates of β-blocker therapy (0% of ICD and amiodarone arm of CASH) ( ). Longitudinal clinical outcomes in secondary prevention Pre-ICD Era Survivors of resuscitated VT/VF arrest have long been known to have increased mortality. Observational cohort studies in the 1970s and 1980s identified a significant rate of recurrent cardiac arrest in this population. , , For example, Furukawa and colleagues observed a curvilinear incidence of recurrent VT/VF arrest in survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) without acute MI, with an 11% incidence in the first 6 months of follow-up, which then reduced to 4% per subsequent 6-month interval. Myerburg and colleagues observed a similar kinetics of recurrent sudden death in survivors of VT/VF OHCA, with a 10% incidence at 1 year and then 5% per year for the subsequent 3 years. In a mode-of-death analysis, these authors observed that two-thirds of mortality was attributable to sudden death (16 of 24 deaths) over 5 years of follow-up. Randomized controlled trials In randomized controlled trials of ICD efficacy for secondary prevention (AVID, CIDS, CASH), total mortality at 1 year ranged from 11% to 17% in the AAD arms and 8% to 11% in the ICD arms of these studies. In mode-of-death analysis in AVID, the incidence of arrhythmic sudden death in the antiarrhythmic arm was 8% at 1 year, in general concordance with older observational cohort studies. Overall in AVID, 40% (79 of 202) of the deaths were adjudicated as arrhythmic and the incidence of arrhythmic death was numerically greater in those who qualified on the basis of VF arrest compared to VT (56% vs 44% in the AAD arms for qualifying VF vs VT), although the survival benefit of ICD therapy was observed independent of qualifying arrhythmia. In those randomized to ICD therapy in AVID, ICD therapy was common and rates of ICD therapy were significantly greater than arrhythmic mortality observed in the AAD arm of the study. For example, over a 3-year follow-up, 75% of patients with index VT and 48% of patients with index VF received appropriate ICD therapy. Recurrent VT was more common in those with index VT vs VF (74% vs 30%); and conversely, subsequent VF was more common in those with index VF vs VT (28% vs 18%). The discordance between rates of ICD therapy and rates of adjudicated arrhythmic death in the AAD arm of AVID highlights the important limitation of using appropriate ICD therapy in historic randomized trials as a surrogate for survival benefit in this population. Contemporary observational cohorts Contemporary longitudinal cohorts have identified similar mortality in secondary prevention ICD recipients. For example, in an evaluation of 46,685 patients enrolled in the National Cardiovascular Data Registry between 2006 and 2009, 1-year mortality was 10% and 2-year mortality 16.4% in patients undergoing ICD implantation. Intriguingly, 2-year mortality rates were similar in patients qualifying on the basis of resuscitated cardiac arrest and VT when compared to those qualifying on the basis of syncope in the setting of structural heart disease, even though the latter group was an inclusion criterion in only 1 of the landmark randomized trials in this population (CIDS). The concordance of mortality rates in this contemporary cohort compared to historic randomized trials is striking given the higher penetrance of factors that would be predicted to lower mortality, including goal-directed medical therapy (β-blockers, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system antagonists), lower prevalence of ischemic heart disease, and more flexible ICD programming. An important limitation of these contemporary administrative database cohort studies is delineation and adjudication of mode of death, which is critical in understanding the impact of secular trends in medical and interventional care on mortality risk in secondary prevention patients. Patients excluded from randomized trials Notable exclusion criteria from landmark secondary prevention trials were the presence of reversible causes of arrhythmia (ie, acute ischemia, electrolyte or metabolic derangement, use of proarrhythmic pharmacotherapy), , , as well as sustained VT without syncope or hemodynamic compromise. In the AVID study, patients deemed ineligible by these factors were enrolled in a registry and followed prospectively. For registry patients deemed to have a transient or reversible mechanism of arrhythmia, 42% underwent in-hospital revascularization and others underwent adjustment of medical therapy including, for example, potassium repletion. Over the interval 3 years, mortality was 29% in this “transient/reversible” group, which was similar to the mortality in the AAD arm of the parent trial. Similarly, when longitudinal outcomes were evaluated in patients with “stable” VT without hemodynamic compromise, 3-year mortality remained high (34%), although it is important to note that this “stable VT” cohort reflected patients with LV dysfunction (mean LVEF 34% ± 13%). Since the observations of AVID, other studies have similarly highlighted the limitations and challenge of adjudicating reversible mechanisms of ventricular arrhythmias. For example, Michaud and colleagues systematically evaluated serum potassium on the day of sustained ventricular arrhythmia and found no relationship between serum potassium concentrations and subsequent arrhythmic risk. In a more contemporary analysis of 792 patients deemed to have a reversible mechanism for arrhythmic cardiac arrest, Ladejobi and colleagues observed a 4-year mortality rate of 40%, similar to that observed in the “transient/reversible” subgroup of the AVID registry. ICD use in this contemporary subgroup was associated with 40% relative risk reduction in all-cause mortality. Intriguingly, the mortality benefit of ICD therapy only accrued to patients with reversible mechanisms unrelated to acute ischemia or MI. While the findings of Ladejobi and colleagues would suggest that contemporary revascularization strategies may abrogate or minimize the survival benefit of ICD therapy in patients with sustained arrhythmias in the setting of acute cardiac ischemia, the role of ICD therapy in this setting remains an open question. , For example, van Dijk and colleagues evaluated the incidence of ICD therapy in patients with prior MI presenting with sustained arrhythmia (67% VF, 33% VT) in the setting of acute coronary syndrome (22% ST elevation MI [STEMI], 68% non-STEMI, 10% unstable angina) and an LVEF ≥35%. Over a mean follow-up of 5 years, appropriate ICD therapy occurred in 46% of patients. As VF is considered to occur more commonly in the setting of acute ischemia, these authors hypothesized that revascularization may mitigate subsequent arrhythmic risk, particularly for patients with an index ischemic VF arrest. They found, however, that appropriate ICD therapy still occurred in 23% of these patients, highlighting the substantial risk of incident ventricular arrhythmias regardless of presenting rhythm in patients with prior MI presenting with acute coronary syndrome and sustained VT/VF. Similarly, over a mean follow-up of 4 years, Gupta and colleagues identified appropriate ICD therapies in 18% of patients with a history of VT/VF in the setting of acute ischemia. Finally, the relative timing of arrhythmia in relation to reperfusion may further modify arrhythmia risk. Podolecki and colleagues observed substantial 5-year mortality (36.2%) in patients with early post-reperfusion VT/VF as compared to those without arrhythmia (5-year mortality: 22.6%) or those with pre-reperfusion VT/VF (5-year mortality 26.2%). In the post-reperfusion arrhythmia cohort, the presence of cardiogenic shock, prior MI, and delayed symptom to balloon time were each predicting of incident arrhythmia. The optimal arrhythmic risk stratification in patients presenting with sustained arrhythmias and acute coronary syndrome remains an area of needed investigation, as we discuss below. Diagnostic evaluation in secondary prevention Survivors of sudden arrhythmic death warrant a systematic evaluation for etiology of arrhythmia ( ). In patients with evidence of STEMI following return of spontaneous circulation, contemporary resuscitation guidelines recommend urgent coronary angiography. For patients without STEMI, guidelines support coronary angiography in those with a suspected cardiac cause of arrest and a strategy of delaying coronary angiography until after neurologic recovery was associated with similar outcomes as immediate coronary angiography. Coronary computed tomography angiography is also an alternative modality to define coronary anatomy and substrate, with a recent study demonstrating robust sensitivity and specificity for the detection of coronary stenoses. Contemporary rates of coronary angiography in the United States in those hospitalized after VT/VF OHCA range from 87% in those with STEMI to 34% in those without. For patients without STEMI, the survival implications of potential underutilization of coronary angiography in survivors of VT/VF OHCA remains unknown. Coronary angiography may additionally identify other nonatherosclerotic mechanisms of cardiac arrest, including anomalous coronary anatomy and coronary vasospasm. In addition to coronary angiography, there is emerging evidence that cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging may have diagnostic and prognostic value in secondary prevention patients. , , , Zorzi and colleagues evaluated the diagnostic and prognostic value of systematic coronary angiography and CMR in survivors of OHCA. For patients with obstructive coronary disease, a clinically relevant culprit lesion was identified in 55%. In this subgroup, CMR was able to identify acute changes consistent with ischemia (ie, myocardial edema on T2 sequences) that were concordant with the territory subtended by the culprit vessel. CMR was additionally able to identify patterns of late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) suggestive of ischemic scar in the remaining patients with nonculprit coronary stenoses. For those with nonobstructive coronary artery disease, CMR identified a potential structural mechanism for arrhythmia in 42%, including dilated cardiomyopathy, acute myocarditis, mitral valve prolapse with associated LGE, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy. Over a mean follow-up of 36 months, the presence of acute myocardial edema at CMR was associated with a benign arrhythmia course. Others have similarly found incremental diagnostic utility for CMR in this population, including reassignment to a new or alternate diagnosis in 25%–76% of patients when compared to standard transthoracic echocardiography. , , Prognostically, both the presence and extent of LGE by CMR have been associated with incident arrhythmia and mortality in survivors of OHCA. For example, Neilan and colleagues found a 7-fold increased risk of ICD therapy or death in those with LGE, even after adjusting for LVEF and other clinical sudden death risk factors. An LGE burden of >8.1% of the myocardium was a particularly high-risk subgroup with a 78% incidence of ICD therapy or death. These data raise the intriguing role of CMR imaging in secondary prevention patients, as a means to delineate etiology of ventricular arrhythmia and to additionally adjudicate the potential “reversibility” of underlying mechanism and prognosticate the risk of incident arrhythmia. For patients with apparently unexplained cardiac arrest including no evidence of coronary artery disease, normal echocardiogram, and normal electrocardiogram, a systematic diagnostic protocol including CMR, signal-averaged electrocardiogram, exercise testing, provocative drug challenge (procainamide for Brugada syndrome, adrenaline or epinephrine for long QT syndrome), and selective genetic and electrophysiological testing can be valuable ( ). Invasive electrophysiology testing can include programmed stimulation, voltage-based phenotyping, and voltage-guided endomyocardial biopsy. Employing such a systematic protocol in the Cardiac Arrest Survivors with Preserved Ejection Fraction Registry (CASPER), Krahn and colleagues identified an etiology of cardiac arrest in 56% of patients, which additionally led to clinically relevant diagnoses in 24% of screened family members. Of those with a delineated etiology, the majority (69%) were reflective of an underlying electrical syndrome (eg, long QT syndrome, catecholaminergic polymorphic VT, Brugada syndrome) and the remainder an underlying structural disease (eg, arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, myocarditis). In this cohort of unexplained cardiac arrest with a preserved ejection fraction, a history of syncope and a family history of sudden death were independently predictive of the presence of a pathogenic genetic variant. While the role of invasive electrophysiology phenotyping in the CASPER protocol was left to the discretion of investigators, in the future, the potential utility of detailed electrical phenotyping—particularly in the era of high-density mapping —may offer important insights into novel electrical phenotypes and further guide risk stratification. Options for defibrillator therapy include transvenous (TV-ICD) and subcutaneous (S-ICD) ICDs. S-ICDs have been associated with lower rates of device and lead complications as compared to transvenous defibrillators, although they do not have the capacity for antitachycardia pacing (ATP), cardiac resynchronization therapy, or antibradycardia pacing. In a contemporary analysis of S-ICD implantation in secondary prevention patients, Boersma and colleagues identified a 16% incidence of appropriate therapies for VT/VF and a 12.3% incidence of inappropriate therapies over 3-year follow-up. First-shock conversion rate in the cohort was 90% and similar to conversion rates in TV-ICDs. In this context, an S-ICD is a reasonable alternative to TV-ICD in secondary prevention patients without an indication for cardiac resynchronization, antibradycardia pacing, or a documented history of ATP-terminable monomorphic VT. An S-ICD may also be favored in patients whose presenting arrhythmia is VF to the extent that future arrhythmias are less likely to be ATP-terminable, although post hoc analysis of AVID did identify a 30% incidence of VT in those with an index VF arrest. For those undergoing TV-ICD implantation, consideration of ICD programming is paramount. Post hoc analysis of the Avoid Delivering Therapies for Non-sustained Arrhythmias in ICD Patients III (ADVANCE III) trial demonstrated that for secondary prevention patients a long detection setting (30 of 40 intervals for ventricular arrhythmia with cycle length ≤320 ms) was associated with a 25% reduction in overall ICD therapies and a 34% reduction in number of shocks compared to nominal settings (18 of 24 intervals). Similar reductions in rates of treated VF episodes were observed in secondary prevention ICD recipients in the PainFree SST study randomized to longer detection intervals (30 of 40) for ventricular arrhythmias with cycle length ≤320 ms. In the PainFree SST analysis, there was no accompanying increase in the incidence of syncope in the longer detection interval arm; and taken together, these studies generally support the use of extended detection intervals for fast ventricular arrhythmias in patients undergoing a secondary prevention ICD. Ultimately, a tailored approach for ICD programming is warranted, integrating physiological/hemodynamic reserve and observed hemodynamic compromise with slower sustained VT. Interventions to reduce arrhythmic risk in secondary prevention The incidence of ICD therapies in secondary prevention patients has declined over the past 30 years, , likely owing to a combination of improved revascularization techniques, idealized pharmacotherapy for heart failure, and liberalized ICD programming. Nevertheless, rates of appropriate ICD therapy remain high even in contemporary cohorts employing long-detection programming (3-year rates of 8%–47%). , , These substantial rates of ICD therapies have significant clinical implications as they have been associated with both an increased mortality and significant reductions in quality of life. , Thus, there has been long-standing interest and need for strategies to reduce incident ventricular arrhythmia that complement the therapeutic role of ICD implantation. Pharmacotherapy Pharmacologic strategies for arrhythmia suppression include use of β-blockers and antiarrhythmic drugs. In the Optimal Pharmacological Therapy in Cardioverter Defibrillator Patients (OPTIC) study, which included 412 patients undergoing secondary prevention ICD (mean LVEF 34%, history of MI in 80%), investigators observed a 40% incidence of appropriate ICD therapy at 1-year in those randomized to β-blocker therapy as compared to 24% in those randomized to sotalol and 10% in those randomized to amiodarone. Of note, rates of study drug discontinuation over 1 year owing to side effects was 5% for β-blockers, 18% for amiodarone, and 24% for sotalol. Recent meta-analysis of randomized trials evaluating the efficacy of antiarrhythmic drug therapy for patients with ICDs and a history of ventricular arrhythmia identified an approximate 70% relative risk reduction in VT recurrence and ICD therapies with amiodarone as compared to standard cardiomyopathy pharmacotherapy including β-blockade. Comparatively, there was no significant risk reduction in either VT recurrence or ICD therapies in meta-analyzed trials of sotalol compared to standard cardiomyopathy pharmacotherapy. Taken together, these data would generally support the use of amiodarone therapy to reduce recurrent VT/VF in the secondary prevention population, at the expense of drug-related side effects in a significant minority.
