Randomisation Participants will be randomised (1:1) to receive either NAS-TNK or standard treatment by a central randomisation system. An adaptive permuted block design with variable block sizes (4/6/8) will be implemented without stratification parameters. Investigators will retrieve computer-generated randomisation sequences through a password-protected portal to establish treatment assignments, ensuring allocation concealment through secured digital infrastructure. Following randomised allocation, protocol-defined interventions will be administered to the patient at the earliest protocol-permitted timepoint. Intervention Qualified participants will be randomly allocated to either of the two groups Standard medical treatment group Standard medical treatment for this group of patients will be provided according to the optimal care standards defined by the Clinical Standardization Guidelines (CSG) for ICH management ( ). NAS-TNK group Participants randomised to the NAS-TNK group will receive the intervention as close to the time of randomisation as possible, and they should aim to arrive in the operating room within 8 hours of randomisation. The implementation of NAS-TNK will follow the study surgical manual ( ). All cases randomised to the NAS-TNK group will have their surgical trajectory planning documented through video recordings or photographs. The lead neurosurgeon will review the first two surgical cases from each centre to objectively assess compliance with the surgical protocol. After surgery, patient care will follow the CSG for management, as detailed in the . Primary outcome The primary efficacy outcome is the proportion of patients achieving a favourable functional outcome, defined as an mRS Score of 0–3 at 180 days. Secondary outcomes Secondary outcomes include the following events: (1) The change of the National Institute of Health stroke scale (NIHSS) Score at 5–7 days or discharge if earlier from baseline. (2) Proportion of patients with adjudicated mRS of 0–3 (good functional status) at 90 days. (3) Ordinal graded mRS (0–6) at 90 days post stroke. (4) Dichotomised Extended Glasgow Outcome Scale (EGOS) Score at 180 days: 4–8 (good) vs 1–3 (poor). (5) All-cause death at 180 days. (6) Dichotomised graded mRS at 180 days post haemorrhage: 0–2 vs 3–6. (7) Ordinal graded mRS (0–6) at 180 days post stroke. (8) Barthel Index and EGOS assessment at 180 days. Safety outcomes The primary safety outcome is the all-cause death at 30 days. Secondary safety outcomes include the following events: (1) all-cause death at 7 days, (2) symptomatic rebleeding events within 6 days post randomisation (defined as a persistent decrease in Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) motor score by more than two points, with a CT scan showing a new haematoma with a CT value greater than 72 Hounsfield Units (HU) and a volume exceeding 5 mL within the haematoma cavity and surrounding area compared with the prior scan), (3) 30-day intracranial bacterial infection, (4) total serious adverse events (SAEs) within 30 and 180 days and (5) total adverse events (AEs) within 30 and 180 days. Rationale for blinded adjudication of outcome Given the involvement of surgical intervention in this study, conducting blinded outcome assessments is not feasible. To reduce bias affecting the primary outcome, a dedicated and blinded adjudication method for the mRS will be established. The NAS-TNK team enlisted skilled neurologists and neurosurgeons, all kept unaware of treatment assignments, to evaluate audio tapes of participants’ mRS assessments. After evaluation, the physicians input their assessments into the electronic data capture system. Discrepancies in mRS scores between the clinical centres and the assessing physicians are resolved through case discussions, with the final decision rendered by the blinded physician. Data safety and monitoring board (DSMB) An independent DSMB will implement protocol-defined reviews with real-time surveillance systems to maintain ethical oversight and participant protection throughout the trial

After evaluation, the physicians input their assessments into the electronic data capture system. Discrepancies in mRS scores between the clinical centres and the assessing physicians are resolved through case discussions, with the final decision rendered by the blinded physician. Data safety and monitoring board (DSMB) An independent DSMB will implement protocol-defined reviews with real-time surveillance systems to maintain ethical oversight and participant protection throughout the trial duration. DSMB members are independent and do not participate in the trial. Their roles and responsibilities are established by the trial’s executive committee before the trial commences. After each meeting, the DSMB shall electronically disseminate consensus-driven advisories to principal investigators holding steering committee oversight authority. Sample size The determination of sample size relies on the occurrence rate of the primary endpoint (180-day mRS score≤3) and the estimated effect size. We used the following assumptions: (1) a two-sided significance level of 0.05; (2) a statistical power of 80%; (3) based on data from the MISTIE III trial, the proportion of patients in the conservative group with an mRS score ≤3 at 180 days is approximately 38.3% and 48.8% in the NAS-TNK group, an improvement of 10.5% in absolute terms (27.4% in relative terms); and (4) a dropout rate of 5%. Under these conditions, each group requires 366 patients, resulting in a total of 732 patients. Follow-up In the follow-up plan for the clinical study, participants will be monitored to evaluate treatment efficacy, patient outcomes and any AEs. For the blinded outcome assessment, all mRS interviews will be face to face (telephone follow-ups will be made when face to face visits are not feasible) and conducted by trained neurologists who were unaware of treatment allocation. For the consistency of the blind outcome assessment, the Principal Investigator (PI) team will train the assessors to conduct the mRS interview. Only if qualified to get through the relevant tests, will an assessor be given a certificate. These assessments will be performed at all predefined follow-up timepoints at day 30 (±7 days), day 90 (±7 days) and day 180 (±14 days) after randomisation. The video or audio recordings will be used for quality control to minimise potential bias. Data will be collected during these visits through clinical assessments. To ensure adherence to the follow-up schedule, reminders will be provided, and procedures are in place to address missed visits. Ethical considerations, including informed consent and participant rights, are prioritised throughout the study. Patients will continue to be followed at least 1 year in a separate follow-up study. Statistical analyses The main analyses of the trial will follow the intention-to-treat (ITT) principle, with supplementary analyses conducted on the per-protocol (PP) group. The ITT population includes all participants who were randomised. Participants will be removed at their final follow-up assessment if they experience a clinical event, at the study’s conclusion or on withdrawal from the study. The PP population is a subset of the ITT population, excluding subjects who have significant protocol deviations. The specific criteria for protocol deviations will be outlined in the statistical analysis plan. The primary endpoint will be examined using a modified Poisson regression model. In the modified Poisson model, the treatment group will be included as the key study factor to estimate the risk ratio (RR) comparing the intervention and control arms for the primary outcome, accompanied by a 95% CI. An analysis adjusted for covariates regarding the primary endpoint will additionally be carried out using a modified Poisson model. In this model, the treatment group will serve as the main study variable, evaluated across subgroups defined by the following covariates: prerandomisation clot volume, age, clot removal, baseline severity of impairment as measured by GCS, ICH location (halamus or basal ganglia; ICH, intraventricular haemorrhage (IVH) or ICH+IVH), and time to treatment. Adjusted RR together with their 95% CI will be derived from the covariate adjusted modified Poisson model. Subgroup analysis will also be performed across the subgroups of the following prespecified covariates using unadjusted (crude) models: prerandomisation clot volume (< or ≥median), age (< or ≥median), clot removal (≤ 15 mL vs medical, >15 mL vs medical), baseline severity of impairment (GCS Score<5–12 or ≥13), ICH location (thalamus or basal ganglia; ICH, IVH or ICH+IVH) and time to treatment (≤24 hours or >24 hours). Secondary dichotomous endpoints will mirror the analytical framework established for the primary endpoint. Time-to-event analyses will employ Kaplan-Meier methodology with treatment-stratified survival estimates, followed by non-parametric groupwise comparisons via log-rank testing. Unadjusted Cox proportional hazards regression models will be used to derive HRs and associated 95% CIs. Ordinal data such as mRS (0–6) at 180 days will be analysed using

Secondary dichotomous endpoints will mirror the analytical framework established for the primary endpoint. Time-to-event analyses will employ Kaplan-Meier methodology with treatment-stratified survival estimates, followed by non-parametric groupwise comparisons via log-rank testing. Unadjusted Cox proportional hazards regression models will be used to derive HRs and associated 95% CIs. Ordinal data such as mRS (0–6) at 180 days will be analysed using generalised OR. Continuous secondary outcomes will be analysed using generalised linear model or win ratio method depending on their distributions. For continuous variables, summaries will include the count of observations, average value with SD and median accompanied by the IQR. In contrast, categorical variables will be described by reporting both the frequency and proportion of occurrences. When comparing groups, hypothesis testing will be performed using a two-tailed significance level set at 0.05 (α=0.05). A comprehensive description of all analyses will be provided in the statistical analysis plan, which is scheduled to be completed before the database is locked and the study is unblinded. Study organisation The trial steering committee offers oversight and strategic guidance. Outcomes, SAEs and brain imaging evaluations are conducted by trained assessors who are blinded to the treatment assignments. Discussion NAS-TNK aims to clarify the effects and safety of the NAS-TNK haematoma dissolution in reducing the disability and mortality rates among patients with acute spontaneous deep cerebral haemorrhage. The study seeks to explore a simple, standardised and stable minimally invasive surgical technique, which holds significant potential for reducing mortality and disability associated with strokes. Current research on ICH indicates that MIPS has been proven to reduce mortality rates in certain patients with ICH. Most studies demonstrate that this technique significantly enhances patient survival rates. However, there remains uncertainty regarding its efficacy in improving neurological functional outcomes and there is a lack of consensus in conclusions across different studies. Some studies suggest that MIPS effectiveness is inferior to optimal medical treatment, and there are discrepancies in conclusions across different studies. Building on this foundation, ongoing research aims to further explore and refine MIPS by incorporating neuronavigation technology and TNK. The objective is to minimise surgical trauma and rapidly reduce haematoma volume, thereby optimising the therapeutic outcomes of minimally invasive treatments. Strengths This study is designed as a multicentre RCT with a large sample size aimed at evaluating the safety and efficacy of neuro-navigation-assisted stereotactic puncture combined with the third-generation thrombolytic agent TNK for the treatment of ICH. The exploration of this RCT will provide important references for clinical treatment protocols. This research is expected to effectively fill a significant evidence gap in the field of minimally invasive treatment for deep ICH and to provide high-level evidence for the updating of clinical practice guidelines. Limitations Our study has three limitations. First, the use of the ABC/2 method via CT scan for measuring haemorrhage volume is fairly basic. Nowadays, more precise imaging techniques or measurements could be used. However, the ABC/2 method is the most basic practical and widely used method for volume calculation of intracerebral haematoma. It has been used in the well-known clinical trials, such as the MISTIE series and ENRICH trial. We acknowledge that more advanced techniques (eg, Artificial Intelligence-assisted segmentation) would provide superior accuracy. However, the RCT study will be conducted in multicentres, the Artificial Intelligence (AI) -assisted more precise imaging techniques or measurements might not be popularised and proficient in use. We will collect all baseline CT scans from enrolled patients and perform centralised AI-based volumetric analysis to quantify potential discrepancies between ABC/2 and AI-calculated volumes and evaluate whether measurement differences significantly impact treatment outcomes. Second, we did not choose outcomes at 1 year because at 1-year follow-up after a surgical intervention, many bias factors such as patients’ variable rehabilitation practices, socioeconomic factors, etc might disproportionately influence longer-term outcomes. We will continue to follow up patients for at least 1 year in a separate follow-up study. Finally, we did not enrol the patients with 50–80 mL because patients with that haemorrhage volume will prefer endoscopic or craniotomic surgeries for rapid haematoma evacuation. This part of the patients would be studied in the future RCT study. Conclusions The NAS-TNK study will provide reliable evidence, offering high-quality clinical proof for MIS for ICH, to evaluate whether NAS-TNK is superior to the current standard treatment in managing patients with deep ICHs of 20–50 mL. documents.title: Guidelines for the management of aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage

chunks.content: Introduction SAH is a life-threatening condition in the central nervous system (CNS), characterized by bleeding in the subarachnoid space, often leading to severe neurological dysfunction and high mortality rates . The pathogenesis of SAH is complex and not yet fully understood, posing significant challenges to its treatment . The pathophysiology of SAH is closely associated with neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier disruption, and neuronal injury, which together trigger a series of cellular and molecular events, resulting in brain damage and functional impairment . Although considerable research has unveiled potential mechanisms of SAH, there is still a lack of in-depth understanding regarding the roles of different cell types in disease progression . During the course of SAH, immune cell infiltration and dysfunction are considered key factors exacerbating brain injury and inflammation . Microglia and astrocytes play important roles in the CNS immune response, particularly in modulating neuroinflammation and responding to tissue damage . However, the functional changes and interactions of these cells in SAH remain insufficiently explored . Traditional histological techniques, while useful for assessing tissue damage, have limitations in identifying the cellular heterogeneity involved in SAH pathology. As a result, our understanding of the cellular composition and microenvironment in SAH remains incomplete . Advances in bioinformatics provide powerful tools to analyze large-scale gene expression data and understand complex biological processes. By integrating transcriptomic data with immune cell infiltration analysis, we can gain a deeper understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying SAH and identify potential key genes as therapeutic targets , . Previous studies have indicated that inflammation, oxidative stress, and cell death play crucial roles in the development of SAH, processes that are often closely associated with changes in specific cell types and immune responses . The goal of this study is to explore the molecular mechanisms of SAH, with a focus on immune cell infiltration and its role in disease progression. We aim to identify key genes and signaling pathways associated with SAH and investigate potential therapeutic strategies. Specifically, we will examine Isorhynchophylline (IRN) as a potential treatment for SAH and analyze its effects on relevant targets and signaling pathways. Through a comprehensive understanding of the pathological features of SAH, this study aims to provide valuable insights into future clinical interventions and treatment strategies. Materials and methods Microarray data source and limma differential analysis We retrieved the GSE36791 dataset from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database . This dataset includes 43 samples from patients with SAH and 18 control samples, all sourced from human peripheral blood. The sequencing of this dataset was carried out on the GPL10558 platform. To identify genes with differential expression, we applied the “Limma” method, which is based on a generalized linear model . The analysis was conducted using the R software package “limma” (version 3.40.7). Initially, we loaded the gene expression data and performed multiple linear regression using the lmFit function. Next, we utilized the eBayes function to apply empirical Bayes moderation to the standard errors, which allowed us to obtain the adjusted t-statistics, F-statistics, and the log odds of differential expression for each gene. In the final step, we identified the genes with statistically significant differential expression. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) We applied the WGCNA method to explore the relationships between genes . Initially, we calculated the median absolute deviation (MAD) for each gene and removed the 50% of genes with the lowest MAD values. Next, we filtered the differentially expressed genes (DEGs) expression matrix using the sample genes function, excluding poor-quality genes and samples, and constructed a scale-free co-expression network. We then determined an optimal “soft” threshold power (β) to calculate the adjacency relationships between genes, derived from their co-expression similarity. In the following step, the adjacency relationships were converted into a topological overlap matrix to evaluate gene co-expression and differences, which provided a more accurate representation of the gene network. Using hierarchical clustering and dynamic tree cutting functions, we detected co-expression modules. The genes with similar expression patterns were grouped into multiple modules using average linkage hierarchical clustering. Finally, we calculated the dissimilarity of module feature genes, selected the appropriate cut-off for the module tree, and merged related modules for further analysis. Each module represented genes with similar expression patterns. To identify key genes potentially involved in the pathology of SAH, we used the VennDiagram tool to find overlaps between core module genes and DEGs. Through these steps, we successfully built a gene co-expression network and identified gene modules that may play crucial roles in SAH. Collection of subarachnoid hemorrhage disease dataset To investigate potential disease targets and their roles, we performed a search using the keyword “Subarachnoid Hemorrhage” in the GeneCards database ( https://www.genecards.org/ ) to identify relevant disease-associated protein targets . The results from these searches were combined and duplicates were removed, resulting in a curated gene set for

Collection of subarachnoid hemorrhage disease dataset To investigate potential disease targets and their roles, we performed a search using the keyword “Subarachnoid Hemorrhage” in the GeneCards database ( https://www.genecards.org/ ) to identify relevant disease-associated protein targets . The results from these searches were combined and duplicates were removed, resulting in a curated gene set for SAH. Protein–protein interaction(PPI)network analysis The STRING database ( https://cn.string-db.org/ ) is a tool used to analyze protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks and their functional relationships – . We uploaded the intersecting genes from the WGCNA core modules, DEGs, and GeneCards-related genes into the STRING database. Genes with a calculated interaction score higher than 0.4 were considered significant. The resulting PPI network was visualized with Cytoscape software (version 3.9.0) ( www.cytoscape.org/ ) . To assess the importance of the genes within the network, we used CytoHubba to evaluate the topological properties and centrality indices of the nodes. In this study, we employed the Degree centrality algorithm, which measures the number of direct connections (edges) a gene has in the network. Genes with higher degrees are considered to play more significant roles in the network. We also used the Betweenness Centrality metric, which evaluates how often a gene acts as a bridge or connector between other genes within the network, and Closeness Centrality, which reflects how close a gene is to all other genes in the network in terms of shortest paths. These three centrality measures (Degree, Betweenness, and Closeness) were calculated to rank the genes based on their importance in the PPI network.We considered genes with higher scores across these centrality metrics to be the most crucial in the network, as they are likely to be involved in key biological processes. The most critical genes were highlighted in red, representing their prominent roles within the network. Based on this analysis, we identified the top four genes, marked in red, as the hub genes for SAH. Functional enrichment analysis To explore the biological roles of the identified genes, we performed functional enrichment analyses using Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathways. The GO analysis covered three main categories: biological processes (BP), cellular components (CC), and molecular functions (MF) . In parallel, KEGG analysis was conducted to identify the signaling pathways relevant to SAH . Functional enrichment was carried out using the R package ClusterProfiler, and the significantly enriched GO terms and KEGG pathways were identified based on an adjusted P -value (FDR < 0.05). Identification of immune-infiltrating cells in disease The immune microenvironment consists of various cell types, including immune cells, inflammatory cells, fibroblasts, along with numerous cytokines and chemokines. Analyzing immune cell infiltration is essential for assessing disease progression and predicting the patient’s response to therapy. To investigate this, we used the CIBERSORT method, which applies linear support vector regression to deconvolve gene expression data. By analyzing RNA sequencing data, we estimated the immune cell proportions in the samples and conducted immune cell infiltration analysis using the CIBERSORT (version 0.1.0) tool , . Single sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) The identified hub genes were analyzed using ssGSEA to explore the key signaling pathways associated with their regulation. We obtained GSEA software (version 3.0) from the official website ( http://software.broadinstitute.org/gsea/index.jsp ) and categorized the samples into two groups based on the expression levels of the selected hub genes: high-expression (≥ 50%) and low-expression (< 50%). We performed the analysis using gene sets from the Molecular Signatures Database ( http://www.gsea-msigdb.org/gsea/downloads.jsp ), specifically focusing on the c2.cp.kegg.v7.4.symbols.gmt subset. The analysis was conducted to identify relevant pathways and molecular mechanisms linked to gene expression patterns and phenotypic groupings. A minimum gene set size of 5 and a maximum of 5000 genes were applied, with 1000 permutations. Pathways with a P -value < 0.05 and a false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.25 were considered statistically significant . ROC curve analysis of hub genes To ensure the accuracy of each candidate hub gene, we performed evaluation using Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves. The “pROC” package was employed for ROC curve analysis , a widely used method for assessing the performance of classification models, especially in terms of accuracy and sensitivity. The ROC curve plots the relationship between the true positive rate (TPR) and false positive rate (FPR), which helps determine the model’s effectiveness at various threshold values. In our study, ROC analysis was used to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of each candidate hub gene for the disease. gene, we performed evaluation using Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves. The “pROC” package was employed for ROC curve analysis , a widely used method for assessing the performance of classification models, especially in terms of accuracy and sensitivity. The ROC curve plots the relationship between the true positive rate (TPR) and false positive rate (FPR), which helps determine the model’s effectiveness at various threshold values. In our study, ROC analysis was used to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of each candidate hub gene for the disease. The “pROC” package was chosen because it offers comprehensive tools to compute the area under the curve (AUC), which is a key metric for classifier performance. A higher AUC value indicates a better-performing classifier. In our research, genes with an AUC greater than 0.70 were considered to potentially have diagnostic value for the disease. This threshold was selected based on prior research and experimental experience, though it may vary depending on the specific disease and research context. By identifying genes with a higher AUC, we were able to highlight their diagnostic significance and provide a solid foundation for further investigation. Hub genes expression and protein localization analysis To investigate the expression of hubs genes across various cell types, we utilized R language packages to create UMAP plots, showcasing the expression profiles of specific genes. The identified key genes were cross-referenced with the Human Protein Atlas (THPA) ( https://www.proteinatlas.org/ ), which provides information on the expression of these proteins in brain-related cells and immune cells. This step helped validate our gene expression findings by matching them against a comprehensive database that compiles the expression of common human proteins across various tissues, cell lines, and immune cell types , . To better interpret the gene expression data, we employed Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP), a dimensionality reduction technique . UMAP plots for subcellular localization were generated using a large collection of confocal microscopy images, which visually represent the spatial distribution of human proteins within cells. This method, integrated into THPA, offers a novel approach to visualize and analyze high-dimensional protein localization data at the subcellular level. To explore the potential cellular functions and localization of the hub genes, we examined subcellular 3D images and confocal microscopy data to pinpoint their precise locations and propose possible mechanisms of action. Drug prediction In this study, we employed bioinformatics techniques to predict potential therapeutic drugs targeting 11 key genes. Initially, we screened existing drugs from public databases such as DrugBank, PubChem, and CTD based on the functions and relevance of these genes. Our focus was primarily on drugs associated with SAH, and we ultimately identified IRN as a promising candidate. To further evaluate its potential, we applied molecular docking techniques to assess the binding affinity between IRN and the target genes. Small molecule agents screening and molecular docking analysis The Connectivity Map (CMap) database ( https://clue.io/ ) is a tool used to investigate the relationships between genes, small molecule drugs, and diseases, facilitating drug discovery by analyzing differential gene expression. To conduct molecular docking, we first retrieve the 3D structure of the target molecule in mol2 format from the PubChem database. Using AutodockTools 1.5.6, we prepare the ligand by adding hydrogen atoms, calculating charge distributions, identifying the root and rotatable bonds, and saving the ligand as a pdbqt file. The 3D structure of the target protein is sourced from the RCSB Protein Data Bank ( www.rcsb.org/ ), and is processed by adding Gasteiger charges, including nonpolar hydrogens, defining it as a receptor, and saving it in pdbqt format. For docking using Autodock Vina, parameters like exhaustiveness are set to 15, with defined box size and coordinates, while other settings are left unchanged. The docking is performed using semi-flexible docking, and the conformation exhibiting the highest binding affinity is chosen as the final docked result . Experimental validation by WB analysis To validate the expression of the core genes identified through bioinformatics analysis, we conducted Western blot experiments using BV2 microglial cells (SaiBeikang Biotechnology Co., Ltd., China). BV2 cells were cultured in DMEM supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Gibco, USA) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin at 37 °C in a humidified incubator containing 5% CO₂. For the inflammatory model, BV2 cells were stimulated with 100 ng/mL lipopolysaccharide (LPS; Sigma-Aldrich, USA) for 24 h. After LPS treatment, cells in the treatment group were exposed to 50 µM of IRN (MedChemExpress, USA) for another 24 h.Cells were then lysed in RIPA buffer containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors (Beyotime, China). The total protein concentration was measured using a BCA assay kit (Thermo Scientific, USA). Equal amounts of protein (30 µg) were separated on 10% SDS-PAGE gels and transferred onto PVDF membranes (Millipore, USA). After LPS treatment, cells in the treatment group were exposed to 50 µM of IRN (MedChemExpress, USA) for another 24 h.Cells were then lysed in RIPA buffer containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors (Beyotime, China). The total protein concentration was measured using a BCA assay kit (Thermo Scientific, USA). Equal amounts of protein (30 µg) were separated on 10% SDS-PAGE gels and transferred onto PVDF membranes (Millipore, USA). Membranes were blocked with 5% non-fat milk for 1 h at room temperature and incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies against CCL20 (1:1000, Abcam, UK), IL6 (1:1000, Cell Signaling Technology, USA), TLR4 (1:1500, Abcam, UK), and MMP9 (1:1000, Proteintech, China). After washing, membranes were incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies (1:5000, CST, USA) for 1 h at room temperature.Protein bands were visualized using enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) detection reagents (Thermo Scientific, USA), and images were captured using a chemiluminescence imaging system (Bio-Rad, USA). Band intensities were quantified with ImageJ software (NIH, USA).All experiments were repeated three times independently. Results Identification of differentially expressed genes We began by acquiring the dataset and proceeded to identify DEGs through the Limma rapid differential analysis method. This process revealed 372 DEGs, with 193 genes showing a down-regulation expression and 179 genes displaying up-regulation. To facilitate the visualization and interpretation of these gene expression patterns, we generated volcano plots and heatmaps. These graphical representations of the DEGs in SAH, shown in (Fig. A,B, and Supplement Table S1), highlight the distinct expression profiles and statistical significance of the differences. These findings provide a strong foundation and clear direction for our subsequent investigations. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis and key module identification For the weighted gene co-expression network analysis, we first determined the appropriate parameter settings, selecting a β-value of 10 as the “soft” threshold, based on the scale-free R² of 0.86 and average connectivity measures (Fig. A,B). The gene clustering dendrograms for both the normal and SAH groups are shown in Fig. C. From this, we identified 14 distinct gene co-expression modules (GCMs), each represented by a unique color (Fig. D). To identify the module most strongly correlated with SAH, we assessed the correlation between each gene co-expression module and the disease status (Fig. E). The green module showed the strongest correlation with SAH, with a correlation coefficient of 0.59 and a P -value of less than 0.01. As a result, this module, containing 1833 hub genes, was selected for further investigation (Supplement Table S2). Next, we analyzed the relationships between genes within the green module and SAH. Our analysis revealed a significant positive correlation between the module’s gene members and their individual gene significance, with an r-value of 0.73 and a P -value of less than 0.01 (Fig. F). This suggests that the green module is closely associated with SAH and warrants further exploration. Screening of subarachnoid hemorrhage hub genes To uncover the hub genes associated with SAH, we constructed a protein-protein interaction (PPI) network by integrating the hub genes identified from the WGCNA analysis with those retrieved from the GeneCards disease database (Supplement Table S3) and the DEGs. This resulted in 18 intersecting genes (Fig. A). We then visualized the PPI network using the STRING database (v11.5) and Cytoscape software, which showed interactions among 11 genes (Fig. B). These 11 genes were selected as potential key genes for SAH. To further assess the importance of these genes within the network, we utilized CytoHubba to evaluate their topological features and centrality. The significance of each node was reflected by the shading, with darker shades indicating higher importance (Fig. C). After further analysis, we identified the top 4 hub genes, which were prioritized for subsequent study. The expression patterns of these genes across different groups are presented in Fig. D. Enrichment analysis We performed functional enrichment analysis on the 11 key genes to uncover their biological roles and pathways in SAH. GO enrichment analysis indicated that these genes were enriched in 325 GO terms (Supplement Table S4), including 235 biological processes (BP), 48 cellular components (CC), and 42 molecular functions (MF). In the category of biological processes, the top 10 significantly enriched terms included -biological adhesion, biological regulation, cellular component organization or biogenesis, cellular process, developmental process, establishment of localization, immune system process, localization, locomotion, metabolic process. For cellular components, significant terms included cell junction, cell part, extracellular matrix, etc. In terms of molecular functions, notable terms were antioxidant activity, binding, catalytic activity among others (Fig. A,B). KEGG pathway analysis revealed that these genes are involved in 114 signaling pathways (Supplement Table S5), with significant enrichment observed in pathways such as TNF signaling pathway, HIF-1 signaling pathway, and IL-17 signaling pathway (Fig. C,D). These pathways are crucial in the development and progression of SAH. Figure E

For cellular components, significant terms included cell junction, cell part, extracellular matrix, etc. In terms of molecular functions, notable terms were antioxidant activity, binding, catalytic activity among others (Fig. A,B). KEGG pathway analysis revealed that these genes are involved in 114 signaling pathways (Supplement Table S5), with significant enrichment observed in pathways such as TNF signaling pathway, HIF-1 signaling pathway, and IL-17 signaling pathway (Fig. C,D). These pathways are crucial in the development and progression of SAH. Figure E presents detailed enrichment results of the key genes in the TNF signaling pathways. The pathways play pivotal roles in the development and progression of SAH. This visualization aids in understanding the specific roles and mechanisms of these genes and pathways in SAH pathology. The enrichment findings offer valuable insights into the molecular mechanisms of SAH and provide direction for future research. Immune infiltration analysis of hub genes in SAH To explore the immune landscape associated with the hub genes in SAH, we applied the CIBERSORT algorithm to assess immune cell infiltration scores. Figure A presents the immune infiltration scores in a stacked bar plot, illustrating the distribution of various immune cell types across SAH and control samples. The analysis revealed that major immune cell types, including NKT cells, monocytes, B cells, Th17 cells, and macrophages, were significantly correlated with the expression of SAH hub genes. Furthermore, Fig. B displays the correlations between different immune cell populations, emphasizing the complex interactions within the immune microenvironment of SAH. Statistical differences in immune cell infiltration between the SAH and control groups were also analyzed and are shown in Fig. C. A ridge plot (Fig. D) further compares the distribution patterns of immune cell types, highlighting significant differences in the expression of immune cells such as CD8 naïve, Tr1, nTreg, Th17, and Tfh between the SAH and normal groups. These findings suggest that these immune cells are markedly infiltrated during the progression of SAH, contributing to the disease pathogenesis. ssGSEA and ROC analysis of SAH hub genes and their diagnostic potential To gain insight into the biological pathways associated with the SAH hub genes, ssGSEA on the four key hub genes identified earlier. The analysis revealed that these genes were significantly enriched in the Apoptosis, Cell Cycle, MAPK signaling, and p53 signaling pathways (Fig. A–D). These findings suggest that these pathways may play a critical role in the pathogenesis of SAH. Additionally, we assessed the diagnostic specificity and sensitivity of each hub gene using Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. We calculated the area under the curve (AUC) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) to evaluate their diagnostic potential. The results showed that CCL20 (AUC = 0.85, CI = 0.75–0.95), IL6 (AUC = 0.70, CI = 0.56–0.84), TLR4 (AUC = 0.79, CI = 0.67–0.91), and MMP9 (AUC = 0.86, CI = 0.75–0.97) all demonstrated high diagnostic value for SAH (Fig. E–H). UMAP analysis reveals distribution patterns of four hub genes in brain tissues and cell subpopulations We utilized UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) to analyze the expression patterns of the four hub genes in various brain tissues and cell subpopulations. The results revealed distinct distribution patterns for each gene across different regions. Specifically, CCL20 showed higher expression levels in the cerebellum and white matter (Fig. A). IL6 was widely distributed across vesicles (Fig. B). TLR4 exhibited a predominant expression in the Golgi apparatus and plasma membrane (Fig. C), while MMP9 was mainly localized to the cytosol (Fig. D). These findings suggest that the four hub genes are differentially expressed in specific brain regions and cellular compartments, which may imply their distinct roles in the pathophysiology of SAH. The differential localization of these genes could contribute to their involvement in various molecular mechanisms, such as inflammation and cell signaling, which are central to the development and progression of SAH. Results of molecular docking and experimental verification by Western blot analysis In this study, molecular docking was utilized to predict the potential of IRN as a therapeutic agent. Initially, bioinformatics analysis identified four key target genes: CCL20, IL6, TLR4 and MMP9. Subsequently, molecular docking simulations were conducted using AutoDock Vina to assess the binding potential of IRN with these target proteins. Figure A illustrates the chemical structure of IRN. Based on the screening outcomes, docking simulations were performed to evaluate the interactions between IRN and the four hub genes (CCL20, IL6, TLR4 and MMP9). Binding energies lower than 0 kJ/mol suggest that spontaneous binding is likely, while values under − 5.0 kJ/mol indicate a stronger binding affinity. Based on the screening outcomes, docking simulations were performed to evaluate the interactions between IRN and the four hub genes (CCL20, IL6, TLR4 and MMP9). Binding energies lower than 0 kJ/mol suggest that spontaneous binding is likely, while values under − 5.0 kJ/mol indicate a stronger binding affinity. The results of the docking simulations revealed favorable binding interactions, with three out of four docking energies falling below − 5 kJ/mol, suggesting a strong affinity between IRN and the target proteins. The docking conformations are visualized in Fig. B–E using PyMOL software. To validate the expression of the core genes CCL20, IL6, TLR4, and MMP9 identified from our bioinformatics analysis, WB analysis demonstrated that LPS stimulation significantly upregulated the expression levels of CCL20, IL6, TLR4, and MMP9 in BV2 microglial cells, compared to the untreated control group ( P < 0.05). Treatment with 50 µM IRN significantly downregulated these proteins’ expression ( P < 0.01). Quantitative densitometric analysis further confirmed the inhibitory effect of IRN on inflammatory gene expression in BV2 cells (Fig. F).These findings validate the bioinformatics predictions and molecular docking results, highlighting the potential of IRN as a therapeutic agent for SAH. Discussion SAH is a life-threatening acute neurological disorder, typically characterized by sudden onset of severe headache, vomiting, and altered consciousness. The disease is associated with high mortality and long-term disability, significantly burdening both patients and society. Epidemiological studies show that the annual incidence of SAH is approximately 6–8 cases per 100,000 people, with 25–50% of patients dying within the first month after onset. Among those who survive, around 50% experience varying degrees of neurological dysfunction . SAH is most commonly caused by the rupture of cerebral aneurysms, although in some cases it may result from cerebrovascular malformations, trauma, or other factors , . Despite advances in early diagnosis and treatment, the prognosis for SAH remains poor, primarily due to acute brain injury, secondary cerebral ischemia, brain edema, and neuroinflammation , . Therefore, a deeper exploration of the molecular mechanisms of SAH, along with the identification of early diagnostic biomarkers and potential therapeutic targets, is of great importance for improving the clinical prognosis of SAH patients . This study systematically investigated the key genes, signaling pathways, and potential therapeutic strategies associated with SAH through bioinformatics analysis, integrating DEGs, immune cell infiltration analysis, and molecular docking simulations. Our approach has revealed the complex biological mechanisms underlying SAH and has proposed new diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. Our ssGSEA results indicate that four key hub genes—CCL20, IL6, TLR4, and MMP9—are predominantly enriched in the apoptosis, cell cycle, MAPK pathway, and p53 signaling pathway. These pathways play crucial roles in cellular responses to damage and stress. In particular, the apoptosis pathway, which regulates programmed cell death, is a key mechanism in brain injury following SAH. Increased apoptotic activity may exacerbate neuronal loss and hinder the repair process after brain injury. The MAPK signaling pathway is widely involved in inflammatory responses, cell proliferation, and stress reactions, and it is activated in SAH, further promoting neuronal damage. The p53 signaling pathway, through its regulation of the cell cycle and apoptosis, may contribute to neuronal death in SAH. Of particular note is the interaction between these pathways. CCL20, IL6, TLR4, and MMP9 are not only involved in separate signaling pathways but also interact with each other to regulate critical cellular processes. For example, TLR4 activation can induce inflammatory responses through the MAPK pathway, while IL6 plays a pivotal role in both inflammation and apoptosis. Additionally, MMP9 is involved in extracellular matrix degradation, which, in conjunction with IL6 and CCL20, could exacerbate blood-brain barrier disruption and neuronal injury in SAH. These genes form a complex regulatory network that modulates the balance between cell survival and death, influencing the overall severity of the brain injury.Understanding how these genes interact within these signaling networks provides valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying SAH and suggests that targeting these pathways could offer novel therapeutic strategies. Modulating the apoptosis and immune response pathways, in particular, may help alleviate neuronal damage and improve outcomes for SAH patients. Through ROC curve analysis, we assessed the diagnostic ability of the four hub genes. The results showed that the AUC values for CCL20, IL6, TLR4, and MMP9 were all above 0.7, with CCL20 reaching an AUC of 0.85, indicating high diagnostic accuracy for SAH. These findings suggest that these genes can serve as reliable biomarkers for the early diagnosis of SAH. Given the challenges in the early diagnosis of SAH, where symptoms overlap with those of other conditions, these biomarkers can assist clinicians in more efficiently identifying high-risk patients. The results showed that the AUC values for CCL20, IL6, TLR4, and MMP9 were all above 0.7, with CCL20 reaching an AUC of 0.85, indicating high diagnostic accuracy for SAH. These findings suggest that these genes can serve as reliable biomarkers for the early diagnosis of SAH. Given the challenges in the early diagnosis of SAH, where symptoms overlap with those of other conditions, these biomarkers can assist clinicians in more efficiently identifying high-risk patients. Due to the strong diagnostic potential of these hub genes, future research should validate their expression levels in clinical samples and further explore their application in assessing disease severity and predicting patient prognosis. Immune cell infiltration plays a critical role in the progression of SAH. Our immune infiltration analysis revealed that immune cells such as NKT cells, monocytes, B cells, Th17 cells, and macrophages were significantly associated with the hub genes in SAH. These immune cells are known to play key roles in the inflammatory response following brain injury, with particular emphasis on the activation of Th17 cells and macrophages, which may be crucial in the immune response during SAH. The increased presence of immune cells suggests an imbalance in the chronic inflammatory response in SAH patients. While immune activation may have protective effects during the early stages of the disease, excessive immune activation can exacerbate neuronal damage and cell death. These findings further underscore the dual-edged role of the immune system in the pathological process of SAH. Future studies should explore strategies to regulate the immune response to enhance neuroprotection and improve patient prognosis. To explore potential therapeutic interventions for SAH, we conducted molecular docking analysis to assess the binding affinity between IRN and the four hub genes. Our docking results showed that three of the hub genes (CCL20, IL6, and MMP9) exhibited binding energies below − 5 kJ/mol, indicating strong binding affinity between these genes and IRN. These findings suggest that IRN may exert its therapeutic effects by binding to these key genes. Further experimental validation is required to confirm IRN’s regulatory effects on the expression of these genes and its therapeutic potential in SAH. So our in vitro WB validation further confirmed that IRN effectively suppresses the LPS-induced overexpression of CCL20, IL6, TLR4, and MMP9 in BV2 microglial cells. These findings suggest that IRN may mitigate neuroinflammation in SAH by modulating these critical inflammatory mediators. This experimental validation supports our molecular docking findings and highlights the translational potential of IRN for SAH treatment. In conclusion, this study systematically identified key genes and signaling pathways associated with SAH, highlighting the critical role of the immune system in disease progression. Among these, CCL20, IL6, TLR4, and MMP9 were identified as not only potential diagnostic biomarkers but also promising therapeutic targets. Through comprehensive molecular docking analysis, we demonstrated a strong binding affinity between IRN and these hub proteins, supporting its potential therapeutic efficacy in SAH. Additionally, WB validation confirmed that IRN significantly downregulates the expression of CCL20, IL6, TLR4, and MMP9 in LPS-induced microglial cells, providing robust experimental evidence for its anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects. Overall, this research not only enhances our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying SAH but also provides important theoretical foundations for the development of new diagnostic tools and therapeutic strategies, paving the way for future advances in the clinical treatment of SAH. chunks.content: 1 Introduction Cardiovascular disease (CVD) represents the leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, accounting for approximately 17.9 million deaths annually and constituting nearly 31 % of all global deaths [ ]. CVD primarily encompasses coronary heart disease, stroke, and other major cardiovascular conditions that collectively contribute to this substantial disease burden [ ]. The global burden of CVD continues to escalate, particularly in developing countries where rapid urbanization and lifestyle transitions have dramatically increased cardiovascular risk factors [ ]. In China, CVD affects approximately 290 million individuals and accounts for more than 43 % of all deaths, imposing substantial economic and social burdens on healthcare systems [ ]. Despite significant advances in primary and secondary prevention strategies, including widespread adoption of statin therapy and evidence-based interventions, many individuals continue to experience cardiovascular events after achieving guideline-recommended treatment targets [ , ]. This persistent residual cardiovascular risk underscores the complexity of CVD pathogenesis and demonstrates the urgent need for enhanced risk assessment tools to better identify high-risk individuals and guide personalized prevention strategies [ , ]. . Traditional cardiovascular risk assessment has relied predominantly on individual risk factors, including low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), blood pressure, and diabetes status [ , , ]. However, this single-parameter approach may inadequately capture the multifaceted nature of cardiovascular risk, particularly the complex interactions between different pathophysiological pathways [ ]. Emerging evidence suggests that integrated biomarker approaches, which simultaneously reflect multiple disease mechanisms, provide superior risk stratification compared to conventional single-biomarker methods [ , , , ]. Among the various biomarkers under investigation, remnant cholesterol (RC) and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) have demonstrated independent associations with cardiovascular outcomes, representing distinct yet interconnected pathways of atherogenic lipid burden and systemic inflammation [ , ]. The recognition that these pathways may interact synergistically in promoting atherosclerotic disease progression has led to the development of composite indices that integrate both parameters [ , ]. The remnant cholesterol inflammatory index (RCII), which combines RC and hs-CRP into a single comprehensive metric, has emerged as a promising tool for integrated cardiovascular risk assessment [ ]. This integrated approach may overcome the limitations of evaluating individual biomarkers in isolation and provide a more holistic assessment of cardiovascular risk profiles [ ]. The RCII represents a recently developed composite biomarker that quantifies the combined burden of atherogenic lipids and systemic inflammation [ ]. While preliminary studies have demonstrated promising associations between RCII and stroke risk, comprehensive evaluation of its relationship with broader CVD outcomes remains largely unexplored. Current evidence is primarily limited to single-endpoint analyses [ ], with most investigations focusing exclusively on cerebrovascular events rather than comprehensive CVD assessment. Furthermore, existing studies have predominantly utilized cross-sectional designs or short-term follow-up periods [ ], leaving critical questions about the long-term predictive value of RCII and the potential clinical benefits of monitoring cumulative exposure over time unanswered. To address these substantial knowledge gaps, we utilized data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) to comprehensively evaluate the association between RCII and CVD in a large, nationally representative cohort of Chinese adults aged 45 years and older. Our investigation aimed to establish whether RCII provides clinically meaningful cardiovascular risk stratification and to assess its potential utility for CVD prediction in clinical practice. 2 Methods 2.1 Study design and participants This study conducted secondary analyses of data from CHARLS, a nationwide prospective cohort study examining the economic, social, and health conditions of Chinese adults aged 45 years and older. The baseline survey was conducted from June 2011 to March 2012, initially enrolling 17,705 individuals. For our analyses, we utilized data from the 2011, 2013, 2015, and 2018 waves to comprehensively evaluate the relationship between RCII and CVD. The CHARLS study was approved by the Biomedical Ethics Review Board of Peking University (IRB00001052-11015), and all participants provided written informed consent prior to participation. We conducted three complementary analyses to provide a comprehensive assessment of the RCII-CVD relationship: (1) a cross-sectional analysis including participants with prevalent CVD to examine the association between RCII and CVD prevalence at baseline; (2) a longitudinal cohort analysis excluding baseline CVD patients to assess the predictive value of baseline RCII for incident CVD risk over 7 years of follow-up (2011–2018); and (3) a cumulative exposure longitudinal analysis to investigate the relationship between long-term RCII exposure and CVD incidence using repeated measurements from 2011 and 2015. For the cross-sectional analysis (1), from the original 17,705 participants, we excluded participants with missing gender data (n = 12), age data or those aged < 45 years (n = 775), missing variables required for RCII calculation (n = 5,718), missing outcome variables (n = 120), cancer patients (n = 111), and those with hs-CRP levels > 10 mg/L (n = 510), resulting in a final sample of 10,459 participants. For the longitudinal cohort analysis

and (3) a cumulative exposure longitudinal analysis to investigate the relationship between long-term RCII exposure and CVD incidence using repeated measurements from 2011 and 2015. For the cross-sectional analysis (1), from the original 17,705 participants, we excluded participants with missing gender data (n = 12), age data or those aged < 45 years (n = 775), missing variables required for RCII calculation (n = 5,718), missing outcome variables (n = 120), cancer patients (n = 111), and those with hs-CRP levels > 10 mg/L (n = 510), resulting in a final sample of 10,459 participants. For the longitudinal cohort analysis (2), from the original 17,705 participants, we excluded those with missing follow-up data (n = 6,079), baseline CVD or missing CVD data (n = 1,751), baseline cancer (n = 102), missing age data or aged < 45 years (n = 389), missing gender data (n = 4), missing variables required for RCII calculation (n = 3,093), and CRP levels > 10 mg/L (n = 261), yielding 6,028 participants for analysis. For the cumulative exposure longitudinal analysis (3), based on the longitudinal cohort, we further excluded participants with missing cumulative RCII calculation variables (n = 2,194), those who developed CVD before or during 2015 (n = 304), and those without follow-up data after 2015 (n = 276), resulting in 3,515 participants for final analysis. 2.2 Assessment of RCII index RCII was calculated by multiplying RC by hs-CRP: RCII = RC (mg/dL) × hs-CRP (mg/L) ÷ 10(21). RC was calculated using the formula: RC = TC − (HDL-C + LDL-C). Due to the markedly skewed distribution of RCII in the population, we performed natural logarithmic transformation for statistical analyses. To handle potential negative or zero values, we first applied a shift transformation when necessary (RCII_shifted = RCII + |minimum value| + 1 if minimum ≤ 0), followed by natural logarithmic transformation (RCII_log = ln(RCII_shifted)), yielding log-transformed RCII for analysis. RCII was also categorized into tertiles for group comparisons and dose–response analyses. For the cumulative exposure longitudinal analysis, the cumulative RCII (CumRCII) was calculated using the formula: CumRCII = [(RCII2011 + RCII2015) ÷ 2] × (2015–––2011). CumRCII was also natural log-transformed using the same approach (CumRCII_log) for statistical analysis. 2.3 Assessment of CVD outcomes The primary outcome of the study was CVD, defined as heart disease or stroke. Consistent with previous studies[ , , ], the definition of CVD was determined by responses to two questions: (1) “Have you been diagnosed with a stroke by your doctor?” (2) “Have you been diagnosed by your doctor with congestive heart failure, coronary heart disease, heart attack, angina pectoris, or other heart problems?” In this study, a confirmed diagnosis of CVD was considered if the answer to either of the two questions was “yes.” The time of CVD occurrence was defined as the difference between the time point of the follow-up and the baseline year of 2011. For participants without reported CVD events, follow-up duration was calculated from baseline assessment to their final survey date. 2.4 Data collection At baseline assessment, trained interviewers administered structured questionnaires to collect comprehensive sociodemographic and health-related data. Demographic variables included age (continuous), gender (male/female), marital status (married/unmarried), residence (urban/rural), and education level (illiteracy, primary school, junior high school, high school or above). Lifestyle factors comprised smoking status (never, former, current) and drinking status (never, former, current). Clinical measurements included systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP), and body mass index (BMI, calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared). Laboratory parameters encompassed TG, LDL-C, HDL-C, TC, fasting blood glucose (FBG), hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), blood urea nitrogen (BUN), serum creatinine, uric acid, and cystatin C. Self-reported physician-diagnosed conditions included hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, liver disease, and kidney disease. Hypertension was defined by systolic blood pressure ≥ 140 mmHg, diastolic blood pressure ≥ 90 mmHg, use of antihypertensive medication, or self-reported physician diagnosis. Diabetes was identified by fasting plasma glucose ≥ 126 mg/dL, glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) ≥ 6.5 %, use of antidiabetic medication, or self-reported physician diagnosis. Missing data were handled using multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE) method. 2.5 Statistical analysis Continuous variables were tested for normality using the Shapiro-Wilk test. Normally distributed continuous variables were reported as means ± standard deviations and compared using analysis of variance (ANOVA), while non-normally distributed variables were presented as medians with interquartile ranges (Q1, Q3) and compared using the Kruskal-Wallis test. Categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages and compared using the chi-square test. For the cross-sectional analysis, the association between RCII and CVD prevalence was quantified using multivariable logistic regression models. For longitudinal analyses, the relationship between RCII and incident CVD was quantified through multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression models RCII was analyzed both as a continuous variable (natural log-transformed) and as categorical tertiles. Three progressive adjustment strategies were

means ± standard deviations and compared using analysis of variance (ANOVA), while non-normally distributed variables were presented as medians with interquartile ranges (Q1, Q3) and compared using the Kruskal-Wallis test. Categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages and compared using the chi-square test. For the cross-sectional analysis, the association between RCII and CVD prevalence was quantified using multivariable logistic regression models. For longitudinal analyses, the relationship between RCII and incident CVD was quantified through multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression models RCII was analyzed both as a continuous variable (natural log-transformed) and as categorical tertiles. Three progressive adjustment strategies were employed across all analyses to control for potential confounding. Model 1 (crude model) included only the exposure variable. Model 2 (minimally adjusted model) incorporated basic demographic factors: for cross-sectional analysis, this included age, gender, and residence; for longitudinal cohort analysis, this included age, gender, and education level. Model 3 (fully adjusted model) additionally included relevant covariates selected using a systematic approach. Covariate selection for Model 3 followed specific criteria: covariates were included if they met any of the following conditions: (1) P-value < 0.05 in univariate analysis, (2) changing the regression coefficient of the exposure variable by > 10 % when added to the basic model, or (3) changing the regression coefficient by > 10 % when removed from the complete model. Specifically, for the cross-sectional analysis, Model 3 adjusted for gender, age, marital status, residence, BMI, smoking status, drinking status, hypertension, diabetes, and liver disease. For the longitudinal cohort analysis, Model 3 adjusted for gender, marital status, education level, hypertension, diabetes, age, BMI, SBP, and cystatin C. For the cumulative exposure longitudinal analysis, Model 3 adjusted for gender, education level, smoking status, drinking status, liver disease, age, BMI, FBG, creatinine, and cystatin C. Restricted cubic spline curves were constructed for the cross-sectional analysis to examine potential non-linear relationships between RCII and CVD risk, adjusting for the same covariates as Model 3. Subgroup analyses were conducted to assess the consistency of associations across different population characteristics, including gender, age groups (≤65 vs > 65 years), BMI categories (≤25 vs > 25 kg/m 2 ), education levels, hypertension status, and diabetes status. Each subgroup analysis also adjusted for the respective covariates identified for Model 3 in each sub-study. All statistical analyses were performed using R software version 4.2.0 and Stata 17.0. Laboratory parameters exhibited notable differences across the tertiles (P < 0.001). After adjusting for potential confounders, we performed stratified analyses based on education level, gender, BMI, age, hypertension, and diabetes. The interaction tests were not statistically significant (all P for interaction > 0.05), suggesting that the association between long-term RCII exposure and CVD risk remained consistent across all demographic and clinical subgroups. 4 Discussion This study provides the first comprehensive evaluation of RCII as a CVD predictor using multiple analytical approaches in a nationally representative Chinese cohort. RCII demonstrated consistent associations with cardiovascular disease across three complementary analyses. In cross-sectional analysis, the highest RCII tertile showed 34 % increased odds of prevalent CVD. Longitudinal analysis established RCII as an independent predictor of incident CVD (26 % increased hazard over 7 years). Cumulative exposure analysis revealed that sustained RCII elevation conferred the strongest cardiovascular risk (32 % increased hazard), supporting the value of long-term biomarker monitoring. Our findings align with recent investigations demonstrating RCII's predictive value for cardiovascular outcomes. Chen et al. established RCII's association with stroke risk (HR: 1.106 per standard deviation increase) in the same CHARLS population [ ]. Our study extends this evidence in two important ways. First, we evaluated composite CVD outcomes (heart disease OR stroke) and performed component-specific analyses across different CVD subtypes, which was not examined in prior stroke-focused research. Second, our component-specific analyses revealed differential predictive value: RCII showed markedly stronger associations with stroke (cross-sectional OR: 2.45; longitudinal HR: 1.49) compared to heart disease (cross-sectional OR: 1.33; longitudinal HR: 1.17, non-significant), demonstrating enhanced specificity for cerebrovascular events. Additionally, our three complementary analytical approaches (cross-sectional, longitudinal, and cumulative exposure) provide more comprehensive evidence than previous single-design studies. The finding that cumulative exposure provides superior risk discrimination adds important evidence supporting temporal integration approaches to composite biomarkers. The robust associations between RCII and cardiovascular disease are biologically plausible and supported by extensive mechanistic evidence. RC represents the cholesterol content of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins and their remnants, including very-low-density lipoproteins (VLDL), intermediate-density lipoproteins (IDL), and chylomicron remnants. Unlike LDL cholesterol, remnant lipoproteins penetrate the arterial wall directly without prior modification, making them particularly atherogenic [ ]. Mendelian randomization studies have provided compelling evidence for the causal role of RC in coronary heart disease, with genetic variants associated with higher RC levels conferring increased cardiovascular risk independent of LDL cholesterol [ ]. Recent systematic reviews and meta -analyses have further demonstrated that elevated RC is associated with increased risks of CVD (RR: 1.53), stroke (RR: 1.43), and cardiovascular mortality (RR: 1.83), independent of traditional risk factors [ ]. Moreover, elevated RC has shown superior predictive accuracy for cardiovascular events compared to LDL-C in high-risk populations [ ]. CRP, the inflammatory component of RCII, serves as a sensitive marker of systemic inflammation and has been extensively validated as an independent predictor of cardiovascular events [ ]. Elevated CRP levels reflect underlying inflammatory processes that directly contribute to atherosclerotic plaque formation, progression, and destabilization [ ]. The CANTOS trial demonstrated that anti-inflammatory therapies targeting interleukin-1β significantly reduce cardiovascular events, providing direct evidence for the causal role of inflammation in cardiovascular disease [ ]. Given the established roles of both components, the biological rationale for combining these parameters stems from their synergistic pathophysiological interaction. Importantly, studies have demonstrated that dual residual risk of cholesterol and inflammation confers significantly higher mortality risk (HR: 1.75) compared to either factor alone, even after standard lipid-lowering therapy [ ]. Mechanistically, remnant lipoproteins activate inflammatory pathways through toll-like receptor signaling [ ], while inflammatory mediators enhance remnant particle atherogenicity through oxidative modification. This bidirectional feedback loop—where RC promotes inflammation and inflammation enhances RC atherogenicity—underscores RCII's value as an integrated assessment of atherogenic lipid burden and vascular inflammation. This investigation demonstrates several methodological innovations that advance cardiovascular risk assessment. Our comprehensive analytical framework employing three complementary approaches—cross-sectional, longitudinal, and cumulative exposure—provides progressive validation across different study designs, creating a complete evidence chain that strengthens confidence in RCII's clinical applicability. toll-like receptor signaling [ ], while inflammatory mediators enhance remnant particle atherogenicity through oxidative modification. This bidirectional feedback loop—where RC promotes inflammation and inflammation enhances RC atherogenicity—underscores RCII's value as an integrated assessment of atherogenic lipid burden and vascular inflammation. This investigation demonstrates several methodological innovations that advance cardiovascular risk assessment. Our comprehensive analytical framework employing three complementary approaches—cross-sectional, longitudinal, and cumulative exposure—provides progressive validation across different study designs, creating a complete evidence chain that strengthens confidence in RCII's clinical applicability. The dose–response analysis using restricted cubic splines revealed a linear association without threshold effects, indicating that even modest RCII elevations contribute to cardiovascular risk. This continuous relationship enables precision risk stratification as a quantitative predictor, with direct therapeutic implications for controlling and reducing RCII levels in CVD prevention. The cumulative exposure assessment represents a particularly significant methodological advancement. The stronger associations observed with cumulative RCII exposure align with the chronic nature of atherosclerotic disease development, building upon established “cholesterol-years” concepts [ ]. The improved statistical significance from longitudinal analysis (P = 0.014) to cumulative exposure assessment (P = 0.003) demonstrates enhanced predictive performance through temporal integration of atherogenic burden. Our findings reveal differential associations with specific cardiovascular endpoints, with consistently stronger effect sizes for stroke compared to heart disease across all analytical approaches. This pattern suggests enhanced sensitivity for cerebrovascular events [ ], potentially explained by RC and inflammatory processes contributing more significantly to stroke risk through small vessel disease and endothelial dysfunction pathways [ ]. Subgroup analyses revealed age-related interactions, with stronger associations in participants ≤ 65 years, suggesting enhanced risk discrimination in younger adults where cardiovascular risk is often underestimated by traditional calculators [ ]. Practical implementation is facilitated by RCII's calculation from routinely available laboratory parameters—standard lipid panels and CRP—enabling immediate clinical application without specialized assays. While this comprehensive investigation provides robust evidence for RCII's clinical implementation potential, several important methodological limitations should be acknowledged when interpreting these findings. First, the observational nature of our study precludes definitive causal inferences about the relationship between RCII and cardiovascular disease, although the biological plausibility and dose–response relationships support a causal interpretation. Second, our study population consisted exclusively of Chinese adults aged 45 years and older, which may limit generalizability to other ethnic groups or younger populations. Third, the cardiovascular disease definition relied on self-reported physician diagnoses rather than standardized clinical criteria or medical record verification, though this approach is consistent with large-scale epidemiological studies and has been validated in similar populations. Fourth, the CHARLS questionnaire assesses heart disease and stroke as composite outcomes without distinguishing specific subtypes (e.g., heart failure vs. myocardial infarction; ischemic vs. hemorrhagic stroke), preventing subtype-specific analyses that could provide insights into differential associations across disease phenotypes. Fifth, our study did not include comparisons with cardiac-specific biomarkers such as troponin or NT-proBNP, as these measurements were not available in the CHARLS database. Sixth, despite comprehensive adjustment for potential confounders, residual confounding from unmeasured variables remains possible. Future research priorities should focus on validation studies in diverse populations to establish broader generalizability across ethnic groups and age ranges. Randomized controlled trials are needed to demonstrate whether RCII-guided therapeutic interventions improve clinical outcomes beyond standard care. Additional investigations should determine optimal RCII-based risk assessment strategies, including measurement intervals and therapeutic thresholds. Cost-effectiveness analyses comparing RCII-based stratification with traditional approaches would inform healthcare policy and guideline development. Mechanistic studies elucidating pathophysiological interactions between RC and inflammatory pathways could identify therapeutic targets within this integrated pathway. Introduction: The Need for Deep Phenotyping in ACS Acute Coronary Syndromes (ACS) remain a time-critical spectrum in which contemporary pathways, despite high-sensitivity troponins, accelerated emergency department (ED) protocols, and ready access to invasive angiography, still leave clinically meaningful uncertainty at the point of care. The objective is no longer limited to confirming myocardial injury but extends to phenotyping the full ACS cascade: defining the plaque substrate, identifying the culprit mechanism, and quantifying the myocardial consequence that determines prognosis and guides secondary prevention [ , , ]. It is essential to acknowledge that invasive coronary angiography remains the undisputed gold standard for the evaluation and treatment of patients presenting with ACS and obstructive coronary artery disease. Emergent catheterisation provides an anatomical diagnosis, which can also be aided by the use of intravascular imaging. Moreover, it provides the opportunity for immediate revascularisation, and its central role in the ACS pathway is firmly established by international guidelines [ , ]. However, angiography does not always reveal significant obstructive lesions, as occurs in approximately 5–15% of ACS presentations (MINOCA). Similarly, when the clinician must decide how best to optimise an intervention, plan a complex procedure, or stratify long-term risk, other invasive and non-invasive imaging modalities become indispensable. The “From Plaque to Perfusion” framework is therefore designed not to replace angiography but to address the clinically important questions that angiography alone cannot answer, such as characterising unstable plaque morphology, quantifying myocardial viability, and refining the prognosis of these patients [ , , ]. This narrative review synthesises high-level evidence from randomized controlled trials and expert consensus documents to establish this clinically pragmatic framework. Rather than viewing imaging modalities in isolation, this approach maps specific technologies to the critical decision points that define the ACS patient journey from emergency department triage and catheterization laboratory intervention to post-event tissue characterisation. Crucially, artificial intelligence (AI) now serves as an essential enabling layer across this continuum. By standardising interpretation and automating complex quantification, AI transforms multimodal imaging outputs into reproducible, actionable metrics that support precision decision-making at scale [ , , , ]. 2. Objectives The primary objective of this narrative review is to introduce and validate the “From Plaque to Perfusion” framework as a clinically pragmatic model for integrating multimodality imaging in the management of acute coronary syndromes. The secondary objectives are: To summarise the current evidence base for each imaging modality within this framework, including CCTA, FFR-CT, PET-CT, OCT, IVUS, and CMR. To evaluate the role of artificial intelligence as an enabling technology that enhances diagnostic precision, automates quantification, and supports scalable decision-making across the ACS continuum. To assess the application of multimodality imaging in the specific clinical scenario of Myocardial Infarction with Non-Obstructive Coronary Arteries (MINOCA). To identify current limitations and future research directions, including ongoing trials. 3. Methodology This narrative review is based on a comprehensive literature search conducted across major medical databases, including PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Embase, and Google Scholar, covering the period from January 2010 to February 2026. The search was conducted on 15 December 2025. Search Strategy: The primary search line combined keywords related to the clinical condition and imaging modalities: (“Acute Coronary Syndrome” OR “Myocardial Infarction” OR “Unstable Angina”) AND (“Coronary Computed Tomography Angiography” OR “CCTA” OR “Optical Coherence Tomography” OR “OCT” OR “Intravascular Ultrasound” OR “IVUS” OR “Cardiac Magnetic Resonance” OR “CMR” OR “Fractional Flow Reserve” OR “FFR-CT” OR “PET-CT”). A secondary search line focused on the role of emerging technologies: (“Artificial Intelligence” OR “Machine Learning” OR “Deep Learning”) AND (“Coronary Imaging” OR “Plaque Characterization” OR “PCI Optimization”). Additional targeted searches were performed for specific trial names (e.g., PLATFORM, ADVANCE, FORECAST, OCTOBER, OCTIVUS, ILUMIEN, PROSPECT, CLIMA, CRISP-CT, ORFAN). Inclusion Criteria: The review included evidence from the following studies: (a) randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing imaging-guided strategies; (b) large prospective natural history and registry studies; (c) systematic reviews and meta-analyses; (d) international expert consensus documents and clinical practice guidelines from the European Society of Cardiology (ESC), the American College of Cardiology (ACC), and affiliated societies; and (e) pivotal studies on AI applications in cardiovascular imaging. Exclusion Criteria: The following were excluded: (a) single case reports and small case series (fewer than 20 patients); (b) articles not published in English; (c) preclinical or animal studies; (d) editorials, letters, and commentaries without original data; and (e) studies focused exclusively on non-coronary cardiac imaging (e.g., valvular or congenital heart disease). Reference lists of included articles were hand-searched to identify additional relevant studies. Given the narrative design, no formal risk-of-bias assessment or pooled statistical analysis was performed. 4. Results 4.1.
