Characteristics of the IE index episode according to collection of follow-up BCs are summarized in . Among the follow-up BCs, in 2 patients (1.3%) the BCs returned a positive result and the patients were deemed to have a recurrent IE episode. The first patient had a prosthetic aortic valve IE due to Streptococcus spp and underwent surgery. Follow-up BCs were obtained 22 days after completion of antibiotic in the absence of fever of clinical suspicion of recurrence within the first month, and were positive for Enterococcus faecalis . The patient was diagnosed with a new definite IE episode. The second patient had a tricuspid valve endocarditis caused by Cutibacterium acnes and also underwent cardiac surgery. Follow-up BCs were drawn 25 days after completion of antibiotic in the presence of fever and were positive for Candida guilliermondii . In both patients, IE was confirmed via transesophageal echocardiography. Both cases fulfilled Duke major criteria for definite IE. There were no cases of true bacteremia unrelated to IE recurrence. On the other hand, in 1 patient (0.7%) cultures were positive but this was later interpreted as a contaminant. This patient had a native-valve aortic endocarditis caused by Enterococcus faecalis , without cardiac surgery. Follow-up BCs were drawn in the absence of fever, and in 1 of 2 sets Cutibacterium acnes was retrieved. The patient received no new antibiotic and subsequent BCs were negative. During the first 12 months of follow-up, 12 recurrences (7.8%) were diagnosed in patients who underwent follow-up BCs, compared to 7 recurrences (9.7%) in those who did not ( P = .789). Although there was a trend toward higher 1-year mortality in patients who did not undergo follow-up BCs (9.7% vs 3.3%, P = .058), only 1 patient in each group died due to IE or its recurrence (1.3% vs 0.7%, P = 1.000). Factors of the Index Endocarditis Episode Associated With Recurrence summarizes characteristics of the index episode according to the presence or absence of recurrence. Patients with subsequent recurrence had more frequent prior IE (21.1% vs 5.3%, P = .035), fungal endocarditis (10.5% vs 1.5%, P = .010), and mycotic aneurism (15.8% vs 1.5%, P = .004). In contrast, patients with recurrence less frequently had Staphylococcus aureus etiology (5.3% vs 23.2%, P = .012), native-valve endocarditis (31.6% vs 54.6%, P = .049), and mitral valve involvement (15.8% vs 44.4%, P = .026). There was no significant association between recurrence and other variables. Importantly, patients who experienced recurrence had a significantly higher 1-year mortality than those who did not (15.8% vs 4.4%, P = .025). DISCUSSION Our main aim was to evaluate the yield of follow-up BCs in the management of patients after an IE episode. Our main findings suggest that, although the presence of recurrence was associated with worse outcomes, the collection of follow-up BCs in afebrile patients had low yield, with only about 1% true positives. Moreover, follow-up BCs did not result in a higher proportion of recurrence diagnoses, nor did it improve the prognosis of patients with recurrence. These findings challenge the current recommendation in the 2023 ESC guidelines, as the benefits do not appear to outweigh the possible risks of unnecessary interventions associated with contaminants. In our cohort, the percentage of recurrence in the first year of follow-up was significant (8.4%). Several recent cohorts have addressed the risk of recurrence after an index episode of IE and found similar risk to our data. It has been estimated that 5%–10% of patients with IE will have a subsequent recurrence, with most recurrences occurring during the first few months [ , ]. Some series also suggest that one-third of recurrences may present without fever [ , , ], implying a theoretical risk of 1%–3% of afebrile recurrence during the first months. The importance of assessing this risk is underscored in our study, which observed that recurrence had a negative impact on survival, consistent with previous findings [ ]. This highlights the need for recurrence prevention strategies and optimized follow-up to enable early detection if recurrence does occur. In this context, our data revealed that, although the recurrence rate was high, a quite low proportion of them were diagnosed by means of follow-up BCs (1.3%). Furthermore, excluding patients with fever at the time of BC collection, the proportion of true-positive BCs was only 0.7%. Of note, the rate of true-positive and contaminants was very similar, even though this contamination rate was notably lower than previously reported in the literature (3%–8%) [ ]. This finding likely reflects recent improvements in BC collection and processing protocols [ , ], but we cannot exclude that a

Furthermore, excluding patients with fever at the time of BC collection, the proportion of true-positive BCs was only 0.7%. Of note, the rate of true-positive and contaminants was very similar, even though this contamination rate was notably lower than previously reported in the literature (3%–8%) [ ]. This finding likely reflects recent improvements in BC collection and processing protocols [ , ], but we cannot exclude that a larger sample size might have revealed a higher rate of contamination and, consequently, increased risk from follow-up BCs. In addition, in our study, the overall 1-year recurrence rate did not differ between patients with and without routine follow-up BCs. The use of follow-up BCs had no impact on mortality during follow-up. Consequently, given the very low pretest probability of IE in asymptomatic patients and possible harm derived from contamination, the use of repeat BC could not be routinely recommended from a diagnostic stewardship view. Remarkably, a recently published work by another group [ ], independent from this one, reached a very similar conclusion. The rate of positive follow-up BC was the same (1.5%), and a significant proportion of recurrences were missed (6%). Accordingly, both studies suggest that routine follow-up BCs in afebrile IE survivors appear to have limited or no clinical utility. However, it should be noted that in both studies the follow-up BCs were performed according to clinical practice and the vast majority of BCs were drawn in the first month. Accordingly, we cannot exclude that a systematic collection of BCs at a more prolonged time-point would be of utility. In our study, we also aimed to identify index episode characteristics associated with risk of recurrence, in order to try to define subgroups of patients who might benefit from targeted follow-up BCs. In our cohort, history of prior IE, fungal etiology, and presence of mycotic aneurysm were associated with higher rate of subsequent recurrence. These factors are in accordance to previous findings in literature [ , , ]. Recent studies have shown that valve replacement surgeries performed for IE are associated with higher risk of subsequent IE than replacements for other indications [ ]. Similarly, fungal IE cohorts report numerically higher recurrence rates than bacterial IE [ ], prompting some experts to recommend suppressive therapy in these cases [ ]. Furthermore, recent data on mycotic aneurysms in IE have linked their presence to subsequent recurrence [ ]. Conversely, we found that IE on native valves (as opposed to prosthetic valve or device-related IE) was associated with lower recurrence risk. The absence of foreign material capable of sustaining a bacterial biofilm, which is difficult to eradicate with antibiotics alone, may explain the lower recurrence rates in native valve IE [ ]. In contrast, we did not corroborate in our cohort other important risk factors described in large recent cohorts. Most notably, the association of enterococcal etiology or absence of cardiac surgery, found in recent cohorts [ ], was not present in our patients. This is likely due to our relatively small sample size. Our study provides important and novel information to help guide follow-up strategies for IE survivors. Nonetheless, it is a retrospective, single-center observational study, with the limitations inherent to this design, some of them worth of specific mention. First, data collection depended on information recorded in medical records, which carries the risk of underreporting of minor symptoms or systematically undocumented variables. However, the consecutive inclusion of all cases and reliance on robust outcomes (recurrence and mortality) support the validity of our results. Second, in more than 90% of patients, follow-up BCs were collected within the first month of follow-up. Only a minority had BCs performed beyond this time frame, and therefore we cannot exclude the possibility that follow-up BCs systematically collected in different moments (ie, at first week, first month, 3 months, 6 months, and 12 months) might have greater yield. Last, our relatively small sample size may have limited the statistical power to assess the utility and risks of BCs, as well as to detect recurrence-associated risk factors. Although our data suggest an unclear benefit of follow-up BCs, our study was not specifically designed to assess net clinical benefit (eg, reduction in mortality through earlier diagnosis) in different time-points or harms from contaminants (eg, unnecessary hospitalizations or invasive procedures). Therefore, our findings should be confirmed by well-designed prospective studies with systematic BC collection at different time-points to definitively determine the utility—or lack thereof—of follow-up BCs in survivors of IE. In conclusion, among patients surviving an episode of IE, follow-up BCs performed in the absence of fever had limited utility, failed to detect a higher proportion of recurrences,

Although our data suggest an unclear benefit of follow-up BCs, our study was not specifically designed to assess net clinical benefit (eg, reduction in mortality through earlier diagnosis) in different time-points or harms from contaminants (eg, unnecessary hospitalizations or invasive procedures). Therefore, our findings should be confirmed by well-designed prospective studies with systematic BC collection at different time-points to definitively determine the utility—or lack thereof—of follow-up BCs in survivors of IE. In conclusion, among patients surviving an episode of IE, follow-up BCs performed in the absence of fever had limited utility, failed to detect a higher proportion of recurrences, and did not improve prognosis. They were also associated with a risk of contaminants. Prospective multicenter studies are needed to evaluate the yield and cost-effectiveness of systematically extracted BCs during follow-up, especially in patients at higher risk of recurrence. chunks.content: Background: Antibiotics are fundamental for managing odontogenic infections and preventing any systemic complications, yet their misuse in dentistry has caused some significant public health concerns [ ]. Several evidence-based guidelines have been issued by the American Dental Association, American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, which emphasize conservative local treatment and reserve antibiotics for cases that show systemic spread or diffuse swelling [ ]. Rough estimation suggests that dentists account for 10% of outpatient antibiotic prescriptions within the United States, with amoxicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, penicillin VK and clindamycin being most frequently used [ ]. Generally, narrow-spectrum penicillin remains a first-line choice, thereby reserving clindamycin for β-lactam-allergic patients to minimize the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection [ ]. The AHA and ADA recommendations restrict prophylactic antibiotics to patients with clearly defined high-risk cardiac conditions, emphasizing a selective, patient-specific approach rather than routine use [ ]. Despite these recommendations, the inappropriate prescribing of antibiotics remains an issue, highlighting the continued need for stronger antibiotic stewardship efforts [ ]. Stewardship initiatives adapted from the CDC's "Core Elements of Outpatient Antibiotic Stewardship" have been integrated into dental practice, promoting education, monitoring and interdisciplinary collaboration with the objective of mitigating these effects [ ]. Therefore, it is of interest to describe the current U.S. guidelines, prescribing patterns, therapeutic indications, prophylactic recommendations, challenges of over-prescription and stewardship strategies that together shape responsible antibiotic use in dentistry. Current U.S. guidelines on antibiotic use in dentistry: Antibiotics play an important role in treating dental infections, but unnecessary overprescribing by dental providers has resulted in serious antibiotic-related adverse effects. In response, several governing bodies in the U.S., including the American Dental Association (ADA), the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) and the American Heart Association (AHA), have released clinical guidelines for dentists to follow. Despite these guidelines, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) reports that about 10% of all outpatients' antibiotic prescriptions are written by dentists, with many not adhering to the recommended practices. The ADA, AHA, AAPD and CDC have consistently emphasized the value of prioritizing definitive dental treatment and limiting antibiotic prescriptions to cases where they are necessary. Following these recommendations would reduce the prevalence of adverse effects and guarantee patients' safety [ , ]. In 2019, an expert panel convened by the American Dental Association (ADA) put forward an evidence-based report with recommendations for antibiotic prescribing when managing pulpal and periapical-related dental pain and intraoral swelling. This guideline parallels that published by the Academy of Pediatric Dentistry (AAPD) recommendations for antibiotic prescribing for children presenting with oral infections. Both U.S.-based institutions recommend avoiding the prescription of antibiotics when a definitive, conservative dental therapy is available. Instead, their use should be limited to situations where the dental infection shows signs of spreading or signs of a systemic infection. When prescribing, it is preferred that dentists provide a narrow-spectrum antibiotic. They stress the importance of antibiotic stewardship and highlight the adverse effects that could result from unnecessary prescriptions, such as C. difficile infection, allergic reactions and microbiome disruption [ , ]. Patients with heart conditions and those who have received prosthetic joints have a higher chance of developing serious, life-threatening infections like infective endocarditis or prosthetic joint infection, respectively. Even though the risk was very low, many dentists would prefer to "play it safe" and choose to prescribe antibiotics. In 2007, the American Heart Association (AHA) published a guideline that it refined in 2021, endorsed by the ADA, restricting the use of antibiotics for high-risk cardiac patients. The guideline recommends that Amoxicillin should be used for procedures that manipulate gingival or periapical tissues or perforates the oral mucosa [ ]. However, patients with prosthetic joints do not require antibiotic coverage according to a statement released by the ADA in collaboration with the American Academy of Orthopedic Surgeons (AAOS) as they failed to demonstrate an association between dental procedures and prosthetic joint infection. Individuals who are immunocompromised, have poorly controlled diabetes or have a history of joint infection are an exception and dentists are encouraged to confer with orthopedic specialists to direct clinical decision making [ ]. Common antibiotics prescribed in dental practice: Dentists prescribed about 25.17 million systemic oral antibiotics, with β-lactam penicillin, specifically Amoxicillin, as the preferred choice according to data provided by the Journal of the American Dental Association (ADA) in 2022 [ ]. This significant number places dentists fourth among prescribers of antibiotics, behind family practitioners, pediatricians and internists [ ]. Amoxicillin, clindamycin, penicillin VK, azithromycin and amoxicillin-clavulanate were the top five antibiotics administered by American dentists, according to a Wisconsin-based study of dental antibiotic use from 2018 to 2021. These findings are consistent with normal clinical practice, which reserves clindamycin for patients with β-lactam allergies and favors narrow-spectrum penicillin when appropriate. Geographical disparities were also noted; dentists in the Northeast

This significant number places dentists fourth among prescribers of antibiotics, behind family practitioners, pediatricians and internists [ ]. Amoxicillin, clindamycin, penicillin VK, azithromycin and amoxicillin-clavulanate were the top five antibiotics administered by American dentists, according to a Wisconsin-based study of dental antibiotic use from 2018 to 2021. These findings are consistent with normal clinical practice, which reserves clindamycin for patients with β-lactam allergies and favors narrow-spectrum penicillin when appropriate. Geographical disparities were also noted; dentists in the Northeast were more likely than those in the West to prescribe antibiotics. Additionally, female patients and older persons were shown to have higher prescribing rates [ ]. Overall, antibiotic prescriptions by dentists have remained consistent over the years, with only minor changes in how those prescriptions are written. Mainly, between 2018 and 2022, a slight decrease in "days' supply" per prescription was observed, indicating a greater understanding of antibiotic stewardship principles. Another difference found is the decrease in the percentage of clindamycin prescriptions, even though it remains the main option for patients who report a penicillin allergy. This could be due to the increase in awareness of its connection to Clostridium difficile infection (CDI) [ ]. commonly prescribed Antibiotics in U.S Dental Practice. Dosing ranges are approximate based on typical dental prescribing patterns. Data summarized from studies and public health reports cited in text. These results demonstrate that amoxicillin is still the most often recommended antibiotic by dentists, with clindamycin and a few other frequently used substitutes following closely behind. It is easier to discuss the therapeutic and preventive uses of antibiotics as well as ways to improve stewardship in dental practice when these prescribing trends are acknowledged [ ]. Therapeutic use of antibiotics in common dental infections: Current evidence-based landscape for the therapeutic use of antibiotics in common odontogenic infections emphasizes the critical role of dental practitioners in global Antimicrobial Stewardship (AMS). Being among the top prescribers of antimicrobials, dental professionals significantly influence the development of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and must adhere strictly to current clinical guidelines [ ]. The definitive role of localized treatment: According to current clinical guidelines established by organizations such as the American Dental Association (ADA) and the American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry (AAPD), systemic antibiotics are not indicated as the primary mode of therapy for most localized odontogenic infections in immunocompetent individuals [ ]. Disease states-such as symptomatic irreversible pulpitis (SIP), pulp necrosis with symptomatic apical periodontitis (PN-SAP) and localized acute apical abscess (PN-LAAA)- are typically confined within the alveolar process. Therefore, the only definitive treatment involves Definitive Conservative Dental Treatment (DCDT), which includes surgical elimination of the microbial source through pulpal debridement, root canal therapy or incision and drainage (I & D) of an abscess. Systematic reviews confirm that for promptly treated localized infections, adjunctive antibiotic use provides no statistically significant improvement in clinical outcomes such as pain or swelling [ ]. The unnecessary prescription of antibiotics in these situations contributes directly to AMR and represents a case of over-prescription [ ]. Indications for systemic therapy: Systemic antibiotics are reserved for cases where the infection extends beyond local containment or poses a threat to patient health. Indications for antibiotic therapy include: [1] Systemic involvement-Signs such as fever (≥100°F), malaise, trismus and lymphadenopathy [2] Diffuse swelling (cellulitis)-The presence of indurated, non-fluctuant swelling in facial or intraoral regions, indicating infection spread to adjacent tissue planes. [3] Compromised host immunity-Patients with systemic diseases ( e.g. , uncontrolled diabetes or severe immunosuppression) whose resistance to infection is reduced. When localized abscesses are present and DCDT must be deferred, a conditional or delayed prescription approach is preferred. The patient is instructed to initiate antibiotic therapy only if systemic symptoms worsen prior to receiving definitive treatment. This approach minimizes risk while upholding AMS principles [ ]. Empirical therapy regimens and duration: Antibiotic therapy in dental infections is largely empirical, aimed at polymicrobial flora consisting of facultative and obligate anaerobes. Treatment should utilize narrow-spectrum agents effective against common odontogenic pathogens. [1] First-line agents: Amoxicillin (500 mg three times daily) or Penicillin VK (500 mg four times daily). In more severe cases, amoxicillin-clavulanate may be indicated. [2] Penicillin allergy: Clindamycin (150-300 mg four times daily) is the preferred alternative, though it carries a risk of Clostridioides difficile infection. The duration of antibiotic therapy should be limited to the shortest effective period-typically 3 to 7 days, depending on the initiation of DCDT and resolution of systemic signs [ ]. Dental professionals are ethically and professionally obligated to follow evidence-based AMS practices. Adhering to guidelines that reserve antibiotics for cases involving systemic spread or compromised immunity protects both individual patients and public health. By prescribing antibiotics only as adjuncts to surgical source control, clinicians

Adhering to guidelines that reserve antibiotics for cases involving systemic spread or compromised immunity protects both individual patients and public health. By prescribing antibiotics only as adjuncts to surgical source control, clinicians help preserve the efficacy of these essential medications [ ]. Building upon the same principles of antimicrobial stewardship, it is equally important to apply evidence-based decision-making in situations where antibiotics are used for preventive rather than therapeutic purposes [ ]. Antibiotic prophylaxis in endocarditis and prosthetic joint patients: Antibiotic prophylaxis helps prevent infective endocarditis (IE) and prosthetic joint infections that can occur after invasive dental procedures. Current recommendations limit its use to patients with conditions that place them at the highest risk of serious complications. Research over the past two decades shows that routine antibiotic use offers minimal added protection while contributing to resistance and adverse reactions. The shift toward targeted prevention and improved oral hygiene reflects a balance between patient safety and responsible antibiotic stewardship [ , ]. Infective endocarditis (IE) is a potentially life-threatening infection of the heart's inner lining, most often caused by viridans group streptococci entering the bloodstream during transient bacteremia. Dental procedures that disturb gingival or periapical tissues can allow such microorganisms to enter circulation. Contemporary prevention strategies emphasize a risk-based approach to antibiotic use, underscoring the clinical rationale behind current recommendations [ ]. Current guidelines for IE prophylaxis: According to the 2021 American Heart Association (AHA) scientific statement, antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures is reserved for clearly defined high-risk cardiac conditions. These include prosthetic heart valves or prosthetic material used in valve repair; a history of previous IE; specific congenital heart anomalies such as unrepaired cyanotic defects or repaired lesions with residual shunts or valvular regurgitation adjacent to prosthetic material; and cardiac transplant recipients with valvular disease. Prophylaxis is indicated only for dental procedures that manipulate gingival tissue, the periapical region or perforate the oral mucosa [ ]. The standard drug regimen consists of amoxicillin 2 g orally, administered 30-60 minutes before the procedure. For patients allergic to penicillin, acceptable alternatives include cephalexin 2 g, azithromycin 500 mg or clarithromycin 500 mg. Clindamycin is no longer advised because of its higher association with adverse reactions and Clostridioides difficile infection [ ]. Prosthetic joint patients: Joint guidelines from the American Dental Association (ADA) and American Academy of Orthopedic Surgeons (AAOS) do not recommend routine antibiotic prophylaxis for individuals with prosthetic joint implants undergoing dental procedures. Prophylaxis may be considered only after interdisciplinary consultation for patients who are immunocompromised, have poorly controlled diabetes or experienced postoperative complications [ ]. This stance reflects the absence of strong evidence linking dental work to prosthetic joint infections and a growing recognition of antibiotic-related risks such as allergic reactions, gastrointestinal upset and the promotion of resistant bacterial strains [ ]. Rationale and risk-benefit considerations: Poor oral hygiene has been shown to pose a greater risk of bacteremia and IE than dental treatment itself. Consequently, prevention now prioritizes daily oral care, patient-specific assessment, and close coordination between dental and medical professionals. Antibiotic prophylaxis should be reserved for patients truly at risk of IE or for select prosthetic joint recipients following professional consultation. Adhering to the AHA and ADA recommendations balances infection prevention with prudent antibiotic stewardship, aligning clinical practice with modern evidence-based standards. Since the 2007 revision of AHA guidelines, national IE incidence has remained stable or even declined- despite a major reduction in prophylactic antibiotic use [ , ]. This trend suggests that widespread administration offers little protective advantage. Conversely, unnecessary exposure increases the likelihood of resistance, C. difficile infection [ ] and hypersensitivity reactions [ ]. Challenges and consequences of antibiotic over-prescription in dentistry: Addressing antibiotic over-prescription: Dentists often prescribe analgesics and antibiotics as part of post-operative management for controlling pain and treating odontogenic infections or related post-operative complications [ ]. Though antibiotic prescriptions are routine in the field, several studies have found a significant proportion of those prescriptions to be unnecessary or inappropriate [ ]. A dentist may follow common practice, educational training or literature and prescribe antibiotics as a precautionary measure. Still, the systemic over-issuance and over-use of antibiotics fuels a systemic risk in global antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and adverse drug events. The resulting financial burden on healthcare systems ultimately comes back to impact the patient [ ]. [ ]. Though antibiotic prescriptions are routine in the field, several studies have found a significant proportion of those prescriptions to be unnecessary or inappropriate [ ]. A dentist may follow common practice, educational training or literature and prescribe antibiotics as a precautionary measure. Still, the systemic over-issuance and over-use of antibiotics fuels a systemic risk in global antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and adverse drug events. The resulting financial burden on healthcare systems ultimately comes back to impact the patient [ ]. Contributing factors: Overlapping or conflicting clinical symptoms are prevalent underlying challenges that surface as diagnostic uncertainty in dentistry. Distinguishing between bacterial infection classes is a primary example of the symptom-based challenges dentists face when prescribing for patients; some infection types require systemic therapy, while more typical inflammatory conditions may be managed with local treatment. Consequently, dentists often find themselves prescribing antibiotics "just in case" endodontic treatment is infeasible or when drainage may be an issue [ ]. Commonly held public beliefs and patient expectations also help contribute to a widespread influence on post-procedural prescriptions. Patient and layman beliefs such as equating antibiotic prescription with quality post-procedure care are often a key driver in dentists choosing to prescribe them, sometimes at the cost of avoiding customer dissatisfaction, complaints and negative reviews [ ]. Dental offices and dentists are frequently pressed for time and most dental offices lack advanced diagnostic tools. In urban areas, this leads to dentists not keeping up with continuing education and technological advances. Rural or underserved locations, on the other hand, frequently suffer from dentists adopting outdated local norms and educational resources. In either case, the lack of structured antimicrobial stewardship programs for dental practices on a national level perpetuates the feedback loop of habits that aren't audited or have clear data-driven sources [ ]. Unintended consequences: The consequences of antibiotic over-prescription surface in clinical and public health settings as allergic responses, short-term gastrointestinal effects and sometimes life-threatening anaphylaxis. Studies have found nearly 4% of all patients receiving dental antibiotic prescriptions to have faced adverse effects, including hospitalization from Clostridioides difficile ( C. diff ) infections [ ]. Dentists commonly prescribe Clindamycin and other broad-spectrum cephalosporins, often associated with Clostridioides difficile infections and gut microbiome disruptions. A "just in case" prescription has a nontrivial chance of endangering patient health and causing financial burden upon the patient and the healthcare system [ ]. When observed at scale, dental antibiotic over-prescription and over-use accelerate the growing risk of global antimicrobial resistance, particularly among oral and systemic bacteria [ ]. Routine dental procedures that depend on effective prophylaxis come under threat of losing efficacy in a growing trend of antimicrobial resistance, especially as resistant strains develop and spread across communities worldwide. Economically, the burden on both patients and healthcare systems compounds as unnecessary or inappropriate antibiotic prescriptions increase medication costs, follow-up care and adverse reaction treatments [ ]. Practical implications and solutions: The answer is clear when looking at the problem from a systemic view - a lack of evidence-based antibiotic stewardship that incorporates regular and required clinical education, as well as clear auditing systems and mechanisms that hold dental practices nationwide accountable to a standard [ ]. Several local treatment options, such as pulpectomies, drainage techniques and extractions, can often be utilized and promoted as definitive local treatments that avoid post-operative necessity for antibiotics, only achievable as a transformation at scale with structured stewardship programs [ ]. Collaboration with public health officials and policy makers, pharmacists and infection control specialists and a structured public-private knowledge base for compliance will also drive a clearer adherence to set standards for prescription. Continuing education programs and stewardship/technological advancement integrations at dental offices are a key step in the required transformation. Digital prescription tracking systems collaborating with national stewardship digital frameworks can maintain accountability across the ecosystem and provide the needed data to observe and remedy over-prescription in geographical areas or even down to an individual dentist [ ]. Stewardship strategies and future directions in US dental practice: Antibiotic stewardship has become an essential part of global efforts to control antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Dentists alone contribute around 10-12% of overall antibiotic prescriptions in the United States [ ]. Although ADA has published updated guidelines, research shows that dentists have continued to over-prescribe, especially for pre-procedural prophylaxis, which is completely unnecessary. To address this issue, stewardship strategies are required to translate policies into actions. According to many studies, it is established that 80% of prophylactic antibiotics prescribed by dentists lack specific indications [ ]. In many cases, prescription patterns highlight that decisions are influenced by patients' demand for antibiotics, diagnostic uncertainty, as well as habits rather than clinical evidence. A combination of stewardship strategies, such as education, monitoring and accountability, is critical for improving prescribing practices. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

guidelines, research shows that dentists have continued to over-prescribe, especially for pre-procedural prophylaxis, which is completely unnecessary. To address this issue, stewardship strategies are required to translate policies into actions. According to many studies, it is established that 80% of prophylactic antibiotics prescribed by dentists lack specific indications [ ]. In many cases, prescription patterns highlight that decisions are influenced by patients' demand for antibiotics, diagnostic uncertainty, as well as habits rather than clinical evidence. A combination of stewardship strategies, such as education, monitoring and accountability, is critical for improving prescribing practices. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) introduced the 'Core Elements of Outpatient Antibiotic Stewardship' emphasizing commitment, policy implementation, tracking and education [ ]. These ideas can be adapted for dental setups to aid prescriptions. For example, whenever prescriptions are provided without an appropriate diagnosis or an antibiotic duration exceeds recommendations, the electronic health record system can flag alerts [ ]. Education is highly imperative for lasting enhancements in this matter. Continuing dental education should be interactive and case-based rather than a one-time lecture. Also, stewardship should be implemented in the undergraduate program curriculum early on [ ]. However, surveys continue to show that dentists extend treatment durations and prescribe broad-spectrum agents unnecessarily [ ]. A systematic approach through regulated feedback and peer comparison can help bridge this gap. The American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry (AAPD) continues to reinforce these stewardship principles. Its 2022 best practices document emphasizes that prophylaxis should be reserved for children at the highest risk of bacteremia induced complications and cautions that evidence in pediatrics is limited [ ]. Robust evidence on how to change prescribing behavior is limited. A 2025 systematic review of dental antibiotic stewardship interventions identified three randomized controlled trials. Audit and personalized feedback combined with behavioral messaging consistently reduced unnecessary prescribing, whereas in person education alone had low certainty evidence and disseminating guideline summaries without interaction was ineffective [ ]. Collaborate with other partners, such as the pharmacists, can help the dentists in choosing the most suitable antibiotic, its dosage and checking for allergies or interactions. Inter-professional association, supported by digital tools and national scrutiny, has already proven effective in medical settings and can bring parallel benefits to dentistry. In the future, a combination of technology, inter- professional teamwork and focus on related education can make antibiotic stewardship a routine part of any dental facility workflow [ ]. Conclusion: A judicious approach is required in antibiotic prescription, which is solely based on evidence and prioritizes definitive local treatment while strictly adhering to guidelines from ADA, AHA, AAPD and CDC. Robust stewardship strategies through early and comprehensive education, monitoring and collaboration with pharmacists etc., are the need of the hour, when over-prescription continues to fuel antimicrobial resistance and adverse outcomes. Patient safety will only be ensured by integrating these principles into daily dental practices which will not only preserve antibiotic efficacy but also advance global public health.

documents.title: Contemporary diagnosis and management of rheumatic heart disease AHA scientific statement

chunks.content: Introduction Rheumatic heart disease (RHD) is a chronic condition resulting from one or more episodes of acute rheumatic fever, an autoimmune inflammatory reaction triggered by group A streptococcal pharyngitis that leads to progressive valvular damage [ – ]. Carditis is the second most common manifestation of acute rheumatic fever and represents the principal determinant of long-term morbidity and mortality, particularly when valvular involvement occurs [ , ]. Globally, the burden of RHD increased from an estimated 15 million cases in 2005 to 40.5 million in 2019, disproportionately affecting low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) [ – ]. Despite WHO recommendations for echocardiographic screening in high-endemic areas to enable early diagnosis and intervention [ , , , ], many patients in LMICs still present with advanced RHD and complications due to limited access to echocardiography and specialist care. Echocardiography using the World Heart Federation (WHF) criteria is crucial for accurately diagnosing definite rheumatic valvular disease and ensuring consistency in outcome studies. Effective management requires optimized medical therapy and, for selected patients, surgical or percutaneous interventions [ , , , – ]; however, limited access in resource-constrained settings contributes to high complication rates and an estimated 350,000 deaths annually [ , , , , , ]. Although global RHD mortality declined by approximately 50% between 1990 and 2015, this reduction has been highly heterogeneous across regions, with substantially smaller declines observed in several LMICs [ , ]. Factors associated with increased mortality include poor socioeconomic status, delayed presentation, limited access to tertiary cardiac care, and advanced disease at diagnosis [ ]. Common complications of late-presenting RHD include heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, atrial fibrillation, embolic stroke, and infective endocarditis, with heart failure and pulmonary hypertension being the most prevalent [ , , , , – ]. Despite the high burden of RHD in Ethiopia and across sub-Saharan Africa, there remains a paucity of long-term outcome data among adults managed without surgical or percutaneous interventions. This gap limits understanding of disease progression and impedes development of targeted interventions. The present study aimed to evaluate the patterns of complications and identify predictors of mortality among adults with RHD receiving longitudinal care at the Cardiac Center of Ethiopia who had not undergone surgical or interventional procedures. Methods and materials Study area, period, and design This retrospective cohort study was conducted at the Cardiac Center of Ethiopia (CCE) in Addis Ababa, the national referral center for cardiovascular care. Adults aged ≥ 18 years with definite RHD diagnosed according to the 2012 WHF echocardiographic criteria [ ] were enrolled between January 1, 2015, and January 1, 2025, and followed until death or loss to follow-up. Outcome data, including survival status and date of death, were ascertained from medical records and telephone follow-up conducted between February 1 and June 1, 2025. At CCE, patients with RHD undergo standardized evaluation including detailed medical history, physical examination with emphasis on cardiac auscultation (upright and left lateral decubitus positions), electrocardiography, chest radiography, and comprehensive transthoracic echocardiography. Echocardiographic studies were performed using standard high-quality machines (Samsung Medison EKO 7, GE Vivid E9, Sonoscape P9) by two senior adult cardiologists experienced in the evaluation and management of RHD, both medically and via percutaneous interventions. Assessments included valvular involvement, left ventricular dimensions, left ventricular ejection fraction, and estimation of pulmonary artery pressures. Diagnosis of rheumatic heart disease RHD was diagnosed using transthoracic echocardiography in accordance with the 2012 WHF criteria for definite RHD [ ], and valve severity was assessed using a standardized protocol based on the 2020 American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA) Valvular Heart Disease Guideline [ ]. Diagnosis required pathological valvular regurgitation and/or stenosis in combination with morphological features characteristic of rheumatic involvement, including leaflet thickening, restricted leaflet motion, commissural fusion, and chordal abnormalities. All echocardiographic data were acquired and interpreted by senior cardiologists with extensive experience in advanced echocardiography and the assessment of RHD at the participating center. Although interobserver variability was not assessed, this approach ensured expert and consistent evaluation of valvular morphology throughout the study period. Only patients fulfilling criteria for definite RHD were included. Study population and eligibility The source population comprised all adults with RHD receiving follow-up care at CCE during the study period. Inclusion criteria were age ≥ 18 years, definite RHD by WHF criteria, and at least one documented follow-up visit. Patients with no echocardiographic evidence of rheumatic valvular disease, prior surgical or percutaneous valvular intervention, or missing outcome data were excluded. Data collection technique and procedure Data were collected using a structured questionnaire developed from a literature review and adapted to the local context. Two trained clinical nurses extracted data from medical records and conducted telephone interviews to verify survival status and dates of death, with deaths confirmed through medical records and/or family interviews. Supervisors and principal investigators ensured data quality through continuous monitoring.

Patients with no echocardiographic evidence of rheumatic valvular disease, prior surgical or percutaneous valvular intervention, or missing outcome data were excluded. Data collection technique and procedure Data were collected using a structured questionnaire developed from a literature review and adapted to the local context. Two trained clinical nurses extracted data from medical records and conducted telephone interviews to verify survival status and dates of death, with deaths confirmed through medical records and/or family interviews. Supervisors and principal investigators ensured data quality through continuous monitoring. A pretest involving 5% of participants at a different hospital was conducted to refine the questionnaire. Collected variables included sociodemographic characteristics; clinical features and comorbidities; echocardiographic parameters; treatment and adherence information; and complications such as NYHA class III–IV heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, atrial fibrillation, infective endocarditis, stroke, pulmonary embolism, major bleeding, and rheumatic recurrence. Data processing and analysis Data were entered into Epi Info version 7 for cleaning and analyzed using Python (Lifelines and Matplotlib packages) and Microsoft Excel 2013. Continuous variables are presented as medians with interquartile ranges (IQR), and categorical variables as frequencies and percentages. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Survival was estimated using Kaplan–Meier methods and compared using log-rank tests. Cox proportional hazards regression was used to identify independent predictors of mortality. Variables with p < 0.20 in bivariable analysis were included in multivariable models. Multicollinearity was assessed using variance inflation factors (VIF), with values > 10 indicating significant collinearity. Results are reported as adjusted hazard ratios (AHR) with 95% confidence intervals. Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05. Terms and definitions A maximum tricuspid regurgitation (TR) velocity ≥ 2.8 m/s was used as the echocardiographic threshold for estimating the probability of elevated pulmonary pressure. Pulmonary hypertension was diagnosed by echocardiography and defined as a mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) ≥ 20 mmHg, estimated from the TR pressure gradient using the modified Bernoulli equation and converted to mean pressure with the formula mPAP = 0.61 × systolic pulmonary artery pressure (sPAP) + 2 mmHg. When pulmonary regurgitation (PR) was present, a PR peak gradient ≥ 20 mmHg was used for diagnosis, with the higher value applied when both TR and PR measurements were available. Atrial fibrillation was diagnosed by ECG showing an irregular rhythm without distinct P waves. Infective endocarditis was defined using the Modified Duke Criteria, and rheumatic recurrence was diagnosed using the Modified Jones Criteria. Rheumatic recurrence over the 10-year follow-up was collected retrospectively from clinic records. Documented episodes of rheumatic fever were identified based on symptoms and supporting laboratory findings according to the Jones criteria, and cases were considered recurrences if the treating cardiologist decided to manage them as such. For analysis, only the first recurrence was counted per patient, even if multiple episodes occurred, and recurrence was defined as at least one episode meeting the Modified Jones Criteria. Adherence to secondary prophylaxis was measured retrospectively through review of medical records and clinic follow-up documentation, including benzathine penicillin administration logbook and medication notes. Patients were considered adherent if there were no recorded missed monthly benzathine penicillin injections or daily oral medications during the preceding six months. Nutritional status was assessed using body mass index (BMI) cutoffs as follows: underweight (BMI < 18.5 kg/m²), normal weight (BMI 18.5–24.9 kg/m²), overweight (BMI 25–29.9 kg/m²), and obesity (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m²). Results Sociodemographic characteristics of individuals with RHD at presentation Of the 1,844 adults with RHD, 1,811 met the inclusion criteria. Table demonstrates the sociodemographic characteristics of individuals with RHD included in this study. The median age was 32 years, with 42.9% aged 29–38 years. Females accounted for 60.7% of participants, yielding a female-to-male ratio of 1.54. One-third were married, and 59.5% resided in rural areas. Farmers and government employees represented 57.4% of the cohort, and 26.8% reported a monthly income < 2,000 Ethiopian birr (≈ 13 USD). Clinical characteristics of individuals with RHD at presentation As seen in Table , the most common symptoms were fatigue and dyspnea (29.9%), followed by dyspnea with orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and fever (23.7%). Nearly half of the participants were underweight, and 14.1% had comorbidities, with systemic hypertension being most frequent. Echocardiography revealed multiple valve involvement in 65.6% of patients, with severe valvular lesions in 57.1%. Isolated mitral valve involvement was most common (23.7%), followed by combined mitral and aortic valve involvement (18.5%). Diuretics were prescribed in 94.9% of cases. Non-adherence was reported in 25.8% for secondary prophylaxis and 47.4% for oral medications. Although all patients met indications for surgical or catheter-based interventions and were referred accordingly, none underwent these procedures within the study follow-up period, largely due to limited surgical availability and long waiting lists. Complications in individuals with RHD at presentation and during follow-up Over a

Isolated mitral valve involvement was most common (23.7%), followed by combined mitral and aortic valve involvement (18.5%). Diuretics were prescribed in 94.9% of cases. Non-adherence was reported in 25.8% for secondary prophylaxis and 47.4% for oral medications. Although all patients met indications for surgical or catheter-based interventions and were referred accordingly, none underwent these procedures within the study follow-up period, largely due to limited surgical availability and long waiting lists. Complications in individuals with RHD at presentation and during follow-up Over a median follow-up of 5 years (IQR 2.5–6.5), 1,037 individuals (57.3%) developed at least one complication, including baseline complications. The most frequent were NYHA class III–IV heart failure with pulmonary hypertension (31.4%) and pulmonary hypertension alone (19.8%) (See Fig. ). Notably, no complications were observed in participants with NYHA class I–II, showing that complications occurred only in those with NYHA class III–IV heart failure. At presentation, 799 participants (44.1%) had complications, predominantly NYHA class III–IV heart failure (37.5%) and pulmonary hypertension (27.6%). During follow-up, incidence of heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, and rheumatic recurrence peaked within the first year, while infective endocarditis, atrial fibrillation, and bleeding increased later (see Fig. ). Overall Survival of Individuals with RHD During the follow-up period, 326 participants (18.0%) died. The majority of these deaths (296, 90.8%) were confirmed from hospital records, while the remaining 30 (9.2%) were reported by families via telephone. Among participants without complications, deaths were rare (0.5%) and occurred suddenly at home. In contrast, mortality was much higher among those with complications (31.1%). Of these, 57.1% had both NYHA class III–IV heart failure and pulmonary hypertension, 15.8% had pulmonary hypertension alone, and 7.1% had NYHA class III–IV heart failure with rheumatic recurrence. Most deaths in this group (86.5%) occurred within the first 48 h of hospital admission (See Fig. ). Figure illustrates survival trends over time. Kaplan–Meier analysis demonstrated significant differences in survival between patients with and without complications (log-rank p < 0.001). The 1-year survival rate was 92.5% overall (100% in the no-complication group vs. 86.9% with complications). At 3 years, survival was 86.3% overall (99.8% vs. 76.1%), declining to 81.7% at 5 years (99.7% vs. 68.0%), and 71.0% at 10 years (97.7% vs. 68.0%). Predictors of mortality in individuals with RHD As depicted in Table , Multivariable Cox regression identified independent predictors of mortality, including the presence of comorbidities (AHR 5.8, 95% CI 3.9–6.2), increased left ventricular internal diameter in diastole (AHR 2.1 per mm, 95% CI 1.1–3.9), monthly income < 2,000 Ethiopian birr (≈ 13 USD) (AHR 1.2, 95% CI 1.1–1.5), NYHA class III–IV heart failure (AHR 2.2, 95% CI 1.9–3.2), and pulmonary hypertension (AHR 2.4, 95% CI 1.9–5.5). Variables excluded from the multivariable model due to multicollinearity included severity of valve lesions and adherence to oral medications or secondary prophylaxis, while major bleeding, stroke, and pulmonary embolism were excluded because of the small number of events. Discussion This study evaluated the patterns of complications, survival outcomes, and predictors of mortality in adults with RHD in Ethiopia, providing important insights into long-term outcomes in a resource-limited setting. Our findings reveal a high burden of early complications and premature mortality, emphasizing the need for timely diagnosis and management strategies. The overall complication rate in our cohort was 57.3%, consistent with reports from other regions, which range from 17.1% to 83.6% [ , , – ]. This variability likely reflects differences in follow-up duration, baseline disease severity, definitions of complications, and demographic characteristics of the study populations. Notably, 44.1% of participants had complications at baseline, and the majority of new complications occurred within the first year of follow-up, indicating that patients often present with advanced disease [ – ]. This underscores the urgent need for early detection and routine echocardiographic screening, particularly in high-prevalence areas where delayed presentation is common [ , , ]. Heart failure was the most frequent complication, affecting 31.4% of participants and accounting for 64.4% of all complications. This aligns with findings from Australia, Fiji, Uganda, and other low- and middle-income countries, where heart failure is consistently reported as the predominant complication of RHD [ – , – ]. Pulmonary hypertension was the second most common complication, with a prevalence of 29.3%, falling within the range reported in Ethiopia, Sudan, Uganda, and Nigeria [ , , , ]. Advanced heart failure and pulmonary hypertension likely reflect chronic valvular dysfunction, left ventricular remodeling, and increased right ventricular afterload, which together contribute to progressive hemodynamic deterioration [ ]. Atrial fibrillation occurred in 16.5% of participants, consistent with reported incidence rates ranging from 2.9% to 63.7% across different cohorts [ – , , , , , ]. The lower incidence of embolic events, including stroke (0.1% per year), may be explained

]. Pulmonary hypertension was the second most common complication, with a prevalence of 29.3%, falling within the range reported in Ethiopia, Sudan, Uganda, and Nigeria [ , , , ]. Advanced heart failure and pulmonary hypertension likely reflect chronic valvular dysfunction, left ventricular remodeling, and increased right ventricular afterload, which together contribute to progressive hemodynamic deterioration [ ]. Atrial fibrillation occurred in 16.5% of participants, consistent with reported incidence rates ranging from 2.9% to 63.7% across different cohorts [ – , , , , , ]. The lower incidence of embolic events, including stroke (0.1% per year), may be explained by the absence of prosthetic valves in our cohort, as prior studies report higher embolic risk among patients with mechanical valves [ ]. Infective endocarditis was observed in 8.5% of participants, higher than reported in Australia (1.6%) and the REMEDY multicenter study (4%), likely reflecting delayed presentation and higher exposure to predisposing conditions [ , , ]. Rheumatic recurrence was relatively low at 8.6%, which may be attributed to moderate adherence to secondary prophylaxis compared to other settings [ , , , , , ]. Mortality in our cohort was 18% over a median follow-up of 5 years, comparable to reports from multicenter studies in low- and middle-income countries, which range from 14% to 18.5% over shorter follow-up periods [ , , , ]. The majority of deaths occurred among participants with complications, particularly those with combined heart failure and pulmonary hypertension, highlighting the cumulative impact of severe cardiac pathology on survival. Our analysis identified several independent predictors of mortality. Advanced heart failure (NYHA class III–IV) and pulmonary hypertension were strong predictors, reflecting severe cardiac dysfunction, chronic pressure overload, and progressive multi-organ involvement [ , , ]. Increased left ventricular end-diastolic diameter was also associated with higher mortality, consistent with prior observations in Uganda and other LMICs [ ]. Ventricular dilation likely indicates chronic volume overload and adverse myocardial remodeling, leading to impaired contractility and poor outcomes. The presence of comorbidities significantly increased the risk of death, demonstrating the additive physiological burden of non-cardiac diseases in patients with RHD [ ]. Finally, lower socioeconomic status (monthly income < 2,000 Ethiopian birr (≈ 13 USD)) was independently associated with higher mortality was independently associated with higher mortality, likely due to delayed care-seeking, poor access to medications, and limited healthcare utilization. The implications of these findings are multifaceted. Clinically, early identification of patients at high risk, those with advanced heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, or ventricular dilation, may allow for targeted monitoring, intensified medical therapy, and timely referral for interventions where available. Public health strategies should address social determinants of health, improve access to primary and secondary prophylaxis, and expand awareness programs to reduce late presentation. The high incidence of complications within the first year highlights the need for routine echocardiographic screening and structured follow-up protocols in endemic regions [ , , , ]. Limitations of the study This study has several limitations. Its retrospective, single-center design may limit generalizability to other populations. Survival outcomes were partly determined via telephone follow-up, which could introduce recall bias. Missing data and the exclusion of variables due to multicollinearity (e.g., adherence and valve lesion severity) may have influenced multivariable analyses. Additionally, cause-specific mortality data were not available, preventing differentiation between RHD-related and unrelated deaths. Although echocardiography was performed by a single experienced cardiologist with expertise in RHD evaluation, interobserver variability was not assessed. Despite these limitations, the study provides valuable long-term outcome data for adults with RHD managed without surgical or percutaneous interventions in a low-resource setting. Conclusion Adults with RHD in Ethiopia face a substantial burden of complications and premature mortality, primarily driven by advanced heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, ventricular dilation, comorbidities, and socioeconomic disadvantage. These findings point to modifiable clinical and social risk factors and the need for early detection, optimized chronic disease management, and interventions addressing broader social determinants to improve survival in resource-limited settings. Limited access to surgical and percutaneous interventions remains an important gap, indicating the need to expand the availability and uptake of these therapies.

documents.title: Cardiovascular considerations in caring for pregnant patients AHA scientific statement

chunks.content: The United States has the highest maternal mortality of all industrialized countries, with an estimated maternal mortality rate of 22.3 per 100,000 births. While maternal mortality has declined worldwide over the past 2 decades, maternal deaths in the United States are rising, particularly among non-Hispanic Black women. , A recent maternal report from the Centers of Disease Control found that over 80% of pregnancy-related deaths were preventable. Cardiovascular (CV) conditions, including hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP), cardiomyopathy, and valvular disease, are among the leading causes of maternal mortality, accounting for nearly 32% of pregnancy-related deaths. , Recent analyses established that failure to identify women at high risk for developing serious cardiac events during pregnancy is an important driver of preventable pregnancy-related death. , Early assessment of patient-specific risks of pregnancy-related CV complications has the potential to significantly reduce maternal morbidity and mortality because it enables more frequent monitoring, additional diagnostic testing, and targeted interventions, but present screening tools are limited to crude markers or require costly diagnostic tests. Assessment of maximal oxygen consumption at peak exercise (peak VO 2 ), an integrative gold standard measurement of cardiorespiratory fitness, has been shown to predict adverse outcomes in many populations, including pregnant women, and may help to identify women at elevated risk for CV complications during pregnancy. , , However, broad access to peak VO 2 with exercise testing is limited due to prohibitive cost and need for specialized equipment and expert interpretation. Among nonpregnant individuals, we previously trained and validated Deep electrocardiogram (ECG)-VO 2 , a deep learning model that accurately estimates cardiorespiratory fitness (as measured by peak VO 2 ) using the resting 12-lead ECG, and demonstrated that lower ECG-estimated cardiorespiratory fitness is associated with future CV events, including myocardial infarction (MI), atrial fibrillation, heart failure (HF), and overall mortality, in an ambulatory care sample (37% women, mean age 46 ± 20 years). , We now apply Deep ECG-VO 2 to a multi-institutional electronic health record pregnancy cohort comprising >56,000 pregnancies to examine the prognostic value of ECG-estimated peak VO 2 for pregnancy-related CV complications occurring from 13 weeks’ gestation through 1 year postpartum ( ). We hypothesize that ECG-estimated peak VO 2 will be significantly associated with incident pregnancy-related CV complications during this prespecified assessment window. Study sample PADME (Predictive Analysis with Deep Learning Models for Maternal Endpoints) is an electronic health record cohort of 56,833 pregnancies among 38,996 individuals who delivered within the Mass General Brigham multi-institutional health care system from 2001 to 2019. Candidate pregnancies were identified from a validated primary care electronic health record cohort (Community Care Cohort Project, C3PO) of 520,868 individuals receiving longitudinal primary care between 2001 and 2019. This cohort selection process and study design have been shown to reduce selection bias and data missingness and enable longitudinal tracking of pregnancy-related CV complications. The PADME study protocol was approved by the Mass General Brigham Institutional Review Board and adheres to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. We included all pregnancy episodes with at least one 12-lead ECG performed within 1 year prior to conception (start of pregnancy) through 13 weeks of gestation. Each pregnancy episode was assigned 1 ECG (ECG assignment is further detailed in the and ). Of note, when multiple ECGs were available for a given pregnancy, we selected the ECG closest to 13 weeks’ gestation to harmonize exposure timing across pregnancies. From this starting sample of 3,957 pregnancies (among 3,718 individuals) with qualifying ECGs, we excluded those with missing body mass index (BMI) and systolic blood pressure (SBP) data (n = 307), yielding a final sample of 3,650 pregnancies (among 3,437 individuals). Estimation of peak VO<sub>2</sub> from the 12-lead electrocardiogram Deep ECG-VO 2 model is a deep learning model that utilizes a pretraining approach, dubbed Patient Contrastive Learning of Representations, which creates numerical (latent) representations of ECG waveforms that accentuate the differences between ECGs from different individuals while highlighting similarities within ECGs. This model was previously trained and validated on individuals who underwent clinical cardiopulmonary exercise testing at Massachusetts General Hospital from 2011 to 2017. Deep ECG-VO 2 incorporates patient age, sex, BMI, and a deep learning–based representation of the resting 12-lead ECG to provide an estimate of peak VO 2 with favorable accuracy against gold standard cardiopulmonary exercise testing (mean error ∼6 mL/kg/min) compared to linear models or standard reference equations. We applied Deep ECG-VO 2 on all ECG tracings from our study sample (details summarized in ). No participants from the original Deep ECG VO 2 training set were used in this analysis. Baseline clinical covariates Clinical covariates, including demographic data, pregnancy characteristics, vital signs, comorbidities, smoking status, and prevalent cardiovascular disease (CVD), were assessed from 1 year preceding the start of the pregnancy episode (gestational age 0) to the end of the first trimester of pregnancy (gestational age 13 weeks), except for smoking status, which was assessed as smoking any time prior to delivery. Maternal age was defined at delivery. Gestation type, including single and multiple gestation, was ascertained using International Classification of Diseases (ICD) or Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) codes. Gravidity and parity were ascertained from clinical notes using regular expressions, as previously described. Prevalent comorbidities, including diabetes mellitus (DM) and hyperlipidemia, were ascertained based on the presence of at least one ICD, CPT, and/or electronic health record–specific diagnosis code corresponding to the relevant disease. Hypertension (HTN) treatment was assessed as antihypertensive medication use beginning 1 year prior to the start of the pregnancy episode (gestational age 0) to the end of the first trimester. Smoking status was ascertained from formal smoking questionnaire data documented in the electronic health record. Prevalent CVD was defined as clinically diagnosed CVD documented in the electronic health record prior to or at the index pregnancy/ECG (eg, venous thromboembolism, cerebrovascular disease/transient ischemic attack, HF/cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, or prior MI). Missingness was present for several baseline covariates, including BMI, SBP, smoking status, alcohol use, parity, and gravidity, and is summarized in the legend. BMI and SBP data were extracted from clinical encounters. Due to significant missingness (>40%) of baseline vital signs in the electronic health record, a natural language processing algorithm and manual review were used to recover BMI and SBP data from unstructured notes. For pregnancies with multiple BMI and SBP recordings, we selected the BMI and SBP value most proximal to 13 weeks of gestation. Primary analyses were restricted to pregnancies with available BMI and SBP after this recovery process. Pregnancy-related cardiovascular complications Pregnancy-related CV complications were defined as the composite of severe HDP, major adverse CV events (MACE), and maternal death, as assessed from the end of the first trimester (gestational age 13 weeks) to 1 year postpartum. Severe HDP included preeclampsia with and without severe features, eclampsia, and hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets syndrome, and was ascertained by previously validated code sets after 20 weeks’ gestation with positive predictive value ≥85%. MACE included MI, HF including peripartum cardiomyopathy, vascular dissection, thromboembolism (venous, pulmonary, and systemic), cerebrovascular disease (transient ischemic attack, hemorrhagic, and ischemic cerebrovascular accident), ventricular and atrial arrythmias, and cardiac arrest. Clinical definitions for MI, HF, and stroke were defined codes using previously validated code sets with positive predictive value ≥85%, while remaining MACE events were defined using previously published ICD-9, ICD-10, or CPT code groupings. , Maternal death was ascertained from the Social Security Death Index or Mass General Brigham internal documentation of death, with cause of death manually adjudicated by a physician reviewer. Statistical analysis The distribution of ECG-estimated peak VO 2 was first winsorized to limit leverage of outliers on analyses, setting the minimum VO 2 as 5 mL/kg/min and maximum as 60 mL/kg/min (24 patients had VO 2 <5 mL/kg/min and 0 patients had VO 2 >60 mL/kg/min before winsorizing to 5 and 60, respectively). Baseline characteristics were tabulated across the total sample, according to ECG-estimated VO 2 quartile, and above and below VO 2 of 14 mL/kg/min (moderate/high vs low fitness) and compared using t -tests, chi-squared tests, or Wilcoxon rank sum tests, as appropriate. In primary analyses, we examined the association of ECG-estimated peak VO 2 with incident pregnancy-related CV complications using mixed-effects logistic regression models with a random intercept per patient to account for within-individual correlation across repeated pregnancies and covariates modeled as fixed effects, consistent with standard analytic practice in obstetrics cohort studies. , Models were first adjusted for maternal age at delivery, and then further adjusted for SBP, HTN medications, DM, and gestation type (singleton or multiple gestation). Covariates were ascertained during the baseline period, defined as 1 year before pregnancy through 13 weeks’ gestation. Because prepregnancy BMI is used in the derivation of ECG-estimated VO 2 , prepregnancy BMI was not included as a covariate in the primary model, but we fit an exploratory model with additional adjustment for prepregnancy BMI. In secondary analyses, we examined the association of ECG-estimated peak VO 2 with incident HDP and MACE, separately. Two-sided P values <0.05 were considered statistically significant. Statistical analyses were performed using R Version 4.4.0. Results We ascertained ECG-estimated peak VO 2 for 3,650 pregnancies from 3,437 individuals (mean maternal age at delivery 33 ± 6 years; 1933/3,650 [53%] non-Hispanic White). Median ECG-estimated VO 2 was 27.0 mL/kg/min (IQR: 21.9-31.2 mL/kg/min) ( ), with 208/3,650 (6%) pregnancies with low estimated cardiorespiratory fitness as defined as VO 2 ≤14 mL/kg/min. Median follow-up time from start of pregnancy (estimated date of conception) was 1.7 years (IQR: 1.6-1.8 years). Baseline characteristics stratified by ECG-estimated VO 2 quartile are displayed in (comparisons with the original Deep ECG-VO 2 cohort are displayed in ). Clinical indications for ECG testing are summarized in . Compared with individuals in the highest ECG-VO 2 quartile, women in the lowest quartile had significantly greater burden of CV comorbidities (obesity: 668/913 [73%] vs 15/913 [2%], HTN: 296/913 [32%] vs 87/913 [10%], DM: 137/913 [15%] vs 22/913 [2%], and hyperlipidemia: 200/913 [22%] vs 108/913 [12%], P < 0.001) and prevalent CVD (151/913 [17%] vs 107/913 [12%], P = 0.019), although 164/913 (18%) of women in the lowest ECG-VO 2 quartile had no traditional CV risk factors. Maternal age, gestation type, gravidity, and parity were similar across VO 2 quartiles. Similarly, women with low ECG-estimated cardiorespiratory fitness (VO 2 ≤14 mL/kg/min) had greater prevalence of cardiac comorbidities and prevalent CVD compared with women with moderate/high cardiorespiratory fitness (VO 2 >14 mL/kg/min) ( ). Among 3,650 pregnancies, 723 (20%; 95% CI: 19%-21%) developed incident pregnancy-related CV complications between 13 weeks of gestation to 1 year postpartum, including 421/3,650 (12%; 95% CI: 10%-13%) severe HDP, 358/3,650 (10%; 95% CI: 9%-11%) MACE, and 2/3,650 (0.05%; 95% CI: 0.01%-0.20%) maternal deaths. Association of ECG-estimated peak VO<sub>2</sub> with incident pregnancy-related CV complications We examined the association of ECG-estimated peak VO 2 with incident pregnancy-related CV complications. In both age- and multivariable-adjusted analyses, ECG-estimated VO 2 was associated with pregnancy-related CV complications (multivariable-adjusted OR adj per 1-U lower metabolic equivalent [MET = 3.5 mL/kg/min] 1.09; 95% CI: 1.03-1.17; P < 0.01) ( ). Specifically, compared with individuals in the highest ECG-estimated peak VO 2 quartile, women in the lowest quartile had >60% higher odds of developing a pregnancy-related CV complication during pregnancy (OR adj 1.61; 95% CI: 1.13-2.30; P = 0.008) ( ). Notably, results were attenuated when further adjusting for BMI in exploratory multivariable-adjusted analyses (OR: 1.35; 95% CI: 0.86-2.10; P = 0.19) ( ). Additional exploratory analyses further adjusting for smoking status demonstrated similar directional trends with primary analyses, but associations were attenuated and no longer statistically significant ( ). Sensitivity analyses restricting to first pregnancies available in PADME and to pregnancies with ECGs performed within the first trimester of pregnancy showed results consistent with our primary analyses ( and ). Finally, as HDP is also a risk factor for pregnancy-related CV complication, we performed sensitivity analyses restricting to pregnancies among nulliparous women ( ) and excluding pregnancies with prevalent HDP among multiparous women ( ), with similar results to our primary analyses. In secondary analyses, we examined the association of ECG-estimated peak VO 2 with severe HDP and MACE outcomes separately ( ). We found that ECG-estimated VO 2 was significantly associated with future risk of severe HDP in both age- and multivariable-adjusted analyses (multivariable-adjusted OR adj 1.11 per 1-U lower MET, 95% CI: 1.04-1.18; P = 0.002). Similarly, women in the lowest ECG-VO 2 quartile had significantly greater odds of developing severe HDP vs women in the highest quartile (OR adj 1.59; 95% CI: 1.12-2.25; P = 0.009, ).
