We found that ECG-estimated VO 2 was significantly associated with future risk of severe HDP in both age- and multivariable-adjusted analyses (multivariable-adjusted OR adj 1.11 per 1-U lower MET, 95% CI: 1.04-1.18; P = 0.002). Similarly, women in the lowest ECG-VO 2 quartile had significantly greater odds of developing severe HDP vs women in the highest quartile (OR adj 1.59; 95% CI: 1.12-2.25; P = 0.009, ). ECG-estimated peak VO 2 was not significantly associated with incident MACE (OR adj 1.06 per 1-U lower MET; 95% CI: 0.97-1.17; P = 0.21) ( ). When examining the association of ECG-estimated cardiorespiratory fitness with incident pregnancy-related CV complications using a clinically significant cutoff of peak VO 2 ≤14 mL/kg/min, risk of incident pregnancy-related CV complications was higher among low (ECG-VO 2 ≤14 mL/kg/min) vs moderate-to-high cardiorespiratory fitness (ECG-VO 2 >14 mL/kg/min), although the association was not statistically significant (OR adj 1.39; 95% CI: 0.86-2.25; P = 0.17) ( ). Subgroup analyses We examined the prognostic value of ECG-VO 2 for incident pregnancy-related CV complications in key subgroups including race/ethnicity, maternal age (≥35 vs <35 years of age), obesity status (BMI <30 vs ≥30 kg/m 2 ), and prevalent CVD ( , ). We found that the associations of ECG-estimated peak VO 2 with incident pregnancy-related CV complications were comparable for race/ethnicity, maternal age, and prevalent CVD subgroups. Notably, heterogeneity of effect was observed for obesity status, with ECG-estimated peak VO 2 more associated with incident pregnancy-related CV complications among women without obesity vs with obesity (OR adj per 1-U lower MET 1.13; 95% CI: 1.02-1.24 in women without obesity vs OR adj 1.09; 95% CI: 0.95-1.24 in women with obesity, P int = 0.03) ( ). Discussion Among 3,650 pregnancies in a contemporary electronic health record–based pregnancy cohort, we demonstrate that cardiorespiratory fitness estimated using deep learning–enabled analysis of the 12-lead ECG before the second trimester is associated with future pregnancy-related CV complications. Our findings are 3-fold. First, lower ECG-derived peak VO 2 is associated with a higher risk of developing a composite of pregnancy-related CV complications, including severe HDP, MACE, and maternal death, although the magnitude of effect was attenuated after adjustment for BMI. Second, women with lower ECG-derived peak VO 2 had greater burden of cardiometabolic disease, including higher BMI and greater prevalence of obesity, HTN, DM, and hyperlipidemia, although nearly 20% of women with low ECG-estimated peak VO 2 were free of any traditional CV risk factors. Finally, ECG-estimated VO 2 was similarly associated with incident pregnancy-related CV complications among women in key subgroups, including race/ethnicity, maternal age, obesity status, and prevalent CVD. Taken together, artificial intelligence–enabled analysis of ECGs performed early in antepartum care may enable efficient and scalable risk prognostication for identifying pregnancies at high risk for developing CV complications. One of the key barriers to reducing preventable pregnancy-related deaths is failure to identify high-risk women early in pregnancy. Currently available risk stratification tools for pregnancy-related CV complications are limited to individuals with pre-existing CVD and/or require extensive disease-specific information or imaging data that are not routinely captured in obstetric populations. , , , Furthermore, current guidance for selecting patients for low-dose aspirin for preeclampsia prevention relies on risk factor-based criteria (eg, prior preeclampsia, chronic HTN, multifetal gestation, etc) and does not incorporate direct physiologic measures of CV reserve. , In this context, ECG-VO 2 could serve as a scalable, low-burden complement to existing risk frameworks by providing an early-pregnancy estimate of cardiorespiratory fitness from a routinely available test for individuals both with and without preexisting CVD and those who do not meet traditional high-risk criteria. Cardiorespiratory fitness, as quantified by cardiopulmonary exercise testing-derived peak VO 2 , has been shown to predict CV outcomes in pregnant populations. , , For example, in a prospective study of 43 women, lower cardiorespiratory fitness measured by cycle-ergometer cardiopulmonary exercise testing was associated with a greater risk of HDP. Similarly, among 33 pregnant women with congenital heart disease who underwent cardiopulmonary exercise testing prior to delivery, lower peak VO 2 was independently associated with adverse maternal events, including HF, sustained arrythmias, cardiac arrest, stroke, and maternal death. By contrast, in a large population-based cohort with prepregnancy treadmill testing, cardiorespiratory fitness was not independently associated with adverse birth outcomes, highlighting that observed associations may depend on outcome definition, timing of fitness assessment, and covariate adjustment. Despite these data, routine ascertainment of peak VO 2 is not feasible for broad pregnancy risk stratification due to limited availability, significant cost, and the need for expert interpretation. , Although exercise testing has been shown to be safe in pregnancy, there is reticence among providers to refer pregnant patients for exercise testing because of perceived maternal-fetal

cardiac arrest, stroke, and maternal death. By contrast, in a large population-based cohort with prepregnancy treadmill testing, cardiorespiratory fitness was not independently associated with adverse birth outcomes, highlighting that observed associations may depend on outcome definition, timing of fitness assessment, and covariate adjustment. Despite these data, routine ascertainment of peak VO 2 is not feasible for broad pregnancy risk stratification due to limited availability, significant cost, and the need for expert interpretation. , Although exercise testing has been shown to be safe in pregnancy, there is reticence among providers to refer pregnant patients for exercise testing because of perceived maternal-fetal safety concerns. , , To circumvent these challenges, our group previously developed Deep ECG-VO 2 , a deep learning model that can accurately estimate peak VO 2 from the resting 12-lead ECG. In the present study, lower ECG-estimated VO 2 is associated with pregnancy-related CV complications, including severe HDP, MACE, and maternal death, with women in the lowest quartile of ECG-estimated peak VO 2 experiencing >60% greater odds of developing a CV complication during pregnancy compared with those in the highest quartile. We hypothesize that this association reflects reduced integrated CV reserve and cardiometabolic health, which may predispose to maladaptive hemodynamic adaptation and endothelial/vascular dysfunction during pregnancy, pathways that are closely linked to severe HDP. Consistent with this, the observed association between lower ECG-predicted VO 2 and pregnancy-related CV complications was most pronounced for severe HDP, with no significant association seen for incident MACE. However, it is important to acknowledge that incident MACE events were rare (n = 358), limiting power to precisely evaluate relationships with MACE. Whether cardiorespiratory fitness during pregnancy is more tightly linked to HDP-related vascular and hemodynamic physiology rather than more cardiac-centric MACE events warrants further investigation in larger prospective pregnancy cohorts. Finally, women with lower ECG-estimated VO 2 had greater burden of cardiometabolic risk, including higher BMI and higher prevalence of obesity, HTN, DM, and hyperlipidemia. Furthermore, inclusion of BMI in multivariable models attenuated the primary associations between ECG-VO 2 and pregnancy-related CV complications, underscoring the close relationship between estimated fitness and adiposity-related risk and supporting ECG-estimated cardiorespiratory fitness as a single integrated measure of underlying cardiometabolic health. Notably, nearly 20% of individuals in the lowest ECG-VO 2 quartile had no documented traditional CV risk factors. This may reflect true heterogeneity in cardiorespiratory fitness among younger women, as supported by cardiopulmonary exercise testing reference standards showing wide distributions of peak VO 2 in women of reproductive age, or clinical selection as ECGs in our sample were often obtained for cardiopulmonary symptoms that may indicate reduced functional capacity even in the absence of documented comorbidity. Although prospective pregnancy cohorts with systematic ECG ascertainment will be important to clarify this phenotype, these findings suggest that ECG-VO 2 may capture additional physiologic vulnerability beyond routinely ascertained cardiometabolic comorbidity. Currently, routine 12-lead ECG testing is not recommended during antenatal care and is largely performed in women presenting with cardiopulmonary symptoms or among women with a history of existing CVD or prior pregnancy-related CV complication. We contend that integration of Deep ECG-VO 2 into routine antenatal screening could further refine risk assessment of CV risk among healthy individuals without symptoms. Indeed, we showed in sensitivity analyses that ECG-estimated VO 2 is an accurate prognosticator of pregnancy-related CV risk even among individuals without prior complications during pregnancy. A key window of opportunity to integrate widespread ECG testing into antepartum care is during first trimester prenatal screening. We therefore examined the prognostic value of Deep ECG-VO 2 for pregnancy-related CV complications during the first trimester and found that ECG-estimated peak VO 2 is similarly associated with incident CV complications during pregnancy in sensitivity analyses restricted to pregnancies with ECGs performed within the first trimester only. Finally, we found that Deep ECG-VO 2 provides prognostic value for pregnancy-related CV complications in key vulnerable subgroups, including women of non-White race and without prevalent CVD. In the United States, non-White women experience substantially higher rates of maternal mortality than White women, with rates of maternal death 3 to 4 times higher among Black women vs White women, emphasizing the need for risk stratification tools with generalizability across diverse populations. , We demonstrate that ECG-estimated VO 2 was associated with pregnancy-related CV complications among both non-White women and White women, highlighting generalizability as a key strength of our model. We similarly found that ECG-estimated cardiorespiratory fitness was associated with pregnancy-related CV complications among women without prevalent CVD and without obesity. Identifying women without traditional risk factors like obesity may discern masked risk for adverse CV events during pregnancy. Furthermore, while studies consistently demonstrate that women with established CVD are at highest risk of developing CV-related complications during pregnancy, most maternal morbidity and mortality occur among patients without established diagnoses of CVD. , , , The ability

We similarly found that ECG-estimated cardiorespiratory fitness was associated with pregnancy-related CV complications among women without prevalent CVD and without obesity. Identifying women without traditional risk factors like obesity may discern masked risk for adverse CV events during pregnancy. Furthermore, while studies consistently demonstrate that women with established CVD are at highest risk of developing CV-related complications during pregnancy, most maternal morbidity and mortality occur among patients without established diagnoses of CVD. , , , The ability of ECG-estimated VO 2 to accurately capture risk among women without prevalent CVD is an important strength as women without prevalent CVD are less likely to be screened and/or closely monitored for the development of pregnancy-related CV complications. Taken together, identification of pregnant individuals at higher risk for CV complications using ECG-VO 2 may enable more targeted prevention approaches, including more frequent monitoring, enhanced access to multidisciplinary care, and provision of preventive therapies (eg, low-dose aspirin for preeclampsia prophylaxis). , Potential downstream actions could include earlier and/or more frequent maternal–fetal medicine and cardio-obstetrics follow-up, closer surveillance of blood pressure and cardiopulmonary symptoms, and lower thresholds for additional evaluation when clinically indicated (eg, natriuretic peptides, echocardiography, or ambulatory rhythm monitoring for dyspnea, edema, or palpitations). Study limitations Our study has several limitations worth noting. First, Deep ECG-VO 2 was derived and validated in fitter men and nonpregnant women, and to date had not been extrapolated to pregnant populations. Second, peak VO 2 was estimated from ECGs obtained for clinical indications, which may introduce selection bias and result in potentially higher event rates in our sample. Compared with the parent PADME pregnancy electronic health record cohort from which our analysis sample was drawn, our sample demonstrated a higher burden of CV comorbidities and greater prevalence of existing CVD, highlighting the need for prospective validation of Deep ECG-VO 2 among pregnant individuals using protocolized ECGs. Notably, availability of prospective pregnancy cohorts with systematic ECG ascertainment is limited, precluding our ability to include an unselected healthy control population. Third, missing data were present for several baseline covariates. Although missingness for most variables examined was not associated with the primary outcome, missingness in parity and gravidity was associated with the outcome, suggesting that pregnancies with incomplete obstetric history data may have differed systematically from those with complete data. Fourth, we examined ECGs prior to 13 weeks’ gestation to standardize exposure assessment and to capture risk information before the onset of many pregnancy-related complications. Because CV reserve is progressively stressed through pregnancy and underlying disease may become symptomatic in the late second trimester, future work should reevaluate whether serial ECG-VO 2 assessment and/or later-pregnancy ECG-VO 2 measurements may provide additional prognostic value beyond early pregnancy alone. Fifth, longitudinal postpartum blood pressure trajectories were not systematically available for incorporation in our primary analyses. Furthermore, because persistent postpartum HTN characterized by elevated diastolic blood pressure may be more prevalent after HDP than isolated SBP elevation, future studies with standardized blood pressure ascertainment across pregnancy and the postpartum period are needed to determine whether incorporating diastolic blood pressure (DBP)-based definitions and postpartum BP trajectories improves performance and clinical utility of ECG-VO 2 -informed risk stratification. Finally, our sample comprised individuals from a single geographical location who predominantly received their obstetrical care in tertiary and quaternary settings, limiting generalizability to diverse populations, particularly as many deliveries occur in community or low-risk settings. Conclusions In a contemporary pregnancy electronic health record sample, we show that lower estimated cardiorespiratory fitness from a validated deep learning model based on the resting 12-lead ECG is associated with higher risk of pregnancy-related CV complications, including severe HDP, MACE, and maternal death. Integration of 12-lead ECG testing into routine antepartum care may identify women with silent risk and enhance early prevention efforts to ameliorate the burden of adverse CV outcomes in pregnant women. Perspectives COMPETENCY IN MEDICAL KNOWLEDGE 1: Cardiorespiratory fitness estimated from the resting 12-lead ECG, derived from a validated deep learning model, is associated with incident pregnancy-related CV complications and may help identify high-risk patients preconception or early in pregnancy. COMPETENCY IN MEDICAL KNOWLEDGE 2: Cardiorespiratory fitness is an established marker of CV reserve and adverse outcomes. This study extends its prognostic relevance to pregnancy-related CV complications using a scalable, ECG-based surrogate. TRANSLATIONAL OUTLOOK: Integration Deep-ECG VO 2 into antepartum care may help identify women are at highest risk of developing pregnancy-related CV complications and support targeted surveillance and preventive strategies. chunks.content: 1 Introduction: the Rise of myocarditis post-COVID-19 The global COVID-19 pandemic, driven by multiple variant strains of Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), has exerted unprecedented consequences on public health systems and the global economy. As reported by the World Health Organization (WHO) COVID-19 dashboard ( https://data.who.int/dashboards/covid19/cases ), by November 23, 2025 over 778 million confirmed cases of SARS-CoV-2 infection and over 7.1 million COVID-19-related deaths have been document worldwide. Though early global estimates during the initial phase of the pandemic reported a mortality rate of about 4 % [ ], a rapid and widespread implementation of evolving critical care practices, targeted antiviral therapies, and messenger RNA (mRNA)-based vaccines has led to a substantial global decline in infection rates and improved mortality outcomes in the post-COVID-19 era. Despite these advances, a growing population of COVID-19 survivors continues to experience persistent, multi-organ complications, collectively described as post-acute COVID-19 syndrome (or post-acute COVID-19 sequelae (PACS) or long-haul COVID [ , , ]. Among the spectrum of long-term cardiovascular complications associated with SARS-CoV-2 infection, myocarditis has emerged as a potentially life-threatening health complication in COVID-19. Studies have indicated around a 15-fold increased risk of developing myocarditis from SARS-CoV-2 infection in comparison with other causes [ , ]. A multifaceted study conducted by Boehmer et al. (2021) including 2116 COVID-19 patients developed myocarditis within one month (89.6 %), or one (6.6 %) or more than two months (3.9 %) after infection [ ]. In another study conducted by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the overall incidence of SARS-CoV-2 infection related myocarditis cases in the United States has been estimated at around 150 per 100,000 individuals in comparison to 9 per 100,000 individuals in non-COVID cases during the same time period [ ]. In contrast to these studies, an autopsy-based study performed by Halushka et al. (2020) reported a modest incidence (7.2 %) of clinically significant myocarditis amongst 277 postmortem cases [ ]. In addition, rare cases of myocarditis have also been reported following COVID-19 mRNA vaccination; however, vaccine-associated cases are generally mild, self-limiting, and occur at a substantially lower incidence than myocarditis following SARS-CoV-2 infection [ ]. Myocarditis is defined as a non-familial inflammatory manifestation of the myocardium with or without myocyte necrosis, and may extend to involve the pericardium and endocardium [ , ]. It remains one of the leading causes of unanticipated cardiac death in both adults and children worldwide. When present, myocarditis is often associated with an unfavourable prognosis, including progression to ventricular dysfunction and cardiac failure [ , , , ]. Based on pathological features and severity, COVID-19-associated myocarditis can be categorized as acute or chronic inflammatory [ , ]. Acute myocarditis typically presents within first few weeks (2–4 weeks) following infection or onset-of symptoms, and is characterized by abrupt myocardial inflammation, ventricular dysfunction, myocyte necrosis, myocardial edema, and, in severe cases, cardiogenic shock [ , ]. In some cases, acute myocardial injury may progress to dilated cardiomyopathy, marked by chronic inflammation and disruption of myocytes, either with or without ongoing viral persistence [ ]. Chronic myocarditis, in contrast, reflects a sustained inflammatory response persisting beyond 3 months after the initial presentation, often accompanied by secondary myocardial fibrosis in the absence of myocyte necrosis [ ]. Emerging evidence suggests that direct invasion of the myocardium by SARS-CoV-2 can induce myocarditis and myocardial injury via interaction with host's angiotensin-converting enzyme II (ACE2), the primary protein receptor mediating viral tropism [ ]. In COVID-19 patients, myocarditis typically manifests during the post-acute phase of infection and presents clinically with unexplained congestive heart failure, persistent chest pain, arrhythmias, heart palpitations, dyspnea, syncope and sudden cardiac death [ ]. Given acute systemic stressors such as infection, hypoxemia, anemia, metabolic derangements and others, it is common for COVID-19 patients to exhibit myocardial injury, which is often reflected by elevated cardiac biomarkers (such as Troponin) and abnormal electrocardiogram (ECG) and cardiac imaging (echocardiographic or cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (cMRI)) findings [ , ]. Though limited in scope, autopsy and endomyocardial biopsy (EMB) studies usually demonstrate hallmark features of myocardial inflammation, including myocardial infiltration by mononuclear cells, diffuse myocardial edema and cardiomyocyte damage [ , ]. Despite growing awareness, the true burden of myocarditis remains substantially underestimated due to the lack of universally standardized diagnostic guidelines on myocarditis and limited systematic surveillance, especially in the younger population. Estimates based on the International Classification of Diseases (9th revision; ICD-9) codes suggest an estimated annual global incidence of about 22 cases per 10000 individuals [ ]. The most recent Global Burden of Disease's pre-pandemic figures have projected the worldwide prevalence of myocarditis and cardiomyopathy ranging from 10.2 to 105.6 cases per 100,000 individuals, with an estimated 1.8 million new cases occurring each year [ , ]. Estimates based on the International Classification of Diseases (9th revision; ICD-9) codes suggest an estimated annual global incidence of about 22 cases per 10000 individuals [ ]. The most recent Global Burden of Disease's pre-pandemic figures have projected the worldwide prevalence of myocarditis and cardiomyopathy ranging from 10.2 to 105.6 cases per 100,000 individuals, with an estimated 1.8 million new cases occurring each year [ , ]. More recent investigations have demonstrated that about 7–28 % of patients with acute COVID-19 experience myocardial injury, with a proportion of recovered patients subsequently developing SARS-CoV-2-mediated myocarditis [ , ]. Although COVID-19-associated myocarditis has been widely reported, the existing literature remains divided across clinical, molecular, and genetic domains. The complex mechanistic interplay by which viral tropism, host immune dysregulation, and genetic predisposition converge to underly disease onset, influence severity and long-term outcomes remain elusive. This review, therefore, seeks to provide a comprehensive synthesis of COVID-19-associated myocarditis by bridging different domains – clinical manifestations, molecular mechanisms, and genetic determinants. By consolidating current knowledge on pathophysiology, diagnostic strategies and emerging therapeutic strategies, this work aims to elucidate the existing knowledgebase on COVID-19-associated myocarditis, address existing debates, highlight translational opportunities, and underscore the importance of early diagnosis and personalized management to mitigate adverse outcomes such as heart failure, sudden cardiac arrest, and cardiac death. 2 Clinical presentation COVID-19-related myocarditis has a wide range of clinical manifestations. Mild symptoms like exhaustion, palpitation, chest pain, or dyspnea with exertion are common in many. Even in individuals with moderate or asymptomatic condition, these symptoms may appear days to weeks after infection, and some exhibit primarily subclinical imaging findings in cMRI. While others experience moderate illness, which manifests as echocardiographic left ventricular dysfunction, increased cardiac biomarkers, and ECG abnormalities. About 7–20 % of COVID-19 hospitalized patients have this kind of cardiac involvement [ ]. According to a Chinese cohort (December 2022–June 2023), approximately 32 % of patients had lower left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF; <50 %) before admission; the majority of these patients recovered with corticosteroids or supportive treatment. Fulminant myocarditis, which can result in arrhythmias, cardiogenic shock, or abrupt death, can occur at the end. The prevalence of SARS-CoV-2 fulminant presentation has been reported at 38.9 % in patients [ ]. Approximately 25 % of patients in a case series needed mechanical support or inotropes, but the majority regained systolic function [ ]. Diffuse hypokinesis, a significantly decreased ejection fraction (less than 25–45 %), and right ventricular involvement or pericardial effusion are all echocardiography findings in fulminant patients [ ]. Importantly, post-acute myocarditis could go unnoticed; however, weeks after the original infection, delayed dysfunction or chronic symptoms may appear [ ]. Researchers hypothesize that factors, including acute coronary syndrome, demand ischemia, microvascular ischemic injury, cellular stress and hypoxia, and comorbidities (including cardiovascular diseases, hypertension, and metabolic syndrome), contribute to the myocardial insults [ ]. 3 Pathogenesis of COVID-19-associated and COVID-19 vaccination associated myocarditis 3.1 SARS-CoV-2 tropism in the human body After gaining entry into the human respiratory tract, SARS-CoV-2 can invade the host's ciliated columnar cells of the respiratory tract, pneumocytes and cardiomyocytes ( (A)). The viral tropism is facilitated by the host transmembrane protease serine 2 (TMPRSS2)-mediated viral spike proteins (S-protein) priming with host cell membrane ACE2 receptors [ ]. One of the characteristic features of the SARS-CoV-2 S-protein is the presence of a four amino acid polybasic or multi-basic insert, a potential cleavage site for the furin protease (a proprotein convertase), at the S1/S2 junction and the S 2 ’ site [ , ]. Viral internalization into the target host cells encompasses activation of the viral S-protein, which involves its host furin-mediated proteolytic cleavage at the S1/S2 junction into S1 and S2 polyproteins [ , ]. While the S1 interacts with the ACE2 receptor, the S2 is involved in the fusion of the viral envelope with the host cell membrane [ ]. Receptor binding and cleavage of S-protein affect tropism and pathogenicity of SARS-CoV-2. Furthermore, the SARS-CoV-2 spread depends on the activity of host TMPRSS2, which is required for SARS-CoV-2 S-protein priming to the host ACE2 receptors [ ]. The viral S1- and S2-polyproteins are cleaved by TMPRSS2 and/or endosomal cysteine protease Cathepsin L. After viral S-protein priming, the virus enters the host target cells via clathrin-mediated endocytosis ( (B)) [ ]. The positive-strand RNA is released into cytoplasm of the host cell, where it undergoes replication to generate genomic copies using virally expressed RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. These copies are translated into polyproteins and structural proteins using the translational machinery of the host cell. After replication of the viral genome followed by the expression of viral structural and non-structural proteins, assembly of the viral component and envelope begins in the Golgi apparatus of the host cell. The immature virions migrate to the endoplasmic reticulum and fuses with the host cell membrane for release. 3.2 Pathogenesis of cardiac involvement in SARS-CoV-2 infection The pathogenic mechanisms underpinning cardiac involvement, especially myocarditis, in patients with SARS-CoV-2 infection remain elusive and are likely multifactorial. However, it may reflect a process of replication and dissemination of the SARS-CoV-2 virus from the infected respiratory tract to the cardiomyocytes via the blood or lymphatic system, where the virus could trigger an inflammatory shock leading to myocardial injury ( (C)). Evidence supports two non-mutually exclusive mechanisms, including direct viral-mediated myocardial injury and indirect immune-driven inflammation [ , ]. 3.2.1 Direct viral invasion versus immune-mediated myocardial damage in SARS-CoV-2 infection Following primary infection of the respiratory epithelium, replication and systemic dissemination of the SARS-CoV-2 virus into the cardiomyocytes via hematogenous or lymphatic routes trigger an inflammatory shock leading to local myocardial inflammation and injury. This process may culminate in myocyte necrosis, interstitial edema, and impaired contractility, particularly in severe or uncontrolled infection. Alternatively, and more prominently, COVID-19-associated myocarditis may be invoked by the maladaptive host immune response to viral invasion rather than direct viral cytotoxicity. Excessive activation of both innate and adaptive immune responses against the SARS-CoV-2 S-glycoprotein and recognition of the viral mRNA as an antigen, provoke cytokine storm (a proinflammatory cytokine surge), deregulated thrombo-inflammation, thrombotic microangiopathy and endothelial dysfunction [ , ]. Elevated levels of pro-inflammatory mediators (including interleukins (IL) such as IL-1β, IL-6, Tumour Necrosis Factor-α (TNF-α), and Interferon-γ (IFN-γ)), a hallmark of the cytokine storm, impairs vascular integrity, encourages coagulation, and contribute to multi-organ dysfunction, including myocardial involvement. Dysregulated interferon responses, persistent innate immune activation, and impaired adaptive immune resolution are key features of the maladaptive immune response. Furthermore, autoimmune mechanisms may further amplify myocardial injury. Processes such as bystander activation, epitope dissemination, and molecular mimicry have been implicated in post-infection autoimmunity. SARS-CoV-2 and surfactant proteins share peptide motifs, which may promote cross-reactive immune responses and the generation of autoantibodies (such as anti-inflammatory and anti-cytokine antibodies), contributing to sustained myocardial inflammation. Similar immune-mediated mechanisms have been described in other post-viral syndromes, such as Guillain-Barré syndrome, raising the possibility of autoimmune contributions to COVID-19-associated myocarditis [ ]. Whether COVID-19-induced myocarditis stems from direct viral-mediated cytopathic effects in the cardiomyocyte or an uncontrolled cardiogenic inflammation remains uncertain [ , ]. 3.2.2 Impact of SARS-CoV-2 infection on myocardial tissue: fibrosis, remodeling, and functional impairment SARS-CoV-2 can directly infect cardiac cells, including cardiomyocytes, pericytes, and endothelial cells, by binding to the ACE2 receptor leading to cardiomyocyte injury, endothelial dysfunction, and microvascular thrombosis [ ]. These events initiate a cascade of cytokine-mediated inflammatory processes (involving IL-1β, IL-6, Transforming Growth Factor-β1 (TGF-β1)) which mediate interstitial remodeling and fibroblast activation within the myocardium leading to myocardial fibrosis. Further, elevated TGF-β1 and SMAD3 signaling promote collagen synthesis through NOX-mediated ROS and CaMKII pathways, significantly raising the expression of profibrotic genes in COVID-19 affected left ventricular (LV) tissue. Through cytokines (IL-4, IL-13, IL-33) and mechanisms underlying endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EndMT), cells including macrophages, T-lymphocytes, and endothelial cells augment fibroblast activation. The cMRI studies frequently reveal diffuse interstitial fibrosis (reflected by extracellular volume expansion) as well as focal replacement fibrosis (detected by late gadolinium enhancement (LGE)). While diffuse fibrosis may partially regress over time (several months), LGE is observed in as many as 60 % of hospitalized patients with COVID-19 [ ]. Pathologic remodeling, which includes ventricular dilatation, hypertrophy, and interstitial scarring, mimics the mechanism of infarction-based remodeling and results in increased stiffness, decreased compliance, and poor systolic/diastolic function. Even in patients with preserved ejection fraction, subclinical dysfunction, manifested as impaired strain or perfusion abnormalities, may persist long after clinical recovery, potentially predisposing individuals to long-term cardiovascular morbidity [ ]. 4 Pathophysiological mechanisms involved in COVID-19 mRNA vaccine associated myocarditis Reports of myocarditis in symptomatic and asymptomatic individuals following mRNA-based COVID-19 vaccination have also raised public health concern regarding the potential safety of these vaccines [ ]. Although post-vaccination myocarditis was considered as a rare adverse complication in the pre-COVID-19 times, an increase in number of post-vaccination myocarditis reports have emerged, especially in young individuals and adolescent males following administration of the BNT162b2-mRNA (Comirnaty®, Pfizer-BioNTech) and mRNA-1273 (Moderna) and Ad26.COV2.S (Johnson & Johnson-Janssen) COVID-19 vaccines [ , ]. The biological basis of COVID-19 mRNA vaccine-associated myocarditis is not well understood. It can be explained as a transient, immune-mediated inflammatory response driven by an exaggerated immune response and plausible molecular mimicry [ ]. However, vaccination driven myocarditis is rare, typically mild, self-limiting, and less severe compared with myocarditis following SARS-CoV-2 infection ( ; ). Several hypotheses have been suggested to explain the plausible pathophysiological mechanisms underlying post-COVID-19 mRNA vaccination myocardial inflammation. Many of these relate heightened immune activation or dysregulated cytokine responses and modifying factors (such as genetic determinants) to the development of myocardial inflammation post-vaccination. Studies have reported an elevated circulating levels of free spike protein (unbound by anti-spike antibodies) in individuals with post-vaccine myocarditis [ ]. Whether circulating intact spike protein introduced via mRNA vaccine is pathogenic remains elusive. A growing body of evidence suggest that spike protein itself can trigger cardiogenic insults such as cardiac inflammation and pericyte dysfunction by down-regulating ACE2 expression and mediating S-signalling via CD147 receptors, or by activating integrin-mediated inflammation with hyperpermeability of the endothelial cell layer, or by limiting bioavailability of endothelial nitric oxide [ , , ]. In addition, molecular mimicry between the spike glycoprotein of SARS-CoV-2 and host self-antigens, and cross-reactivity of antibodies (released against spike proteins) with myosin heavy chain may lead to myocardial damage [ , ]. 5 Plausible genetic determinants of COVID-19-associated myocarditis Although myocarditis most often stems from an exaggerated immune or autoimmune response secondary to the viral infection, the molecular mechanism underpinning COVID-19 related myocarditis and inter-individual predisposition to myocarditis following SARS-CoV-2 infection remains poorly understood. Emerging evidence implicates host genetic factors in influencing disease onset, severity, and diverse clinical outcomes, thereby contributing to the marked heterogeneity among affected individuals [ ]. Genetic variants influencing cardiomyocyte cytoskeletal components and varied immune responses to other viral infections suggest genetic diversity among myocarditis patients. A prospective genetic analysis of three sudden death cases linked to non-SARS-CoV-2 viral myocarditis by Campuzano et al. (2015) demonstrated pathogenic variations in the desmosomal genes, including DSC2 , DSP , JPH2 , MYH7 , PKP2 and TTN , may cause disruptions in desmosome leading to myocardial inflammation underlying myocarditis [ ]. Genetic susceptibility to inflammation-induced tissue injury may provide a plausible mechanistic association between cardiomyopathy-associated variants and myocarditis-related outcomes. So far, direct evidence defining underlying genetic determinants for COVID-19-related myocarditis remains limited. Researchers across the globe are investigating the potential influence of genetic predispositions on SARS-CoV-2-related myocarditis susceptibility and prognosis through clinical investigations, animal-based experimental studies, and integrative bioinformatics approaches. Genetic variants within the human leukocyte antigen ( HLA ) loci have been proposed to drive myocarditis risk following mRNA vaccination [ , ]. A study by Bolze et al. (2022) reported an increased predisposition of HLA-A∗03:01 allele-harboring individuals to fever, chills, and stronger side effects of the Pfizer-BioNTech COMIRNATY® vaccine in patients [ ]. The authors proposed a plausible role of HLA-A∗03:01 allele in inducing pronounced symptoms after the second vaccination dose; activation of CD8 + T-cells by COVID-19 vaccines in individuals carrying this variant allele may enhance the immune response. A case study by Aguilar-Gallardo et al. (2011) reported a plausible association of a likely pathogenic, splice-site variant in the gene MYBPC3 , a gene associated with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, with lymphocytic COVID-19 related myocarditis [ ]. High-throughput transcriptomic and bioinformatics studies have further expanded insight into the molecular landscape of SARS-CoV2-associated myocarditis. Zhang et al. (2022) demonstrated the differential gene expression profile amongst different gene expression datasets representing patients with SARS-CoV-2 related myocarditis and SARS-CoV-2 infected cardiomyocytes derived from human induced pluripotent stem cells and identified ten potential drugs (including Etoposide, Ciclopirox, Genistein, Methotrexate, Lucanthone, Thalidomide, etc.) aiming COVID-19 myocarditis [ ]. They identified about 850 differentially expressed genes (DEGs), including 449 up-regulated and 401 down-regulated genes, and 159 significant genes in turquoise modules, mainly linked to cell-cycle and ubiquitin-protein hydrolysis. Out of these genes, six genes (including CDC20 , CDK1 , KIF2C , KIF20A , PBK , UBE2C ) were identified as critical genes. Another study published by Yan et al. (2024) investigated DEGs in patients with COVID-19-related myocarditis and the prognosis for ECMO support [ ]. The study identified about 229 overlapping DEGs attributed to contractile actin filament bundle, actomyosin, T-cell activation, cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterase activity, and cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction. Out of these DEGs, they found 30 screened DEGs that involved 15 intersecting hub genes and neighbouring genes, and implicated APOE , CCL2 , COL6A3 , GZMB , IL6 , IL15 , ITGA1 , ITGB3 , ITGB5 , ITGB8 , LAMA4 , LAMC2 , PTK2 , TNFRSF9 , and VCAM1 as prognostic markers/therapeutic targets in COVID-19-related myocarditis patients for preventing myocarditis progression and adverse cardiovascular events. It is to be noted that these genes are involved in key processes such as cytokine signaling and cell adhesion, both of which are critical in the progression of myocarditis and subsequent cardiovascular events. Furthermore, germline genetic variants in host genes governing SARS-CoV-2 entry, tropism and innate immunity may influence susceptibility to this viral infection [ ]. It is recently suggested that an increased expression of ACE2 receptors in susceptible hosts may likely contribute to relatively high cardiovascular involvement, especially in genetically susceptible COVID-19 patients or patients with co-morbidities [ ]. Of further interest is the role of host's dysregulated/deficient innate immunity in the pathogenesis of SARS-CoV-2-related myocarditis and varied clinical outcomes in the myocarditis patients [ ], which is characterized by disrupted expression of immunomodulators within immune cells such as eosinophils, neutrophils, mast cells, innate lymphoid cells, monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, T-lymphocytes and B-lymphocytes. While data specific to the involvement of immunomodulatory genetics in SARS-CoV-2-related myocarditis remain sparse, mechanistic insights from non-SARS-CoV-2 viral myocarditis animal models are quite informative. Studies in coxsackievirus B3-induced myocarditis mice models and patients have demonstrated that disruption in innate immunity related genes (such as TLR3 , TLR4 , MyD88 ) and associated ligands (S100A8, S100A9) may alter early interferon host responses and influences disease severity and outcomes [ , , ]. In humans, TLR3 variants have been associated with increased incidence of acute enteroviral myocarditis, while TLR3-deficient coxsackievirus mice model was observed to develop fulminant disease [ , ]. Since viral myocarditis across diverse cardiotropic viruses including SARS-CoV-2 converges on highly conserved innate immune pathways [ , , ], genetic determinants identified in these study models may be directly relevant to SARS-CoV-2-myocarditis. Genetic variants affecting these conserved pathways, therefore, may likely modulate susceptibility, disease severity, and clinical outcomes across viral myocarditis patients and warrant further investigation. 6 Incidental differences Data on the prevalence of myocarditis secondary to SARS-CoV2 infection is mainly documented as case reports, case series and retrospective studies. Several epidemiological studies have reported variable incidental rates of myocarditis in COVID-19 patients belonging to different population groups since the pandemic had ensued. However, a clear male predominance has been consistently observed in SARS-CoV-2-mediated myocarditis similar to classical viral myocarditis. Large cohort studies and registry-based analyses report that approximately 60–70 % of COVID-19-related myocarditis cases occur in males, with higher disease severity and worse short-term outcomes compared with females [ , , , , ]. Indeed, age-, sex-, region- and study-based incidental differences are quite evident among individuals with COVID-19- and COVID-19 mRNA vaccine-associated myocarditis. 6.1 Age- and sex-related incidental differences in COVID-19-associated myocarditis Myocarditis affects individuals of all ages, yet its prevalence is higher in infants and the younger population below the age of 40, with incidence reported to be higher in males than in females [ , , , ]. It is regarded as the most common predisposing etiological factor of diminished cardiac function and failure and sudden unexpected death in the pediatric population [ ]. But due to heterogeneity of the clinical manifestation, only 17 % of pediatric patients receive a confirmed diagnosis during their first clinical examination [ ]. But due to heterogeneity of the clinical manifestation, only 17 % of pediatric patients receive a confirmed diagnosis during their first clinical examination [ ]. In children aged 0–15 years, the estimated annual incidence of myocarditis is 1.95 per 100,000 children accounting for about 0.05 % of all pediatric hospitalizations [ ]. Nevertheless, the gender-based incidental differences in the pediatric population are strongly age-dependent. For children aged 0–5 years, no gender variation in the incidence rate of myocarditis is reported. In a statewide research conducted in Finland, boys aged 6–10 years were found to have a considerably higher risk of developing myocarditis than the age-matched girls [ ]. Furthermore, an analytical study by Ozierański et al. (2022) on adult clinically diagnosed myocarditis patients from Poland revealed that myocarditis is primarily a male-predominant disease, and its incidence in males decreased significantly with age [ ]. The same study suggested an increase in diagnostic rates in women of post-menopausal age, which is likely linked to decreased estrogen levels. It is believed that sex hormones are the major contributors to sex-based incidental differences in myocarditis patients [ ]. In both physiological and pathological states, sex hormones significantly influence the immune system. Studies based on virus-infected animal models have demonstrated that sex steroid hormones play an essential role in the development of myocarditis by influencing viremia and virus localization. For instance, the male sex hormone testosterone promotes viral replication and inhibits anti-inflammatory cells. The administration of exogenous testosterone may increase the expression of virus receptors on endothelial cells and myocytes and increase inflammation in the heart following viral infection. In contrast, gonadectomy demonstrated inhibition of cardiac inflammation in experimental animal models [ , ]. Furthermore, studies based on mouse models have also demonstrated the myocarditis-inducing role of progesterone. Exogenous hormonal treatment or infection of female mice under the diestrus phase of the menstrual cycle demonstrated aggravation of experimental myocarditis [ , ]. On the contrary, estrogen plays a protective role in myocarditis by mediating Th2-type immune response, stimulating inhibitory T-regulatory cells, inhibiting proinflammatory T-cells, and preventing the apoptosis of cardiomyocytes, cardiac hypertrophy, and fibrosis, as demonstrated by some molecular studies [ , , , ]. Myocarditis linked to COVID-19 affects people with underlying comorbidities, and the results might vary greatly. A comprehensive narrative of analysis of 108 fulminant cases (mean age 34.8 years) showed that 9.3 % were ≥60 and 27.8 % were ≤20; the main comorbidities were pre-existing cardiac or connective tissue illness, obesity, diabetes, hypertension, and asthma. Even though 935 patients had significantly decreased LVEF (≤40 %) upon presentation, 77.6 % of them survived with intensive treatment (such as ECMO) [ ]. In an Italian cohort, Twelve (mean age-78) of the 1169 hospitalized COVID-19 patients had suspected myocarditis; 66.7 % had previous heart disease, and 25 % passed away, indicating higher mortality and longer hospital stays in older, comorbid adults [ ]. In 2020, a nation-wide investigation of 6455 myocarditis cases from 1.66 million hospitalizations in the United States revealed that patients with myocarditis were more likely to have diabetes, CKD, CAD, and a history of myocardial infarction. In multivariate models, comorbidities did not significantly predict mortality, but older age (>50 years), ventilation, shock, and AKI were associated with worse outcomes, and in-hospital mortality was 30.5 % (compared to 13.1 %) [ ]. 6.2 Age- and sex-related incidental differences in COVID-19 mRNA vaccine related myocarditis The incidence of COVID-19 vaccine-related myocarditis varies widely based on vaccine type, age, and gender. It was in Israel for the first time that reports of vaccine-related myocarditis cases surfaced, mostly in young men and usually after the second dose of COVID-19 vaccination ( https://www.gov.il/en/departments/news/01062021-03 ; https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/israel-examining-heart-inflammation-cases-people-who-received-pfizer-covid-shot-2021-04-25 ). A six-months long active surveillance program initiated by the Israeli Ministry of Health monitored adverse events related to COVID-19 vaccines and reported 136 cases of myocarditis among a total of recorded 5.1 million vaccinated individuals and about 95 % of these had a mild course of the myocarditis [ ]. Since then, several heterogeneous reports of myocarditis related to COVID-19 vaccination have been reported across the globe [ , , , , , , , , , , , , ]. These vary due to different inclusion criteria, subject parameters, diagnostic criteria for post-vaccination myocarditis, types and doses of vaccines, and follow-up time duration after vaccination used in their studies. Most of the post-vaccination myocarditis cases were invariably reported within 2–3 days after the second dose of mRNA vaccine, and presented symptoms such as chest pain, fever, and myalgia [ ]. A cross-sectional survey by Kohli et al. (2022) reported occurrence of mRNA COVID-19 vaccine-related adverse events in children aged between 12 and 17 years from 57 pediatric institutions across the US [ ]. Myocarditis was reported in about 4.3 % of the cases of vaccine-related adverse events, and most of these were mild or moderate in severity and got resolved. 7 Outcomes of COVID-19-related myocarditis and factors influencing recovery in patients 7.1 Short-term outcomes SARS-CoV-2-related myocarditis is a serious complication of long COVID-19, often associated with poor outcomes including dilated cardiomyopathy, left ventricular dysfunction and cardiac failure [ , , ]. Although long-term data are limited, patients who are diagnosed promptly often recover well, but their recovery may be prolonged and require continued medical care after hospital discharge. Close monitoring is, therefore, essential to detect persistent or late-onset issues like chronic heart failure or clinically significant arrhythmias. Inflammation and myocardial injury are central to the pathogenesis of COVID-19-related myocarditis. Established biomarkers such as cTnl, BNP, and CRP can be useful as early-stage biomarkers of myocardial involvement, whereas emerging inflammatory and immune-nutritional indices such as CAR (C-reactive protein/albumin ratio) and PNI (Prognostic Nutritional Index) have gained attention as adjunctive prognostic markers to assess systemic inflammation, immune competence and nutritional status [ , , ]. These biomarkers may help predict recovery and predict outcomes in COVID-19-related myocarditis patients. Notably, persistently low PNI values (reflecting impaired immune-nutritional status) and elevated CAR values (reflecting heightened inflammatory burden) have been independently linked to increased mortality and disease progression among hospitalized COVID-19 patients with cardiovascular risk [ , ]. 7.2 Long-term outcomes Myocarditis is linked to an increased long-term risk of hospitalization, death, and heart failure in younger individuals with an underlying cardiovascular condition and even those who were free of cardiac episodes and heart failure medication a year after their hospital discharge, necessitating the support of pacing device or ICDs (implantable cardioverter defibrillators) in comparison to age- and sex-matched controls from the general population [ ]. The outcomes are relatively better for children with COVID-19-related myocarditis than for adults [ ]. Although children with SARS-CoV-2-linked MIS present with severe cardiac dysfunction and may require intensive care, mechanical ventilation, and sometimes extra-corporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), reports have suggested a full and quicker improvement of their heart function than people with traditional myocarditis [ , , ]. Furthermore, COVID-19-related myocarditis patients with concomitant pneumonia were found to have a worse prognosis compared with cases of isolated acute myocarditis. Early recognition and prompt initiation of therapy are critical, as delayed treatment has been associated with increased risk of persistent cardiac dysfunction and adverse long-term outcomes [ ]. Furthermore, differences in cardiovascular outcomes have been observed among patients with myocarditis of different causes, underscoring their distinct pathophysiological and prognostic profiles. Several studies have demonstrated a significantly higher risk of cardiovascular outcomes in COVID-19 patients relative to non-COVID-19 controls, with a significant risk of their development in the early post-infection period [ , ]. In contrast, a large-scale, population-based study of 154,302 Korean patients reported no significant difference in incidence of cardiovascular outcomes in hospitalized COVID-19 as well as non-COVID-19 pneumonia patients [ ]. Prolonged post-COVID-19 ailment has also been related to a higher risk of developing psychological distress in the patient group, which may be characterized by anxiety, depression, panic attacks, psychosis, sleep disorders, and/or insomnia, somatic symptoms, and post-traumatic stress disorder [ , , ]. Existing meta-analyses and large-cohort studies indicate that neuropsychiatric symptoms prevail in as much as one-third of individuals who have suffered from SARS-CoV-2 infection [ , , ]. A recent small-scale cross-sectional, survey-based study has documented high rates of depressive symptoms, general anxiety, and traumatic distress in about 44.8 %, 21.9 % and 34.4 % of the myocarditis patients (n = 96) of viral and non-viral causes with a similar incidence [ ]. Furthermore, a significant sex-based dichotomy in the prevalence and severity of psychiatric symptoms exists, with women more likely to develop depression co-occurring with cardiovascular problems than men [ , , ]. 7.3 Factors influencing recovery Recovery in patients with COVID-19-associated myocarditis may be influenced not only by factors such as age, gender, comorbidities and genetic predisposition, but also by lifestyle-related factors [ , ]. Although direct evidence regarding the impact of lifestyle on this specific condition remains limited, lifestyle modification is well-established to improve cardiovascular health and clinical outcomes in patients with cardiovascular disease. Furthermore, because COVID-19-associated myocarditis results in cardiac injury via both direct viral effects and dysregulated inflammatory responses, compounds exhibiting anti-viral, anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, cardioprotective or metabolic effects are particularly relevant. Herbal and marine natural products (such as curcumin, quercetin, marine algae polysaccharides, taurine, various polyphenols, and many others) have demonstrated promising anti-viral, anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory and cardioprotective activities [ , , , ]. Although none of these compounds are currently considered as standard therapeutic molecules, yet they are being actively investigated for their potential as adjunct therapies in the clinical management of COVID-19-associated cardiovascular complications. Some preclinical in vitro and in vivo studies have shown encouraging outcomes, supporting their further evaluation in translational and clinical research settings. It is further suggested that the risk of developing myocarditis is higher in younger population and those infected with Omicron EG.5 (Eris) variant than BA.5.2 variant of SARS-CoV-2 [ ]. 7.4 Repeated SARS-CoV-2 infection, persistent inflammation and the risk of chronic myocardial injury Repeated SARS-CoV-2 infections and the cumulative inflammatory burden are increasingly recognized as clinically important in the development and persistence of myocardial involvement. The plausible reason for reinfections can be newly emerging, immunity evading variants of SARS-CoV-2 virus [ ]. Population-level data shows that SARS-CoV-2 reinfection is associated with a higher risk of post-acute sequelae affecting multiple organ systems, including cardiovascular issues compared with no reinfection. Extended follow-up studies have reported that individuals with documented reinfection exhibited a substantially increased risks of all-cause mortality, adverse cardiovascular outcomes and sequelae in both the acute and post-acute phases of reinfection, and this risk increased with the number of infections, suggesting a cumulative risk effect of repeated inflammatory insults from SARS-CoV-2 infection [ ]. A higher incidence of reinfections and hospitalizations in unvaccinated than vaccinated individuals is also been reported [ ]. Furthermore, accumulating evidence demonstrates that individuals with SARS-CoV-2 reinfection have a significantly higher relative risk of post-infection myocarditis and arrhythmias compared with those experiencing only a single infection episode [ ]. This is consistent with the broader finding that reinfection potentiates the risk of persistent post-acute sequelae across systems, including cardiac outcomes. Mechanistically, repeated episodes of SARS-CoV-2 infection may amplify systemic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and procoagulant states that can potentiate myocardial injury, exacerbate residual cardiac inflammation, and impair resolution of prior injury, thereby, increasing the likelihood of delayed recovery, adverse myocardial remodeling, and progression toward chronic dysfunction or cardiomyopathy. Prolonged or recurrent inflammatory responses reflected in biomarkers such as elevated CRP, CAR, and persistently low PNI may, therefore, identify patients at particular risk of adverse long-term cardiac outcomes after repeated infection [ , ]. SARS-CoV-2 infection may amplify systemic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and procoagulant states that can potentiate myocardial injury, exacerbate residual cardiac inflammation, and impair resolution of prior injury, thereby, increasing the likelihood of delayed recovery, adverse myocardial remodeling, and progression toward chronic dysfunction or cardiomyopathy. Prolonged or recurrent inflammatory responses reflected in biomarkers such as elevated CRP, CAR, and persistently low PNI may, therefore, identify patients at particular risk of adverse long-term cardiac outcomes after repeated infection [ , ]. Although these markers have not yet been specifically validated in longitudinal studies, sustained abnormalities in PNI and CAR may relate to long-term cardiac sequelae (involving progression from acute to chronic myocarditis). 8 Emerging diagnostic approaches 8.1 Biomarkers, MRI, echocardiography, and other advanced techniques The preliminary diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2-related myocarditis is highly dependent upon clinical suspicion. It can be misleading since patients often exhibit prodromal symptoms that are not recognized to be infection-related in the initial stages of infection. About 1–3 weeks post-SARS-CoV-2 infection, the patients may develop cardiac issues, including fatigue, chest tightness, dyspnea, palpitation, and shortness of breath [ ]. Acute myocarditis can be easily overlooked unless a high index of suspicion is maintained. However, the diagnosis may not be obvious until a fulminant disease manifests itself. Diagnostic conclusions rely primarily on determining myocardial dysfunction and active viral infection in the suspected individuals. When patients present with manifestations suggestive of cardiac involvement (including chest pain, acute or sub-acute dyspnea, palpitations, and syncope), they must be screened accordingly. The European Society of Cardiology (ESC) recommends selective coronary angiography and EMB in all clinically suspected myocarditis patients [ ]. The diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2-related myocarditis is similar to that of other viral myocarditis and is primarily based on determining the extent of cardiac involvement in the patients. It is typically defined by clinical symptoms, elevated blood markers (such as persistently elevated troponin levels in the absence of coronary artery disease and elevation in the levels of BNP (brain natriuretic peptide)), histological evidence of inflammation in the myocardium, abnormal electrocardiogram, and radiographic findings, or direct molecular evidence of viral load [ , ]. Blood tests for cardiac troponin, an echocardiography, and a 12-lead ECG are usually recommended for individuals exhibiting symptoms of cardiac involvement [ ]. In COVID-19 related acute myocarditis patients, frequently observed hematological abnormalities include elevated white blood cell count, inflammatory markers including procalcitonin, ferritin, interleukin-6, and CRP [ ]. About 95 % of patients present with elevated cardiac biomarkers, including D-dimer, troponins, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and NT-pro-BNP or BNP [ , , ]. Elevation of these blood and cardiac biomarkers suggests a hyperinflammatory state and myocardial damage, which can be related to acute myocarditis. In addition, patient evaluations via coronary angiography (CA) tests, such as invasive CA (ICA) or computed tomography CA (CTCA) and computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA), can be performed to rule out acute myocarditis or other pathological features [ ]. The 12-lead ECG and transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) are considered alternative techniques to assess myocardial dysfunction in both adult and pediatric patients [ ]. The use of endomyocardial biopsy (EMB) has proven instrumental not only for confirming the diagnosis of myocarditis but also for guiding therapy and assessing prognosis [ , , , , ]. However, it is required to define myocarditis via EMB using the Dallas criteria [ , ]. It allows histological, immunohistochemical, and molecular virological evaluations of the specimens, which are prerequisites for the precise diagnosis of viral myocarditis [ ]. The EMB may facilitate the detection of immune cell infiltrates, viral DNA and RNA, and quantification of viral load in a cardiac biopsy sample. Due to low detection sensitivity (ascribed to sampling error) and several inherent risks associated with this invasive method, including cardiac perforation, atrial tachyarrhythmia and others, its routine use for myocarditis diagnostics in the pediatric parients is far less extensive than adults [ , , ]. 8.2 Diagnostic challenges and the role of advanced imaging techniques Due to the lack of reliable diagnostics, non-specific symptoms, and clinical signs that overlap with acute coronary syndromes, diagnosing COVID-19-associated myocarditis is still difficult. Despite being the gold standard, endomyocardial biopsy (EMB) is invasive and infrequently used in COVID settings because of the low yield in diffuse myocardial disease and the dangers involved in the procedure [ ]. The non-invasive diagnostic mainstay is cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (cMRI). By identifying myocardial inflammation, edema, and fibrosis, the updated 2018 Lake Louise Criteria, which include native T1/T2 mapping and extracellular volume (ECV) quantification, provide high sensitivity and specificity. Common observations include increased T2- T2-weighted signals and sub-epicardial or mid-wall late gadolinium enhancement (LGE), especially in the lateral wall [ ]. The use of other modalities is growing. Echocardiography is still crucial for preliminary evaluation since it can show anomalies in wall motion or a decreased ejection fraction. Particularly when

Common observations include increased T2- T2-weighted signals and sub-epicardial or mid-wall late gadolinium enhancement (LGE), especially in the lateral wall [ ]. The use of other modalities is growing. Echocardiography is still crucial for preliminary evaluation since it can show anomalies in wall motion or a decreased ejection fraction. Particularly when CMR is contraindicated, cardiac CT (with delayed iodine enhancement) aids in the exclusion of coronary disease and the visualization of the myocardial damage. The identification of active inflammation and immune cell infiltration is made possible by FDG-PET/CT. By measuring myocardial strain, speckle-tracking echocardiography can identify early subclinical impairment even in cases when EF is preserved. The best method for diagnosing and tracking COVID-19 myocarditis, particularly in cases with diverse clinical presentations, is to use a multimodal approach that integrates CMR, echo, CT, PET, and biomarkers [ , ]. A comparison between the diagnostic utility of these techniques in diagnosis of viral myocarditis has been provided in . 8.3 Molecular diagnostics The ESC guidelines call for a quantitative analysis of the cardiotropic viral genome in EMB samples [ ]. Advanced molecular biology techniques such as conventional Polymerase chain reaction (PCR), real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR), and next-generation sequencing (NGS) have proven instrumental in rapid, specific and sensitive detection of the viral genome in patients (both children and adults) suffering from viral myocardial infection [ , , , ]. An emerging single-cell RNA sequencing technology (scRNA-seq) has been proven instrumental in the characterization of an array of molecular processes underpinning COVID-19-associated and post-vaccine associated myocarditis and identification of associated therapeutic targets [ , , , ]. This technology has significant potential to advance our understanding of the COVID-19-associated and post-vaccine associated myocarditis etiology, enabling researchers to explore cellular heterogeneity and immune responses at an unprecedented resolution. These diagnostic modalities can be employed in conjunction and correlating their findings may substantially enhance diagnostic sensitivity. 9 Current pharmacological interventions: antivirals, immunosuppressants, and novel therapies SARS-CoV-2 infection causes multi-system damage with a wide spectrum of clinical manifestations that vary considerably among patients. There are no definitive therapeutic recommendations for the management of post-COVID myocarditis in the patients. Although symptomatic therapy and supportive care remain the cornerstones of the therapeutic management, it should be tailored according to the patients’ varied disease phenotype, severity and underpinning risk factors [ ]. In context to SARS-CoV-2 associated myocarditis, the therapeutic management follows similar recommendations as that of heart failure, which is usually based on managing the clinical manifestations (such as arrhythmia and/or ventricular dysfunction) and providing supportive care to the patients. It includes pharmacological therapy, fluid management, and advanced therapies in cases of unresponsive or cardiogenic shock. Using antivirals to limit the virus load and targeted immunomodulators (such as corticosteroids, anti-IL-6 6/IL 1, and JAK inhibitors) to stop cytokine storm are still the central therapeutic approaches. In selective cases, therapies such as tocilizumab, anakinra, colchicine, and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) blockers have been proven effective [ ]. 9.1 Antiviral Therapy The role of antiviral therapy in the management of myocarditis is debatable. The use of molnupiravir and nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (Paxlovid) remain the first-line therapy within five days of symptom onset to limit viral replication and systemic spread [ ]. Remdesivir has been used extensively for treating COVID-19 patients, although its effectiveness in preventing or treating myocarditis has not been conclusively demonstrated [ ]. 9.2 Immunosuppressive & immunomodulatory therapies • Immunosuppressive and immunomodulatory agents are primarily used to counteract excessive immune activation and cytokine-mediated myocardial injury. Glucocorticoids (such as Methylprednisolone 200–500 mg IV) are often used to treat fulminant myocarditis, followed by a gradual tapering of oral prednisone over the course of weeks to months [ ]. • Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) may be beneficial for fulminant patients, although robust randomized data remain limited [ ]. • IL-inhibitors, including IL-1 blockers (such as anakinra) and IL-6 inhibitors (such as tocilizumab), are used particularly in patients presenting with shock and elevated inflammatory profiles [ ]. • JAK inhibitors, such as baricitinib and ruxolitinib, have demonstrated potential in treating severe systemic illness and myocardial inflammation [ ]. 9.3 Supportive/cardiac-directed therapies • Standard guideline-directed therapeutic interventions for cardiac issues remains essential inn patients with COVID-19-associated myocardial involvement. Administration of ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs), and inotropes or mechanical circulatory assistance (including ECMO; in case of hemodynamic instability) is usually recommended for the therapeutic management of COVID-19-associated myocarditis patients [ ]. 9.3.1 Novel and investigational therapies • Furthermore, several emerging therapies are under active investigation. Administration of ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs), and inotropes or mechanical circulatory assistance (including ECMO; in case of hemodynamic instability) is usually recommended for the therapeutic management of COVID-19-associated myocarditis patients [ ]. 9.3.1 Novel and investigational therapies • Furthermore, several emerging therapies are under active investigation. DFV890, an oral NLRP3 inflammasome inhibitor that targets cytokine-driven damage, is currently undergoing testing [ ]. • Beyond anecdotal evidence, JAK inhibitors are being studied for their therapeutic potential in myocarditis [ ]. • Advanced biological and regenerative approaches, including APOSEC secretome, stem cells, and CXCR3-targeted biologics, further represent cutting-edge strategies; however, they are still in the preclinical stages [ , ]. 9.4 Cardiac rehabilitation in managing post-COVID myocarditis An emerging topic in the management of post-COVID myocarditis is the role of comprehensive cardiac rehabilitation (CR). The role of CR in improving the well-being and quality of life of patients with cardiovascular problems and reducing associated mortality and morbidity burden has already been established. The American Heart Association (AHA) recommends CR as the first step in secondary prevention of cardiovascular manifestations [ ]. With the main aim of reversing the physiological and psychological impacts of cardiovascular diseases, comprehensive CR programs help optimize disease management, reduce adverse cardiovascular events and hospitalizations, improve functional capacity, occupational status, and psychosocial status of the patients, and reduce the health-related economic burden. The key components of these programs include patient assessment and education, physical training, respiratory muscle training, occupational therapy, counseling for daily life activities, and lifestyle management (diet, sleep, and hygiene management, physical activity), psychosocial counseling and management, and vocational support [ ]. Patients with cardiovascular manifestations from COVID-19, pre-existing heart conditions with worsening symptoms after COVID-19, and cardiovascular complaints are typically candidates for comprehensive CR (such as palpitations, dyspnea, fatigue) of long COVID-19. The rehabilitation program for post-COVID myocarditis cases is tailored to their varied functional capacities and secondary ailments. It primarily relies on regular monitoring of oxygen saturation while walking, performing daily life activities, and/or during telemetric monitoring [ ]. Exercise stress test, Cardiopulmonary Exercise Test (CPET), and/or field tests such as the 6-Minute Walk Test can determine the functional capacity of the COVID-19 patients, following the general indications and contraindications of these tests [ ]. Nevertheless, clinical guidelines concerning physical exercise for patients recovering from post-COVID myocarditis exist. Current recommendations from the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC) and the European Sports Cardiology Section of the European Association of Preventive Cardiology (ESC/EAPC) advise against physical exercise in individuals with active pericarditis and/or myocarditis and to resume it only after their complete recovery [ , ]. Therefore, to ensure the biological and clinical resolution of the cardiac dysfunction, it is advised that patients with confirmed myocarditis refrain from engaging in physical exercise programs for at least a period of three to six months [ , ]. Patients who have acute myocarditis should not undergo CPET because of an increased risk of cardiac dysfunction in them [ ]. Exercise stress test can be performed in patients with COVID-19-related myocarditis after three-to six-months after the initial illness. 10 10.1 9.6 The role of vaccination in reducing myocarditis risk, especially in younger populations The risk of developing myocarditis following SARS-CoV-2 infection is considerably decreased by the COVID-19 vaccine. Rarely, young guys (aged 12–29) get vaccine-associated myocarditis, usually mild and self-limiting, mainly following mRNA vaccinations. On the other hand, myocarditis, brought on by infections, happens more frequently and is more severe. Numerous extensive studies attest to the fact that immunization reduces long-term consequences, including cardiac injury. The safety profiles of booster dosages have been favourable. Vaccination is strongly recommended by the overall benefit-to-risk ratio, especially for adolescents and young adults [ , , ]. In contrast to patients with post-COVID-19 myocarditis, both adult and pediatric patients with post-COVID-19 mRNA vaccine-related myocarditis are reported to have a milder clinical course and recover from the ailment more rapidly [ ]. At 18 months after infection, their cardiovascular problems are less common than those of people with traditional myocarditis. Nonetheless, patients (mostly young men) might need medical supervision for several months following their release from the hospital. Of 4635 hospitalized myocarditis patients recruited in a nationwide follow-up cohort study from France, about 558 cases with post-vaccine myocarditis presented less severe cardiovascular events at 18 months of follow-up than 298 post-COVID-19 myocarditis cases and 3779 cases with conventional myocarditis [ ]. 11 10.
