In addition to abnormal aortic gradients, anatomic evidence for CoA is necessary and is well characterized by MRI or CT. Adult congenital guidelines have reported the best evidence to proceed with intervention to correct CoA, including hypertension, BP differential between upper and lower extremities, and TTE-derived gradients across the coarctation. For individuals with native or recurrent CoA and appropriate anatomic characteristics, endovascular treatment with stenting is typically performed. , , , – , Open surgical repair of CoA may include subclavian flap aortoplasty, resection and end-to-end anastomosis, interposition grafting, or bypass grafting, with the choice of procedure informed by patient- and anatomic-specific characteristics. , In adults who have undergone a previous open surgical CoA repair and develop recoarctation, aneurysm, or pseudoaneurysm, an endovascular approach (assuming there is adequate iliofemoral access and absence of involvement of the supra-aortic trunks) avoids the need for reoperation. , , , , Patients with CoA are at risk for complications of hypertension, including heart failure, stroke, coronary artery disease, and aortic complications, so hypertension should be assessed and in accordance with current guidelines. Multiple studies have shown that persistent hypertension is common after CoA correction. , , , , Ambulatory BP monitoring and exercise testing may be useful in the evaluation and treatment of hypertension in patients with native CoA and after repair. , , Screening studies suggest that adults with CoA have an 10% prevalence of intracranial aneurysms (compared with a prevalence of 2% in the normal adult population), with the greatest risk among older adults and those with hypertension. – , Cost-effective analysis supports screening for intracranial aneurysms in adults with CoA, but preferred screening strategies remain unknown. Because many of the intracranial aneurysms detected by screening will be very small and not require treatment, shared decision-making about screening may be informed by age, risk factors, and anticoagulation considerations. , 9.4.2. Other Arch Abnormalities 9.4.2.1. Aberrant Subclavian Artery, Kommerell’s Diverticulum Synopsis Anomalies of the aortic arch are usually detected incidentally on a CT of the chest or neck ordered for other reasons. An ASCA arises as the fourth branch from the aorta, distal to the left subclavian artery (or right subclavian artery in the case of a right-sided aortic arch). It courses through the posterior mediastinum behind the esophagus in its path to perfuse the arm and can cause a vascular ring around the trachea and esophagus that results in dysphagia, respiratory symptoms, or recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy. Kommerell’s diverticulum is a persistent remnant of the fourth primitive dorsal aortic arch because of failed regression and may be present in 20% to 60% of patients with an aberrant right or left subclavian artery. The risk of rupture or dissection of a Kommerell’s diverticulum has been reported to be as high as 50% in case series, although high-quality data on the natural history are very limited. The 2020 SVS clinical practice guidelines recommend surgical intervention for Kommerell’s diverticulum when the diverticulum orifice is >3.0 cm, the combined diameter of the diverticulum and adjacent descending aorta is >5.0 cm, or both. Successful repair has been described using open, endovascular, and hybrid approaches depending on patient anatomy and comorbidities. Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text Variant aortic arch anatomy has been found to be significantly associated with TAA in several single-center retrospective observational series, with 33% of patients with right-sided aortic arch having concomitant TAA. Left-sided aortic arch with aberrant right subclavian artery was also significantly associated with TAD but only occurred in 2% to 8% of those patients. Consequently, if the imaging study that detected the ASCA did not include imaging of the thoracic aorta, then a dedicated CT or MRI to evaluate for an associated aortic aneurysm is reasonable. Case series have reported rupture and/or dissection of Kommerell’s diverticulum for diverticula ranging from 4.0 cm to 10 cm (mean size, 5.0 cm). The measurement of the Kommerell’s diverticulum may be difficult, and various strategies to standardize measures have been proposed. Based on CT, 2 diameter measurements should be obtained ( ) using cross-sectional imaging: the diverticulum orifice (radially and longitudinally at the aortic wall) and the combined diameter of the diverticulum and adjacent descending thoracic aorta (measured from the tip of the diverticulum to the opposite aortic wall ). Repair of Kommerell’s diverticulum has been suggested when the orifice diameter is >3 cm or the combined diameter of the diverticulum and adjacent descending thoracic aorta is >5.0 cm. , , 9.4.2.2. Aberrant Left Vertebral Artery Origin Synopsis The most common anatomic variant for the left vertebral artery is arising directly from the aortic arch; 6% of adults have a left vertebral artery

cross-sectional imaging: the diverticulum orifice (radially and longitudinally at the aortic wall) and the combined diameter of the diverticulum and adjacent descending thoracic aorta (measured from the tip of the diverticulum to the opposite aortic wall ). Repair of Kommerell’s diverticulum has been suggested when the orifice diameter is >3 cm or the combined diameter of the diverticulum and adjacent descending thoracic aorta is >5.0 cm. , , 9.4.2.2. Aberrant Left Vertebral Artery Origin Synopsis The most common anatomic variant for the left vertebral artery is arising directly from the aortic arch; 6% of adults have a left vertebral artery that arises from the arch between the left carotid and left subclavian arteries, , rather than of a branch of the left subclavian artery. There is a paucity of data on the management of the left vertebral artery arising from the aortic arch in patients undergoing thoracic aortic repair. For patients undergoing elective open surgical partial or total arch repair or undergoing TEVAR for TAA or dissection, revascularization of the left subclavian artery is recommended to preserve left vertebral artery perfusion and reduce the risk of symptomatic vertebrobasilar insufficiency, SCI, and stroke. This may be particularly important in patients with a dominant left vertebral artery or a nonintact circle of Willis. Vertebral artery revascularization via either an open bypass or transposition technique can be accomplished with good outcomes. , Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text In patients undergoing elective TEVAR with planned left subclavian artery coverage, preoperative revascularization of the left subclavian artery has been shown to decrease the risk of stroke and SCI, – presumably by maintaining perfusion through the posterior circulation via the left vertebral artery. In a small series of 9 patients with an aberrant left vertebral artery origin undergoing open aortic arch replacement, no neurologic complications were reported among patients who first underwent revascularization of the left vertebral artery. 9.4.2.3. Bovine Arch (Common Innominate and Left Carotid Artery) Synopsis The most common anatomic pattern of great vessel origin, occurring in approximately 70% of adults, is a type I arch, in which the 3 great vessels originate directly from the aorta. Bovine arch variants are the most common arch anomalies, and 2 types are described: In type II-A, found in 9% of the population, the left common carotid artery arises directly from the innominate artery ( ); in type II-B, found in 13% of the population, the innominate and left common carotid arteries arise from a common origin ( ). The term “bovine arch” is a misnomer, because the arch vasculature in cattle has a single, large brachiocephalic vessel that subsequently trifurcates into 2 subclavian arteries and a bicarotid trunk. Others have referred to the bovine aortic arch pattern as an aortic arch with a common origin of the innominate and left carotid artery. Some authors have suggested that a bovine arch increases the risk of aortic dissection, but the data are limited. , Among patients with acute type A aortic dissection, a bovine arch was highly predictive of an arch tear (OR, 5.9; 95% CI, 2.89–12.04; P <0.001) and increased perioperative stroke (OR, 2.69; 95% CI, 1.2–6.0; P =0.016) based on multivariable analysis, although it was not associated with worse long-term survival. Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text A bovine aortic arch appears to be a marker for TAD and more rapid aortic expansion. Among patients with TAD, the prevalence of a bovine arch was 26.3%, compared with 16.4% in controls ( P <0.001). Moreover, among patients with TAA, the annual aortic growth rate was 0.29 cm/y among those with a bovine arch versus 0.09 cm/y among those with normal arch anatomy. A recent meta-analysis found that the proportion of TAD among patients with bovine arch was 41.5%, compared with 34.0% among patients with standard arch configuration. If aortic dilation or aneurysm is found on imaging, subsequent surveillance imaging may be obtained. 9.5. Tumors Tumors of the thoracic aorta are usually secondary, resulting from contiguous or metastatic spread of primary malignancies, especially lung and esophageal. , Primary malignant tumors of the aorta, which are extremely rare, are most often primary sarcomas that protrude into the lumen but leave the aortic wall intact. Aortic sarcomas are aggressive tumors with a propensity for arterial embolization, disseminated metastases, and rapid clinical deterioration, , usually with limited survival after initial diagnosis. , Tumors of the thoracoabdominal aorta may exhibit nonspecific symptoms. On imaging, aortic tumors are often initially mistaken for atherosclerosis or aneurysmal disease (although PET imaging may suggest tumor metabolic activity over metabolically quiescent atherosclerosis), so the diagnosis is often made by histologic examination of embolic debris or surgical specimens – ; in some cases, the diagnosis is made postmortem. Combined therapy with surgery (resection and reconstruction of the segment of aorta containing the neoplasm) and chemoradiotherapy provide the best survival results, although the overall

embolization, disseminated metastases, and rapid clinical deterioration, , usually with limited survival after initial diagnosis. , Tumors of the thoracoabdominal aorta may exhibit nonspecific symptoms. On imaging, aortic tumors are often initially mistaken for atherosclerosis or aneurysmal disease (although PET imaging may suggest tumor metabolic activity over metabolically quiescent atherosclerosis), so the diagnosis is often made by histologic examination of embolic debris or surgical specimens – ; in some cases, the diagnosis is made postmortem. Combined therapy with surgery (resection and reconstruction of the segment of aorta containing the neoplasm) and chemoradiotherapy provide the best survival results, although the overall prognosis remains poor. 10. PHYSICAL ACTIVITY AND QUALITY OF LIFE Synopsis As surgical outcomes for aortic disease improve, a focus on patient-reported health-related quality of life (HRQOL) outcomes is becoming increasingly important, because patients have become increasingly concerned about HRQOL issues such as returning to work, pain management, risk of infection, activity recommendations and restrictions, and neurologic complications. The most common measures of HRQOL are generic patient-reported outcome measures (eg, SF-36), although validated aneurysm-specific measures have been developed. , , In patients with Marfan syndrome in the GenTAC registry, HRQOL was slightly below the population norm. Better HRQOL was independently associated with socioeconomic factors (eg, private insurance, active employment) but not factors related to disease severity or comorbidities. , Although aneurysms are usually asymptomatic before diagnosis, surgical aortic repair is associated with an initial deterioration in HRQOL at 3 months, including decreased physical, cognitive, and social function that generally returns to preoperative levels after 6 to 12 months. Standardized reporting of preoperative and postoperative HRQOL measures is needed to guide further improvements in interventional strategies and improve the overall patient experience. Patients with aortic aneurysms, who have adequate BP control, may have improvements in overall cardiovascular health when undertaking moderate intensity aerobic activity at least 3 to 4 days per week, 30 to 60 minutes per session. – Although resistance training may be beneficial to patients with cardiovascular disease, it increases central aortic BP and, therefore, benefits for those with aortic aneurysm are less well understood because, theoretically, increases in BP could contribute to subsequent aortic growth, complications, or both. Further longitudinal study is warranted. – Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text In patients with aortic disease, limited data are available to guide recommendations regarding the forms of exercise that are safe and promote cardiovascular health versus those that pose an acute or long-term risk of aortic growth or rupture. But evidence exists regarding the physiologic benefits of exercise and the hemodynamic consequences of various form of exercise and exertion in case series and relevant animal models. There has been a uniform consensus among numerous expert committees on aortic disease that it is wise to avoid intense isometric exertion or exercises that require the Valsalva maneuver, given that heavy lifting with Valsalva can produce acute increases in SBP to >300 mm Hg. There is also a consensus that light weightlifting and low-intensity aerobic exercise are safe and likely improve both physical and mental health. No uniform consensus exists about the safety of intermediate-level static and aerobic exercise. Recommendations for exercise intensity are best individualized, informed by multiple factors that include underlying aortic pathology, aortic diameter and ASI, aortic growth rate, age, family history, and any other high-risk features (eg, uncontrolled hypertension). Ongoing investigation is needed to better define the levels of resistance activities that would be considered low-risk for adverse aortic events, favoring greater exercise restrictions among patients at higher risk of dissection. , – , Although data are limited, cardiac rehabilitation has been shown to be useful and safe for patients after aortic surgery. , , , A randomized trial of exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation in patients who have undergone surgery for type A aortic dissection showed improved peak oxygen uptake, maximal workload, and HRQOL. Fear of a repeat cardiac event can cause patients who are post–aortic dissection to decrease or stop exercise and sexual activity, but mild-to-moderate intensity exercise may be cardioprotective. Because of deconditioning, patients may be unable to exercise initially at the recommended level. An intensity of 3 to 5 metabolic equivalents of task is recommended, while avoiding strenuous lifting, lifting to the point of exhaustion, or other activities that entail maximal exertion. , In a retrospective study, patients with small AAA went through a modified cardiac rehabilitation program before surgery, and the rate of aortic growth was slower in the rehabilitation group. High-intensity athletic training in 1 study has been shown to be an independent predictor of aortic growth, although these data were limited to the aortic root and did not include AAA. In a recent study in 442 athletes of mean age 61 years, aortic root enlargement by z-score was present in 24% of participants and, after multivariate analysis, elite competitor status was found to be an independent

entail maximal exertion. , In a retrospective study, patients with small AAA went through a modified cardiac rehabilitation program before surgery, and the rate of aortic growth was slower in the rehabilitation group. High-intensity athletic training in 1 study has been shown to be an independent predictor of aortic growth, although these data were limited to the aortic root and did not include AAA. In a recent study in 442 athletes of mean age 61 years, aortic root enlargement by z-score was present in 24% of participants and, after multivariate analysis, elite competitor status was found to be an independent predictor of aortic growth. Less is known about the potential effects of mild-to-moderate intensity aerobic activity on aortic growth, but it is known to improve overall cardiovascular health, including among patients with TAA – and AAA. , , A recent meta-analysis suggests that that higher physical activity is associated with a reduced risk of AAA. In 1 study of a mouse model of Marfan syndrome, rates of aortic root growth were significant slower in mice that exercised daily on a treadmill compared with sedentary mice. In another study of mice with Marfan syndrome, both mild and moderate—but not strenuous—aerobic exercise protected the structural integrity of the aortic wall, as evidenced by reduced elastin fragmentation and reduced expression of matrix metalloproteinases 2 and 9 within the aortic wall, compared with sedentary controls. Depression and anxiety often occur in patients with aortic disease, regardless of surgical status. Posttraumatic stress disorder after dissection is a particular risk. Screening patients and providing resources for assistance may prevent mental health issues from becoming more severe and lead to an increased HRQOL. , The SF-36 is a common tool for assessing mental health for these patients , , , but may not cover all patient concerns, such as activity restriction, family life, and losing ability to earn income. More studies are needed with both pre- and postoperative HRQOL data to improve shared decision-making and patient outcomes. , , Exercise may decrease depression. Education before procedures helps most patients feel more satisfied with their procedures and improve postoperative HRQOL. Patients and clinicians can define surgery success differently, showing the importance of discussing expectations and risks. 11. COST AND VALUE CONSIDERATIONS Although assessment of cost and value in development of guidelines is of growing importance, studies are limited on the cost-effectiveness of aortic disease treatment and lack standard methods for comparison. Screening for AAA among men ≥65 years of age has been shown to be cost-effective, , although data for screening women are less clear. Women have a lower incidence of AAA but higher risk of rupture and longer life expectancy, so incremental cost-effectiveness is similar to men and may justify screening, especially in those with a history of smoking. In patients with AAA, studies comparing EVAR to open surgical repair generally show lower initial costs for EVAR based on shorter hospital stays; however, ongoing expenses for EVAR surveillance and reinterventions may minimize long-term cost advantages after 2 to 5 years. – In addition, significant variability in costs across organizations and countries, and changing efficiencies in techniques, makes it difficult to make recommendations on preferred interventional approaches based primarily on relative costs. , , Findings are mixed but similar for descending TAA, with trends toward lower initial hospital costs with TEVAR compared with open surgery stemming from shorter length of stay, but the long-term results are more neutral. – Few data examine the cost-effectiveness of management strategies of TAA. For the management of AAS, the costs are not easily modifiable. However, for management of chronic TAD, patients often see a host of specialists, including both cardiologists and surgeons, have follow-up visits with specialists in both the community and at tertiary or quaternary centers, or both. Moreover, diagnostic imaging is often duplicated because of differences in imaging protocols or quality, or simply because images are not readily transferrable. Consequently, there are likely opportunities for significant cost savings if redundant clinician visits and imaging could be reduced through common protocols, common imaging platforms, and coordinated care. 12. EVIDENCE GAPS AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS Most of the current recommendations for patients with aortic disease are based on expert opinion and data from observational studies, large registries, and prospective studies, but few are from randomized clinical trials. More data are needed from basic science studies and RCTs to guide prevention, early diagnosis, and advanced treatment for aortic disease. In the future, precision medicine and patient-centered approaches will enable clinicians to develop care plans to optimize outcomes for each patient. Future research should include diverse populations and examine race, ethnicity, and sex differences to ensure that all patient groups are represented and that questions pertinent to their aortic health are answered. 12.1. Biomarker Studies Although interest in using circulating biomarkers for risk stratification of

observational studies, large registries, and prospective studies, but few are from randomized clinical trials. More data are needed from basic science studies and RCTs to guide prevention, early diagnosis, and advanced treatment for aortic disease. In the future, precision medicine and patient-centered approaches will enable clinicians to develop care plans to optimize outcomes for each patient. Future research should include diverse populations and examine race, ethnicity, and sex differences to ensure that all patient groups are represented and that questions pertinent to their aortic health are answered. 12.1. Biomarker Studies Although interest in using circulating biomarkers for risk stratification of patients with aortopathy has increased, biomarker expression has not been clearly associated with relevant clinical aortic events. Most studies have focused on protein-based biomarkers and noncoding RNAs in patients with bicuspid aortopathy. These emerging biomarkers and other better, early-stage biomarkers, along with advanced noninvasive imaging modalities, may help us precisely identify the risk associated with adverse outcomes in these patients. In addition, noncoding RNAs such as microRNA are biological molecules whose expression can be modified through targeted mechanisms and present opportunities to identify new treatment options for patients with aortic disease. – In addition, developing image-based cardiac and aortic markers derived from large-scale imaging studies with automated machine learning–based analysis might provide a wealth of information for guiding the optimal care of these patients. 12.2. Genetic and Nongenetic Factors Various genes have been associated with and linked to TAA and dissection. Consequently, genetic testing can identify pathogenic mutations in specific genes that increase a patient’s risk of aneurysm, dissection, or both and may inform the optimal timing of aortic repair. As the prevalence of genetic testing increases, the discovery of more genes will help in the earlier diagnosis of asymptomatic nonsyndromic TAA. In addition to the contribution of genetic variants, environmental factors and lifestyle habits may contribute to aortic aneurysm formation. Further research on these factors may provide evidence to guide lifestyle modifications that could reduce a patient’s lifelong aortic risk. Recent evidence suggests that fluoroquinolone use is associated with an increased risk of aortic aneurysm and dissection, but the pathways through which this effect is mediated are unknown. Future research investigating the potentially protective or harmful effects of other pharmacologic agents on aortic health might further elucidate the pathophysiology of aortic disease. – 12.3. Biomechanics of the Aorta Emerging evidence suggests that aortic diameter alone is an insufficient predictor of risk for aortic dissection. Understanding the distribution of biomechanical wall stress in the various anatomic locations of the aorta, as well as potential contributions of hemodynamic flow disturbances such as those from aortic valve stenosis or regurgitation, or even from a well-functioning BAV, may improve risk stratification strategies and, in turn, patient outcomes, filling a knowledge gap on wall stress distribution in patients with aortic aneurysms. – 12.4. Sex, Race, and Ethnicity Conflicting data exist in the literature on the association between sex and outcome in patients with aortic disease. Studies have shown different rates of aortic aneurysm growth and dissection risk in male versus female patients. Nevertheless, the data are inconsistent, because some outcome studies indicate that sex affects prognosis, whereas others show no impact of sex. Clearly, further research is needed to elucidate the impact of sex on the incidence and progression of aortic disease, the risk of aortic dissection, and the outcomes of intervention. Even more challenging is the fact that few studies have been published on racial and ethnic disparities among patients with aortic disease and those undergoing aortic intervention. Moreover, it is unclear that all patients with aortic disease have equal access to skilled practitioners to care for them, so it is imperative that we seek ways to actively minimize such health care disparities. – Similarly, efforts should be made to broaden clinical trials to represent the diverse populations that we treat; study design, methodology, reporting, and implementation should be designed to be more inclusive. , 12.5. Quality of Life in Patients With Aortic Disease Baseline HRQOL assessment in patients with aortic disease is lacking, and the few studies that have targeted HRQOL have been conducted only in patients receiving endovascular or open aortic repair. The impact of physical, mental, emotional, sexual, and professional status on the psychosocial well-being, tolerance of medical therapies, and recovery from aortic intervention has not been well studied. The long-term effects on physical and mental HRQOL after aortic repair are unknown. In addition, evidence-based knowledge on studies targeting quality of life in patients with heritable TAA is narrow or limited only to patients with Marfan syndrome; almost no studies have been performed in patients with Loeys-Dietz syndrome or vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, for example. Furthermore, only scattered studies have examined strategies for boosting the psychological health of patients with aortic disease and those undergoing aortic surgery. Aortic diseases require a

status on the psychosocial well-being, tolerance of medical therapies, and recovery from aortic intervention has not been well studied. The long-term effects on physical and mental HRQOL after aortic repair are unknown. In addition, evidence-based knowledge on studies targeting quality of life in patients with heritable TAA is narrow or limited only to patients with Marfan syndrome; almost no studies have been performed in patients with Loeys-Dietz syndrome or vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, for example. Furthermore, only scattered studies have examined strategies for boosting the psychological health of patients with aortic disease and those undergoing aortic surgery. Aortic diseases require a lifetime of treatment and surveillance, so research is needed on ways to improve and sustain patient engagement, especially among those who are disadvantaged or at a lower educational level. – 12.6. New Endovascular Technology Advances in endovascular technology have dramatically impacted treatment strategies in patients with aortic disease requiring intervention. Despite this significant progress, current endovascular designs are limited in their application because of the differing hemodynamic and anatomic challenges presented by each segment of the aorta and individual differences in aortic anatomy. In addition, operator knowledge and experience, as well as methodical patient selection, are important for obtaining optimal outcomes from endovascular procedures. Continued evolution in stent-graft design, focused on flexibility and durability, improved vascular imaging technology, and advances in simulation training for operators, will likely further reduce the risk of reinterventions and improve long-term outcomes. – 12.7. Optimal Exercise and Rehabilitation Protocols Very limited research has been conducted on optimal exercise in patients with aortic disease. Moreover, no specific rehabilitation strategies exist for patients who still have untreated diseased aortic segments after surgical aortic repair and who do not meet the surgical threshold for intervention. Developing patient-centric rehabilitation protocols and individualized exercise programs for patients with aortic disease is an unmet need that requires further study. – 12.8. Equitable Care and Training Opportunities Sociodemographic disparities can pose challenges to patients and clinicians who seek and offer cardiovascular and aortic care. Market competition, a relatively modern phenomenon, and physician market concentration can drive decision-making and subsequently affect optimal care. Providing optimal cardiovascular and aortic care will depend on widespread regional quality improvement projects to determine best practices, minimize variations in areas where evidence-based medicine has finite benchmarks, and standardize patient selection and case management. Physician participation in these programs should be encouraged, and educational interventions and training should be provided to disseminate knowledge and improve performance, which will help increase awareness for patients and physicians in less-populated, underserved areas. – Supplementary Material Supplemental Material

documents.title: AHA-ASA guidelines for adult stroke rehabilitation and recovery

chunks.content: Background With the aging of the population and the rising prevalence of chronic conditions, rehabilitative care has become a central component of healthcare systems worldwide, addressing the needs of patients with various pathological conditions [ ]. Rehabilitation interventions are inherently complex, as they aim to address multiple functional domains (including motor, cognitive, emotional, and social), and must be tailored to each patient’s unique profile, underlying pathology, and comorbidities [ ]. This complexity makes Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs) in rehabilitation particularly challenging [ , ], as RCTs require standardized protocols and interventions that are difficult to implement in the presence of substantial inter-patient variability. Methodological rigor in rehabilitation trials depends not only on intervention design, but also on the quality and consistency of clinical outcome assessment [ ] which defines patient disability profiles and tailored goals [ ]. Over the last decade, rehabilitation research has benefited from substantial advances in outcome assessment methodology [ ], driven by coordinated efforts from professional societies, national institutes, and international guideline panels. As a matter of fact, clinical practice guidelines and consensus statements have promoted the adoption of core outcome sets and standardized performance measures for neurological rehabilitation, including stroke, with the explicit goal of improving consistency, interpretability, and comparability across studies [ , ]. Recent international and regional guidelines—such as those from the European Stroke Organisation and the World Stroke Organization—further emphasize structured, multidimensional assessment frameworks spanning motor function, activity, participation, and quality of life, while underscoring the importance of assessor training, certification, and treatment fidelity in rehabilitation trials [ , ]. Collectively, these efforts have had a positive impact on the design and conduct of multicenter rehabilitation RCTs, even if recent analyses highlight that the historic lack of standardization in collecting rehabilitation outcomes continues to prevent the effective aggregation of data across health systems [ ]. Even within rigorously designed trials employing certified assessors and validated outcome measures, practical challenges remain at the level of data capture and longitudinal data management. Rehabilitation trials often involve repeated administration of numerous outcome measures across multiple time points and sites. This increases operational complexity and the risk of data entry errors, incomplete records, and inconsistencies in interpretation of data items [ , ]. As such, robust data collection in rehabilitation remains an open challenge. As noted by Arienti et al. [ ], methodological inconsistencies in data description frequently undermine research quality. Robust electronic data capture systems play a critical role in supporting rehabilitation research. One of the most widely used tools for electronic data capture is REDCap [ – ]. An important feature of REDCap is its nature as a collaborative platform. Users can develop new modules and make them available to the REDCap community, for example, by sharing their implemented instruments within the REDCap shared library. As of today, the REDCap shared library contains 4,401 heterogeneous instruments, representing both validated scales and custom instruments. Notably, 89% of the instruments are implemented in English. In this paper, we describe the development and implementation of an electronic repository of both custom and clinically validated outcome scales as REDCap instruments [ ] to be shared with the research community to foster data collection standardization in rehabilitation trials. The developed REDCap instruments were exploited to collect patient’s clinical information within an Italian multicenter pragmatic RCT (named StrokeFit4) evaluating robotics-assisted rehabilitation in post-stroke patients. Specifically, this work was carried out by the trial’s data management, informatics and clinical team within the StrokeFit4 trial. In this context, the developed REDCap instruments span key rehabilitation domains (e.g., motor function, cognition, independence, quality of life), which can be reused in future clinical studies, including but not limited to stroke patients. The implemented instruments are available in both Italian and English, enabling use in international contexts. The present publication is meant to describe the development and implementation of the research data capture through REDCap. As such, this publication does not focus on the trial’s protocol (which can be found in [ ]), and does not focus on the clinical results of the StrokeFit4 trial, which will be described in a separate publication. Methods This Methods section is organized to reflect the stepwise development and deployment of the data infrastructure supporting the StrokeFit4 multicenter clinical trial. First, we briefly summarize the clinical study context and outcome assessment framework underlying the data collection ( section). We then describe the design and implementation of the centralized REDCap project, including its governance through REDCap Data Access Groups and the implementation of validated and study-specific instruments ( section). Finally, we present the rationale, development, and operational workflow of the Data Quality Dashboard, which was designed to support longitudinal, cross-site data quality monitoring throughout the trial ( section). Clinical study description The StrokeFit4 trial started in August 8th, 2024 and will last approximately up to 31st of July 2026. It is currently recruiting acute and sub-acute stroke patients. Its goal is to evaluate the non-inferiority of a rehabilitation treatment integrated with Robots and Allied Technologies (RADTs), compared to traditional rehabilitation, in the recovery of activities of daily living (ADLs). Briefly, recruited patients undergo 5 weeks of rehabilitative training, consisting of 25 sessions. The traditional arm will undergo conventional rehabilitation with the physiotherapist. The RADTs arm also utilizes instruments, such as exoskeleton or treadmill, possibly enhanced with software for cognitive training. Thirteen clinical centers are involved in the trial. The detailed protocol is described in a previous publication [ ]. StrokeFit4 is one of the 20 pragmatic clinical trials launched within the Fit4MedRob Initiative [ ], a large-scale research program funded by the Italian Ministry of University and Research. The Initiative aims to foster the development and evaluation of innovative, technology-enhanced rehabilitation strategies designed to improve the effectiveness and cost-efficiency of care for neurological conditions, including stroke, neuromuscular disorders, and Parkinson’s disease. This effort is particularly relevant in Italy, where population aging is placing increasing pressure on healthcare systems. At the national level, the results of the Fit4MedRob trials are expected to inform the design of new rehabilitation frameworks tailored to the needs of an aging population. More broadly, the Initiative seeks to promote the sharing of standardized practices, data models, and methodological tools with the international research community, supporting reproducibility, comparability, and collaboration in rehabilitation research. At the time of writing, the StrokeFit4 trial is ongoing, and it is expected to recruit a total sample size of 596 stroke patients by July 2026. The trial sample size has been computed in order to demonstrate non-inferiority of the robotic rehabilitation approach with respect to the traditional one in improving independence in daily activities. More details can be found in the protocol publication [ ]. During the development of the StrokeFit4 trial protocol, healthcare professionals identified several key domains that are needed for comprehensively characterizing stroke patients and their recovery, according to the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) [ ], following ICF-based guidelines [ – ]. In particular, an initial selection of a broad range of assessments was performed in order to allow for an extensive characterization and profiling of patients at admission, including demographic and clinical characteristics as well as genetic analyses. With regard to outcome measures, a primary outcome was identified as being suitable for capturing the overall effectiveness of a multidomain intervention. Subsequently, specific outcome measures were selected for each treatment domain (upper and lower limb sensorimotor domain, balance domain, and cognitive domain). Finally, additional scales were included in accordance with the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) framework, covering the domains of body functions, activities, and participation. This multidomain, ICF-based approach to outcome assessment is also consistent with recent perspectives in neurorehabilitation research, which emphasize the need to move beyond single-domain or single-cause frameworks when evaluating recovery after neurological injury. In particular, a recent editorial in The Lancet Neurology highlighted that neurorehabilitation outcomes should explicitly account for the complex interactions between biological, psychological, and environmental factors, advocating for assessment frameworks that reflect the multidimensional nature of health and recovery [ ]. Accordingly, the rehabilitative and assessment protocols adopted in StrokeFit4 were designed to capture this complexity through the systematic collection of outcomes spanning body functions and structures, activities and participation, and contextual factors. Twenty-eight validated clinical scales are exploited to depict the patient (Table , Supplementary Materials). Some of them are measured both at baseline, during, and after rehabilitation. The primary outcome of the trial is the Modified Barthel Index (MBI), which measures a patient’s level of independence in ADLs. This scale is often used to evaluate older adults, people with mobility limitations, and those with neurological problems, such as stroke, Parkinson’s disease and spinal cord injury [ – ]. Secondary outcomes of the trial include the Fugl–Meyer Assessment for the upper and lower extremities [ ] and the Berg Balance scale [ ]. The complete list of implemented REDCap instruments is available at https://github.com/bmi-labmedinfo/REDCap_Rehabilitation_Measures . REDCap project development REDCap represents a secure, web-based software platform designed to support data collection for research studies. REDCap provides (1) an intuitive interface for validated data capture; (2) audit trails for tracking data manipulation and export procedures; (3) automated export procedures for seamless data downloads to common statistical packages; and (4) procedures for data integration and interoperability with external sources. The REDCap infrastructure for the StrokeFit4 trial was designed to explicitly reflect the multicenter structure of the trial. A single centralized REDCap project was implemented for the entire study, within which REDCap Data Access Groups (DAGs) were used to manage site-level data segregation. One DAG was created for each participating clinical center. For each center, two to three physiotherapists were designated as data entry operators and assigned to the corresponding DAG. This configuration ensures that users within a given DAG have visibility—both for data entry and export—only to the records of patients enrolled at their own clinical center. In contrast, designated data managers and monitoring users (two data managers and four monitors) were granted cross-DAG permissions, allowing them to view and export the complete dataset across all centers for centralized data analysis and data quality monitoring. This structure enabled standardized data collection within a unified project while preserving site-level data isolation and supporting centralized oversight. Validated clinical scales REDCap implementation Each clinical scale specified in the protocol was implemented as a dedicated REDCap instrument (i.e., a data collection form or survey within a REDCap project). To facilitate the scale administration, whenever necessary, we added text instructions and demonstration videos on how to carry on the evaluation. Calculated fields, such as partial and global scores, are implemented for each quantitative scale. When implementing the various instruments, we followed the Coding guidelines for REDCap Curated Forms and Instruments (REDLOC), to ensure consistency and clarity in data collection, and reusability of forms ( https://projectredcap.org/wp-content/resources/redcap_library_coding_guidelines.pdf ). A more extensive description is provided in Table and in the supplemental materials. When a scale requires computation of one or more scores (global and/or partial), this is performed automatically. REDCap also allowed implementing branching logic to facilitate and shorten the scale completion. StrokeFit4-specific REDCap instruments In addition to the clinically validated scales, we developed several REDCap instruments to support comprehensive data collection throughout the trial. First, instruments were created to collect demographic and clinical background data, such as gender, age, height, weight, and information regarding the acute neurological event. Then, patient status within the study (e.g., regular or drop-out) is tracked using a repeatable instrument (“Patient Status and Notes”), allowing data entry operators to document key events over time. A dedicated “Timing” instrument captures the dates of relevant trial milestones (e.g., T0, T1, etc.). We also implemented a “diary” form to record details of each rehabilitation session, including the actual number of minutes completed. For patients in the robotic intervention groups, the specific device(s) used can also be noted. StrokeFit4 data quality dashboard In multicenter clinical trials, ensuring data quality is a challenge, particularly when multiple clinical scales are collected across sites. First, inconsistencies may arise from the use of different versions or formats of the same clinical scales, or from variations in how items are interpreted, ultimately undermining the comparability of outcomes. For this reason, to prepare the kick-off of the trial, multiple meetings involving physicians, therapists, data entry operators, and developers were carried out, in order to determine guidelines for data collection. Second, despite the use of structured data collection platforms such as REDCap, variability in data entry practices persists, as clinicians may interpret or input responses differently, especially when free-text fields are involved. This heterogeneity introduces bias and reduces the reliability of aggregated data. To limit heterogeneity, when possible, we define the data type of Text Box variables (such as Integer or Float), and set the valid set of values. Moreover, we give additional information for data entry within Field notes to support consistent data entry across centers and to reduce variability and errors in the recording of complex clinical outcome measures (Fig. ). Finally, the high volume of forms required per patient further increases the risk of human error or omissions. Even within REDCap, manual data entry under time pressure or by personnel unfamiliar with the platform can lead to typos or selection errors, thereby compromising data integrity and necessitating substantial data cleaning efforts. Finally, the high volume of forms required per patient further increases the risk of human error or omissions. Even within REDCap, manual data entry under time pressure or by personnel unfamiliar with the platform can lead to typos or selection errors, thereby compromising data integrity and necessitating substantial data cleaning efforts. Although REDCap provides a built-in Data Quality module, its functionality is mainly limited to identifying missing values and can be difficult to apply in the context of repeated measures. To enable a more effective longitudinal assessment of data quality, we developed a new DQD using Python and Streamlit (an open-source Python framework that allows users to easily and quickly create interactive web applications for data visualization and exploration). The dashboard was developed by the data managers. It is intended for monthly use by data managers and monitoring users to automatically detect missing and abnormal values at the patient level. Each month, the data managers download the raw .csv file containing patients’ data of the entire REDCap project (i.e. across all clinical centers). The data managers and monitoring users manually upload the .csv file to the dashboard. Given that, for each patient, the trial spans several months, including follow-up assessments, the dashboard automatically accounts for patient enrollment date when defining whether a value is truly missing. For instance, if a patient has just completed the 5-week treatment phase (T1), follow-up outcomes are not expected in the database and should not be flagged as missing. In addition to automated checks, the dashboard generates interactive figures allowing users to manually inspect clinical scales, demographic data, and other relevant characteristics at a patient level, and allows users to log potential issues directly within the system. Finally, the dashboard can automatically generate a structured Data Quality report in CSV format for further analysis and documentation. This report is generated for each clinical center by selecting its associated REDCap DAGs, and it is sent by the data managers by email to the corresponding data entries. Data entries are then required to solve the data issues as soon as possible and to provide feedbacks to the data managers and monitoring users. Results REDCap project development We implemented a total of 28 clinical scales, 20 of which are not subject to copyright restrictions and are therefore shared openly on GitHub, both in Italian and English. In the context of the StrokeFit4 trial, starting from August 8th, 2024 and lasting approximately up to 31st of July 2026, the scales briefly described in Table are exploited to assess the patients at baseline and during the study, according to ICF domains, as reported by the Rehabilitation Measure Database. StrokeFit4 data quality dashboard The DQD can be run locally. The workflow for using it is organized into four main steps (Fig. ). First, the .csv file exported from REDCap is manually uploaded by the data managers and monitoring users into the Streamlit-based dashboard (Step 1). Once the data are uploaded, users can filter the analysis by REDCap Data Access Group (DAG), to analyse the data from each clinical center participating in the multicenter trial; by default, the analysis includes all centers (Step 2). In Step 3, the dashboard allows exploration of the general characteristics of the patient population where mousing over a data point reveals the patient record ID. For example, in Fig. , Step 3, we can see that two patients have a reported age equal to 0, which is clearly an error. In our REDCap forms “Demographics and anamnestic data”, the data entry operator must select the patient’s date of birth from a Text Box formatted as a date. The age is then automatically computed using the date of birth, compared with the enrollment date. For these patient, the dates of enrollment were incorrectly entered as the date of birth, leading to the wrong age calculation. Therefore, at this stage, users can also manually log potential data quality issues to be included in the quality report. Finally, in Step 4, the different clinical scales are inspected at various time points, and the system can automatically generate a comprehensive data quality report in .csv format by clicking on the “Save Data Quality Report” button (Fig. step 4). The report is intended to be delivered to data entry operators in each DAG (clinical center) to fix the errors. For their convenience, each row of the report provides the patient record-id, the event, the instrument, and the related problem (Fig. ). The report is intended to be delivered to data entry operators in each DAG (clinical center) to fix the errors. For their convenience, each row of the report provides the patient record-id, the event, the instrument, and the related problem (Fig. ). Discussion Rehabilitation RCTs are inherently complex because they require the integration of multiple outcome domains—motor, cognitive, psychological, and social—while at the same time ensuring standardized administration across sites. With this work, we describe the implementation of a REDCap project to support data collection in the StrokeFit4 randomized controlled trial, particularly focusing on a comprehensive set of validated rehabilitation outcome measures. While REDCap is widely used in RCTs [ , , , ], we lack shared instruments in rehabilitation. Recent work on stroke patients [ ] has already shown the usage of REDCap within a rehabilitation RCT. However, unlike our study, the previous trial has focused on upper limb rehabilitation, implementing a relatively small number of instruments, which, in addition, were not publicly shared. Adopting a broader rehabilitation perspective, aiming to assess multiple functional domains, including motor, cognitive, psychological, and functional aspects, our protocol involves a substantially larger and more heterogeneous set of clinical outcome measures to comprehensively characterize patient status over time. By digitizing 28 clinical scales, 20 of which are openly shared, we contribute to addressing the lack of publicly available, standardized REDCap instruments for rehabilitation research. At present, the REDCap Shared Library provides access to more than 4,000 implemented instruments, the vast majority of which are available exclusively in English. To our knowledge, no instruments are currently available in Italian. Notably, among the 19 copyright-free validated clinical scales used in our trial, only one (the Cumulative Illness Rating Scale, CIRS) is available in the REDCap Shared Library, and only in its English version. This resource has the potential to facilitate harmonization across studies and support reusability of outcome measures in future clinical trials and observational studies. Several methodological aspects emerged as crucial in our implementation. First, automatic scoring and branching logic embedded in REDCap instruments could substantially reduce the burden on clinicians and minimize the risk of errors associated with manual calculations. Second, the adoption of structured fields with validation rules (e.g., integer, float, predefined ranges) and descriptive instructions ensures consistency in data entry across different centers. Nonetheless, despite the advantages of REDCap, ensuring data quality in a multicenter rehabilitation trial remains challenging. Variability in interpretation, time pressure on clinicians, and the high number of forms to be completed can still introduce errors or missing values. To mitigate these issues, we developed the Data Quality Dashboard using Python and Streamlit, which extends REDCap’s native data quality module. The dashboard allows both automated and manual checks of longitudinal data, while accounting for the specific point in time along the patient pathway to avoid false positives for expected missing values. Importantly, the dashboard supports center-specific monitoring through REDCap DAGs and produces structured reports that can be used for iterative data cleaning. This approach is particularly relevant in rehabilitation trials, where repeated measures over extended follow-up periods are the norm. Additionally, the StrokeFit4 trial is expected to enroll nearly 600 patients, a sample size that substantially exceeds the median number of participants typically reported in stroke rehabilitation randomized controlled trials [ ]. Managing data collection and ensuring data quality at this scale necessitates a high degree of automation, both to maintain consistency across centers and to reduce the risk of errors associated with manual data handling. Although the Data Quality Dashboard was developed to address the specific operational needs of the StrokeFit4 trial, its underlying design principles are broadly applicable to other multicenter rehabilitation studies. The dashboard architecture—based on standardized REDCap exports, longitudinal consistency checks, and patient-level quality monitoring—can be readily adapted to trials with repeated outcome assessments across multiple sites. In particular, studies that adopt similar REDCap-based instrument implementations may reuse or extend the proposed workflow with minimal customization. This work has been carried out in the context of the Fit4MedRob Initiative [ ], a large-scale national program aimed at strengthening rehabilitation research and innovation within the Italian healthcare system. Despite the growing clinical importance of neurorehabilitation, structured data infrastructures and standardized outcome assessment frameworks for multicenter rehabilitation trials remain unevenly developed across countries and health systems [ ]. Fit4MedRob represents a coordinated effort to address this gap by promoting shared methodologies, interoperable data models, and scalable digital tools to support complex rehabilitation studies. Within this context, the REDCap project and Data Quality Dashboard described here constitute foundational components for enabling high-quality, multicenter rehabilitation research at scale.

Despite the growing clinical importance of neurorehabilitation, structured data infrastructures and standardized outcome assessment frameworks for multicenter rehabilitation trials remain unevenly developed across countries and health systems [ ]. Fit4MedRob represents a coordinated effort to address this gap by promoting shared methodologies, interoperable data models, and scalable digital tools to support complex rehabilitation studies. Within this context, the REDCap project and Data Quality Dashboard described here constitute foundational components for enabling high-quality, multicenter rehabilitation research at scale. While similar infrastructures exist in some research-intensive settings, their systematic adaptation, open dissemination, and integration into national rehabilitation initiatives remain limited. By making rehabilitation-specific REDCap instruments openly available and by documenting a reproducible approach to longitudinal data quality monitoring, this work aims to support not only the StrokeFit4 trial, but also future rehabilitation studies in Italy and in other countries seeking to strengthen research capacity in this domain. Our study has limitations. The current REDCap implementations include several copyrighted scales that cannot be shared, potentially limiting reuse by the wider community. Additionally, while we have emphasized technical standardization, challenges such as ceiling and floor effects of some outcome measures remain intrinsic to rehabilitation research and require careful consideration in trial design and data quality analysis. While detecting some quality problems (such as the one reported in Fig. ) can be trivial, other issues (such as abnormal patterns of clinical scales for a patient over time) might be more difficult to spot. Future work should focus on further automating cross-scale consistency checks and validating whether the adoption of these tools translates into measurable improvements in data quality and trial efficiency. To this end, we previously developed a clinical outcome scale ontology described in [ ]. In future work, we plan to extend it with an explicit representation of data constraints and relationships, enabling the Data Quality Dashboard to automatically generate warnings whenever collected data violates these rules. Additionally, multilingual forms could be implemented. Conclusion We implemented a large set of validated rehabilitation outcome measures within REDCap and complemented them with a tailored Data Quality Dashboard to support the StrokeFit4 multicenter RCT. This dual approach—standardized electronic data capture combined with longitudinal data quality monitoring—addresses critical challenges of rehabilitation trials, including the complexity of outcome assessment and risk of data entry errors. By openly sharing 20 non-copyrighted scales, we also provide a resource that can promote harmonization and reproducibility in future rehabilitation studies. Taken together, our work demonstrates how informatics tools can enhance the methodological rigor of rehabilitation research and contribute to generating more reliable evidence on the effectiveness of innovative interventions such as robotics-assisted rehabilitation. documents.title: AHA scientific statement aphasia and stroke

chunks.content: Strengths and limitations of this study There is limited guidance for health professionals working with the complex condition of aphasia to implement best practice across the continuum of care. The aim of this study was to develop and validate a set of best practice statements for use in post-stroke aphasia rehabilitation. An aphasia rehabilitation Community of Practice developed eight areas of care that provided the framework for the development of an initial 74 best practice statements. These statements were then validated using the RAND/UCLA Appropriateness Method in two rounds of ratings with nine panel members. During the rating, items were added, divided or deleted so that there was panel agreement on a final set of 82 best practice statements over eight domains of care. These evidence-based and expert endorsed care standards form part of the Australian Aphasia Rehabilitation Pathway (AARP), and have been formulated into a dynamic web-based implementation tool with increasing attention to care standards for culturally and linguistically diverse, and indigenous populations. The literature reviews may not be exhaustive given the continuing development of the published evidence. The best practice statements may require some adaptation for other regions; however, the majority of the data should be common and internationally applicable. This process sets a benchmark for the development and dissemination of best practice post-stroke aphasia rehabilitation statements to other areas of practice where research evidence is in its foundational stage. Introduction Aphasia is an acquired neurological disorder of language processing that affects speaking, listening, reading, writing and gesture. Approximately 30–35% of stroke survivors have aphasia on discharge from hospital following stroke, with the prevalence of speech (dysarthria) and language (aphasia) disability 6 months after stroke reported as 30–50/100 000. People with aphasia have higher healthcare costs (8.5% or $1700 attributable cost) and longer length of stays in hospital (6.5%) compared with stroke survivors without aphasia. People with stroke-related aphasia may require additional services to address their communication disability in hospital and also during community life, and such services might reduce their length of length of stay or incidence of adverse events. However, the management of swallowing disorders (dysphagia) may be prioritised over aphasia services in acute hospital settings due to inadequate staffing ratios and lack of appropriate therapy space/resources. Additionally, people with aphasia have poor long-term outcomes after stroke, including consequences such as social isolation, depression and poor quality of life for themselves and their family members. As a chronic disability, aphasia generates a number of long-term service needs, including therapy to enable functional and socially relevant communication. Provision of quality, efficient, evidence-based care is critical for people with aphasia, their families, and healthcare systems. Stroke clinicians and teams need to make daily decisions about the management of people with aphasia from the acute phase through to community-based care. However, a variety of challenges exist to the implementation of best practice in aphasia rehabilitation. Using the AGREEII and ADAPTE guideline appraisal tools, Rohde et al , documented a significant lack of high quality, comprehensive guidance for clinicians working with people with aphasia. Most recommendations identified were included within broader stroke guidelines and frequently lacked details on management of aphasia. The Australian National Stroke Foundation Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management were identified as high-quality guidelines. These guidelines contain 11 items that are focused specifically on aphasia from screening, goal setting, provision of health information, therapy and counselling to communication partner training for family/carers. Despite the availability of these guidelines and the fact that their use has been shown to result in improved patient outcomes, documented evidence to practice gaps continue to exist. For example, in provision of health information, only 56% of a sample of 170 Australian hospitals provided at least ‘some’ information in tailored, ‘aphasia friendly’ formats to people with aphasia as the guidelines recommend. Additionally, some people with aphasia are not receiving treatment, despite a recent Cochrane review that found that aphasia therapy was generally effective. While the above two examples are centred on Australian stroke rehabilitation practice, evidence to practice gaps in stroke rehabilitation have also been documented internationally. Clinicians report that implementation of best practice is challenging because recommendations are often too broad and the evidence-base is limited in some areas. For example, while the Cochrane aphasia rehabilitation review concluded that therapy was generally effective, an additional difficulty for clinicians is that there is still insufficient evidence to indicate the best approach to provision of aphasia therapy for specific individuals with aphasia. Clinicians report they require more in-depth information and research and accompanying resources (eg, standardised clinical resources such as aphasia friendly information handouts) to bridge the evidence to practice gap. Evidence to practice gaps are of concern as consumers report a lack of consistency in the provision of aphasia care and difficulty accessing communication therapy services, especially in the chronic phase. Consumers also emphasise

Cochrane aphasia rehabilitation review concluded that therapy was generally effective, an additional difficulty for clinicians is that there is still insufficient evidence to indicate the best approach to provision of aphasia therapy for specific individuals with aphasia. Clinicians report they require more in-depth information and research and accompanying resources (eg, standardised clinical resources such as aphasia friendly information handouts) to bridge the evidence to practice gap. Evidence to practice gaps are of concern as consumers report a lack of consistency in the provision of aphasia care and difficulty accessing communication therapy services, especially in the chronic phase. Consumers also emphasise the importance of the rehabilitation journey and the need for a comprehensive road map to understand what to expect at different phases of their recovery. The Centre for Clinical Research Excellence (CCRE) in Aphasia Rehabilitation is an Australian research centre that was funded for 5 years by the Australian National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC). The CCRE in Aphasia Rehabilitation drove a national collaborative effort to enhance the quality and consistency of rehabilitation care provided to people with aphasia. To address the above issues of a lack of a detailed road map, comprehensive recommendations and accessible implementation resources, the CCRE in Aphasia Rehabilitation developed the Australian Aphasia Rehabilitation Pathway (AARP). This care pathway was developed to provide the basis for a road map containing important domains of care and was populated with detailed best practice statements (BPS) for each domain of the pathway. The mode of delivery of the AARP is a web-based dynamic tool that contains resources to assist with implementing each of the BPS recommendations. BPS are a recent development and intended to guide practice and promote a consistent, cohesive and achievable approach to care. These address an area of care where there is variation in practice due to limited robust evidence; the BPS attempt to incorporate professional consensus in the absence of a rigorous evidence base. One method of developing BPS is the RAND/UCLA Appropriateness Method (RAM). The RAM consists of the development and validation of quality indicators through a literature review and a two-round modified-Delphi method with a panel of experts. The RAM has been used to develop validated, expert endorsed indicators in a wide range of fields, including paediatric traumatic brain injury rehabilitation, osteoarthritis and pharmacy. The process has been particularly recommended for areas of practice with an emerging evidence base because it seeks to combine both research (literature review) and clinical evidence (expert panel opinion). The aim of this study was to develop a comprehensive set of evidence-based, expert endorsed BPS for post-stroke aphasia rehabilitation utilising the RAM. Method Design We utilised the RAM to develop and validate the Australian Aphasia Rehabilitation Best Practice Statements. The RAM consists of a literature review and development of a list of ‘indications’, which we termed best practice statements. These statements were then rated for their degree of appropriateness by an expert panel in two rounds using a modified Delphi technique. The RAM approach has produced results that are valid and reliable. An overview of the process involved in developing and validating the RAM statements is found in , while a detailed timeline of processing and events can be found on the AARP website ( http://www.aphasiapathway.com.au/flux-content/aarp/pdf/Australian-Aphasia-Rehabilitation-Pathway-RAM-Timeline.pdf ). The first round of ratings was conducted via email, while the second round of ratings was conducted face-to-face. The inclusion of a face-to-face round has been described as advantageous compared with traditional Delphi methods because it allows for greater opportunities for discussion and clarification of statement wording and evidence. Development of best practice statements In developing and organising the statements, we were guided by eight overarching areas of care developed through a national consultative programme with the CCRE in Aphasia Rehabilitation Community of Practice (CoP). The CoP consisted of over 250 aphasia clinicians and managers, researchers, people with aphasia (Australian Aphasia Association) and policymakers (National Stroke Foundation) who were collectively interested in aphasia care, policy and practice. The eight areas of care were developed through an iterative process that occurred through face-to-face workshops, teleconferences, written feedback using Google Docs (a web-based word processing programme) and review of the research literature on consumer (patient and family) experiences with their care and goal setting. The agreed areas of care were: (1) receiving the right referrals, (2) optimising initial contact, (3) setting goals and measuring outcomes, (4) assessing, (5) providing intervention, (6) enhancing the communicative environment, (7) enhancing personal factors, (8) planning for transitions and discharges. From January to August 2013, a core team of researchers from the CCRE in Aphasia Rehabilitation (see ) conducted multiple literature reviews to provide a synthesis of the evidence-base for each area of care identified (see , earlier). The synthesis, construction and refinement of the BPS was an iterative, cyclical process. Within each content area, research questions

From January to August 2013, a core team of researchers from the CCRE in Aphasia Rehabilitation (see ) conducted multiple literature reviews to provide a synthesis of the evidence-base for each area of care identified (see , earlier). The synthesis, construction and refinement of the BPS was an iterative, cyclical process. Within each content area, research questions were created by the project manager in conjunction with the core literature review group. Initially, the literature was searched for secondary level evidence. We accessed available guidelines that were identified by Rohde et al as being of high quality, including the Australian Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management. Other major sources of secondary evidence were: Trip Database ( http://www.tripdatabase.com ); Evidence Based Reviews of Stroke Rehabilitation ( http://www.ebrsr.com ); the Cochrane Library and American Speech and Hearing Association's Evidence Maps: Aphasia ( http://ncepmaps.org/aphasia/tx/ ). We also accessed systematic reviews and then conducted a manual search of their bibliographies. If no secondary evidence was available, search terms were then developed for each area of care and applied to the following databases: The Cochrane Library (2005–2013), CINAHL (1981–2013), Medline (1946–2013), Pubmed (1948–2013), speechBITE (1956–2013) and Google Scholar (2009–2013). All quantitative research designs were included (eg, systematic reviews, randomised controlled trials, cohort studies, single case experimental designs) as well as qualitative research studies. Additional experts in each care area (see ) were contacted and requested to provide any applicable literature (both published literature and grey literature). Evidence was synthesised by the project manager and sent back to key experts and the CCRE executive team (core group) via email. Limited published literature was identified for Section 6 (Enhancing the Communicative Environment) and Section 7 (Enhancing Personal Factors). Therefore greater input was required from experts. One CCRE researcher with specialist expertise working with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people led a team to prepare the literature review and development of BPS in this area. Likewise, a CCRE postdoctoral researcher led the development of the BPS in regards to Culturally and Linguistically Diverse (CALD) populations. The quantitative literature was graded according to the NHMRC Levels of Evidence and Grades of Recommendation. This grading system was chosen because it aligns with the Australian Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management and is the system endorsed by the Australian NHMRC peak body. As the NHMRC levels of evidence do not include a level for every type of study design, single case experimental designs studies were assigned a grading of IV, and the qualitative literature, if used to support a best practice statement, was listed as ‘Qual’. It must be emphasised that this system only allows for the level of study design to be assessed, which is different to the grade of evidence. The grade of evidence (eg, A, B, C, D) takes into account the level of evidence along with evidence quantity, quality, consistency, clinical impact, generalizability and applicability. This additional step was not feasible at the time of the development of the BPS. Qualitative studies were not rated due to the lack of current consensus methods for grading of qualitative studies; however, only studies that were judged to be rigorous were included. Where expert opinion was utilised as the evidence for a statement, we followed the procedures in the Australian Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management and labelled the level of evidence as a ‘Good Practice Point’ (GPP). All 250 members of the CoP were invited to provide feedback on the synthesis of each area. This process has been previously described (see http://www.aphasiapathway.com.au/flux-content/aarp/Thomas-KTEaphasia-pathway-JCPSLP-2014.pdf ). Briefly, of the CoP members, a group of CCRE researchers (n=25) and clinical affiliates (n=45) expressed interest in providing regular feedback and formed the constituents of a feedback mail group. The core CCRE Aphasia Rehabilitation working group then translated the evidence into a list of BPS and additional input was sought from researchers who had specific expertise in each of the areas of care (see additional experts listed in ). Further feedback was then obtained on the initial draft of statements from the feedback mail group using an online programme ‘Google Documents’. Feedback from the CoP in the refinement of the BPS was mostly provided by CoP speech pathologists. Two representatives of the Australian Aphasia Association provided consumer feedback throughout the process. However, they had most input for the workshops that established the areas of care rather than for the detailed refinement of the BPS. Development of the specific sections on personal factors associated with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander populations did include input from Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. The final document contained 74 BPS
