chunks.content: Nonstandard Abbreviations and Acronyms CDI Cardiac Distress Inventory CDI‐SF Cardiac Distress Inventory Short Form EFA exploratory factor analysis GAD‐7 Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7‐item scale PHQ‐9 9‐item Patient Health Questionnaire PTGI Posttraumatic Growth Inventory SCAD spontaneous coronary artery dissection SDI Spontaneous Coronary Artery Dissection Distress Inventory Research Perspective What Is New? The Spontaneous Coronary Artery Dissection (SCAD) Distress Inventory, a condition‐specific tool codesigned with survivors of SCAD and developed using best‐practice instrument methodology, is the first dedicated measure of SCAD‐related psychological distress. The 33‐item SCAD Distress Inventory captures the distinctive psychological impacts of SCAD across 4 empirically derived domains: challenges to sense of self, fear of recurrence, concerns about reduced capacity, and lack of support and validation. What Question Should Be Addressed Next? Future studies should replicate and confirm the SDI's 4‐factor structure, further evaluate its psychometric robustness, and establish its clinical utility across diverse SCAD populations and international contexts. Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) is a highly distressing cause of acute myocardial infarction (AMI), marked by its sudden onset, uncertain optimal management, and relatively high recurrence rate. , , , , Unlike typical cases of atherosclerotic AMI, SCAD‐induced AMI predominantly affects individuals with few traditional cardiovascular risk factors and without significant atherosclerotic disease, , , , , , making it poorly suited to conventional cardiovascular management approaches. , As a result, survivors of SCAD often experience psychological shock, confusion, uncertainty, frustration, and emotional distress while navigating their recovery. , , , , , , , Rates of post‐SCAD anxiety and depression are notably high. , , , , , , Indeed, emotional stress is a recognized trigger for SCAD events. , , , , , Although the past decade has seen increasing attention to the psychosocial sequelae of SCAD, research progress has been limited by the absence of a SCAD‐specific measure of distress. While numerous qualitative studies have offered rich, nuanced insights into the diverse psychosocial impacts of SCAD, , , , , most quantitative studies have relied on generic instruments such as the Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7‐item scale (GAD‐7), the 9‐item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ‐9) and, less commonly, the Screening Tool for Psychosocial Distress (STOP‐D) and the Cardiac Distress Inventory (CDI), to assess distress after SCAD. , , , , , , , While these tools are useful for comparing rates of anxiety, depression, and distress across cardiac populations, they fall short in capturing the unique and multifaceted nature of SCAD‐related distress. The development of a SCAD‐specific instrument would facilitate more precise assessment and longitudinal monitoring of the specific and unique psychological challenges encountered by survivors of SCAD and enable targeted evaluation of the impact of interventions and support programs on personally relevant aspects of distress. We previously developed the CDI, a comprehensive, cardiac‐specific tool to assess the multifaceted psychological distress experienced by people after typical atherosclerotic cardiovascular events. , Designed to fill a gap in existing measures, which fail to capture the full spectrum of distress unique to patients with cardiac disease, the 55‐item CDI has been shown to have both empirical and clinical utility: It has excellent psychometric properties and has recently been included in European Society of Cardiology recommendations for cardiac‐related mental health assessment. , The CDI has been translated into French, Chinese, Turkish, German, Thai, Italian, Swedish, Gujerati, and Farsi and validated in diverse populations, , , confirming its validity and cross‐cultural applicability. A 12‐item CDI Short Form (CDI‐SF) has been developed for use as a screening tool in primary care and cardiac rehabilitation settings. The aim of the present study was to develop a SCAD‐specific measure of psychological distress following methods similar to those used to develop the CDI. The new instrument, the SCAD Distress Inventory (SDI), was designed for use in both research and clinical practice to assess the unique and multifaceted distress that can occur after SCAD. Given that the CDI has been well received in the research and clinical community, it is anticipated that the SDI will similarly be found to have both empirical and clinical utility. Methods Ethical Statement The present study conformed to the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki and was undertaken with the approval of the Human Research Ethics Committee of St Vincent's Hospital Sydney, Australia (Approval No. 2019/ ETH03171 October 5, 2021; Amendment HREC/16/SVH/338, January 18, 2023). Written informed consent was received from all study participants. Data Availability The data set generated from the focus group study is not publicly available due to ethical requirements based on the sensitive nature of the data and the risk of participant identification. Data will be made available by the authors upon reasonable request and with permission of the Human Research Ethics Committee of St Vincent's Hospital Sydney. The data set generated for the online survey is available in the University of Melbourne Figshare repository at https://doi.org/10.26188/24654414.v1 . Study

Data will be made available by the authors upon reasonable request and with permission of the Human Research Ethics Committee of St Vincent's Hospital Sydney. The data set generated for the online survey is available in the University of Melbourne Figshare repository at https://doi.org/10.26188/24654414.v1 . Study Design This was a cross‐sectional instrument development and psychometric evaluation study. The study involved the development of a pool of relevant distress items, which were then included in a questionnaire that was part of a larger survey of survivors of SCAD. Statistical analysis of questionnaire responses informed the selection of items for inclusion in the final inventory. Development of the SCAD Distress Item Pool The methodology used to develop the SCAD distress item pool involved an extensive review of the published literature and consultation with relevant experts and stakeholders, including those with lived experience of SCAD. The specific steps were as follows: Step 1: Review of extant literature relating to the psychosocial experiences of survivors of SCAD. This review included both qualitative and quantitative studies published before November 2022. , , , , , , , , , , , , Step 2: Consultation with SCAD survivors through focus groups, conducted between November 2022 and February 2023, to explore lived experience of the psychosocial impacts of SCAD (N=30 participating survivors of SCAD). The development of the focus group discussion guide was informed by the literature review undertaken in step 1. Focus group findings have been reported in detail elsewhere as qualitative themes and subthemes and included confusion and uncertainty about what SCAD was and how to manage it; feelings of shock, sadness, vulnerability, frustration, unfairness, guilt, embarrassment, isolation, and loneliness; loss of self‐confidence and reduced sense of self; fear about the future including concerns about SCAD recurrence and death; concern, confusion, frustration, and helplessness in self‐management efforts; negative impacts on roles and relationships, including work restrictions and family stress; and feeling dismissed by health professionals and abandoned by the health care system. Step 3: Generation of a pool of SCAD‐related distress items based on each of the themes and subthemes identified in focus groups undertaken in step 2. Step 4: Review by the multidisciplinary investigator group to reach consensus on items to be tested and the response scale to be used in the survey. The investigator group had expertise due to lived experience of SCAD and qualifications and experience in cardiology, psychology, and instrument design. Survey of SCAD Survivors Participants and Procedure Recruitment and data collection for the survey occurred between March 10 and May 6, 2023. Participants were recruited by the Victor Chang Cardiac Research Institute from a database of SCAD survivors participating in a larger genetic study (Victor Chang Cardiac Research Institute Arteriopathies and SCAD Cohort). , At the time of recruitment, the Victor Chang Cardiac Research Institute Arteriopathies and SCAD Cohort involved 433 participants aged >18 years who had had at least 1 SCAD event (confirmed by a cardiologist or angiography), with no exclusion based on time since SCAD. All participants had adequate English language proficiency to read and understand the participant information and consent form. This was the same database from which participants were recruited for the earlier focus group study. Potential survey participants (N=433) were emailed a unique link to access the participant information and consent form, which they completed to access the online questionnaire, available via the Research Electronic Data Capture platform. No identifying information was collected as no participant follow‐up was involved. As it was possible for an individual to gain access to and complete the Research Electronic Data Capture questionnaire more than once, with no way of restricting repeat access, the possibility of duplicate entries was assumed. All respondent data were collected by self‐report. The questionnaire then took ≈25 minutes to complete. The full sample of survey participants (N=310) has been described in a previous publication that reported on the prevalence ratings for each of the 48 distress items. Only those participants who provided full data on all 48 items and the validated psychological instruments required for psychometric testing of the final instrument (N=293) were included in the current analysis to develop the SDI. In the present study, the latter were used for validation purposes. for each of the 48 distress items. Measures The online questionnaire comprised the 48 SCAD distress items, together with sociodemographic and medical questions and psychological questionnaires validated in cardiac populations. In the present study, the latter were used for validation purposes. For each of the 48 SCAD distress items, respondents were asked to indicate how much they had experienced the issue during the first 6 months after their most recent SCAD. Items were rated on a 4‐point scale where 0=not at all, 1=a small amount, 2=a moderate amount, and 3=a large amount. Sociodemographic information included sex, age, partner status, living arrangements, employment status, highest education, and health insurance status. Medical information included number of SCAD‐related AMIs, time since most recent SCAD, and presence (yes/no) of SCAD‐specific risk factors (fibromuscular dysplasia, migraine headache, connective tissue disorder, inflammatory disorders), traditional cardiovascular risk factors (high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, gestational diabetes, obesity, sleep apnea, smoking), and comorbidities (musculoskeletal conditions, stroke, cancer). Cardiac distress was assessed using the 12‐item CDI‐SF, which has excellent reliability and validity in assessing cardiac‐specific distress. Anxiety was assessed using the Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7‐item scale (GAD‐7), while depression was assessed using the 9‐item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ‐9). The GAD‐7 and PHQ‐9 are the recommended tools for assessment of anxiety and depression in patients with cardiac disease. Posttraumatic growth was assessed using the 21‐item Posttraumatic Growth Inventory (PTGI), which has been validated with patients with cardiac disease. Statistical Analysis Deidentified survey data (N=341) were exported from Research Electronic Data Capture and imported into SPSS Statistics version 27.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY) for analysis. Initial data cleansing involved the removal of duplicate entries (n=31), identified by identical sociodemographic profiles; in these cases, either the first or most complete entry was retained. Of the remaining 310 cases, 293 contained complete responses for all 48 SCAD distress items and the instruments required for psychometric evaluation (CDI‐SF, GAD‐7, PHQ‐9, PTGI). The statistical analysis followed a 4‐stage process, modeled on the methodology used in the development and validation of the CDI. , Stage 1: Item Refinement Item suitability for exploratory factor analysis (EFA) was evaluated using several methods. Before statistical analysis and throughout the refinement process, the investigator group reviewed items for specificity, clarity, uniqueness, and clinical relevance, removing those deemed too general for a SCAD‐specific instrument, unclear in meaning, duplicative in meaning with another item, or lacking clinical relevance. Items with low communalities (<0.40) were also removed. The suitability of the data for EFA was confirmed using the Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin measure of sampling adequacy (>0.80), a significant Bartlett's test of sphericity ( P <0.05), and visual inspection of the scree plot. Stage 2: EFA EFA was conducted using Jeffrey's Amazing Statistics Program version 0.19.1 and SPSS version 27.0 to identify the underlying factor structure of the SDI. The optimal number of factors was determined via parallel analysis using a polychoric correlation matrix, which is suitable for ordinal data. The minimum residual method was used to estimate factor structure, given its robustness in handling skewed item distributions, a common feature in questionnaire data. Since correlation between factors was assumed, multiple nonorthogonal rotation methods were tested to evaluate model fit, with oblimin rotation selected for its alignment with both clinical and theoretical interpretations. Factor loadings were suppressed below 0.40 to aid interpretability; items failing to load above this threshold were removed and the model reevaluated. Stage 3: Rasch Analysis Rasch analysis was performed using WINSTEPS software version 5.5.1. This analysis aimed to ensure that all items worked together consistently to measure a single underlying dimension or trait. Given the uniform response format (0, 1, 2, 3) of each question, the rating scale model was applied across all analyses. At each iteration, model fit was assessed, and items were removed if they failed to meet Rasch assumptions, with the goal of improving the scale's overall measurement quality and internal consistency. Unidimensionality was assessed using several criteria to ensure that each subscale of the SDI measured a single construct. First, positive point‐measure correlations indicated agreement between observed responses and the Rasch model. Second, each subscale was checked for a potential secondary dimension using principal components analysis of Rasch residuals. Unidimensionality was assumed if the variance explained by the data was at least 40% and the eigenvalue of the first residual contrast was <2. If the eigenvalue was >2, the principal components analysis of Rasch residuals loadings were examined to assess whether a second dimension was likely. Third, Wright's unidimensionality index was calculated by dividing the person separation index using real standard errors by the person separation index using model standard errors. A value

indicated agreement between observed responses and the Rasch model. Second, each subscale was checked for a potential secondary dimension using principal components analysis of Rasch residuals. Unidimensionality was assumed if the variance explained by the data was at least 40% and the eigenvalue of the first residual contrast was <2. If the eigenvalue was >2, the principal components analysis of Rasch residuals loadings were examined to assess whether a second dimension was likely. Third, Wright's unidimensionality index was calculated by dividing the person separation index using real standard errors by the person separation index using model standard errors. A value of ≥0.90 suggested unidimensionality, while a value of ≤0.50 indicated multidimensionality. In addition, the properties of individual items were evaluated to ensure they performed as expected according to Rasch model measurement theory. First, residual correlations were inspected, with values >0.30 potentially suggesting local dependence or multidimensionality. , Second, monotonicity of each rating scale category was assessed by checking that average category measures increased monotonically across the subscale. Third, within each subscale, item fit was evaluated using infit and outfit mean square statistics and standardized Z scores. Items had adequate fit if their mean square values were between 0.5 and 1.5. If the mean square was outside this range, standardized Z score values of ≥2.0 were used to confirm misfit. Fourth, differential item functioning was used to determine if items functioned differently across subgroups, such as age and education. A logit difference of ≥0.5 and a Rasch–Welch test P value of <0.05 were considered problematic. Finally, a number of Rasch model indices were calculated to demonstrate item and person fit in relation to item endorsement. Item and person separation indices were used to assess the spread of items and individuals along the endorsement continuum. Values of ≥2.0 indicated acceptable separation. Rasch person reliability indicates how well the instrument distinguishes between individuals of different abilities with standard cutoffs being >0.70, the minimum acceptable level for group‐level analysis, and at >0.80, the instrument is sensitive enough to distinguish between high and low performers. Rasch item reliability estimates the replicability of item placement within the Rasch measurement model if these same items were given to another sample of persons with similar abilities. Values ≥0.80 were considered acceptable and values ≥0.90 were preferred. Stage 4: Evaluating the Psychometric Properties of the SDI Psychometric evaluation of the SDI was guided by the Consensus‐based Standards for the Selection of Health Measurement Instruments (COSMIN) framework. Internal consistency was assessed using McDonald's ω, which provides a robust estimate of reliability in multidimensional scales, alongside reliability indices derived from Rasch analysis. McDonald's ω values of ≥0.70 are considered acceptable for research purposes and ≥0.80 considered good. An ω value ≥0.90 is considered excellent and is typically required for clinical diagnosis or high‐stakes decision making. Concurrent validity of the SDI was examined through its correlations with established measures of cardiac distress, anxiety, and depression, namely, the CDI‐SF, GAD‐7, and PHQ‐9. Discriminant validity was examined through its correlation with a measure of a construct that is unrelated to distress, namely, the PTGI, which measures posttraumatic growth. Distribution‐based estimates of the minimum clinically important difference were derived using 2 approaches based on the standard error of measurement. The standard error of measurement for each subscale was calculated as SD×√(1−α), where SD is the baseline standard deviation and α is Cronbach's α. First, the minimum detectable change at 95% confidence was calculated as 1.96×standard error of measurement, representing the smallest change exceeding measurement error at a single assessment occasion. Second, the reliable change index threshold was calculated as 1.96×√2×standard error of measurement, which accounts for measurement error at both baseline and follow‐up assessments and thus provides a more conservative estimate. Changes exceeding this threshold can be interpreted as statistically reliable ( P <0.05) rather than attributable to random measurement variability. Finally, receiver operating characteristic curve analysis was used to identify the optimal cutoff point for discriminating between responders and nonresponders, as defined by the clinical cutoff point of ≥13 on the CDI‐SF. The optimal cutoff point for each subscale was determined by maximizing Youden's J index (sensitivity+specificity−1), which equally weights the probability of correctly identifying true responders and true nonresponders. , These analyses were conducted using the user‐written cutpt command in Stata (StataCorp, College Station, TX). Sample Size Requirements Guidelines for sample size in instrument development recommend a minimum of 5 participants per item for EFA. For Rasch modeling conducted for exploratory purposes, a sample size of at least N=100 is considered acceptable, with N=250 preferred to ensure stable and reliable parameter estimates. Of note, ratings on distress items did not differ significantly on the basis of time since the most recent SCAD event. Initial Assessment of Item Suitability The initial pool of 48 SCAD‐related distress items is shown in Table . Before factor analysis, 6 items were removed, due to duplication in meaning (items 1, 10, 27, and 44) or communalities <0.4 (items 39 and 48). The remaining 42 items, which demonstrated high suitability for factor analysis (measure of sampling adequacy, 0.848; Bartlett's test of sphericity, χ 2 (861)=14116.17; P <0.001), were included in the EFA. Exploratory Factor Analysis Initial EFA of the 42 items revealed 4 items that did not load on any factor and had questionable clinical relevance: Items 18 and 25 were considered too general, item 43 referred to a cognitive rather than an emotional response, and item 29 had low endorsement across the sample. The subsequent EFA of 38 items revealed 1 item that loaded on 2 factors and was considered too general (item 4). The final EFA with parallel analysis (37 items) resulted in a 3‐factor solution, with the 3 factors comprising 12, 14, and 11 items. The scree plot is shown in the Figure . The first factor showed a dominant eigenvalue (15.6), with a clear elbow occurring after the third factor. The horizontal line represents Kaiser's criterion (eigenvalue=1.0). Correlations between factors ranged from 0.46 to 0.63, confirming nonorthogonality. All correlations were positive, reflecting unidimensionality and shared variance in the latent construct of SCAD distress. The rotated 3‐factor model explained 59.1% of the variance. The 3‐factor EFA solution is presented as Table , as these did not form part of the final factor solution due to changes made following Rasch analysis, as outlined below. The polychoric correlation matrix for the final 3‐factor EFA is also presented as Table . RASCH Analysis A separate Rasch analysis was run for each of the 3 factors identified by the EFA. After consideration of item fit, separation of items on the Wright map, dimensionality and differential item functioning, the following changes to the 3 factors identified in the EFA were made: factor 1, item 41 removed; factor 2, items 14 and 21 removed; and factor 3, item 47 removed. A potential issue with dimensionality for factor 2 was identified from the principal components analysis of Rasch residuals (eigenvalue >2), indicating the possibility of 2 subfactors. A PCA was conducted on the 12 items that remained after initial item removal with 2 subfactors emerging. Additional Rasch analyses were conducted for each of these 2 factors, with all items retained. The final 33‐item inventory therefore included 4 factors: Factor 1, challenges to sense of self, comprised 7 items (5–7, 12, 13, 16, and 30); factor 2, fear of recurrence, comprised 5 items (2, 3, 9, 17, and 26); factor 3, concerns about reduced capacity, comprised 11 items (11, 20, 28, 31, 33, 34, 36, 38, 42, 45, and 46); and factor 4, lack of support and validation, comprised 10 items (8, 15, 19, 22–24, 32, 35, 37, and 40). Item fit statistics are presented in Table . All item infit and outfit statistics fell within the recommended fit criteria. All items had positive point measure correlations within each scale with Wright's unidimensionality index ranging from 0.93 to 0.94, indicating excellent unidimensionality of the latent construct within each subscale. The internal consistency of each subscale was good to excellent, with ω ranging from 0.88 to 0.92. All subscales were significantly skewed. These reliability estimates supported the calculation of distribution‐based minimum clinically important difference thresholds. The minimum detectable change at 95% confidence for the total SDI was 8.55 points, with subscale values ranging from 2.45 (fear of recurrence) to 4.87 (concerns about reduced capacity). The more conservative reliable change index thresholds, which account for measurement error at both assessment occasions, were 12.25 for the total score and ranged from 3.46 to 6.89 across subscales. Receiver operating characteristic curve analysis using Youden's J index identified optimal clinical cutoff scores for detecting clinically significant distress, using the CDI‐SF cutoff (>13) as the external anchor. The estimated cutoff for the total SDI was ≥62, with subscale cutoffs ranging from ≥11 (challenges to sense of self) to ≥16 (concerns about reduced capacity). Estimated clinical cutoff scores are presented in Table . Concurrent validity of the total SDI score was established through significant subscale ordinal correlations with the CDI‐SF and, to a lesser extent, the GAD‐7 and PHQ‐9, as shown in Table . Discriminant validity was established through the lack of significant correlation ( P >0.05) with the PTGI, also shown in Table . On the whole, correlations with the SDI subscales were significantly lower for the PTGI than for the other psychological instruments (95% CIs not overlapping, apart from PHQ‐9 and PTGI on subscales 1 and 2), confirming significant discriminant validity. When the correlation analyses were restricted to respondents who had a more recent SCAD (N=36), to optimize temporal consistency across instruments, the pattern of results remained the same, with correlations becoming slightly higher for the CDI‐SF, GAD‐7, and PHQ‐9 and slightly lower for the PTGI (Table ). The final 33‐item SDI and scoring instructions are presented as Supplementary Data . The scoring syntax includes mean imputation to account for missing data, provided at least half the scores in the subscale are available. Importantly, the current study asked participants to reflect on the first 6 months following their most recent SCAD event, ensuring a consistent focus on the early recovery period after SCAD regardless of time since the event. In contrast, the final SDI uses a shorter, more immediate time frame of “the past 4 weeks” to better capture respondents' emotional state. This shift allows the tool to monitor changes over time in the distress levels of survivors of SCAD, whether naturally occurring or in response to specific interventions, in both research and clinical settings. Discussion The present study reports on the successful development and psychometric testing of a 33‐item SDI, a comprehensive and codesigned measure of SCAD‐related distress. The development of the SDI followed best practice guidelines in instrument design: the inclusion of people with lived experience of SCAD; reference to previous literature; consultation with experts in psychology, cardiology, and instrument development in generating the initial item pool; and refinement of the item pool through recommended statistical techniques, namely, EFA and Rasch analysis. The SDI demonstrated good to excellent internal consistency and good concurrent and discriminant validity. The 4 domains of the SDI are highly reflective of the extant qualitative literature that has documented the psychological impacts of SCAD. The 4 subscales—challenges to sense of self, fear of recurrence, concerns about reduced capacity, and lack of support and validation—are consistent with themes reported by several other research teams. , , , , , This consistency across studies further supports the content validity of the SDI. The SDI offers a comprehensive and tailored measure of the psychological consequences of SCAD. Most previous quantitative investigations of SCAD impacts have measured generic constructs such as anxiety and depression. , , , , , , , While useful for comparative analyses across populations, generic measures such as the GAD‐7 and PHQ‐9 do not capture the unique and multifaceted nature of SCAD‐related distress. Inclusion of the SDI in future cross‐sectional and longitudinal studies will enable more precise assessment and monitoring of SCAD‐specific distress, potentially revealing how it differs between subgroups of survivors of SCAD and how it changes over time. The inclusion of the SDI in trials of therapeutic interventions will enable targeted assessment of intervention benefits in reducing distress, both broadly and in regard to the specific domains assessed in the 4 subscales. The SDI is also likely to have utility as a clinical tool to identify the specific areas of distress faced by survivors of SCAD. Clinicians could either administer the total scale or choose specific subscales relevant to their patient group, clinical setting, and/or therapeutic approach. For example, use of the inventory or specific subscales in cardiac rehabilitation settings will help to identify fears about returning to or initiating exercise (subscale 2), specific areas of reduced capacity (subscale 3), confusion about medications and health advice (subscale 4), and ongoing support needs (subscale 4).

Clinicians could either administer the total scale or choose specific subscales relevant to their patient group, clinical setting, and/or therapeutic approach. For example, use of the inventory or specific subscales in cardiac rehabilitation settings will help to identify fears about returning to or initiating exercise (subscale 2), specific areas of reduced capacity (subscale 3), confusion about medications and health advice (subscale 4), and ongoing support needs (subscale 4). Use of the inventory before psychological counseling has potential to assist in identifying personally relevant issues and challenges, for example, threats to identity (subscale 1), thereby assisting in the tailoring and targeting of psychosocial therapies and interventions for individual clients. A stepped approach to interpretation may be advised: First, identify patients exceeding clinical cutoffs who may require intervention; subsequently, use minimum clinically important difference thresholds to monitor treatment response and inform decisions about treatment continuation or modification. Study Limitations There are some limitations of the present study that should be acknowledged. First, the study relied on participant self‐report, which cannot be objectively validated. Importantly, though, the participants were drawn from a population of patients with SCAD objectively confirmed either by a cardiologist or on angiography. Second, the study sample was predominantly English language–speaking female survivors of SCAD, potentially limiting the representativeness of the findings. Use of the SDI with larger samples of male survivors of SCAD is required to assess its relevance for men, while cross‐cultural translation and validation of the inventory, including in men, is warranted to enhance its utility in broader SCAD populations. Third, validation of the SDI was potentially limited by the large range in time since respondents' most recent SCAD and the differing time frames used for the SDI items (the 6 months after most recent SCAD) and the psychological instruments used for validation (the 4 weeks before survey participation). Importantly, though, participants' ratings on neither the SCAD distress items nor the GAD‐7 and PHQ‐9 scales varied in terms of time since event, , providing support for the approach taken in validating the SDI. Moreover, when the analysis was restricted to participants whose SCAD event was closer to the time of questionnaire completion, the pattern of findings slightly improved, further supporting the concurrent and discriminant validity of the inventory. Finally, the length of the 33‐item inventory, while ideal for broad assessment of SCAD‐related distress, may be prohibitive in some studies or clinical settings. Development of a short form of the SDI is underway. Conclusions While previous quantitative investigations have relied on generic measures to assess the psychological sequelae of SCAD, the SDI offers a more tailored and nuanced assessment of the specific fears and concerns experienced by survivors of SCAD. The SDI has been developed following best practice guidelines for instrument development, including codesign with relevant stakeholders and adherence to recommended statistical techniques, and the initial results presented here suggest that it is psychometrically sound. Its 4‐factor structure reflects the multidimensional and nuanced nature of SCAD‐related distress. Confirmatory factor analysis in a separate sample is warranted to replicate and validate the 4‐factor model. The SDI has potential in both research and clinical settings, offering relevance as an assessment tool in studies of, and before, interventions with survivors of SCAD. Revisions to the SDI may be required as knowledge about SCAD management evolves. Further research on clinical uses of the instrument, including in assessing treatment outcomes, is needed before firm conclusions can be drawn about its clinical utility. Future cross‐cultural translation and validation of the SDI, including in larger representative samples, will enable assessment of its empirical and clinical utility in broader SCAD populations and international settings. chunks.content: Introduction The reproductive period is a critical time for establishing risks of chronic diseases in offspring later in life. Nutrition plays a vital role during this developmental period, and because it is a determinant of lifetime risk of disease, it is potentially a modifiable risk factor. Although the World Health Organization (WHO) provides guidelines for antenatal care, comprehensive guidelines detailing nutritional needs of women throughout reproduction from preconception through pregnancy and lactation are lacking. The role of optimal nutrition for the continuum beginning at preconception, during pregnancy, at birth, and beyond extending through childhood and adolescence has received too little attention from researchers, clinicians, and policy experts in the past but has recently become a frequent topic of discussion, including a recent National Academies of Science, Engineering, and Medicine workshop. The need for additional well-designed research on this topic became apparent in a recent series of systematic reviews from the US Department of Agriculture (USDA): Nutrition Evidence Systematic Review, Pregnancy and Birth to 24 Months Project. Of note, 29 of the most important questions related to pregnancy and infant milk-feeding practices were systematically reviewed, with the highlights related to nutrition during pregnancy presented in . Each topic was summarized by a conclusion statement and was assigned a grade based on the quality of evidence. For 5 conclusion statements, a grade was not assignable, and the remaining 3 pregnancy questions received a grade that reflected only limited available evidence. , For the infant milk topics, 4 received a grade indicating moderate evidence, 10 had limited evidence, and a grade was not assignable for 21 questions. The uncertain conclusions of the aforementioned systematic reviews underscored the need for more well-conceived studies to address specific questions regarding the role of nutrition in pregnancy. However, the inadequate numbers of studies capable of meeting the strict criteria of the reviews, do not negate the large number of robust studies on related topics, from which the scientific community may benefit. In this review, we have included such studies that give important insight into the many aspects of nutrition for women during their reproductive years. In the past, public policy guidelines did not include pregnant or lactating women or infants under the age of 2. Fortunately, the 2020 to 2025 Dietary Guidelines for the first time include recommendations for infants, toddlers, and pregnant women that will provide added benefits for healthcare professionals and the public. The USDA released its final guideline document (USDA 2020–2025 Dietary Guidelines) in December 2020. Although this report was not available at the time of the Nutrition in Pregnancy: Lifelong Impact conference in 2019, which was the motivation for this review, the findings and recommendations of this document were nevertheless consistent with the new USDA guidelines. Other reviews on this topic bring additional clarity to the issue. The conclusions offered herein come from recommendations from assembled experts on (1) the health benefits of consuming nutritious food before, during, and after pregnancy, (2) the value of promoting improved nutrition among pregnant women, and (3) the gaps in knowledge regarding nutrition during reproductive years that require urgent attention. Although the meeting was largely focused on women in the United States, there were also important insights from global partners. The consumption of a beneficial dietary pattern before and during pregnancy is associated with a reduced risk of disorders of pregnancy, including gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), preterm birth, obesity-related complications, and, in some populations, preeclampsia and gestational hypertension. Nutrition therapy provides the foundation for the treatment of GDM and is especially important for pregnant women with obesity who have undergone bariatric surgery or who have preexisting diabetes mellitus (DM). A diet with balanced macronutrient intake provides the best chance for a healthy pregnancy and optimal perinatal outcomes. Nutritious diets are those that include ample quantities of vegetables, fruits, whole grains, nuts, legumes, fish, oils enriched in monounsaturated fat, and fiber and are lower in fatty red meat and refined grains. Furthermore, healthy diets avoid simple sugars, processed foods, and trans and saturated fats. A diet that consistently and substantially restricts any macronutrient should be avoided during pregnancy. Fad diets as promoted by the popular press are widespread and may be especially harmful during pregnancy because of the resulting nutrient imbalance and consequent nutrient deficiencies or ketosis. Growing evidence indicates that maternal prepregnancy body mass index (BMI) impacts the influence of gestational weight gain (GWG) on complications of pregnancy. Although the optimal time to improve maternal body weight and nutrition-related lifestyle is well before conception occurs, GWG goals, including a diet that limits nonnutritive, calorie-dense foods, maybe more achievable intervention targets for some women than weight modification before pregnancy. Human milk is uniquely suited to meet the nutritional needs of normal infants born at term for the first 4 to 6 months of life, and its consumption during infancy is associated with lower risks of chronic disease in later life. Human milk composition is influenced by maternal dietary intake during lactation and maternal adipose nutrient stores, which together influence maternal milk and nutrient production and composition. Among women with GDM, there is evidence that exclusive breastfeeding for at least 6 months decreases the risk of type 2 DM (T2DM) for the mother and is protective for the risk of childhood obesity in her offspring. The regular consumption of multivitamin and mineral supplements that contain optimal amounts of folic acid, among other micronutrients, is recommended for all reproductive-age women to augment a balanced diet, starting at least 2 to 3 months before conception and continuing throughout pregnancy until the cessation of lactation or at least 4 to 6 weeks after delivery. Women who become pregnant after bariatric surgery need additional supplements and close monitoring before and during pregnancy. It is imperative that healthcare providers have the time, knowledge, and means to discuss optimal nutrition and provide educational support to women of reproductive age to improve their health before, during, and after pregnancy. This perspective encouraged pregnant women to restrict their diet and minimize GWG in the middle 20th century. Infants with LBW were assumed to be “skinny” but “relatively untroubled.” However, current evidence found that maternal body size, dietary practices, and nutritional status before and during pregnancy are important factors for fetal health. Both inadequate nutrition and excessive nutrition and weight before and during pregnancy contribute to complications related to fertility (maternal and paternal); conception; development of the placenta, embryo, and fetus; fetal size; and perinatal complications, resulting in suboptimal pregnancy consequences for the mother and infant ( ). , – , , Animal models and human studies have suggested that maternal nutrition and maternal pre-pregnancy metabolic condition regulate fetal-placental gene expression, organ structures, metabolism, and growth during critical periods of development, affecting offspring risk of cardiovascular, metabolic, respiratory, immunologic, neuropsychiatric, and other chronic conditions starting during childhood development and into adulthood, with and without LBW. , – The intrauterine environment can establish poor trajectories of health that may be increased when nutrient restriction in utero is followed by postnatal nutrient excess. , To illustrate, in Holland during World War II, where the population recovered from the Dutch Hunger Winter famine relatively quickly, exposure to famine early in pregnancy was associated with a higher risk of offspring obesity and cardiovascular disease (CVD) in adulthood, whereas exposure to famine in the second half of pregnancy led more commonly to T2DM. Opportunities for positive impact Unfortunately, recognition of the importance of preconception nutrition, except for micronutrients, such as folate for the prevention of neural tube defects, is limited among healthcare workers, policymakers, and the public. The WHO Report of the Commission on Ending Childhood Obesity recognized preconception and pregnancy care as 1 of 6 key areas of action and called for clear guidance and support for the promotion of good nutrition and dietary counseling in antenatal care. Although healthy eating and physical activity counseling for adequate weight gain is recommended, the availability of effective support during pregnancy is limited. Weight gain in pregnancy in low-to-middle–income countries (LMICs) is not monitored routinely in some countries, and prepregnancy BMI is generally unknown. In addition, culturally acceptable, affordable, nutritious food supplements are urgently needed in areas where the prevalence of maternal undernutrition and poor food quality is high. Comprehensive improvements in nutrition and health status of women before conception and during pregnancy may have immediate effects on fetal growth, obstetrical outcomes, and perinatal survival. In a recently completed multicountry trial in which the effects of a comprehensive nutrition intervention initiated before conception was compared with the same intervention initiated late in the first trimester of pregnancy (vs no intervention), birth outcomes, including birth length and birthweight, LBW, SGA, and stunting, were strongly impacted by the nutritional intervention, with the largest effects in the preconception arm. Nulliparity and preconception anemia were strong effect modifiers of the response to intervention with more modest effects by baseline BMI. , The WHO global guidance for antenatal care recommends several central nutritional and health interventions for a healthy pregnancy, including multiple micronutrient supplements containing iron and folic acid, calcium supplementation for the prevention of preeclampsia in low intake contexts, and balanced energy and protein supplementation for undernourished populations to reduce LBW. Poor and Inappropriate Maternal Nutritional Status is Causally Associated with Abnormal Fetal Growth Patterns Including Low Birthweight (<2500 g), Small for Gestational Age (<10% Birthweight for Gestational Age) or Fetal Growth Restriction, Macrosomia (>4–4.5 kg), and Large for Gestational Age (>90% Birthweight for Gestational Age), Each of Which is Associated with Increased Risks of Developing Childhood and Adult Chronic Diseases Background and status Examples of the powerful influence of maternal nutrition on fetal development are demonstrated by the pregnancy outcomes associated with neonates at the extremes of birthweight: (1) neonates below the 10th percentile in weight for gestational age at birth are defined as SGA, and (2) neonates born exceeding the 90th percentile in weight for age are defined as LGA. These birthweights represent, in part, the nutritional status of the mother before and during pregnancy but do not necessarily reflect infant body composition (lean and fat mass). One of the WHO’s global nutrition targets calls for a 30% reduction in LBW. A recent Lancet paper estimated that 20.5 million infants will be born with LBW globally; thus, progress toward achieving the target has been slow. Maternal nutritional status, including low and high prepregnancy BMI scores, inadequate weight gain, short stature, anemia, and micronutrient deficiency, were causally associated with LBW, which may be a result of preterm birth, impaired fetal growth, or both. Impact of maternal nutrition on pregnancy outcomes During extremes of maternal undernutrition, the fetus develops chronic FGR, , a prime example of “survival at the expense of growth.” This phenotype includes decreased pancreatic growth, development, and insulin secretion; increased capacity for glucose uptake in peripheral tissues (such as skeletal muscle) ; reduced utilization of amino acids for protein synthesis and cell growth; and development of hepatic insulin resistance with increased glucose production in an ovine model that produced hypoxia and reduced nutrient supply in the fetus. We now know that the FGR phenotype, especially when followed by later life excess caloric intake, is a risk of the development of obesity, insulin resistance, and DM later in life. , Unfortunately, no strategy has emerged that improves growth and development of the FGR fetus once diagnosed in pregnancy. Previous attempts (maternal oxygen supplementation, bed rest, augmented nutrition, and medications) have either not worked or caused harm. Therefore, current management of pregnancies with FGR involves fetal surveillance and delivery of the fetus when adverse physiology becomes apparent, in hopes that the neonate with FGR can be treated more effectively outside the uterus. Although there is no direct nutritional strategy for treating FGR, recent studies in sheep have revealed that uteroplacental gene therapy involving vascular endothelial growth factors safely increased fetal growth velocity and reduced the incidence of FGR. In addition, recent data indicated that nutritional support and exercise before pregnancy may be more efficacious in promoting healthy placentation and fetal growth than during pregnancy. Moreover, the current postnatal strategy in which infant weight is a primary criterion for neonatal intensive care unit or hospital discharge may contribute to excessively rapid catch-up growth, especially for body fat mass, as parents and providers are motivated to align newborn intake and nutrition to meet weight gain targets rather than to maintain normal fetal in utero growth trajectories. , At the other extreme, fetal overnutrition from maternal obesity, DM, and high fat and sugar intake may result in macrosomia or LGA. These conditions that present excess glucose and lipid supply to the fetus are increasingly common and associated with several complications. Fasting and pulsatile postprandial hyperglycemia promote fetal insulin secretion, contributing to excess glycogen storage and fat accretion in the fetus, especially in pregnancies complicated by T2DM, GDM, and type 1 DM (T1DM), particularly when complicated by obesity. Although pregnancies complicated by DM are commonly associated with macrosomia and/or LGA, most cases of these infants are born to mothers with obesity alone, which now affects up to 1 of 3 women. Even greater fetal fat mass accumulation occurs with the combination of high maternal plasma glucose and lipid concentrations. – Recent evidence suggested that maternal triglycerides, made available to the fetus by placental lipases that hydrolyze the triglycerides to free fatty acids (FFAs), are primary drivers of fetal fat mass growth in pregnancies with obesity and contribute to accelerated fat mass accumulation in the fetus. , , Fetuses have limited capacity for fatty acid (FA) oxidation , but can store fat. Excess fat mass accreted in utero might contribute to later obesity, but postnatal fat mass accretion especially during the first 1 to 2 years of life can persist into later life leading to obesity in childhood. In a nonhuman primate model, a maternal Western-style diet resulting in intermittently higher postprandial glucose and lipid exposure to the fetus resulted in the 3-year-old offspring demonstrating higher glucose excursions. Furthermore, the child’s pancreatic islets secreted more insulin, suggesting that these islets were primed before birth to hypersecrete insulin. In contrast, extremely high and relatively constant glucose concentrations in the fetus actually can suppress insulin production and response to glucose stimulation. This, along with abnormal placentation and decreases in placental perfusion, may explain why some women with long-standing T1DM complicated by vascular diseases will have neonates who are not only SGA but also at increased risk of later metabolic disease, especially when exposed to an obesogenic environment. , There is increasing evidence that persistent, very high fetal glucose concentrations can inhibit fetal neuronal development, leading to reduced neuronal number, dendritic proliferation, and synapse formation, ultimately leading to reduced cognitive function in such offspring later in their lives. In humans, a recent study in adolescent offspring from women with T1DM showed that cognitive function was significantly diminished, with lower intelligence scores and greater learning difficulties in the offspring whose mothers had more severe hyperglycemia associated with DM. Moreover, the rates of congenital heart defects and major malformations of the central nervous system derived from the neural tube, such as caudal regression syndrome, were higher in offspring of mothers with both T1DM and T2DM, and the risk period during organogenesis (<8 weeks) was often before women knew they were pregnant. However, stillbirth risk near term is the highest in mothers with T2DM, especially when associated with obesity, , both conditions associated with excess maternal caloric intake and malnutrition. In addition, maternal overnutrition plays an important role in the early origins of childhood obesity and inflammatory diseases, such as nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), the most common liver disease worldwide affecting 1 in 3 youth with obesity. A “multiple-hit” pathogenic model has been suggested to explain the progressive liver damage that occurs among children with NAFLD. Data in humans demonstrated that liver fat is 68% higher in neonates born to mothers with obesity and GDM and is strongly correlated with maternal prepregnancy BMI and, perhaps, maternal triglycerides before subcutaneous fat stores are fully developed. , Moreover, evidence from the national pediatric nonalcoholic steato-hepatitis (NASH) network showed that high birthweight or LBW, even when adjusting for childhood BMI, doubles the risk of advanced fibrosis in youth with biopsy-confirmed NAFLD, suggesting that changes at birth may precede and possibly predict the rapid onset of NASH in at-risk youth for reasons that remain poorly understood. Without effective treatments, children with NASH are at risk of developing cirrhosis and liver-related mortality in early adulthood. Opportunities for positive impact All women of childbearing age should receive preconception counseling and guidelines on nutrition, physical activity, and optimal GWG, with particular attention to those with undernutrition or overnutrition; those with a prepregnancy BMI that indicates underweight, overweight, or obese status; and those with medical complications, including DM, prediabetes mellitus, insulin resistance, history of GDM, chronic hypertension, and any chronic medical disease (cardiopulmonary, obstructive sleep apnea, rheumatologic, NAFLD, gastrointestinal, etc.). Medical management of any chronic condition should be optimized before pregnancy, and women should be provided with options for effective contraception until the timing of pregnancy is optimal. Many Adolescent Mothers Face Multifaceted Socioeconomic and Lifestyle Difficulties that Require Professional and Social Support to Aid in Optimizing their Diets and Other Aspects of their Health and Social Care Before, During, and After their Pregnancies Background and current status The physiology of pregnancy may differ in adolescents from that in adult pregnant women. Young maternal age (particularly <16 years) is a significant risk factor for stillbirth, preterm delivery, LBW, and neonatal mortality. – The probability of these adverse outcomes is the greatest when pregnancy coincides with continuing and/or incomplete growth of the adolescent mother. , Sheep paradigms involving nutritional management of weight and adiposity in young biologically immature adolescents have replicated this competition for nutrients between the mother and offspring in the womb. – Although poor nutrient reserves at conception play a modest role, dietary manipulation of the maternal growth trajectory during pregnancy has the most profound impact on pregnancy outcomes. Overfeeding adolescent sheep to promote rapid maternal growth during pregnancy is particularly detrimental. It leads to abnormal placental growth and development, reduced uteroplacental blood flow, and reduced fetal nutrient delivery. In the sheep model, these led to high rates of premature delivery of LBW lambs and increased rates of intrauterine growth restriction. In addition, initial lactation was impaired, and neonatal morbidity was high. In contrast, when maternal growth after conception is prevented by underfeeding adolescent sheep, the progressive depletion of the mother’s nutrient reserves resulted in only a small reduction in birthweight independent of any change in placental size or length of gestation. Appropriate caloric intake maintains maternal adiposity throughout gestation, and this optimizes fetoplacental growth and birth outcomes. Maternal and placental endocrine systems are differentially altered in both overnutrition and undernutrition with downstream effects on fetal endocrine systems, organ development, and body composition. Approaches to reverse these effects in sheep have been explored: notably, improving nutrition during late gestation in the undernourished model restores fetal nutrient supply, normalizes fetal adiposity, and partially restores birthweight. , Following delivery, growth-restricted lambs of both sexes born to overfed adolescents and who are fed according to appetite have altered metabolic and body composition phenotypes, which persist into adulthood, whereas offspring of underfed adolescent sheep were largely unaffected. Impact on pregnancy outcomes This body of work using sheep models has public health implications for human adolescents living in both low- and high-income countries. Adolescents have been found to consume higher levels of snack and processed foods, less fruit and vegetables, and take fewer nutritional supplements than adult women. Irrespective of geographic location, both nutrient reserves at conception and gestational dietary intake are likely to be powerful determinants of fetal growth in very young girls whose own growth is still ongoing or incomplete. Data from human pregnancies in adolescent mothers concerning overnutrition and undernutrition remain limited. , Opportunities for positive impact In settings where women have chronically inadequate diets, intervening during pregnancy has shown limited benefit in perinatal outcomes. , Intervention strategies among poorly nourished women are more effective if initiated months before conception. Adolescent nutrition has been neglected, particularly in LMICs. The Lancet Commission on Adolescent Health drew attention to both overnutrition and undernutrition burdens in this age group that composed approximately 18% of the world’s population. As adolescent girls have not historically been prioritized in global research, there is a significant data gap regarding the burden of underweight and stunting within adolescent girls in LMICs and the knowledge of interventions needed to optimize this period of rapid growth and development. , High-energy nutritional intakes that promote rapid maternal growth during pregnancy in adolescents may constrain placental development and function and are potentially more detrimental than restricted nutritional intakes that prevent maternal growth. In areas where early marriage soon after menarche is the norm, there is evidence that girls with a low BMI should be advised to gain weight and achieve a normal BMI before conception to decrease the risk of preterm birth and neonatal underweight. Thereafter, dietary intakes should be sufficient to maintain maternal nutrient reserves throughout pregnancy. Nutrition Therapy Provides the Foundation for the Treatment of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus and is Especially Important for Pregnant Women with Obesity Who have Undergone Bariatric Surgery or Who have Preexisting Diabetes Mellitus Gestational diabetes mellitus Nutrition therapy is the foundation for the treatment of GDM. Rooted in carbohydrate restriction, the rationale for this approach can be traced to the pre-insulin era, when restriction of carbohydrates to ≤ 10% of calories was among the few interventions that could prolong life in those with T1DM. , Pioneers in the field of DM in pregnancy recognized that in utero environmental conditions that influence fetal growth are shaped by maternal nutrition. Moreover, contemporary evidence in the previous 2 to 3 decades has supported associations between fasting and postprandial glucose and infant birthweight, solidifying the need for control of maternal glucose to prevent fetal overgrowth in pregnancies affected by DM. The restriction of dietary carbohydrates leads to the risk of increasing dietary fat intake because of the replacement of carbohydrates with fat calories, particularly in obesogenic environments influenced by the easy availability of processed foods and low-carbohydrate fad diets promoted by the popular press. At the same time, mounting evidence supports that high saturated fat diets result in elevated FFAs, which inhibit insulin signaling and result in insulin resistance, which may increase fetal exposure to excess nutrients. Furthermore, fetal exposure to excess maternal lipids, especially triglycerides, is linked with fetal overgrowth and excess adiposity, both potent predictors of later childhood obesity and metabolic disorders. , , In 2005, the American Diabetes Association acknowledged the concern for excess fetal lipid exposure secondary to maternal diet, de-emphasizing restriction of carbohydrate, and worldwide, there is no consensus on the optimal approach to the treatment of GDM with nutrition therapy. , When a woman receives a diagnosis of GDM, regardless of the exact diagnostic criteria, nutrition therapy is the first line of treatment. There is high hope across the field that nutrition therapy alone in the absence of adjunct treatment with insulin or oral diabetes agents can effectively and economically treat the growing number of women with GDM. More recent data underscored the metabolic similarities in patterns of glycemia and lipidemia between diet-controlled GDM and maternal obesity without GDM. , This highlights an opportunity to more thoughtfully target women with obesity outside of GDM for treatment with nutrition. Moreover, the importance of good nutrition for all pregnant women was recently highlighted by data demonstrating strong associations between fasting and postprandial triglycerides and neonatal adiposity in both women with normal weight and women with obesity (without GDM), further supporting a role for targeting these nutrition-sensitive indicators. Unfortunately, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) using diet and lifestyle changes, although resulting in slightly less GWG, have overall not been successful in preventing GDM. Currently, the evidence does not support 1 particular nutritional approach to the treatment of GDM. It was recently shown that, globally, advice for nutrition in GDM is mixed between carbohydrate restriction and more liberal carbohydrate intake, with the focus on choosing low glycemic index foods, consuming more complex carbohydrates, increasing dietary fiber, and limiting consumption of saturated fats. The quality of the available evidence is poor, with high heterogeneity across studies, lack of control for confounding medications, poor reporting of GWG, and low dietary compliance. , Very recently, a controlled trial in which women with GDM were randomized to a lower carbohydrate and higher fat (40% carbohydrate and 45% fat) diet vs a higher-complex carbohydrate diet (60% carbohydrate and 25% fat) (both eucaloric and all meals provided for the duration of pregnancy) found no difference in birthweight, newborn adiposity by Peapod, or cord C-peptide supporting that complex carbohydrate can be liberalized by 20% above conventional recommendations and similarly normalize fetal growth, expanding nutrition options in GDM. Pregnancy after bariatric-metabolic surgery Preconception weight loss for women with obesity holds great promise to improve maternal and fetal health but is difficult to achieve through lifestyle alone. In contrast, bariatric-metabolic surgery (currently the most common being Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and, recently, sleeve gastrectomy) can result in total weight loss averages that approach 25% to 30% with accompanying benefits in, and often resolution of, most obesity-related comorbidities, including GDM. Greater numbers of women with severe obesity are now undergoing bariatric-metabolic surgeries and subsequently are becoming pregnant. Although meta-analyses of study outcomes of this population of mothers have typically demonstrated favorable outcomes concerning lower rates of HDP (62% lower), GDM (80% lower), and fewer babies born who are LGA (69% fewer); furthermore, they have reported a slight increase in preterm delivery (odds ratio [OR], 1.35) and a higher likelihood of SGA (OR, 2.16), especially when compared with women matched for presurgical BMI. The close timing of bariatric surgery concerning subsequent pregnancies in addition to the type of surgery is likely an important risk factor for SGA. Because women are in an active weight loss phase during the first year after bariatric surgery, pregnancy should be avoided. Furthermore, micronutrient deficiencies, such as iron, vitamin D, and vitamin B12, are common in patients who have undergone bariatric surgery, especially with Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, and must be adequately resolved before and during pregnancy. Less clear are the longer-term ramifications of postsurgical maternal weight, metabolic, and micronutrient changes on infant and childhood development and their risk of chronic diseases of adulthood (eg, obesity, DM, and CVD); however, the lower risk of GDM and LGA would seem to confer a benefit. Preeclampsia and preterm delivery The pathophysiology of preeclampsia is believed to be related to poor placentation accompanied by oxidative and endoplasmic reticulum stress in placental cells in addition to abnormal angiogenesis. These processes maybe modifiable by nutrition, and hence, a good deal of attention has been directed to the role of nutrition in preeclampsia. Unfortunately, these concepts have not been well studied, and in many cases, conclusions have been opposed (overnutrition vs undernutrition, too much vs too litde dietary salt, etc.). Current information on diet has recently been thoroughly reviewed ( ), and the role of micronutrients in preeclampsia has been a subject of increasing scrutiny. However, because of the challenges of studying the role of nutrition in the prevention of preeclampsia, their relationship remains largely unresolved. In 4 studies of nutrition before and during pregnancy to modify preeclampsia and gestational hypertension risk, limited data suggested a reduced risk with a diet higher in vegetables, fruits, whole grains, nuts, legumes, fish, and vegetable oils and lower in meat and refined grains. This information was from healthy White European women with access to medical care. Data were insufficient to estimate this relationship in minority women or women of low socioeconomic status. Micronutrient studies have provided a few helpful insights regarding their role in the prevention of preeclampsia. Calcium supplementation has been shown to be useful in settings with low calcium intake, leading to the conclusion that replacement, not supplementation, is relevant. Therapy with vitamins C and E as administered in several large studies has not proven effective to prevent preeclampsia. , Several other micronutrients, including folic add, , vitamins A and D, zinc, iodine, omega-3 FAs, and arginine, are supported by some, but not all, supplementation studies. A meta-analysis restricted to LMICs reported a significant effect of omega-3 supplementation on preeclampsia (risk ratio [RR], 0.40; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.21–0.77; I 2 , 0%; 6 studies, n=1343), but there was no difference in severe preeclampsia, eclampsia, or gestational hypertension. Moreover, some intriguing possibilities deserve further studies, including periconceptional vitamins, – dietary nitrates, reduced sodium intake, and antioxidants other than vitamins C and E, but thus far, none has been of proven benefit. Recent evidence has shown that among women with obesity, the degree of prepregnancy obesity predicts adverse outcomes for pregnancy to a greater degree than does GWG. This adds more urgency to targeting interventions to help women achieve the healthiest possible weight before and between conceptions. Nonetheless, there is also evidence that low weight gain, especially in women who are underweight or women with normal weight, or excessive GWG is associated with adverse maternal and child outcomes. , Offering opportunities during prenatal care for pregnant women may be a more feasible intervention than helping women optimize their weight before pregnancy. In the United States, the measurement of weight is routine at each prenatal care visit. However, this practice is not consistently found in all other countries, and even in the United States, real-time patient feedback and counseling related to weight tracking are not routinely practiced. Clinicians continue to identify insufficient time and knowledge related to counseling best practices as barriers to improving weight-related tracking and counseling. Furthermore, in generating weight gain guidelines, the IOM committee did not have adequate evidence to identify specific advice by subclasses of obesity. Therefore, they recommended at least 5 kg of weight gain for all women entering pregnancy with a BMI of >30 kg/m 2 , regardless of obesity class. Epidemiologic data published since then suggest that the ideal GWG varies by obesity class. For obesity grades I (BMI, 30–34.9 kg/m 2 ) and II (BMI, 35.0–39.9 kg/m 2 ), studies suggested that maternal gains less than the lower limit of the IOM recommendation may not increase adverse outcomes and may decrease LGA and GDM, , , although other studies indicated an increased risk of SGA and infant mortality with weight loss and very low weight gain. – However, for women with obesity grade III (BMI, ≥40.0 kg/m 2 ), lower levels of gain, or even weight loss, may be optimal, but the current evidence is observational and based on weight alone, not maternal diet or lifestyle behaviors. , , Because of insufficient evidence at the time, the 2009 guidelines did not provide evidence-based recommendations regarding diet or physical activity changes that would best help women to achieve recommended gains. Among Women With Gestational Diabetes Mellitus, There is Evidence That Exclusive Breastfeeding For At Least 6 Months Decreases The Risk of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus For The Mother And is Protective For The Risk of Childhood Obesity in Her Offspring Human milk provides personalized nutrition and is associated with long-term health benefits for infants and mothers. , According to the 2012 American Academy of Pediatrics policy statement, “Given the documented short- and long-term medical and neurodevelopmental advantages of breastfeeding, infant nutrition should be considered a public health issue and not only a lifestyle choice.” Milk composition is influenced by maternal dietary intake during lactation and maternal adipose nutrient stores, which together are responsible for the nutrients available for milk biosynthesis and ultimately maternal milk and nutrient production. To meet all infant nutritional needs, human milk is constantly changing, composition varies by infant age, between breasts, within a feed, throughout the day, during lactation, among women, and among populations. In light of these significant variations, accurate assessment of milk composition remains a challenge for researchers. The evaluation of donor milk pools assumed to come from women not only with adequate milk production to meet their infants’ nutritional needs but also with sufficient quantity to nourish other infants showed significant variations in composition. Among donor pools from the first and third quartiles, milk demonstrated up to a 33% difference in fat content, 22% difference in protein, and 16% difference in energy content. Importantly, individual women showed a greater difference in milk composition compared with variation by age of infant or length of time breastfeeding. , Regarding individual macronutrients, maternal diet does not have a major impact on milk protein content or the total amount of fat in human milk, but it affects the types of FAs present in breast milk. , Maternal adipose stores remain an important source of nutrients for human milk, although women with greater fat mass do not produce more or higher fat milk. Different lipids are the most variable component of human milk. Lipid composition variability is inversely related to the degree of breast fullness and milk volume. In addition to macronutrients and essential micronutrients, there is moderate evidence that flavors from the maternal diet during lactation are transferred into breast milk and that infants can detect diet-transmitted flavors, which may impact future taste preferences. The ratio of omega-6 vs omega-3 FAs in human breast milk seemed to promote postnatal fat development; however, this relationship requires further study. Interestingly, human milk from women with obesity or T2DM does not seem to expose the infant to a different macronutrient composition; however, it has been shown to have higher insulin levels and to influence the early infant microbiome population; moreover, any effects on infant appetite or growth remain unclear. , Women with GDM who breastfeed have decreased risk of developing T2DM, with a longer duration and increased intensity of breastfeeding associated with a lower 2-year incidence of T2DM. , Furthermore, breastfeeding is associated with a decreased maternal risk of metabolic syndrome, CVD, and cancer. Unfortunately, women who are overweight or women with obesity commonly experience difficulties in lactation and are less likely to meet exclusive breastfeeding goals, which suggests additional physiological barriers. Key Questions Question 1: What are the unique nutritional requirements of a normal pregnant woman and what unique features of diets produce optimal health and growth of her fetus and infant? The WHO defines good nutrition as “intake of food necessary for optimal growth, function, and health. Good nutrition is defined as a well-balanced diet that provides all essential nutrients in optimal amounts and proportions, whereas poor nutrition is defined as a diet that lacks nutrients (either from imbalance or [from] overall insufficient food intake) or one in which some components are present in excess.” Additional features of a healthy diet include foods that are accessible, acceptable, affordable, safe, culturally appropriate, and composed primarily of whole foods consumed in moderation. There is growing evidence that diet and nutritional status at preconception, starting as early as childhood and adolescence, seems to be equally or even more important than during pregnancy, because of growing evidence that nutrition affects fertility and the early development of the placenta and fetus, which occur well before a woman recognizes that she is pregnant About half of US women of childbearing age consume unhealthy diets that are too high in processed ingredients, fat, sugar, and other refined carbohydrates and do not meet current nutritional recommendations. , , Although it is commonly said that pregnant women are “eating for two,” for most women, average energy requirements increase only modestly. In contrast, assuming that the preconception diet was adequate, prenatal needs for some micronutrients, for example, folate and iron, increase by one-third to one-half, respectively. The WHO has declared iodine deficiency as the single most common cause of brain damage, after starvation, and mild iodine deficiency is still a public health concern in both developing countries and Western industrialized nations, especially Europe. Iodine requirements are increased during pregnancy and in nursing mothers from 250 to 300 μ g per day (compared with 150 μ g outside of pregnancy). These requirements begin very early because of the fetal need to synthesize thyroid hormone, critical for early neurogenesis, proliferation migration, differentiation, neurite outgrowth and guidance, synaptogenesis, and myelination. The fetal thyroid begins to concentrate iodine at 10 to 12 weeks of gestation and begins making thyroid hormone with complete independence from maternal thyroid hormone production by 18 weeks of gestation. , It has been demonstrated that mild-moderate iodine deficiency, which is common in pregnancy, is associated with a 10-point decrease in total intelligence quotient score and an increase in attention-deficit and hyperactivity disorder in the offspring. Question 2: What is the optimal balance of macronutrients during pregnancy and lactation to support and maintain appropriate nutrient supply to the infant through lactation? Diet planning is especially important for women planning to conceive, during pregnancy, and during lactation. Dietary patterns are an evolving area of research involving the entirety of the diet rather than focusing on individual nutrients or foods. There is limited but consistent evidence primarily in healthy White women with access to healthcare that dietary patterns before and during pregnancy higher in vegetables, fruits, whole grains, nuts, legumes, fish, and vegetable oils and lower in meat and refined grains are associated with a reduced risk of disorders of pregnancy, including preeclampsia, gestational hypertension, GDM, and preterm birth. – Conclusions about the association between dietary patterns during pregnancy and birthweight outcomes is less consistent and restricted by inadequate adjustment of birthweight for gestational age and sex variation in study design, lack of measures of infant body composition, dietary assessment methodology that rely on recall rather than robust biomarkers of nutritional intake, and adjustment of key confounding factors. However, in a recent cohort of 354 fully breastfeeding mother-infant dyads, in utero exposure to a higher-quality maternal diet, based on the HEI-2015, was inversely associated with the percentage of infant fat mass. Avoiding simple sugars, processed foods, and trans and saturated fats and limiting red and processed meats are recommended. A diet that severely restricts any food group should be avoided, specifically the ketogenic diet that lacks carbohydrates, the Paleo diet because of dairy restriction (promoting deficiencies in calcium and vitamin D), and any diet containing excess saturated fats. Foods with a high saturated fat content containing high omega-6 vs omega-3 FAs constitute a proinflammatory diet, with some evidence of impact on obesity in the offspring and increased postnatal adipose tissue development. , Literature on the effects of nutrition of lactating women on their infants’ later health is scarce. Eating a healthy diet is a way for lactating mothers to support their health and the health of their infants during lactation. The quality of a mother’s diet, particularly dietary fats, including saturated vs unsaturated fat, is an important way for mothers to ensure a healthy start for infant growth and development. What is the best way to ensure that the embryo and fetus have adequate micronutrients throughout gestation? A balanced diet that includes fish twice a week for docosahexaenoic acid and whole grains for folate, vitamin B12, iron, and choline is recommended as is supplementation of iodine by 150 μ g to ensure that pregnant women have a total intake of 250 μ g/day. For women with dietary restrictions, consultation with a nutritionist is recommended. A daily multivitamin that contains optimal amounts of folic add and iron is recommended for women who are planning to become pregnant. Because only a small percentage of women will eat a complete diet that includes all required nutrients, appropriate dietary supplementation with optimal levels of iron and folic add and other micronutrients is recommended. A dietitian may recommend other supplementation regimens for women at risk of insufficiency of specific micronutrients.
